  • InfluxDB Prometheus Logger - Cloud logging setup
  • MQTT Logger - MQTT publishing configuration

docs.title: How to Configure Environment Variables
docs.text: Use environment variables to configure Profinity for flexible deployments across different environments.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed
  • Access to system configuration files
  • Understanding of environment variable syntax

docs.title: Step 1: Understand Environment Variable Usage
docs.text: Environment variables allow you to: - Change configuration without editing files - Use different settings for different environments - Deploy the same configuration across multiple systems

docs.title: Step 2: Set Environment Variables
docs.text:
Windows: 1. Open System Properties → Environment Variables 2. Add new variables or edit existing ones 3. Click OK to save 4. Restart Profinity for changes to take effect

Linux/macOS: 1. Edit your shell profile (.bashrc, .zshrc, etc.) 2. Add: export VARIABLE_NAME=value 3. Or set in systemd service file (for services) 4. Restart Profinity

Docker: 1. Set in docker-compose.yml: 

environment:
  - HTTP_PORT=18080
  - LOG_LEVEL=Info
2. Or use .env file 3. Restart containers

docs.title: Step 3: Reference Variables in Config Files
docs.text:
In your Config.yaml or Profile.yaml files:

http:
  port: ${HTTP_PORT:-18080}  # Use HTTP_PORT or default to 18080
  address: ${HTTP_ADDRESS:-0.0.0.0}

logging:
  level: ${LOG_LEVEL:-Info}

docs.title: Step 4: Use Variables in Docker Compose
docs.text:
Create a .env file:

HTTP_PORT=18080
HTTPS_PORT=18443
LOG_LEVEL=Info
PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile

Reference in docker-compose.yml:

services:
  profinity:
    environment:
      - HTTP_PORT=${HTTP_PORT:-18080}
      - LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-Info}

docs.title: Step 5: Verify Configuration
docs.text:
1. Check environment variables are set correctly
  2. Restart Profinity
  3. Verify settings are applied
  4. Check logs for configuration details

docs.title: Common Environment Variables
docs.text:
• HTTP_PORT - HTTP server port (default: 18080)
  • HTTPS_PORT - HTTPS server port (default: 18443)
  • LOG_LEVEL - Logging level (Info, Debug, Warning, Error)
  • PROFILE_NAME - Default profile name
  • CONFIG_NAME - Configuration name
  • ENABLE_SCRIPTING - Enable scripting (true/false)

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Environment Variables - Complete environment variable reference
  • Docker Installation - Docker environment setup

docs.title: How to Connect Profinity to AI
docs.text: Connect Profinity to AI tools and LLMs using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server integration.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • Admin access to system configuration
  • An AI tool or LLM that supports MCP (e.g., Claude Desktop, Cursor IDE)
  • Understanding of MCP protocol

docs.title: Step 1: Enable MCP Server in Profinity
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → System Configuration
  2. Find MCP Server section in Application Configuration
  3. Enable MCP Server option
  4. Click Save

Note: The MCP server will be available at http://localhost:18080/sse (using the default Profinity web server port).

docs.title: Step 2: Create Service Account and Get Token
docs.text:
The MCP server requires authentication using JWT tokens. Users must have the SystemRead security role to access MCP endpoints.

  1. Create a user account with the SystemRead role:
  2. Navigate to ADMIN → User Management
  3. Create a new user (e.g., "mcp-service")
  4. Set Service Account to true
  5. Assign the SystemRead security role

  6. Save the user

  7. Generate a JWT token for the service account:

  8. Authenticate via the Profinity API: POST /api/v2/Users/Authenticate
  9. Use the service account username and password
  10. Save the token from the response (service account tokens never expire)

Example API call: 

curl -X POST http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Users/Authenticate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"mcp-service","password":"your-password"}'

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Your AI Tool
docs.text:
The following should be taken as examples only, check with your tools documentation on how to configure MCP over SSE to your tool.

Examples on using SSE with OLLAMA are also available on the Prohelion GitHub page https://www.github.com/prohelion.

Example For Claude Desktop:

  1. Open Claude Desktop settings
  2. Navigate to MCP server configuration
  3. Add MCP server with authentication: 
    {
  "mcpServers": {
    "profinity": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "@modelcontextprotocol/server-fetch",
        "http://localhost:18080/sse"
      ],
      "env": {
        "AUTHORIZATION": "Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE"
      }
    }
  }
}
    Note: Replace YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE with the JWT token from Step 2.
  4. Restart Claude Desktop

docs.title: Step 4: Verify Connection
docs.text:
1. In your AI tool, try querying Profinity data
  2. Check MCP server responds correctly
  3. Verify you can access component data, profiles, and dashboards

docs.title: Step 5: Use AI Features
docs.text:
Once connected, you can:

  • Query component data
  • Analyse dashboards
  • Generate scripts
  • Troubleshoot issues

docs.title: Example Queries
docs.text:
• "What components are in my active profile?"
  • "Show me the current battery voltage from the BMU"
  • "Create a dashboard for monitoring motor controller temperatures"
  • "Help me write a script to log data every 5 seconds"

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start Simple: Begin with basic queries to verify the connection
  • Check Logs: Monitor Profinity logs for MCP connection issues
  • Firewall Settings: Ensure the MCP port is accessible if connecting remotely
  • Authentication: Use strong credentials for production deployments

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Connection Failed: Verify MCP server is enabled and port is correct
  • No Data Available: Ensure you have active components and profiles
  • Authentication Errors: Check credentials match in both systems

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• MCP Server - Complete MCP server documentation
  • Scripting - Learn about Profinity scripting
  • APIs - REST API documentation

docs.title: How to Connect to CAN Bus
docs.text: Connect Profinity to your CAN bus network using a supported adapter.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed
  • A supported CAN bus adapter (Peak USB, SocketCAN, CAN-Ethernet Bridge, etc.)
  • Adapter drivers installed (if required)
  • Access to create components in Profinity

docs.title: Step 1: Install Adapter Drivers (if required)
docs.text:
For Peak USB Adapters: 1. Install the Peak drivers before starting Profinity 2. Use Peak tools to verify the adapter is working 3. Verify the adapter appears in device manager (Windows)

For SocketCAN (Linux/macOS): 1. Ensure SocketCAN is enabled in your kernel 2. Install socketcand if using remote SocketCAN 3. Verify CAN interfaces are available

docs.title: Step 2: Connect Your Adapter
docs.text:
1. Connect your CAN bus adapter to your computer
  2. USB adapter: Plug into USB port
  3. Ethernet bridge: Connect to network
  4. SocketCAN: Configure CAN interface
  5. Connect the adapter to your CAN bus network
  6. Verify physical connections are secure

docs.title: Step 3: Auto-Discover the Adapter
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the ADD COMPONENT window
  2. Look for the Discovered category
  3. Your adapter should appear in the discovered list
  4. Click on your adapter to add it

If your adapter doesn't appear in the discovered list, proceed to manual configuration.

docs.title: Step 4: Add Adapter Manually (if needed)
docs.text:
1. Click ADD COMPONENT in Profinity
  2. Select CAN Bus Adapter or your specific adapter type
  3. Enter adapter details:
  4. Name: Give your adapter a unique name
  5. Type: Select your adapter type
  6. Network Interface: Select the network interface (for Ethernet bridges)
  7. CAN Interface: Select CAN interface (for SocketCAN)
  8. Click Add or Save

docs.title: Step 5: Configure Adapter Settings
docs.text:
1. Click on your adapter in the sidebar
  2. Open Change Settings (gear icon)
  3. Configure settings:
  4. Auto Connect: Enable to auto-connect on startup
  5. Allow Loopback Traffic: Enable if needed (Tritium adapters only)
  6. Bitrate: Set CAN bus bitrate (must match network)
  7. Click Save

docs.title: Step 6: Connect the Adapter
docs.text:
1. Click the Connect button on your adapter dashboard
  2. Wait for the adapter to connect
  3. Check the status indicator:
  4. Green: Connected and receiving data
  5. Yellow: Connected but no data arriving
  6. Red: Connection error (check logs)
  7. Grey: Not connected

docs.title: Step 7: Verify Connection
docs.text:
1. Check that the status indicator turns green
  2. Open the SEND & RECEIVE CAN window
  3. Verify CAN messages are appearing in the activity panel
  4. If no messages appear, check:
  5. CAN bus bitrate matches network
  6. Physical connections are correct
  7. Adapter is properly powered

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Adapter Not Discovered: - Check adapter is powered and connected - Verify network connectivity (for Ethernet bridges) - Check firewall settings - Verify drivers are installed

No Data Arriving: - Verify CAN bus bitrate matches all devices - Check physical CAN bus connections - Ensure devices on CAN bus are powered - Check adapter status for errors

Connection Errors: - Check adapter logs in Profinity - Verify adapter is not in use by another application - Restart Profinity and try again - Check adapter documentation for specific issues

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• CAN Bus Adapters - Complete adapter documentation
  • Adding New Components - General component setup
  • Virtual CAN Adapter - Using virtual adapters

docs.title: How to Create a Custom Component
docs.text: Add any CAN bus device to Profinity by creating a Custom Component with a DBC file and optional dashboard.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A DBC file for your CAN bus device
  • (Optional) A dashboard YAML file
  • Access to create components in Profinity

docs.title: Step 1: Create a New Custom Component
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → Components
  2. Click Add Component
  3. Select Custom Component

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Basic Settings
docs.text:
1. Enter a Component Name (e.g., "My CAN Device")
  2. Set the CAN ID if required
  3. Configure connection settings

docs.title: Step 3: Add Your DBC File
docs.text:
Option A - Using DBC Editor: 1. Click the DBC Editor icon in the toolbar 2. Paste your DBC content or upload a DBC file 3. Editor validates your DBC syntax 4. Save the DBC configuration

Option B - Upload DBC File: 1. Find the DBC file upload option in settings 2. Click Browse and select your .dbc file 3. Upload the file 4. Profinity parses and validates the DBC file

docs.title: Step 4: (Optional) Add a Custom Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Click the Dashboard Editor icon
  2. Start with "Hello World" template or upload existing YAML
  3. Create dashboard with data bindings: 
    bind:
  - target: value
    source: '{COMPONENT_NAME}.YourMessage.YourSignal'
  4. Save the dashboard

docs.title: Step 5: Save and Activate
docs.text:
1. Click Save to save your Custom Component
  2. Component appears in your component list
  3. Add it to your active profile if needed

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Component
docs.text:
1. Check component appears in the sidebar
  2. View component dashboard to see data
  3. Verify CAN messages are being received
  4. Check signals are displaying correctly

docs.title: Using Your Custom Component
docs.text:
Once created, your Custom Component:

  • Receives CAN messages defined in your DBC file
  • Displays signals in the dashboard (if configured)
  • Can be logged to InfluxDB, Prometheus, or files
  • Can be monitored in real-time
  • Can be used in scripts via the Profinity API

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test with CAN Log Replay: Use the CAN log replay feature to test your component with recorded messages
  • Start Simple: Begin with a basic dashboard and add complexity gradually
  • Validate DBC: Ensure your DBC file is valid before uploading
  • Use Examples: Look at existing component dashboards for reference

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No data appearing: Check that CAN messages are being received and match your DBC definitions
  • Dashboard not loading: Validate your YAML syntax in the dashboard editor
  • Signals not found: Verify signal names match exactly (case-sensitive)

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Custom Components - Complete Custom Component guide
  • DBC Documentation - Understanding DBC files
  • Dashboard Development Guide - Creating dashboards
  • Data Binding - Connecting data to dashboards

docs.title: How to Create a Custom Dashboard
docs.text: This guide walks you through creating your first custom dashboard for a Custom Component.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A Custom Component created in Profinity
  • Basic understanding of YAML syntax
  • Access to the Dashboard Editor

docs.title: Step 1: Open the Dashboard Editor
docs.text:
1. Navigate to your Custom Component in the sidebar
  2. Click the Dashboard Editor icon (pencil/edit icon) in the toolbar
  3. The dashboard editor opens with a "Hello World" template

docs.title: Step 2: Add Your First Data Binding
docs.text:
Replace the static label with a data binding:

- value:
    label: TEMPERATURE
    precision: 1
    bind:
      - target: value
        source: '{COMPONENT_NAME}.Temperature.Value'

Note: {COMPONENT_NAME} is automatically replaced with your component's actual name at runtime.

docs.title: Step 3: Add More Components
docs.text:
Add additional readouts:

- pillgroup:
    items:
      - value:
          label: TEMPERATURE
          precision: 1
          bind:
            - target: value
              source: '{COMPONENT_NAME}.Temperature.Value'
      - value:
          label: PRESSURE
          precision: 2
          bind:
            - target: value
              source: '{COMPONENT_NAME}.Pressure.Value'

docs.title: Step 4: Validate and Save
docs.text:
1. The editor validates your YAML in real-time
  2. Check for error messages at the bottom
  3. Click Save when validation passes
  4. Your dashboard updates immediately

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Learn about Core Elements for more complex layouts
  • Explore Component Reference for available components
  • See Examples for complete dashboard examples

docs.title: How to Create a New Profile
docs.text: Create a new profile to manage different configurations for different setups or locations.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • Admin access to create profiles

docs.title: Step 1: Access Profile Management
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → Profiles
  2. Profile management window opens

docs.title: Step 2: Create New Profile
docs.text:
1. Click New Profile or Add Profile button
  2. Enter a Profile Name (e.g., "Production Site", "Test Rig")
  3. Click Create or Save

docs.title: Step 3: Load the Profile
docs.text:
1. Select your new profile from the list
  2. Click Load Profile or Set as Active
  3. Profile becomes the active profile

docs.title: Step 4: Configure Profile
docs.text:
1. Add components to your new profile (see Add Component to Profile)
  2. Configure component settings
  3. (Optional) Upload a custom dashboard (see Create Profile Dashboard)

docs.title: Step 5: Save Profile Settings
docs.text:
1. Profile settings are saved automatically
  2. Switch between profiles using ADMIN → Profiles
  3. Each profile maintains its own configuration

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use Descriptive Names: Name profiles clearly (e.g., "Site A - Production")
  • Profile-Specific Dashboards: Each profile can have its own custom dashboard
  • Component Isolation: Components in one profile don't affect another profile
  • Profile Switching: Switch profiles without restarting Profinity

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Profiles - Complete profile documentation
  • Profile Dashboard - Profile dashboard configuration

docs.title: How to Create a Profile Dashboard
docs.text: Replace the default Profinity home page with a custom dashboard for your profile.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An active profile in Profinity
  • A dashboard YAML file ready to upload
  • Admin access to profile settings

docs.title: Step 1: Create Your Dashboard YAML
docs.text:
1. Create a dashboard YAML file in the dashboard editor or a text editor
  2. Your dashboard should start with: 
    dashboard:
  items:
    - titlebar:
        # Your titlebar configuration
    - row:
        items:
          # Your dashboard content
  3. For examples, see the Dashboard Development Guide

docs.title: Step 2: Access Profile Settings
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the ADMIN tab
  2. Click on Profiles
  3. Select your profile from the list
  4. Click on the profile to open its settings

docs.title: Step 3: Upload the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. In profile settings, find "Upload Default Dashboard"
  2. Click Choose File or Browse
  3. Select your dashboard YAML file
  4. Click Upload or Save

docs.title: Step 4: Verify the Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the home page (click home icon or refresh)
  2. Your custom dashboard should display instead of the default home page
  3. Dashboard is active whenever this profile is loaded

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test First: Test your dashboard in the Dashboard Editor before uploading
  • Backup: Keep a copy of your dashboard YAML file
  • Validation: Ensure your YAML is valid - invalid dashboards won't load
  • Profile-Specific: Each profile can have its own custom dashboard

docs.title: Removing a Profile Dashboard
docs.text:
To revert to the default home page:

  1. Go to Profile settings
  2. Remove or clear the uploaded dashboard file
  3. Save the profile

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Profile Dashboard - Detailed information about profile dashboards
  • Dashboard Development Guide - Complete dashboard development reference

docs.title: How to Debug Dashboard Issues
docs.text: Troubleshoot and fix common dashboard problems.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • A dashboard with issues
  • Access to dashboard editor

docs.title: Step 1: Check Dashboard Validation
docs.text:
1. Open dashboard editor
  2. Check for validation errors at the bottom
  3. Fix any YAML syntax errors shown
  4. Common errors:
  5. Missing colons or commas
  6. Incorrect indentation
  7. Invalid property names

docs.title: Step 2: Verify Data Bindings
docs.text:
1. Check data binding sources: 
    bind:
  - target: value
    source: '{COMPONENT_NAME}.Signal.Value'  # Verify source exists
  2. Verify component name is correct
  3. Verify signal path matches your DBC file
  4. Check signal is receiving data

docs.title: Step 3: Check Component Status
docs.text:
1. Verify components are active (green status)
  2. Check components are receiving CAN data
  3. Verify data is available for binding
  4. Check CAN bus connection

docs.title: Step 4: Test with Simple Components
docs.text:
1. Start with a simple readout: 
    - readout:
    label: "TEST"
    value: 42.5  # Static value first
  2. Verify it displays correctly
  3. Then add data binding

docs.title: Step 5: Check Image and Asset References
docs.text:
1. Verify images exist in /Profile/Images/
  2. Check filenames match exactly (case-sensitive)
  3. Verify file paths in HTML components: 
    <img src="/Profile/Images/logo.png" />  # Correct

docs.title: Step 6: Review Dashboard Logs
docs.text:
1. Check Profinity logs for dashboard errors
  2. Look for data binding errors
  3. Check for missing component or signal errors
  4. Review validation messages

docs.title: Step 7: Compare with Working Dashboard
docs.text:
1. View source of a working dashboard
  2. Compare structure with your dashboard
  3. Check for differences in formatting
  4. Copy working patterns

docs.title: Common Issues and Solutions
docs.text:
Issue: Dashboard Not Loading - Check YAML syntax is valid - Verify dashboard structure is correct - Check for missing required properties

Issue: No Data Displaying - Verify components are active - Check data bindings are correct - Verify CAN data is arriving

Issue: Images Not Showing - Check image files exist in /Profile/Images/ - Verify filenames match exactly - Check file format is supported

Issue: Styling Not Applied - Verify CSS file exists in /Profile/Styles/ - Check CSS is linked in HTML component - Verify class names match

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Troubleshooting Guide - Complete troubleshooting guide
  • FAQ - Frequently asked questions
  • Dashboard Validation - Schema validation information

docs.title: How to Log Data to the Cloud (InfluxDB)
docs.text: Configure Profinity to log CAN bus data to InfluxDB for cloud-based data analytics and visualization.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • An InfluxDB instance (cloud or self-hosted)
  • InfluxDB database created and accessible
  • Network access to your InfluxDB server
  • Admin access to Profinity

docs.title: Step 1: Set Up InfluxDB
docs.text:
Option A - InfluxDB Cloud: 1. Sign up for InfluxDB Cloud 2. Create a new organization 3. Create a new bucket for your data 4. Generate an API token with write permissions 5. Note: Organization Name, Bucket Name, API Token, InfluxDB URL

Option B - Self-Hosted: 1. Install InfluxDB on your server 2. Start InfluxDB service 3. Create a bucket: influx create bucket my-profinity-data 4. Generate an API token: influx auth create --org my-org --all-access

docs.title: Step 2: Add InfluxDB Logger Component
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → Components
  2. Click Add Component
  3. Select InfluxDB Prometheus Logger
  4. Click Add

docs.title: Step 3: Configure InfluxDB Connection
docs.text:
1. Set Component Name (e.g., "InfluxDB Cloud Logger")
  2. Set Logger Type to "InfluxDB"
  3. Enter InfluxDB URL:
  4. Cloud: https://us-east-1-1.aws.cloud2.influxdata.com
  5. Self-hosted: http://your-server:8086
  6. Enter Organization name
  7. Enter Bucket/Database name
  8. Enter API Token

docs.title: Step 4: Select Components to Log
docs.text:
1. Find Components to Log section
  2. Select components to send to InfluxDB:
  3. Check individual components, or
  4. Select "All Components"
  5. (Optional) Use filters to include/exclude specific components

docs.title: Step 5: Configure Logging Interval
docs.text:
1. Set Logging Interval (e.g., 1-5 seconds)
  2. Typical values: 1-5 seconds for most applications
  3. Higher frequency = more granular but more bandwidth
  4. Lower frequency = less bandwidth but coarser data

docs.title: Step 6: Test Connection
docs.text:
1. Click Test Connection (if available)
  2. Verify connection successful
  3. Check for error messages
  4. Review connection status

docs.title: Step 7: Save and Activate
docs.text:
1. Click Save to save logger configuration
  2. Ensure logger is added to active profile
  3. Logger starts automatically when profile is active

docs.title: Step 8: Verify Data Logging
docs.text:
1. Log into InfluxDB web interface
  2. Navigate to Data Explorer
  3. Query your data: 
    from(bucket: "my-profinity-data")
  |> range(start: -1h)
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r["_measurement"] == "component_name")
  4. Verify data is arriving
  5. Check Profinity logs for connection errors

docs.title: Data Structure in InfluxDB
docs.text:
Profinity logs data with this structure:

  • Measurement: Component name
  • Tags: Component ID, signal names
  • Fields: Signal values
  • Timestamp: Data timestamp

Example Data Point: 

measurement: "Prohelion BMU"
tags:
  componentId: "bmu-001"
  signal: "PackVoltage"
fields:
  value: 400.5
timestamp: 2024-01-17T10:30:00Z

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start with One Component: Test with a single component first
  • Monitor Bandwidth: Cloud logging uses network bandwidth
  • Optimize Intervals: Balance data granularity with cost
  • Use Tags Efficiently: Tags are indexed and help with queries
  • Set Retention Policies: Configure data retention to manage costs
  • Monitor Costs: Cloud InfluxDB charges based on data usage

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Connection Failed:
  • Verify InfluxDB URL is correct and accessible
  • Check firewall settings
  • Verify API token is valid

  • Test network connectivity

  • No Data Arriving:

  • Verify components are selected
  • Check that components are receiving data
  • Verify logging interval is set

  • Check InfluxDB write permissions on token

  • Authentication Errors:

  • Verify API token is correct
  • Check token has write permissions
  • Verify organization name matches

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• InfluxDB Prometheus Logger - Complete logger documentation
  • Data Logging Overview - General data logging guide
  • InfluxDB Documentation - Official InfluxDB documentation

docs.title: How to Replay CAN Bus Logs
docs.text: Replay recorded CAN bus messages to test your system without live CAN bus data.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • A recorded CAN bus log file (.csv format)
  • CAN bus adapter connected (optional for testing)

docs.title: Step 1: Access CAN Replay Tool
docs.text:
1. Navigate to CAN Utilities → Replay CAN Logs
  2. Or click Replay in the CAN Activity window
  3. CAN Replay window opens

docs.title: Step 2: Load Your CAN Log File
docs.text:
1. Click Load Log File or Browse
  2. Select your .csv log file
  3. File loads into the replay tool

docs.title: Step 3: Configure Replay Settings
docs.text:
1. Replay Speed: Select replay speed:
  2. Real-time: Replay at original speed
  3. Faster: Speed up replay (2x, 5x, 10x)

  4. Slower: Slow down replay (0.5x, 0.25x)

  5. Loop: Enable to loop replay continuously

  6. Filter: (Optional) Filter specific CAN IDs or time ranges

docs.title: Step 4: Start Replay
docs.text:
1. Click Start Replay or Play button
  2. Messages are sent to the CAN bus network
  3. Watch the CAN Activity panel to see messages being replayed

docs.title: Step 5: Monitor Replay
docs.text:
1. Check CAN Activity panel shows replayed messages
  2. Verify components are receiving data
  3. Check dashboards update with replayed data
  4. Monitor replay progress

docs.title: Step 6: Stop or Pause Replay
docs.text:
1. Click Stop to stop replay
  2. Click Pause to pause (resume with Play)
  3. Use Seek to jump to specific time in log

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test Without Hardware: Use replay to test dashboards without CAN hardware
  • Debug Issues: Replay logs to debug component configurations
  • Record First: Use CAN logging to record logs for later replay
  • Filter Messages: Filter replay to focus on specific CAN IDs

docs.title: Related Documentation
docs.text:
• Logging and Replaying CAN Bus Messages - Complete CAN logging guide
  • Send/Receive CAN Messages - CAN message tools

docs.title: How to Send and Receive CAN Bus Messages
docs.text: Send and receive CAN bus messages using Profinity's built-in CAN tools.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • CAN bus adapter connected and active
  • User privileges to send/receive CAN messages
  • Active profile with adapter configured

docs.title: Step 1: Enable User Privileges
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → Users
  2. Select your user account
  3. Ensure Send CAN Messages privilege is enabled
  4. Ensure Receive CAN Messages privilege is enabled
  5. Click Save

docs.title: Step 2: Open the Send & Receive CAN Window
docs.text:
1. Click on SEND & RECEIVE CAN in the menu
  2. The CAN Activity window will open
  3. You'll see all CAN messages currently on the network

docs.title: Step 3: View Received CAN Messages
docs.text:
The CAN Activity panel shows:

  • CAN ID: Message identifier
  • Data: Message data bytes
  • Direction: Incoming or outgoing
  • Count: Number of times message was seen
  • Time: Timestamp of last message

View Options: - Spaced Data: Breaks data into individual hex bytes (default: on) - Heatmap: Highlights frequently changing bytes in warm colours (default: on)

docs.title: Step 4: Filter and Sort Messages
docs.text:
1. Click column headers to sort by that column
  2. Use filters to show specific CAN IDs or data patterns
  3. Click on a message to see details

docs.title: Step 5: Add a Scheduled CAN Packet
docs.text:
1. Click the + icon in the Scheduled CAN Packets panel (bottom of window)
  2. Or double-click a message in the CAN Activity panel and click +

docs.title: Step 6: Configure the CAN Packet
docs.text:
1. CAN ID: Enter the CAN message ID (hex or decimal)
  2. Endian: Select byte order (default: little endian)
  3. Data Format: Choose how to enter data:
  4. Bytes: Enter individual byte values
  5. Int16: Enter 16-bit integer values
  6. Int32: Enter 32-bit integer values
  7. Floats: Enter floating-point values

  8. Raw Data: Enter raw hex data

  9. Interval (ms): Set how often to send (e.g., 100ms = 10 times per second)

  10. Leave blank for manual send only

docs.title: Step 7: Enter Message Data
docs.text:
Example - Entering Bytes: - Byte 0: 0x01 - Byte 1: 0x02 - Byte 2: 0x03 - Raw data updates automatically

Example - Entering Int16: - Int16[0]: 1234 - Int16[1]: 5678 - Values are converted to bytes automatically

docs.title: Step 8: Save the Packet
docs.text:
1. Click Save to add packet to scheduled list
  2. Packet appears in Scheduled CAN Packets panel
  3. If interval is set, packet starts sending automatically

docs.title: Step 9: Send Packet Manually (if not scheduled)
docs.text:
1. Select the packet in Scheduled CAN Packets panel
  2. Click the Send arrow button
  3. Or select the packet and press Space key
  4. Packet is sent immediately

docs.title: Step 10: Verify Packet Transmission
docs.text:
1. Check the CAN Activity panel
  2. Your sent message should appear with outgoing direction
  3. Verify the CAN ID and data match your configuration

docs.title: Stop a Scheduled Packet
docs.text:
1. Select the packet in Scheduled CAN Packets panel
  2. Delete the interval value or delete the packet
  3. Packet stops sending

docs.title: Edit a Scheduled Packet
docs.text:
1. Select the packet in Scheduled CAN Packets panel
  2. Click Edit or double-click
  3. Modify settings
  4. Click Save

docs.title: Delete a Scheduled Packet
docs.text:
1. Select the packet in Scheduled CAN Packets panel
  2. Click Delete or press Delete key
  3. Packet is removed from schedule

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test First: Send packets manually before scheduling
  • Monitor Activity: Watch CAN Activity panel to see your messages
  • Check Bitrate: Ensure CAN ID and data format match network expectations
  • Use Heatmap: Heatmap helps identify active messages
  • Save Packets: Scheduled packets are saved in your profile

docs.title: Important Notes
docs.text:
• Scheduled Packets Continue: Scheduled packets continue sending even after logging off
  • Profile-Based: Scheduled packets are saved with your profile
  • Manual Restart: Packets don't auto-start after profile change or restart

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Packet Not Sending: - Check adapter is connected (green status) - Verify user has send privileges - Check CAN ID is valid - Ensure interval is set or use manual send

Packet Not Appearing in Activity: - Check filters aren't hiding your message - Verify adapter is receiving traffic - Check CAN bus bitrate matches

Wrong Data Format: - Verify endian setting matches your system - Check data format conversion (bytes vs. integers) - Review raw data to confirm values

docs.text:

  • Connect to CAN Bus - Setting up CAN adapters
  • CAN Bus Adapters - Adapter documentation

docs.title: How to Set Up Profinity as a Kiosk Application
docs.text: Configure Profinity to run as a kiosk application that automatically launches in fullscreen mode.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed as a service or in Docker with automatic start enabled
  • Profinity must be running before configuring the browser for kiosk mode
  • Admin access to the system
  • A profile configured and ready to display
  • Understanding of your operating system's kiosk mode features

docs.title: Step 1: Configure Kiosk Mode in Profinity
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → System Configuration
  2. Find Kiosk Mode section
  3. Enable Kiosk Mode
  4. Configure settings:
  5. Auto-Start: Enable
  6. Fullscreen: Enable
  7. Startup Profile: Select profile to load
  8. URL: Set initial URL/page
  9. Click Save

docs.title: Step 2: Configure Browser for Kiosk Mode
docs.text:
Important: Ensure Profinity is installed as a service or in Docker with automatic start, and that it is running before configuring the browser. The browser will fail to connect if Profinity is not already running.

Windows: 1. Create desktop shortcut 2. Right-click → Properties 3. In Target, add: --kiosk http://localhost:18080 4. Example: "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --kiosk http://localhost:18080 5. Press Win + R, type shell:startup 6. Copy shortcut to startup folder

Linux: 1. Create systemd service: sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/profinity-kiosk.service 2. Add service file: 

[Unit]
Description=Profinity Kiosk Mode
After=graphical.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=your-username
ExecStart=/usr/bin/chromium-browser --kiosk --noerrdialogs http://localhost:18080
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=graphical.target
3. Enable: sudo systemctl enable profinity-kiosk.service 4. Start: sudo systemctl start profinity-kiosk.service

macOS: 1. Open Automator 2. Create new Application 3. Add "Run Shell Script" action 4. Script: /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --kiosk http://localhost:18080 5. Save as application 6. System Preferences → Users & Groups → Login Items 7. Add kiosk application

docs.title: Step 3: Configure System Startup
docs.text:
1. Ensure Profinity starts automatically - Profinity must be installed as a service or in Docker with automatic start enabled
  2. Verify Profinity is running - Before configuring the browser, ensure Profinity service is running and accessible at http://localhost:18080
  3. Configure browser to start after Profinity (with a delay to ensure Profinity is fully started)
  4. Test startup sequence

docs.title: Step 4: Secure Kiosk Mode
docs.text:
1. Disable browser navigation
  2. Disable keyboard shortcuts (Alt+F4, Ctrl+Alt+Del)
  3. Hide taskbar/system tray
  4. Configure timeouts if needed

docs.title: Step 5: Test Kiosk Mode
docs.text:
1. Restart the system
  2. Verify Profinity starts automatically
  3. Verify browser opens in kiosk mode
  4. Verify correct profile loads
  5. Verify fullscreen display works

docs.title: URL Parameters for Kiosk Mode
docs.text:
You can use URL parameters when launching:

http://localhost:18080?profile=MyProfile&fullscreen=true

docs.title: Auto-Refresh Dashboard
docs.text:
Configure dashboards to auto-refresh:

# In your dashboard YAML
chart:
  refreshInterval: 1000  # Refresh every second

docs.title: Prevent User Exit
docs.text:
• Disable browser's exit shortcuts
  • Configure system to restart on browser exit (Linux systemd)
  • Use Windows Group Policy to lock down the system

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Test Thoroughly: Test all functionality in kiosk mode before deployment
  • Monitor Performance: Ensure system has adequate resources
  • Backup Configuration: Keep a backup of your kiosk configuration
  • Update Process: Plan how to update Profinity without breaking kiosk mode
  • Remote Access: Consider remote monitoring for kiosk systems

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Browser Not Starting: Check system startup order and service dependencies
  • Wrong Profile: Verify startup profile setting in Profinity
  • Display Issues: Check display configuration and resolution settings
  • Performance Issues: Monitor system resources and optimize dashboard complexity

docs.text:

docs.title: How to Style Your Dashboard
docs.text: Apply custom CSS styling to your dashboard elements for branding and visual customization.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed
  • A dashboard to style
  • Basic CSS knowledge
  • Access to /Profile/Styles directory

docs.title: Step 1: Create CSS File
docs.text:
1. Navigate to your profile directory
  2. Go to Styles folder (create if needed)
  3. Create a CSS file (e.g., custom-dashboard.css)

docs.title: Step 2: Write Your CSS
docs.text:
Example CSS file:

.custom-panel {
    background-color: #f0f0f0;
    border: 2px solid #007bff;
    border-radius: 8px;
    padding: 1rem;
}

.custom-readout {
    font-size: 1.2em;
    color: #333;
    font-weight: bold;
}

.status-indicator {
    background-color: #28a745;
    color: white;
    padding: 0.5rem;
}

docs.title: Step 3: Link CSS in Dashboard
docs.text:
Using HTML Component:

- html:
    content: |
      <link rel="stylesheet" href="/Profile/Styles/custom-dashboard.css" />
      <div class="custom-panel">
        <h2>Styled Content</h2>
      </div>

docs.title: Step 4: Apply CSS Classes
docs.text:
Use class property in dashboard components:

- group:
    class: "custom-panel"
    items:
      - readouts:
          items:
            - readout:
                label: "Temperature"
                class: "custom-readout"

docs.title: Step 5: Verify Styling
docs.text:
1. Save your dashboard
  2. Verify CSS file is loaded
  3. Check elements are styled correctly
  4. Test on different screen sizes

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use Descriptive Class Names: Name classes clearly
  • Keep Styles Modular: Separate CSS files for different purposes
  • Test Responsive: Ensure styles work on different screen sizes
  • Use CSS Variables: For consistent theming

docs.title: How to View Dashboard Source
docs.text: Access the YAML source code of existing dashboards to learn from examples and modify them.

docs.title: Step 1: Access Dashboard Source for Component Dashboards

1. Navigate to the component in the sidebar

docs.title: Step 2: Access Profile Dashboard Source

docs.title: Step 3: Copy Dashboard Source

docs.title: Step 5: Learn from Dashboard Structure

docs.title: How to Write Your First Script
docs.text: Create your first Profinity script to automate tasks and interact with your CAN bus system.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed and running
  • An active profile with components configured
  • Basic understanding of JavaScript, Python, or C#
  • Scripting enabled in Profinity configuration

docs.title: Step 1: Enable Scripting
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → System Configuration
  2. Find Scripting section
  3. Enable Enable Scripting
  4. Click Save

docs.title: Step 2: Choose Your Script Type
docs.text: For your first script, use Run Script: - Run Scripts - Execute on-demand or on a schedule - Receive Scripts - Triggered when CAN messages are received - Service Scripts - Long-running background services

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Script Editor
docs.text:
1. Navigate to ADMIN → Scripts
  2. Click New Script or Add Script
  3. Select Run Script
  4. Script editor opens

docs.title: Step 4: Write Your First Script
docs.text:
JavaScript Example: 

async function main() {
    const components = await profinity.getComponents();
    for (const component of components) {
        const data = await profinity.getComponentData(component.id);
        console.log(`Component: ${component.name}`);
    }
}
main().catch(console.error);

Python Example: 

import profinity

def main():
    components = profinity.get_components()
    for component in components:
        data = profinity.get_component_data(component.id)
        print(f"Component: {component.name}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

docs.title: Step 5: Configure Script Settings
docs.text:
1. Set Script Name
  2. Select Language (JavaScript, Python, or C#)
  3. Add Description
  4. Configure Trigger:
  5. On Demand - Run manually
  6. Scheduled - Run on schedule (cron)
  7. On Startup - Run when Profinity starts

docs.title: Step 6: Test Your Script
docs.text:
1. Click Run or Test
  2. Check console output for results
  3. Review error messages
  4. Fix issues and test again

docs.title: Step 7: Save and Deploy
docs.text:
1. Click Save to save your script
  2. Script appears in your scripts list
  3. Run on demand or according to schedule

docs.title: Reading Component Data
docs.text:
// Read specific component data
const bmuData = await profinity.getComponentData('Prohelion BMU');
const voltage = bmuData.PackMeasurement.PackVoltage;
console.log(`Battery Voltage: ${voltage}V`);

docs.title: Sending CAN Messages
docs.text:
// Send a CAN message
await profinity.canBus.sendMessage({
    id: 0x123,
    data: [0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04],
    extended: false
});

docs.title: Accessing System State
docs.text:
// Access system properties
const activeProfile = await profinity.profiles.getActive();
const systemInfo = await profinity.system.getInfo();

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start Simple: Begin with basic scripts that read data
  • Use Console Logging: Use console.log() to debug your scripts
  • Test Incrementally: Test small parts of your script as you build it
  • Review Examples: Look at example scripts in the documentation

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Script Not Running: Check that scripting is enabled
  • No Data Available: Ensure components are active and receiving data
  • Syntax Errors: Validate your code syntax before running
  • Permission Issues: Verify your script has necessary permissions

docs.title: Installing Profinity On Docker
docs.text:
Available Profinity Releases

Profinity is currently available on Windows machines as a standard desktop application, for selected Unix Platforms (including macOS and Linux) and as a Docker container for Docker enabled environments and Cloud setups.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Installation using Docker
    • Prerequisites
    • Simple Setup
    • Starting and Stopping Profinity
    • Accessing Profinity
  • Complex Setup for Production Deployments
    • Using Environment Variables for Configuration
    • Docker Compose with Environment Variables
    • Environment File (.env)
    • Using Environment Files with Docker Compose
    • Deployment Strategies

docs.title: Installation using Docker
docs.text: Profinity can be deployed onto most devices capable of running Docker, including macOS and Linux machines as well as several single-board computers such as Raspberry Pi, BeagleBone Black, etc.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
The following items are required to be able to install Profinity:

  • Docker installed on the target device
  • A device capable of running ASP .Net 9, with Docker support from Microsoft
  • Docker Compose installed on the target device (included with Docker Desktop, available as plugin on Linux machines)
  • A suitable CAN adaptor for the target device

docs.title: Simple Setup
docs.text:
On the target device, create a new empty directory and a file titled docker-compose.yml in the new directory. The contents of the docker-compose.yml file should be

services:
  profinity:
      image: prohelion/profinity:latest
      restart: always
      #On linux hosts you can run in host mode to enable autodiscovery
      #network_mode: host
      ports:
        - 18080:18080
        - 18443:18443
        - 5000:5000
        - 4876:4876

For more information about Docker Compose, see the official Docker documentation.

docs.title: Starting and Stopping Profinity
docs.text: The Profinity Docker container is started and stopped using commands from the Docker Compose toolset. First, navigate to the directory containing the docker-compose.yml file.

docs.title: Basic Commands
docs.text:
Start Profinity: 

docker compose up

Start in background (detached mode): 

docker compose up -d

Stop Profinity (keeps containers): 

docker compose stop
This stops the running containers but keeps them. You can restart them later with docker compose start.

Stop and remove Profinity (removes containers): 

docker compose down
This stops the containers and removes them. You'll need to run docker compose up again to recreate and start them.

View logs: 

docker compose logs -f

For more information about Docker Compose commands, see the official Docker Compose reference.

docs.title: Accessing Profinity
docs.text:
Once started, open the URL defined in your configuration to access the Profinity web client. The default URL is http://localhost:18080 on the local machine or http://[Your IP Address]:18080 if accessed remotely.

Connecting to the Profinity web client will direct you to the Profinity login page.

Profinity login page

A fresh install of Profinity will only have the administrator user active. To log in, use the following login details.

Username: admin

Password: password

After logging in, you will arrive at the Profinity homepage.

Profinity homepage

To stop Profinity temporarily (keeping containers), use docker compose stop. To stop and remove containers, use docker compose down.

docs.title: Complex Setup for Production Deployments
docs.text: It is not necessary to use environment variables to configure Profinity. However, for full production environments and deployments that involve many Profinity instances you will likely find that Environment Variables are the most simple way to configure the product.

docs.title: Using Environment Variables for Configuration
docs.text: Profinity supports environment variable substitution in configuration and profile files, making it easy to create flexible Docker deployments. For detailed information about environment variables, including default values and syntax, see the Environment Variables documentation.

docs.title: Docker Compose with Environment Variables
docs.text:
You can configure Profinity using environment variables in your docker-compose.yml file. Docker Compose supports environment variable substitution in compose files, allowing you to use variables for port mapping and service configuration.

services:
  profinity:
    image: prohelion/profinity:latest
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-18080}:18080"
      - "${HTTPS_PORT:-18443}:18443"
      - "${API_PORT:-5000}:5000"
      - "${UDP_PORT:-4876}:4876"
    environment:
      # Profinity Configuration
      - CONFIG_NAME=${CONFIG_NAME:-Production Configuration}
      - HTTP_ADDRESS=${HTTP_ADDRESS:-0.0.0.0}
      - HTTP_PORT=${HTTP_PORT:-18080}
      - LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-Info}
      - ENABLE_SCRIPTING=${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-true}

      # Profile Configuration
      - PROFILE_NAME=${PROFILE_NAME:-Docker Profile}
      - ADAPTER_IP=${ADAPTER_IP:-192.168.1.100}
      - ADAPTER_PORT=${ADAPTER_PORT:-8080}
    volumes:
      - ./profiles:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Profiles
      - ./config:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Config

For more information about Docker Compose environment variables, see the official Docker documentation.

Docker Volumes

The volumes section mounts local directories into the container, allowing Profinity to persist configuration and profile data. Profinity stores data in /root/Prohelion/Profinity/ by default (when running as root user). For more information about Docker volumes, see the official Docker documentation.

Validating Profile Paths

To verify where Profinity is storing profiles and config files, you can exec into the running container: 

docker compose exec profinity bash
ls -la /root/Prohelion/Profinity/
This will show the actual directory structure used by Profinity inside the container.

docs.title: Environment File (.env)
docs.text:
Docker Compose automatically loads environment variables from a .env file in the same directory as your docker-compose.yml. This is the recommended way to manage environment-specific configuration.

Create a .env file in the same directory as your docker-compose.yml:

# Profinity Configuration
CONFIG_NAME=Production Configuration
HTTP_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
HTTP_PORT=18080
LOG_LEVEL=Info
ENABLE_SCRIPTING=true

# Profile Configuration
PROFILE_NAME=Docker Profile
ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.100
ADAPTER_PORT=8080

# Network Configuration
HTTP_PORT=18080
HTTPS_PORT=18443
API_PORT=5000
UDP_PORT=4876

For more information about .env files in Docker Compose, see the official Docker documentation.

Using Environment Variables in Config and Profile Files

When using environment variables with Docker, you can reference them directly in your Profinity Config.yaml and Profile.yaml files. These files should be placed in the mounted volume directories that map to /root/Prohelion/Profinity/Config and /root/Prohelion/Profinity/Profiles inside the container. When Profinity starts in Docker, it will automatically substitute the environment variables in these files with the values from your .env file or Docker Compose environment section.

For complete examples and detailed information about using environment variables in Config.yaml and Profile.yaml files, including syntax, default values, and variable naming rules, see the Environment Variables documentation.

docs.title: Using Environment Files with Docker Compose
docs.text:
If you're using multiple .env files for different environments:

# Start with specific environment file
docker compose --env-file .env.production up

# Start with development environment
docker compose --env-file .env.development up

# Use specific compose file with environment file
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file .env.production up

For more information about Docker Compose environment files, see the official Docker documentation.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies
docs.text:
You can create different Docker Compose files for different environments. This approach allows you to use the same base configuration while customizing settings for development, staging, and production.

Development Environment 

# docker-compose.dev.yml
services:
  profinity:
    image: prohelion/profinity:latest
    environment:
      - CONFIG_NAME=Development Configuration
      - LOG_LEVEL=Debug
      - ENABLE_SCRIPTING=true
      - PROFILE_NAME=Development Profile
      - ADAPTER_IP=127.0.0.1
    volumes:
      - ./dev-profiles:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Profiles
      - ./dev-config:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Config

Production Environment 

# docker-compose.prod.yml
services:
  profinity:
    image: prohelion/profinity:latest
    restart: always
    environment:
      - CONFIG_NAME=Production Configuration
      - LOG_LEVEL=Info
      - ENABLE_SCRIPTING=false
      - PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
      - ADAPTER_IP=${PRODUCTION_ADAPTER_IP}
    volumes:
      - ./prod-profiles:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Profiles
      - ./prod-config:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Config
      - ./logs:/root/Prohelion/Profinity/Logs

For more information about Docker Compose file overrides, see the official Docker documentation.

Directly Accessing Devices

Docker deliberately does not expose all devices through to the containers that run the applications. In some cases you may wish to expose additional devices to Docker so that you can access things like SocketCAN Natively or discover components that use UDP for broadcasting. See the official Docker documentation for how to expose these devices to your Docker container.

docs.title: Environment Variables in Profinity
docs.text: Profinity supports environment variable substitution in both configuration files and profile files, allowing you to create flexible, environment-specific configurations without hardcoding values.

docs.title: Table of Contents
docs.text:
• Overview
  • Syntax
    • Basic Usage
    • Default Values
    • Variable Naming Rules
  • Supported File Types
    • Configuration Files
    • Profile Files
  • Setting Environment Variables
    • Windows
    • Linux/macOS
    • Docker Deployment
  • Variable Behavior
    • Defined Variables
    • Undefined Variables
    • Mixed Values
  • Complete Examples
    • Configuration File Example
    • Profile File Example
  • More Information

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Environment variables enable you to:

  • Use different settings across development, staging, and production environments
  • Keep sensitive information out of configuration files
  • Share configuration templates across teams
  • Easily modify settings without editing files

This functionality makes Profinity configurations flexible and maintainable across different environments and deployments.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text: Environment variables use the ${VARIABLE_NAME} syntax and are automatically substituted when Profinity loads configuration or profile files. Profinity also supports Docker-style default values using the ${VARIABLE_NAME:-default} syntax.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
# Example configuration with environment variables
Name: ${PROFILE_NAME}
Description: Production configuration
Components:
  Adapter1:
    IpAddress: ${ADAPTER_IP}
    Port: ${ADAPTER_PORT}
    Timeout: ${ADAPTER_TIMEOUT:-2000}  # Uses 2000 if ADAPTER_TIMEOUT is not set

docs.title: Default Values
docs.text:
Profinity supports default values for environment variables using the ${VARIABLE_NAME:-default} syntax. If the environment variable is not set or is empty, the default value will be used instead.

Examples:

# Variable without default - must be set
IpAddress: ${ADAPTER_IP}

# Variable with default value
Port: ${ADAPTER_PORT:-8080}  # Uses 8080 if ADAPTER_PORT is not set

# Variable with empty default
Timeout: ${ADAPTER_TIMEOUT:-}  # Uses empty string if ADAPTER_TIMEOUT is not set

# Variable with default in Logs section
RollsizeMB: ${LOG_ROLLSIZE:-100}  # Uses 100 if LOG_ROLLSIZE is not set

# Boolean with default
EnableScripting: ${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-true}  # Uses true if ENABLE_SCRIPTING is not set

Behavior: - If the environment variable is set and has a value, that value is used - If the environment variable is not set or is empty, the default value (after the :-) is used - Variables without defaults must be set, or the configuration will fail to load

docs.title: Variable Naming Rules
docs.text:
Environment variable names must:

Requirement Description Example Use word characters only Letters, numbers, and underscores ${PROFILE_NAME}, ${VAR123} Be enclosed in brackets Must use ${} syntax ${ADAPTER_IP} Be case-sensitive Uppercase and lowercase matter ${Profile_Name} ≠ ${profile_name}

Valid examples: - ${PROFILE_NAME} - ${ADAPTER_IP} - ${BMU1_BASE_ADDRESS} - ${_UNDERSCORE_VAR} - ${VAR123}

Invalid examples: - ${VAR-WITH-DASH} (hyphens not allowed) - ${VAR WITH SPACES} (spaces not allowed) - ${VAR.WITH.DOTS} (dots not allowed)

docs.title: Supported File Types
docs.text: Environment variables are supported in both Profinity Config and Profile files, enabling flexible deployment across different environments.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
Environment variables work in the main Profinity configuration file (Config.yaml):

Name: ${CONFIG_NAME}
AppSettings:
  ProfinityServer:
    HttpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS}
    HttpPort: ${HTTP_PORT}
  Logs:
    LogLevel: ${LOG_LEVEL}
    RollsizeMB: ${LOG_ROLLSIZE:-100}  # Default to 100 if not set
  EnableScripting: ${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-true}  # Default to true if not set
Options:
  WebServer:
    Enabled: true
    HttpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS}
    HttpPort: ${HTTP_PORT}

docs.title: Profile Files
docs.text:
Environment variables are also supported in profile files for component configuration:

Name: ${PROFILE_NAME}
Description: ${PROFILE_DESCRIPTION}
Version: ${PROFILE_VERSION}
Components:
  Tritium1:
    Protocol: UDP
    AdapterIpAddress: ${ADAPTER_IP}
    BusNo: ${BUS_NUMBER}
    UdpTTL: ${UDP_TTL}
    Type: TritiumAdapter
  SocketCan1:
    BusName: can0
    IpAddress: ${SOCKET_IP}
    Port: ${SOCKET_PORT}
    Timeout: ${SOCKET_TIMEOUT}
    Type: ProhelionSocketCANdAdapter
  BMU1:
    ParallelStrings: ${BMU_PARALLEL_STRINGS}
    MilliValid: ${BMU_MILLI_VALID}
    BaseAddress: ${BMU1_BASE_ADDRESS}
    Type: ProhelionBMU

docs.title: Setting Environment Variables
docs.text: Environment variables can be set using various methods depending on your operating system and deployment method.

docs.title: Command Prompt
docs.text:
set PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
set ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.100
set ADAPTER_PORT=8080

docs.title: PowerShell
docs.text:
$env:PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile"
$env:ADAPTER_IP="192.168.1.100"
$env:ADAPTER_PORT="8080"

docs.title: System Environment Variables
docs.text:
1. Open System Properties → Advanced → Environment Variables
  2. Add variables to User or System variables
  3. Restart Profinity for changes to take effect

docs.title: Bash/Shell
docs.text:
export PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile"
export ADAPTER_IP="192.168.1.100"
export ADAPTER_PORT="8080"

docs.title: Persistent Configuration
docs.text:
Add to your shell profile file (~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, or ~/.zshrc):

echo 'export PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export ADAPTER_IP="192.168.1.100"' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'export ADAPTER_PORT="8080"' >> ~/.bashrc

docs.title: Environment File (.env)
docs.text:
Create a .env file in your project directory:

PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.100
ADAPTER_PORT=8080
BMU_PARALLEL_STRINGS=2
BMU_MILLI_VALID=750

docs.title: Docker Run Command
docs.text:
docker run -e PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile" \
           -e ADAPTER_IP="192.168.1.100" \
           -e ADAPTER_PORT="8080" \
           profinity

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
version: '3.8'
services:
  profinity:
    image: profinity
    environment:
      - PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
      - ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.100
      - ADAPTER_PORT=8080
    env_file:
      - .env

docs.title: Variable Behavior
docs.text: Environment variables are processed when Profinity loads configuration or profile files. Understanding how they behave is crucial for successful deployment.

docs.title: Defined Variables
docs.text:
When an environment variable is defined and has a value, it will be automatically replaced:

# Original configuration
IpAddress: ${ADAPTER_IP}

# With ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.100
IpAddress: 192.168.1.100

docs.title: Undefined Variables
docs.text:
When an environment variable is not defined or is empty, the placeholder remains unchanged:

# Original configuration
IpAddress: ${UNDEFINED_IP}

# Result (variable not defined)
IpAddress: ${UNDEFINED_IP}

Configuration Loading Errors

If an undefined variable results in invalid values (like ${UNDEFINED_IP} for an IP address field), the configuration or profile will fail to load with an appropriate error message.

docs.title: Mixed Values
docs.text:
You can combine environment variables with static values in the same configuration:

Components:
  SocketCan1:
    BusName: can0  # Static value
    IpAddress: ${DEVICE1_IP}  # Environment variable
    Port: ${DEVICE1_PORT}  # Environment variable
    Timeout: 2000  # Static value
  SocketCan2:
    BusName: can1  # Static value
    IpAddress: 192.168.1.100  # Static value
    Port: ${DEVICE2_PORT}  # Environment variable
    Timeout: ${DEVICE2_TIMEOUT}  # Environment variable

docs.title: Complete Examples
docs.text: These examples demonstrate how to use environment variables in both configuration and profile files.

docs.title: Configuration File Example
docs.text:
Config.yaml: 

Name: ${CONFIG_NAME}
Description: ${CONFIG_DESCRIPTION}
Version: 1
ReadOnly: false
AppSettings:
  ProfinityServer:
    HttpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS}
    HttpPort: ${HTTP_PORT}
    HttpsRedirect: false
    Enabled: true
  Logs:
    RollsizeMB: ${LOG_ROLLSIZE:-100}  # Default to 100 if not set
    MaxLogFiles: ${MAX_LOG_FILES:-10}  # Default to 10 if not set
    LogLevel: ${LOG_LEVEL}
  EnableScripting: ${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-true}  # Default to true if not set
Options:
  WebServer:
    Enabled: true
    HttpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS}
    HttpPort: ${HTTP_PORT}
    HttpsRedirect: false
    RestAPI:
      Enabled: true

Corresponding environment variables: 

CONFIG_NAME=Production Configuration
CONFIG_DESCRIPTION=Main production configuration
HTTP_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
HTTP_PORT=8080
LOG_ROLLSIZE=100
MAX_LOG_FILES=10
LOG_LEVEL=Info

docs.title: Profile File Example
docs.text:
Profile.yaml: 

Name: ${PROFILE_NAME}
Description: ${PROFILE_DESCRIPTION}
Version: ${PROFILE_VERSION}
ReadOnly: false
Components:
  Tritium1:
    Protocol: UDP
    TritiumProtocolVersion: V1
    AdapterIpAddress: ${ADAPTER_IP}
    BusNo: ${BUS_NUMBER}
    UdpTTL: ${UDP_TTL}
    AutoConnect: false
    Type: TritiumAdapter
  SocketCan1:
    BusName: can0
    IpAddress: ${SOCKET_IP}
    Port: ${SOCKET_PORT}
    Timeout: ${SOCKET_TIMEOUT}
    AutoConnect: false
    Type: ProhelionSocketCANdAdapter
  BMU1:
    ParallelStrings: ${BMU_PARALLEL_STRINGS}
    MilliValid: ${BMU_MILLI_VALID}
    BaseAddress: ${BMU1_BASE_ADDRESS}
    Type: ProhelionBMU
    SendControllerHeartbeat: true

Corresponding environment variables: 

PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
PROFILE_DESCRIPTION=Main production profile with all components
PROFILE_VERSION=2
ADAPTER_IP=192.168.1.50
BUS_NUMBER=14
UDP_TTL=64
SOCKET_IP=10.0.0.100
SOCKET_PORT=5678
SOCKET_TIMEOUT=3000
BMU_PARALLEL_STRINGS=2
BMU_MILLI_VALID=750
BMU1_BASE_ADDRESS=101

docs.title: More Information
docs.text:
For additional information on Profinity configuration and profiles, see:

  • Profinity Profiles - Detailed profile management
  • System Configuration - System-level configuration options
  • Getting Started with Profiles - Basic profile concepts

docs.title: Migration from Profinity V1 to V2
docs.text:
Profinity V2 Overview

Profinity V2 represents a significant architectural upgrade from V1. While V2 maintains all the functionality of V1 and adds many new capabilities, the systems are not backwards compatible.

Profinity V2 is not backwards compatible with Profinity V1. This means:

  • V2 profiles cannot be opened in V1: Profile formats have changed and V1 cannot read V2 profile files
  • V2 configurations are incompatible: System configuration formats differ between versions
  • API changes: The API structure and endpoints have changed significantly
  • No downgrade path: Once you migrate to V2, you cannot revert profiles or configurations back to V1

docs.title: Functionality Preservation
docs.text:
While the formats are incompatible, V2 includes:

  • All core functionality from V1
  • Enhanced features and capabilities
  • Improved architecture and performance
  • Modern web-based interface
  • Expanded API capabilities

docs.title: Recommended Approach: Clean Installation
docs.text:
Recommended: Clean Installation

We recommend performing a clean installation of Profinity V2, removing V1 before installing V2.

  1. Backup V1 Data: Before uninstalling, backup your V1 profiles, configurations, and any custom scripts or data
  2. Document Configuration: Document any custom V1 settings you want to replicate in V2
  3. Uninstall V1: Remove Profinity V1 using standard uninstallation procedures
  4. Install V2: Install Profinity V2 following the installation guides
  5. Recreate Configuration: Set up your V2 installation and recreate your profiles using V2 tools

docs.title: Co-Existence (Not Recommended)
docs.text:
While it is technically possible to run both V1 and V2 on the same machine, this is not recommended because:

  • Port conflicts may occur if both try to use the same network ports
  • Profile confusion between versions
  • Resource usage from running both systems
  • Potential data synchronization issues

If you must run both versions temporarily:

  • Use different ports for each version
  • Run each version under different user accounts
  • Keep profiles and configurations clearly separated
  • Plan to migrate completely to V2 as soon as practical

docs.title: 1. Pre-Migration Planning
docs.text:
• Review your current V1 setup and document all components
  • Identify all profiles in use
  • Document any custom scripts or configurations
  • Plan which V2 features you want to adopt

docs.title: 2. Backup Existing Data
docs.text:
• Export all V1 profiles (save copies)
  • Backup configuration files
  • Document component settings and addresses
  • Save any custom DBC files or scripts

docs.title: 3. Uninstall V1 and Install V2
docs.text:
• Follow the appropriate installation guide for your platform
  • Use your V1 installer to Uninstall V1 and remove all files in your Profile directory
  • Install V2 as a new installation (not upgrading V1)
  • Verify V2 is running correctly before proceeding

docs.title: 4. Recreate Configuration
docs.text:
• Create new profiles in V2
  • Add components using V2's improved interface
  • Import or recreate DBC files as needed
  • Configure system settings for your environment

docs.title: 5. Verify and Test
docs.text:
• Verify all components are detected and configured correctly
  • Test critical functionality before putting into production
  • Review security settings and user accounts
  • Ensure all expected features are working

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you encounter issues during migration:

  • Review the Installation Guides for your platform
  • Check the Administration documentation for configuration guidance
  • Contact Prohelion Support for assistance
  • Use the Feedback feature in Profinity to report issues
