Parameter Description Default Name The name of the component. Must be unique. The adapter name Auto Connect Connects to the adapter automatically when the profile loads. On

The remaining parameters depend on the type of adapter.

docs.title: Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridge
docs.text:
The Tritium Can to Ethernet Bridge adapter connects to a Prohelion or Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridge.

Parameter Description Default Network Protocol UDP or TCP. UDP Tritium Protocol Version V1 or V2. Must match the firmware of the bridge. V1 IP Address The IP address of the bridge. TCP only. 127.0.0.1 Bus Number The virtual bus number of the bridge, from 0 to 13 for V1 and 0 to 32767 for V2. 13 UDP TTL The time to live of the UDP packets that Profinity transmits, from 1 to 1024. 128 Forward Address The lowest CAN identifier that the bridge forwards. TCP only. 0x0 Forward Address Range The size of the identifier range that the bridge forwards. TCP only. All CAN identifiers Allow Loopback Traffic Shows the packets that the bridge receives back from its own transmissions. UDP only. Off

UDP uses the multicast group 239.255.60.60 on port 4876, so several clients can share one bridge. TCP connects to the IP address of the bridge on port 4876, and a physical bridge accepts only one TCP connection. The forwarding range is described in CAN-TCP Bridging.

Auto Discovery sets the Tritium Protocol Version to match the bridge firmware. A profile can hold only one Tritium or Virtual adapter for each bus number. Two bridges that share a bus number on one Ethernet network join their CAN buses into one virtual bus, so give every bridge a unique bus number unless you are joining two buses deliberately (refer to Network Topologies).

The bridge holds the CAN bit rate (default 500 kbit/s), so this adapter has no bit rate parameter. The bit rate, static IP address, and bus number of the bridge itself are set in the bridge firmware, as described in CAN Bridge Configuration.

docs.title: SocketCANd
docs.text:
The SocketCANd Adapter connects over TCP to the socketcand daemon on another machine.

Parameter Description Default Bus Name The SocketCAN interface on the machine running socketcand, such as can0. can0 IP Address The IP address of the machine running socketcand. 127.0.0.1 Port The port that socketcand listens on, from 1 to 65535. 29536 Timeout The TCP timeout in milliseconds, from 0 to 60000. 2000

The machine running socketcand sets the bit rate of the interface, not Profinity.

docs.title: Peak CAN adapter
docs.text:
The Peak Systems CAN Adapter connects to a Peak CAN to USB adapter through the Peak driver.

Parameter Description Default PCAN Channel ID The channel of the adapter: USB 01 to USB 16, LAN 01 to LAN 16, or PCI 01 to PCI 16. Auto Discovery fills it in. USB 01 PCAN BaudRate 5K, 10K, 20K, 33K, 47K, 50K, 83K, 95K, 100K, 125K, 250K, 500K, 800K, or 1M Baud. 500K Baud

On Linux, the adapter appears as a SocketCAN interface, so use the SocketCAN adapter instead.

docs.title: Peak CAN FD adapter
docs.text:
The Peak Systems CANFD Adapter connects to a Peak adapter that supports CAN with Flexible Data-rate (CAN FD). It has the same PCAN Channel ID as the Peak CAN adapter, and the following bit rate parameters.

Parameter Description Default Connect With CAN FD Runs the adapter in CAN FD mode. Off PCAN BaudRate The classic CAN bit rate, used when Connect With CAN FD is off. Same values as the Peak CAN adapter. 500K Baud PCAN BaudRate FD The CAN FD bit rate, used when Connect With CAN FD is on: J2284_4 (500 kbit/s, data 2 Mbit/s) or J2284_5 (500 kbit/s, data 5 Mbit/s). J2284_4

docs.title: Ewert CANdapter
docs.text:
The Ewert CANdapter adapter connects to an Ewert Energy CANdapter over its USB serial port.

Parameter Description Default Candapter COM Port The USB serial port, such as COM3 on Windows or /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux and macOS. Required. None Candapter BaudRate 10K, 20K, 50K, 100K, 125K, 250K, 500K, 800K, or 1M Baud. 500K Baud

docs.title: Native SocketCAN
docs.text:
The SocketCAN Adapter connects to a SocketCAN interface on the machine running Profinity, and is available on Docker and Linux installations only.

Parameter Description Default Bus Name The SocketCAN interface, such as can0. can0

The operating system sets the bit rate of the interface, not Profinity.

For the status colours of an adapter and the bit rate that every device on the bus must share, refer to CAN bus adapter troubleshooting.

docs.title: CAN bus adapter troubleshooting
docs.text: This page covers the adapter status indicator, a Peak adapter that needs its driver, a CAN to Ethernet bridge that Auto Discovery does not find, and the bit rate that every device on a CAN bus must share. The adapters are listed on CAN bus adapters.

docs.title: Adapter status
docs.text:
Once the adapter is added to the Profile, a coloured status indicator appears in the sidebar next to the device name. Green is the state of a working adapter.

Colour Meaning Green Good: the adapter is connected and data is arriving. Amber Warning: the adapter is connected but no data is arriving. Red Error: the Profinity System Logs have the details. Grey Not applicable: the adapter is not connected.

If the indicator is amber, check that the bit rate matches the bus, that the bus is terminated and that another device is transmitting. If it is red, read the Profinity System Logs, then check the Peak driver, the IP address and port of a TCP bridge or the interface name of a SocketCAN adapter.

docs.title: If a Peak adapter is not found
docs.text:
The Peak CAN to USB Adapter needs the Peak driver installed on the machine that runs Profinity, as set out in CAN bus adapters. Without the driver, the adapter does not appear in the Discovered category, and an adapter already in the Profile shows a red status with the message "The Peak driver is not installed. Install the latest Peak drivers from the Peak website, then restart Profinity."

Install the latest driver from the Peak System website, confirm with the Peak tools that the adapter works, then restart Profinity. Peak updates its driver often, and an out-of-date driver also stops the adapter connecting, so update the driver if the adapter is plugged in and still shows red. On Linux, a Peak adapter appears as a SocketCAN interface instead, so use the SocketCAN adapter and no Peak driver is needed.

docs.title: If a CAN to Ethernet bridge is not found
docs.text:
Profinity discovers a CAN to Ethernet bridge from the UDP heartbeat datagrams that the bridge sends periodically (refer to Bridge Heartbeat). If the bridge does not appear in the Discovered category, check the following:

  • The bridge and the PC are on the same subnet, because Auto Discovery does not work across subnets. Across subnets, add the bridge manually with its IP address and the TCP protocol.
  • Any firewall allows UDP and TCP port 4876 for the bridge. For SocketCANd, the firewall must allow UDP port 42000 for discovery and TCP port 29536 (or the configured Port) for the connection.
  • A WiFi router passes broadcast UDP.

The bridge documentation covers further troubleshooting: the CAN to Ethernet bridges, the Quickstart, the Supported Network Setups and Common Problems and Solutions.

docs.title: Set the same bit rate on every CAN device
docs.text:
Every device on the CAN bus, including the adapter that connects Profinity, must operate at the same bit rate to communicate. Prohelion devices ship with a factory default of 500 kbit/s, which is also the default of the bridge, the Peak adapter and the CANdapter in Profinity. Prohelion devices support 1 Mbit/s and 500, 250, 125, 100 and 50 kbit/s, so a device changed from the default constrains the rest of the network. The CAN to Ethernet bridge does not terminate the bus, so terminate the CAN bus with 120 ohm resistors at each end (refer to the bridge DB9 connector datasheet).

For the parameters of each adapter, refer to CAN bus adapter settings.

docs.title: CAN bus adapters
docs.text:
An adapter connects Profinity to a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus. Profinity supports the following adapters.

Adapter Connection Prohelion and Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridges, listed as Tritium Can to Ethernet Bridge Ethernet, over UDP or TCP Prohelion Virtual CAN to Ethernet Bridge, covered on the Prohelion Virtual CAN Bus Adapter page Ethernet, relaying to another adapter SocketCANd, using the socketcand daemon Ethernet, over TCP Peak CAN to USB Adapter, including a Peak adapter running CAN FD USB Ewert Energy CANdapter USB (COM port) Native SocketCAN The local operating system, on Docker and Linux installs only

Native SocketCAN is available when Profinity runs in Docker or on a Linux host, including a Linux archive install, and is not available on Windows or macOS. SocketCAN is a Linux kernel feature. A Peak or CANdapter adapter that you plug into a Linux host also appears there as a SocketCAN interface, so on Linux use the SocketCAN adapter, or the SocketCANd adapter from another machine, instead of the Peak or CANdapter adapter.

Install the Peak driver before starting Profinity, because the Peak CAN to USB Adapter needs it. Use the supplied Peak tools to confirm the adapter works, then add the adapter with Auto Discovery as normal.

Adapters are added in one of two ways, through Auto Discovery or manually. The parameters that manual configuration asks for are in CAN bus adapter settings.

docs.title: Adapter auto discovery
docs.text:
Auto Discovery finds the supported CAN bus adapters that are visible to Profinity. If an adapter is visible on the network but is not yet in the current Profile, a Discovered category appears in the ADD COMPONENT window and lists every adapter that Profinity can currently see. An adapter that is missing from the list has configuration issues that need manual configuration, or is not discoverable.

Add an Adapter via AutoDiscovery

If a CAN to Ethernet bridge does not appear in the Discovered category, refer to If a CAN to Ethernet bridge is not found. For the adapter status colours and the bit rate that every CAN device must share, refer to CAN bus adapter troubleshooting.

For the steps to connect a CAN bus, refer to How to Connect to CAN Bus.

docs.title: Prohelion Virtual CAN Bus Adapter
docs.text:
The Prohelion Virtual CAN Bus Adapter is added to a Profile as the Prohelion Virtual CAN to Ethernet Bridge component. It relays Controller Area Network (CAN) traffic between the other CAN adapters in the Profile and any client that connects to it, and it presents itself to those clients as a Tritium / Prohelion CAN to Ethernet bridge. Use it to run tools that were developed for the Tritium and Prohelion bridges, such as the bridge configuration and firmware tools, when no physical bridge is present.

In the Virtual Adapter topology, a client connects to the Virtual Adapter, which works together with a Peak USB adapter to reach the physical CAN network. Traffic is routed in both directions.

Virtual Adapter

A different CAN connection technology, such as SocketCAN or the Peak USB adapter, connects Profinity to the CAN network. The Virtual Adapter has no setting that selects its partner adapter. It forwards traffic between itself and every other active CAN adapter in the Profile, so add the Peak or SocketCAN adapter to the same Profile first.

docs.title: Virtual adapter settings
docs.text:
To relay traffic, add a Virtual Adapter to the Profile after the adapter for the physical CAN network, and set the following.

Parameter Description Default Network Protocol TCP or UDP. UDP is always available, even when TCP is running. TCP Bridge Protocol Version V1, V2 or All. All Network Adapter The network interface on which the Virtual Bridge runs. The first available multicast interface Bus Number The bus number of the bridge. Profinity limits it to 0 to 13 for V1 or All, because the version 1 protocol allows only a 4-bit bus number. 13 UDP TTL The time to live of the UDP packets that Profinity transmits, from 1 to 1024. 128 Auto Connect Enables the adapter automatically when the profile loads. On

The Virtual CAN Bridge runs inside Profinity, so the operating system of that machine sets its IP address. The CAN Bridge Config tools and Profinity cannot change the address remotely, and Profinity can only select the network interface.

Two bridges with the same bus number relay data between each other

Two bridges with the same bus number on one network relay data from one bridge to the other. This joins two separate CAN bus networks into one virtual bus over Ethernet. Two bridges on the same CAN bus that are also on the same Ethernet network form a cyclic network, in which every message is resent indefinitely until the CAN bus is overloaded. Give each bridge a unique bus number unless you are joining two buses deliberately. Refer to Network Topologies and the bus number guidance for the physical bridge.

If a client cannot connect, check that the Network Adapter is the interface the client can reach and that the client speaks a protocol version covered by the Bridge Protocol Version.

docs.title: Multi-protocol support
docs.text:
Tritium and Prohelion CAN to Ethernet bridges have two major firmware releases, V1 and V2, which speak different protocols and differ in the width of the bus identifier (4 bits for V1 and 16 bits for V2, as set out in CAN-UDP Bridging). Refreshing the firmware of a V1 bridge updates it to V2, but many bridges remain on V1 firmware.

Tritium software tools shipped in either a V1 or a V2 variant. A V1 tool cannot talk to a V2 bridge, and the Fundamentals page recommends using the tools that match the bridge version.

The Virtual Bridge resolves this by speaking both protocols at once (the All option) and presenting itself as two bridges, one V1 and one V2. A tool then finds the bridge version that it can speak to.

Multi-Protocol Support

The Virtual Bridge also lets a physical V1 bridge talk to tools designed for the V2 protocol. In the scenario below, the Virtual Adapter sits in front of a Tritium V1 bridge and routes its traffic, so the bridge can communicate with tools that support the V2 protocol.

V1 and V2 Protocol Support

docs.title: Multi-client support
docs.text:
The physical bridge handles a single TCP connection at a time, so a second TCP connection fails and UDP is the alternative for several clients. The Virtual Bridge handles multiple clients at once. It can therefore act as a TCP CAN bridge server, where many clients connect over TCP and keep the connection open to receive CAN data, which suits real-time CAN monitoring in remote locations.

Multi-Client Support

For the physical adapters that the Virtual Adapter relays to, refer to CAN bus adapters. For the bridge that the Virtual Adapter imitates, refer to the CAN to Ethernet bridge documentation.

docs.title: Chargers and power supplies
docs.text:
Profinity charges a battery pack by controlling a charger and a Prohelion Battery Management Unit (BMU) together.

  • Charger components: choose a TDK Power Supply, Siglent Power Supply or Elcon Charger and add it to a Profile.
  • Charger settings: look up the charger and supply limits and the network and CAN settings.
  • Start a charge: select the battery, set the current and Charge To level, and press START.
  • Charging troubleshooting: fix the controller messages and a pack that does not engage.

docs.title: Charger components
docs.text:
Profinity charges a pack by controlling a charger and a Prohelion Battery Management Unit (BMU) together. A charger that can be controlled remotely is needed because a BMS that can only switch a charger on and off gives slow or poor balancing of the cells, which is described in the D1000 Gen1 Charger Control documentation. The D1000 Gen1 BMU raises the charge current setpoint until the highest cell voltage reaches the Balance Threshold and then reduces it to hold that voltage. On a D1000 Gen2 the BMS hardware handles charging, so refer to the D1000 Gen2 documentation for how charging is managed there.

Profinity supports three charger types, a Prohelion BMS in the same Profile supplies the pack data, and a user needs the Control charging permission to see the charging controls (refer to Roles and Permissions).

Siglent Charger

docs.title: Supported chargers
docs.text:
• TDK Power Supply controls TDK programmable power supplies such as the Genesys family using Standard Commands for Programmable Instruments (SCPI) over TCP. A TDK supply that only has a serial interface needs a TCP to serial converter between it and the network so that Profinity can reach it over TCP.
  • Elcon Charger controls an Elcon charger over CAN, so the charger must be connected to a CAN adapter that is already configured in the Profile.
  • Siglent Power Supply controls Siglent programmable power supplies that accept SCPI commands over TCP, such as the SPD3303X-E, which suits desktop testing.

docs.title: Add a charger to the Profile
docs.text:
A charger is a component, so it is added from ADD COMPONENT in the same way as any other device (refer to Add a Component to a Profile). The Profile must also contain a Prohelion BMS, and that BMS must have Control Pack switched on, because Control Pack is off by default and Profinity can only engage and disengage the pack, which a charge needs, when it is on. Once the charger is added it appears under Chargers & Power Supplies in the main menu with its own dashboard.

Add a Charger

Every charger asks for its own limits and the limits of the supply that feeds it, which Charger settings lists. To run a charge from the dashboard, refer to Start a charge, and for the messages and faults that stop one, refer to Charging troubleshooting.

docs.title: Charger settings
docs.text:
Profinity asks for these settings when a charger component is added to a Profile.

Every charger asks for its own limits and the limits of the supply that feeds it. Each charger type starts with its own default limits, and Supply Voltage Limit and Supply Current Limit start at 240 V and 10 A, so set all five to match the actual charger and the wall circuit before charging.

Setting TDK Siglent Elcon Notes Charger Voltage Limit 300 V 32 V 198 V Maximum voltage, in volts, that the charger can output, from 1 to 1000. Charger Current Limit 10 A 3.2 A 46 A Maximum current, in amps, that the charger can output, from 1 to 1000. Charger Power Limit 3000 W 102 W 6600 W Maximum power, in watts, that the charger can output, from 1 to 1000000. If unsure, use maximum voltage multiplied by maximum current, or less. Supply Voltage Limit 240 V 240 V 240 V Maximum voltage, in volts, that the wall socket supplies, from 1 to 1000. Supply Current Limit 10 A 10 A 10 A Maximum current, in amps, that the wall socket supplies, from 1 to 1000.

The TDK and Siglent supplies are reached over the network and share these communication settings.

Setting Default Notes Charger IP Address 127.0.0.1 Address of the supply on the network. Charger Port 5025 TCP port the supply listens on, between 1 and 65535. Comms Timeout 5000 Time in milliseconds Profinity waits for the supply to answer. Auto Connect Off Connects to the supply when the Profile loads. With it off, the supply is not connected until the user connects it with the Connect / Disconnect toggle in the component's menu. Auto Reconnect On Keeps trying to connect in the background, both when the supply is off at start and after it disconnects. With it off, Profinity makes one attempt and reports a failure. Reconnect Interval 5000 Time in milliseconds between connection attempts, between 500 and 600000. Shown only when Auto Reconnect is on. Charger ID 0 TDK only. The ID the TDK supply is set to. Channel ID 1 Siglent only. The channel in use on a multi-channel supply.

The Elcon charger has no connection step, because it communicates over CAN, and asks for the following instead.

Setting Default Notes Elcon Command CAN Bus Id 0x1806E5F4 CAN address Profinity sends commands to. Elcon Status CAN Bus Id 0x18FF50E5 CAN address Profinity receives status messages from. Milliseconds Valid 5000 Time in milliseconds the CAN traffic from the charger stays valid before Profinity treats the connection as lost, between 1 and 60000.

docs.title: Current and voltage limits
docs.text:
Set the supply and charge limits before charging

The charger and supply limits in the Profile are the maximums Profinity works to, so a Supply Current Limit above what the wall circuit is rated for can overload that circuit. Profinity does not know the cell specification beyond what the BMU reports, so keep the charge current at or below the cell manufacturer's recommended charge current to avoid damaging the battery.

To run a charge with these limits, refer to Start a charge.

docs.title: Charging troubleshooting
docs.text:
Charging needs both the charger and the BMS to work as expected, so first confirm that every device in the Profile shows the green circle in the Profile window. A grey or red device needs fixing before a charge runs. The controller panel then reports most problems in a message above the controls.

Message Cause Fix No Battery: No battery can be found in this profile The Profile has no Prohelion BMS. Add a Prohelion BMS to the Profile. Battery Control Limited: You cannot software control this battery Control Pack is off on the BMS, so the current, Charge To and START controls are disabled. Switch Control Pack on in the BMS settings, or use the screen to monitor the charger only. Charger Not Available: The charger is not connected or not available The charger is not connected or does not exist in the Profile. Connect the charger, and check its IP address and port (TDK and Siglent) or the CAN adapter (Elcon). Charger Issue: There is an issue with your selected charger The charger, its hardware or its communications report an error. Check the COMMUNICATIONS and CHARGER STATUS lamps and the Profinity logs, and resolve the error before charging. SOC Warning: You have already reached that charge level Charge To is lower than the current state of charge. Raise Charge To above the current state of charge.

If START does nothing and no message is shown, check that the battery and charger lamps are not grey or red, because the button is disabled while either is unavailable.

docs.title: The pack does not engage
docs.text:
A common problem is current flowing from the battery into the charger during precharge. Any load that draws current while the pack precharges slows or stops the rise of the output voltage, so precharge does not finish in the expected time and the pack does not engage (refer to Precharge). On a D1000 Gen2 the PRECHARGE FAIL REASON lamps report the failure, for example PRECHARGE TIMEOUT or PRECHARGE STABLE CURRENT, and the Firmware V1.2 Messages and Signals page lists them.

To test this outside a charge, try to engage the pack from the BMU dashboard while the charger is connected. If the contactors do not engage while the charger is connected, the problem exists. The fix is a diode of suitable rating in the charger circuit, so that current can only flow from the charger to the pack.

To run a charge once the fault is fixed, refer to Start a charge.

docs.title: Start a charge
docs.text:
Start a charge from the dashboard of a charger component that is in the same Profile as a Prohelion BMS with Control Pack switched on (refer to Charger components).

Open the charger from Chargers & Power Supplies. The dashboard shows the Charger Status lamps (CHARGER STATUS, TEMPERATURE, COMMUNICATIONS, AC SUPPLY and DC OUTPUT), the Charge Current (Amps) chart and, for a user with the Control charging permission, the Charger / Power Supply Controller panel. With Auto Connect off on a TDK or Siglent supply, the charger must be connected first, and the message above the controls shows Ready with the text "Charger is ready. You can start charging." once it is.

The controls run left to right. The battery selector chooses which Prohelion BMS to charge when the Profile has more than one. The current control sets the charge current in amps, in steps of 0.5 A, up to the maximum the screen allows. Charge To sets the state of charge, in percent, at which charging stops. START begins the charge and becomes STOP while charging is running.

Start the Charge

The following steps start a charge.

  1. Select the battery to charge.
  2. Set the maximum charge current, at or below the cell manufacturer's charge limit.
  3. Set Charge To to the state of charge at which charging should stop.
  4. Press START.
  5. Check that the charge has started. The button changes to STOP, the message above the controls shows Charging Status with the charging current and voltage (for example "Charging at 5.0A • 280.4V • On"), the DC OUTPUT lamp is green, and the Charge Current (Amps) chart rises above zero. If the message stays on Ready or START returns, refer to Charging troubleshooting.

Pressing START engages the pack itself, so there is no separate step to close the contactors. Profinity sets the charger to the estimated pack voltage, checks that the charger is ready for precharge, engages the pack through the BMS and then starts the charge. If any of those stages fails, Profinity stops the charge and disengages the pack. Pressing STOP stops the charger and disengages the pack.

Set the supply and charge limits before charging

A Supply Current Limit above what the wall circuit is rated for can overload that circuit, and a charge current above the cell manufacturer's recommended charge current can damage the battery. Set the limits described in Charger settings before a first charge.

If a charge does not start, refer to Charging troubleshooting.

docs.title: Prohelion Cloud Dashboard
docs.text:
The Prohelion Cloud Dashboard component publishes the values of selected tag collections from a Profile to a device in Prohelion Cloud at a fixed interval, where they can be viewed on cloud-hosted dashboards. Prohelion Cloud is an Internet of Things (IoT) platform that stores the data reported by field devices and lets an organisation monitor and manage those devices and assets remotely.

Rules, Dashboards, and Tag Relays cover many of the functions that Prohelion Cloud provides, so new deployments are usually better served by those features. The Cloud Dashboard remains available for existing customers.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Server["Profinity server"]
        Tags --> Collections["Tag collections"] --> Component["Prohelion Cloud Dashboard"]
    end
    subgraph Cloud["Prohelion Cloud"]
        Device
    end
    Component --> Device
The Prohelion Cloud Dashboard component sends tag collections from the Profinity server to a device in Prohelion Cloud over MQTT

Licence required

The Prohelion Cloud Dashboard component requires the Data Relay licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the component is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Get access to Prohelion Cloud
docs.text: Access to Prohelion Cloud is by request. Raise an access request in the Prohelion Support Portal, and Prohelion support assists with device onboarding, dashboard set-up and integration with existing systems. The component needs an access token and a device ID for the device in Prohelion Cloud, so have both to hand before adding it. Both are shown in your account on the Prohelion Cloud dashboard.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text:
Only one Prohelion Cloud Dashboard component can exist in a Profile. Add it from ADD COMPONENT (refer to Add a Component to a Profile), choose Prohelion Cloud Dashboard and complete the following settings.

Setting Default Notes Name Prohelion Cloud Dashboard The name shown in the Profile. Prohelion Access Token None The access token for the device. Required, and stored encrypted. Prohelion Device ID None The device ID in Prohelion Cloud. Required. Update Interval (Seconds) 60 Seconds between samples sent to Prohelion Cloud, from 1 to 86400. Collections None The tag collections to send. At least one is required, because the component does not start until a collection is selected. Logging mode Snapshot Chooses between Snapshot, On Change and Everything. Refer to Logging modes for what each mode sends. Auto Connect On Starts sending when the Profile loads.

The component connects out from the Profinity server to Prohelion Cloud using MQTT on TCP port 1883, so the firewall or network must allow that outbound connection. No inbound port is needed.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: The component cannot be saved without an access token and a device ID, and reports "You must provide a device access token." or "You must provide a device ID." when either is empty. If the component is added but no data reaches Prohelion Cloud, check that the Profile has the Data Relay feature licensed, that the token and device ID match the device in Prohelion Cloud, that at least one collection is selected, and that outbound traffic on port 1883 is allowed, then read the Profinity logs for the connection error. For the shared settings of MQTT components, refer to MQTT Publisher.

docs.title: Using a Custom Component
docs.text:
A Custom Component allows a developer to create a new component for Profinity, and as of Profinity 2.3 it can carry an optional DBC (CAN database) file, a dashboard, a rules file, a long-running script, operator actions, and settings and firmware maps. Once it is in a profile it is monitored, graphed, and logged the same way as a built-in component. Built-in components such as the Elmar Solar MPPT and the WaveSculptor already include their own DBC support, so Messages and Signals is available on those components without a separate file, and a Custom Component can do the same for a third-party CAN device, or for a component whose live values a script publishes as tags.

Licence required

Custom Components need the Custom Plugins licensed feature, which is included from the Desktop edition upward. The script a Custom Component runs, set under Scripts, needs the Scripting licensed feature, which is included from the Desktop edition upward, so a profile without it can use the DBC, dashboard, and rules files but not the script. The Profinity SDK used to pack a component is a separate add-on. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

To make a first Custom Component, follow Make your first Custom Component. To attach optional files afterwards, refer to How to create a Custom Component. The files that make one up, and how to pack it for another installation, are in Custom Components, which also compares a Custom Component with a Dashboard Component and a dynamic-link library (DLL) plugin.

docs.title: What appears in the profile
docs.text:
After the component is saved it is listed in the side menu and opens onto its dashboard. Loggers, rules, and scripts bind to it the same way they bind to any other component.

Component settings are arranged as Settings, Pack files, Scripts, and Security, with Security last. Pack files is where the DBC, dashboard, rules file, actions file, settings map, firmware map, and firmware file are uploaded. Scripts is where the main script and Auto Start Main Script are set. A component installed from a content pack hides Pack files and Scripts, because those files belong to the pack, and shows Name, Tag tree path, menu placement, and the fields declared in the pack's settings map.

docs.title: Optional capabilities
docs.text:
A Custom Component can have a DBC file, a dashboard, or both. Each is optional, uploaded under Pack files, and the two can be used on the same component.

  • DBC file. With a DBC file the component gets Messages and Signals and Edit DBC File in its menu, so its CAN traffic can be read as named messages and signals. If the file fails to parse, the component stays in the profile and Messages and Signals is left out until the file is fixed. Refer to CAN bus DBC, and to How to create a Custom Component for the Rebase DBC setting that shifts message identifiers to a different base address.
  • Dashboard. The dashboard is the component's page in the profile. With none uploaded, Profinity creates a template dashboard named after the component, and the dashboard editor on the component opens that file so it can be edited into the finished dashboard. Refer to the Profinity dashboard development guide and How to create a custom dashboard.

Live values that a script publishes are tags, and a dashboard binds those tags whether or not a DBC file is present.

docs.title: Packing for other installations
docs.text:
As of Profinity 2.3, a Custom Component that works in one profile can be packed and installed on other systems, with no rebuild of the component. The Profinity SDK includes profinity-component-pack, which validates the component's files and packs them as a .zip or a .nupkg. An administrator then uploads the package by opening ADMIN and then Components & Plugins, and the component appears in ADD COMPONENT under the name the author gave it.

The pack is a bundle of the component's own files (DBC, dashboard, scripts, and maps), not a compiled DLL plugin. The catalogue name is set in component_metadata.yaml. Refer to Component metadata. Packing and installing are covered in Component Pack CLI, and the kit is available from Prohelion.

docs.title: Dashboard Component
docs.text:
A Dashboard Component is a built-in profile component that renders a dashboard defined entirely in YAML and can be edited using the visual dashboard editor.

Use it for human-machine interface (HMI) style screens that bind only to tags that already exist.

It is included in every edition, and it differs from a Custom Component in that it has no DBC, script, or pack files, so there is nothing to upload except the dashboard itself.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text: Add the component from ADD COMPONENT (refer to Add a Component to a Profile), where it is listed under Dashboards. Its only setting besides the name is Upload Dashboard (Optional), which takes a .yaml dashboard file. When no file is uploaded, Profinity creates a template dashboard named after the component, and the dashboard editor on the component opens that file so it can be edited into the finished dashboard. A component name that matches an existing dashboard file in the profile is rejected with the message "There is already a component in this profile with that name".

docs.title: Building the dashboard
docs.text:
Dashboards are written in YAML and can be edited in the Visual Editor, with the same layout, data, and interactive components available as on any other dashboard.

Dashboard visual editor

A relative tag path in a Dashboard Component starts at the Dashboard Component itself, which has no DBC, so a path such as DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage finds no tag there. Bind to the tags of another component with an absolute path that starts with /, such as /Prohelion BMU/DBC/PackStateOfCharge/SOCPercent.

Refer to Data Binding to connect the dashboard to tags and the Component Reference for each element. Worked guides are How to Create a Custom Dashboard and How to Create a Profile Dashboard.

docs.title: Historians
docs.text:
A historian is a logging component that writes the history of your tags to a database and, unlike a logger, also allows that history to be read back out again through the APIs. Dashboards, trend charts and integrations that ask for long-range tag history are answered from the historian, so a profile that needs more than the recent in-memory values needs one.

Data out of Profinity. Historians (InfluxDB v2, InfluxDB v3, TAG SQL) store and read data back, publishers and subscribers (MQTT, Webhook) stream it in both directions, loggers (file, SFTP, InfluxDB v1, Prometheus) stream it out, and a Prohelion Cloud dashboard gives hosted monitoring.

Profinity provides three historians, and each selects the tags it records through collections, in the same way as a logger. Historians require the Historians licensed feature, included in the Desktop, Server and Enterprise editions, and Licensing shows whether it is available on your instance.

All three allow the history to be read back through the APIs, and all three have the Designated tag historian reader setting described under Designating the historian that is read from.

Component Direction Stores data in Selects data by Licence Interval setting InfluxDB v2 Historian Out, and read back through the APIs An InfluxDB v2 server, using a bucket and organisation Collections Historians feature Update Interval (Seconds), default 10, from 1 to 86400 InfluxDB v3 Historian Out, and read back through the APIs An InfluxDB v3 server, using a database Collections Historians feature Update Interval (Seconds), default 10, from 1 to 86400 TAG SQL Historian Out, and read back through the APIs A SQL database: SQLite, SQL Server / Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL, or Oracle Collections Historians feature Update Interval (Seconds), default 10, from 1 to 86400

The InfluxDB v2 Historian needs InfluxDB Bucket, InfluxDB Organisation and InfluxDB Token, all required, and the InfluxDB v3 Historian needs InfluxDB Database and InfluxDB Token, both required. The TAG SQL Historian needs a Database Provider, which defaults to SQLite, and a required Connection String.

docs.title: Which InfluxDB component do I need
docs.text: Check which InfluxDB version your server runs before adding a component, because InfluxDB v1, v2 and v3 are incompatible and a component only connects to the version it was built for. An InfluxDB v2 server organises data into buckets that belong to an organisation, so it needs the InfluxDB v2 Historian, which asks for a bucket, an organisation and a token. An InfluxDB v3 server stores data in a single database, so it needs the InfluxDB v3 Historian, which asks for a database and a token. Both are documented in InfluxDB historians. An InfluxDB v1 server needs the InfluxDB v1 Logger, which is a logger rather than a historian and is documented under InfluxDB v1 Logger.

docs.title: Designating the historian that is read from
docs.text:
More than one historian can write in the same profile, but long-range tag and history queries are answered from exactly one of them. Enable Designated tag historian reader on that one component and leave it disabled on the others. If no component is designated, or more than one is, Profinity has no store to read history from and the long-range queries are not answered. An InfluxDB historian is designated only while its Allow Retrieval setting is also enabled.

To set up logging, refer to How to Configure Data Logging.

docs.title: InfluxDB historians
docs.text:
The InfluxDB v2 Historian and the InfluxDB v3 Historian write the values of the tags in the collections you select to an InfluxDB server, and allow that history to be read back out through the APIs. They sit in the Historians category. Each recorded value belongs to a tag, identified by its tag tree path.

Use the InfluxDB v2 Historian if your InfluxDB server stores data in buckets that belong to an organisation. Use the InfluxDB v3 Historian if your InfluxDB server stores data in a single database. Both authenticate with a token. InfluxDB Cloud is supported as well as a server you host: enter the Cloud URL and a token in the same way.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Profinity["Profinity"]
        Tags --> Collections["Tag collections"] --> Historian["InfluxDB historian"]
    end
    subgraph Server["InfluxDB server"]
        Store["InfluxDB"]
    end
    Historian --> Store
An InfluxDB historian writes the tags in the selected collections to the InfluxDB server, and the APIs read the history back

Licence required

The InfluxDB v2 Historian and the InfluxDB v3 Historian require the Historians licensed feature. Refer to Licensing for the editions that include them.

Use the InfluxDB v2 Historian only with an InfluxDB v2 server, and the InfluxDB v3 Historian only with an InfluxDB v3 server. The component type must match the InfluxDB version, and a mismatch causes connection failures. Historians explains how to choose.

docs.title: Adding an InfluxDB historian
docs.text:
To start recording, install InfluxDB v2 or v3 and confirm that it is running, then:

  1. Add an InfluxDB v2 Historian or an InfluxDB v3 Historian to your profile from the Historians category.
  2. For the v2 historian, enter InfluxDB Bucket, InfluxDB Organisation and InfluxDB Token. For the v3 historian, enter InfluxDB Database and InfluxDB Token.
  3. Under Collections, add at least one tag collection. The component does not start until one is configured.
  4. In Influx Server URL, enter the endpoint URL that InfluxDB is running on, or keep the default http://localhost:8086/.

Settings cannot be saved while a required field is empty.

These settings identify where the data is stored, and differ between the two historians.

Setting Applies to Default Purpose InfluxDB Bucket InfluxDB v2 Historian None The InfluxDB bucket that the data is stored in. Required. InfluxDB Organisation InfluxDB v2 Historian None The InfluxDB organisation that owns the bucket. Required. InfluxDB Database InfluxDB v3 Historian None The InfluxDB v3 database that the data is stored in. Required.

These settings are the same on both historians.

Setting Default Purpose InfluxDB Token None The security token of the InfluxDB user that Profinity connects as. Required, and stored encrypted. Influx Server URL http://localhost:8086/ The endpoint URL that InfluxDB is running on. Dashboard URL Blank The URL of the InfluxDB dashboard. Optional, and leaving it blank shows no dashboard link. InfluxDB Health Check On Checks the health of the InfluxDB server when the component connects and again about every 30 seconds while it runs. Turn it off for InfluxDB Cloud. Collections None The tag collections whose tags are recorded. At least one collection must be configured before the component starts. Update Interval (Seconds) 10 The interval, in seconds, at which data is sent. From 1 to 86400. Logging mode Snapshot Sets what is sent on each interval: Snapshot, On Change or Everything. Refer to Logging modes. Auto Connect On Starts the historian when the profile is loaded. When off, start it with Start Logger. Allow Retrieval On Allows data to be retrieved through this historian using the APIs. Designated tag historian reader Off Makes this historian the store that long-range tag and history queries are read from. Enable it on one component in the profile only, and it takes effect only while Allow Retrieval is on. Refer to Historians.

Every sample is written with its quality in a quality field. A Good sample also has a value field, and a Stale sample keeps its last value with quality Stale. A tag that is Unavailable or Bad is written as a gap, with a quality field and no value, so a chart can show the gap instead of an invented reading. Only tags that hold a number are written, and a query for readings should ask for the value field.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
Each sample is stored as one point in a measurement named after the profile. For example, a motor speed signal on a component called Inverter is stored like this:

Part Example Meaning Tag component Inverter The component that owns the tag. Tag message Status The CAN message the signal belongs to. Tag signal Speed The signal name. Tag full_tag_id Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed The tag's path when the sample was written. Field value 23.4 The reading. Field quality Good The quality of the reading.

In InfluxDB line protocol, that point is:

MyProfile,profile=MyProfile,component=Inverter,message=Status,signal=Speed,full_tag_id=Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed value=23.4,quality="Good" 1792315200000000000

The component, message and signal tags identify the tag in the history. A CAN signal is stored under its component, message and signal names from its DBC file, and a component property is stored with the message _Property_ and its dotted name as the signal, for example Settings_Name. Any other tag is stored with the message _TagPath_, and its place inside its component, joined with underscores, as the signal. Characters other than letters and digits in these names are replaced with underscores.

InfluxDB Cloud does not support the InfluxDB Health Check API, so turn off InfluxDB Health Check when InfluxDB Cloud stores your data. For the full procedure, refer to How to Log Data to the Cloud (InfluxDB).

docs.title: If data does not arrive
docs.text:
The Profinity system logs name the cause, and Logs describes where to read them. When the component cannot connect, it logs one error for the outage, in the form <component name>: could not connect (<reason>). Retrying every 5 s. The reason tells you what to check:

Reason in the log Meaning credential validation failed (likely an invalid token) The token is wrong or lacks access. the health check failed (InfluxDB Cloud has none; switch Health Check off in the settings) The server did not answer the health endpoint. Turn InfluxDB Health Check off for InfluxDB Cloud. Any other text The connection failed for another reason, and the text is the underlying error. Check the Influx Server URL first.

For the steps to set up data logging, refer to How to Configure Data Logging. InfluxDB v1 servers use the InfluxDB v1 Logger, which is described in InfluxDB v1 Logger.

docs.title: TAG SQL Historian
docs.text:
The TAG SQL Historian writes the values of the tags in the collections you select to a table in a SQL database, and allows that history to be read back out through the APIs. It sits in the Historians category. Use it when the history needs to live in a database that you already operate and query with ordinary SQL tools, rather than in a time-series database such as InfluxDB. Each row the historian writes belongs to one tag, identified by its tag tree path.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Profinity["Profinity"]
        Tags --> Collections["Tag collections"] --> Historian["TAG SQL Historian"]
    end
    subgraph Server["SQL database"]
        Table
    end
    Historian --> Table
The TAG SQL Historian writes the tags in the selected collections to a table in the SQL database, and the APIs read the history back

Licence required

The TAG SQL Historian requires the Historians licensed feature. Refer to Licensing for the editions that include it.

docs.title: Adding the historian
docs.text:
To start recording, add the component and point it at a database:

  1. Add a TAG SQL Historian to your profile from the Historians category.
  2. Choose the Database Provider and enter its Connection String.
  3. Under Collections, add at least one tag collection. The component does not start until one is configured.
  4. Save the settings. With Auto Create Table on, the historian creates the table when it starts.

The following tables describe every setting.

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Database Provider The SQL engine to connect to: SQLite, SQL Server / Azure SQL, PostgreSQL, MySQL or Oracle. Defaults to SQLite. Connection String The connection string for the chosen database provider, in that provider's own format. Required, and stored encrypted at rest. Table Name The table the historian writes rows to, which may contain letters, digits, and underscores only and cannot start with a digit. Defaults to TagChangeLog. Auto Create Table Creates the table when the historian starts, if it does not already exist. Enabled by default.

docs.title: Logger settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Collections The tag collections whose tags are recorded. Logging mode Chooses between Snapshot, On Change and Everything. Defaults to Snapshot. Refer to Logging modes for what each mode writes. Auto Connect On by default. Starts the historian when the profile is loaded. When off, start it with Start Logger. Update Interval (Seconds) The interval that controls snapshot timing, or how often changes and samples are flushed to the database. Defaults to 10, and accepts 1 to 86400. Designated tag historian reader Makes this historian the store that long-range tag and history queries are read from. Enable it on one component in the profile only. Refer to Historians.

docs.title: Table layout
docs.text:
Every sample is written with its quality. A Stale sample keeps its last value, and a tag that is Unavailable or Bad is written with its quality and an empty value, so the table shows the gap.

When Auto Create Table is enabled the historian creates a table with the following columns, and the names are the same on every provider.

Column Contents Id An automatically generated row identifier. RecvTime The time the value was received. TagId The path of the tag. ValueType The data type of the value. Value The recorded value. UtcTimestamp The UTC timestamp of the sample. Quality The data quality of the sample: Good, Stale, Unavailable, or Bad. Reason Why the sample was recorded. Message An optional message.

For example, a motor speed tag is stored as this row:

Column Example Id 1 RecvTime 2026-10-18T09:15:02.1234567+10:00 TagId Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed ValueType Double Value 23.4 UtcTimestamp 2026-10-18T09:15:02.0000000Z Quality Good Reason ok Message empty

A row for a tag that is Unavailable or Bad has the same layout with an empty ValueType and Value, and its Quality says why there is no reading.

The columns follow the same field set as the tag change file logger described in Tag file and SFTP loggers, so history written by either can be interpreted in the same way. If you create the table yourself, disable Auto Create Table and make sure the account in the connection string can insert into and read from it.

docs.title: Example connection strings
docs.text:
The connection string uses the format of the chosen provider. The examples use placeholder names and passwords.

Provider Example SQLite Data Source=/var/lib/prohelion/profinity/history.db. SQLite creates the file at the path you give, so use a full path to a folder the Profinity service can write to. SQL Server / Azure SQL Server=dbhost,1433;Database=Profinity;User Id=profinity;Password=<password>;Encrypt=True PostgreSQL Host=dbhost;Port=5432;Database=profinity;Username=profinity;Password=<password> MySQL Server=dbhost;Port=3306;Database=profinity;User ID=profinity;Password=<password> Oracle User Id=profinity;Password=<password>;Data Source=dbhost:1521/ORCLPDB1

The account in the connection string needs permission to insert into and select from the table. With Auto Create Table on, it also needs permission to create the table, and you can remove that permission after the first start.

docs.title: If the historian does not start
docs.text:
Settings cannot be saved without a connection string (You must provide a connection string for the database.) or with an invalid table name (Table name must use letters, digits, and underscore only, and cannot start with a digit.).

If the settings save but no rows arrive, the Profinity system logs (refer to Logs) show one of two messages:

  • The component name followed by could not connect and the reason, for a connection that failed. The historian shows Error and retries every 5 seconds until the database is reachable.
  • Failed to write to the followed by the component name, for a failed write.

Check the connection string, that the database is reachable from the Profinity server and that the account can write to the table.

Moving a component starts a new history in this historian

This historian records history under the tag's path, so moving a component changes its tag paths and the history recorded under the old paths is not carried across. Queries for the new path return a new series with no earlier points. The InfluxDB historians and loggers and the Prometheus logger identify a tag by its component, message, and signal instead, so their history carries on after a move. Refer to Change the path on a deployed component.

For the steps to set up data logging, refer to How to Configure Data Logging.

docs.title: Industrial protocols
docs.text:
Profinity connects to the industrial systems a site already runs through a set of protocol plugins. Each plugin brings data in as ordinary Profinity tags, and the OPC UA plugin can also expose Profinity's tag tree to third-party clients.

The plugins are not included in the standard Profinity installation. Prohelion supplies them on request, so contact Prohelion to arrange access to the protocols you need. Install each one like any other DLL plugin, and then add its components from the Industrial Protocols group, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile.

Protocol plugins and Profinity tags

Licence required

The protocol plugins also require the Industrial Protocols licensed component group, an add-on to your Desktop, Server, or Enterprise edition. Installing a plugin does not make its components available without it. Refer to Licensing to check your instance, where the group is listed as Industrial Protocols under Licensed component groups.

docs.title: Available protocol plugins
docs.text:
Each plugin has its own page describing its settings and point map, and each page lists every supported device family. The OPC UA plugin has one page for each component, and OPC UA certificates covers the certificate folders that both components use.

Plugin Role Typical use BACnet BACnet/IP client that polls values into Profinity tags Building automation and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems EtherNet/IP Common Industrial Protocol (CIP) tag client that polls values into Profinity tags Rockwell programmable logic controllers (PLCs) such as ControlLogix, CompactLogix, Micro800, PLC-5 and SLC Modbus TCP and RTU master that polls values into Profinity tags Industrial devices and distributed input/output (I/O) OPC UA Client Client that polls values from a remote OPC UA server into Profinity tags Enterprise and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system integration OPC UA Server Read-only server that exposes Profinity's tag tree to third-party OPC UA clients Enterprise and SCADA system integration S7 S7comm client that polls values into Profinity tags Siemens PLCs such as S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500

Every protocol component has Auto Connect off by default. The components, what they connect to, and how a point map row identifies a value are:

Plugin Component Connects to A point map row identifies a value by BACnet BACnet Device One BACnet device, over BACnet/IP only and not BACnet MS/TP Object type and Instance EtherNet/IP EtherNet/IP PLC One PLC PLC tag Modbus Modbus Device One Modbus slave, over TCP or over a serial line using RTU framing Table and Address OPC UA OPC UA Client A remote OPC UA server NodeId OPC UA OPC UA Server Listens for OPC UA clients Not applicable, because it exposes the readable scalar tags in the profile's tag tree S7 S7 PLC One PLC Area and Offset, and DB number when the area is DataBlock

For a Siemens S7-1200 or S7-1500, the S7 plugin reads absolute addresses, and the OPC UA client reads symbolic tags by name from the PLC's own OPC UA server.

Once polled, a value from any of these protocols behaves the same as a tag from a CAN device. It can be shown on a dashboard that you build, included in a collection, watched by a rule, or read by a script. The dashboard each component shows for itself is described on its own page, and viewing it needs the Security administration permission, which is set under Roles and Permissions. The polling components of all five plugins connect, retry, and log failures in the way described in Connections and reconnecting.

To build your own component instead, refer to Custom Components for how a compiled plugin compares with a Custom Component pack, and to Component Pack CLI.

docs.title: BACnet
docs.text:
The BACnet Device component is a Building Automation and Control Networks (BACnet) over IP client. It connects to one BACnet device on your network and polls the present-value of the objects you list in its point map, publishing each one as a Profinity tag. BACnet is used for building automation and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems.

flowchart LR
    Device["BACnet device"]
    subgraph Profinity
        Component["BACnet Device"] --> Tags
    end
    Device --> Component
The BACnet Device component in Profinity polls the objects in its point map from one BACnet device and publishes each as a Profinity tag

Licence required

The BACnet plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add a BACnet Device to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. Add one component for each BACnet device you want to read. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

The component supports BACnet/IP only, not BACnet MS/TP (Master-Slave/Token-Passing). It reads and writes the device at the Remote host address you configure, and it does not discover devices on the network with Who-Is.

docs.title: Communications settings
docs.text: Setting Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Local UDP port The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) port Profinity uses locally. Between 1 and 65535. The default is 47808, the standard BACnet/IP port (0xBAC0 in hexadecimal). Remote host The IP address of the BACnet device. Required, and it is the address Profinity sends every request to. The default is 127.0.0.1. Device instance The BACnet device instance number of the device, which is the instance in the device's own Device object. Between 0 and 4194302. The default is 0. Profinity still sends every request to the Remote host, but it reads the Device object of the device at that address each time it connects and compares the two numbers, and it does not connect while they differ, so that a changed address never leads to another device being read. Set this to the instance of the device you are connecting to, which a BACnet configuration tool or the device's own display shows, even when that instance is 0. Poll interval (ms) How often the point map is read, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 600000. The default is 1000. Request timeout (ms) How long Profinity waits for the device to answer a request, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 60000. The default is 1000. Reconnect delay (ms) How long Profinity waits between connection attempts, in milliseconds. Profinity keeps trying when the device is down at start and after a connection is lost, as described in Connections and reconnecting. Between 0 and 600000. The default is 2000. Auto Connect Connects to the device automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default.

docs.title: Point map
docs.text:
The point map lists the BACnet objects to read. Each row becomes one tag.

Column Description Name The name of the tag, published under the component's Points tags. Use a unique name for each row. Object type The type of BACnet object: AnalogInput, AnalogOutput, AnalogValue (the default), BinaryInput, BinaryOutput or BinaryValue. Instance The BACnet object instance number. Writable Allows Profinity to write to the object's present-value from the tag. Off by default. Unit An optional unit label for the tag.

Analog objects are published as number tags, and binary objects are published as boolean tags. Profinity reads and writes the object's present-value property, and it polls each object on the Poll interval (ms) rather than subscribing to changes.

Writing to a device

A write can change how the building plant behaves, so turn Writable on only for points that must be controlled from Profinity.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The component dashboard shows the connection STATUS, whether the device is CONNECTED, and the number of values read (RECEIVED) and values written (SENT). Use the Connect / Disconnect menu action to start or stop polling manually. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

Polled values behave like any other tag, so they can be shown on a dashboard, logged, watched by a rule, or read by a script.

docs.title: If a point shows bad quality
docs.text:
If a point cannot be read, its tag is marked as bad quality. The usual causes are a wrong Remote host, an Object type or Instance that the device does not have, and a device that does not answer within the Request timeout (ms). Check these before reading the Log. The Log records the first failed read of an outage as a warning, repeat failures in the same outage at debug level, and the first success afterwards at information level, as described in Connections and reconnecting. The first success is the first poll in which every point reads correctly.

A Device instance that differs from the device at the Remote host puts the component in the Error status, marks every point as bad quality, and shows and logs a message of the form The device at 192.168.1.20 reports Device instance 1234, but Device instance is set to 0. Profinity tries again every Reconnect delay, so correcting the setting or the device connects it without a restart. Set Device instance to the number in the message, or correct the Remote host if the address now belongs to a different device.

Profinity reads the identity with the standard "wildcard" read of the Device object (instance 4194303), which BACnet requires every device to answer from protocol revision 4 (2004) onwards. A device older than that, or one that does not allow its Device object to be read, answers with a BACnet error, and the component shows that error as the reason. A device that does not answer the identity read, or that does not allow its Device object to be read, puts the component in Error in the same way, with a message that the device did not answer, and Profinity tries again every Reconnect delay. A device that is replaced on the same address after it was connected is caught at the next failed read, and the component then shows Error until the instance matches.

docs.title: EtherNet/IP
docs.text:
The EtherNet/IP PLC component is a Common Industrial Protocol (CIP) tag client for Allen-Bradley (Rockwell) programmable logic controllers (PLCs). It connects to one PLC and polls the PLC tags you list in its point map, publishing each one as a Profinity tag. It supports ControlLogix, CompactLogix, Micro800, PLC-5 and SLC controllers.

flowchart LR
    PLC["Allen-Bradley PLC"]
    subgraph Profinity
        Component["EtherNet/IP PLC"] --> Tags
    end
    PLC --> Component
The EtherNet/IP PLC component in Profinity polls the PLC tags in its point map from one PLC and publishes each as a Profinity tag

Licence required

The EtherNet/IP plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add an EtherNet/IP PLC to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. Add one component for each PLC you want to read. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

You list each PLC tag by name in the point map. The component does not browse the PLC's CIP objects to discover tags for you.

docs.title: Communications settings
docs.text: Setting Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Gateway The IP address of the PLC, or of the gateway module that the PLC sits behind. Required. The default is 127.0.0.1. CIP path The route to the PLC's CPU (central processing unit), as comma-separated values passed to the PLC library as entered. The default is 1,0, which is the backplane (1) and slot 0; for a CPU in slot 2 of the same chassis, enter 1,2. Leave it empty to send no path. For a CPU reached through a bridge module, enter the route as pairs of port and address, one pair for each hop, as the PLC library expects. A PLC-5, SLC or MicroLogix controller on EtherNet/IP needs no path: the PLC library ignores a path for these controllers unless it is a route through a DH+ bridge, so the default 1,0 does no harm, and you can clear it. Micro800 controllers ignore this setting even when it is filled in. PLC kind The family of PLC: ControlLogix (the default), CompactLogix, Micro800, PLC-5 or SLC. Poll interval (ms) How often the point map is read, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 600000. The default is 1000. Request timeout (ms) How long Profinity waits for the PLC to answer a request, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 60000. The default is 1000. Reconnect delay (ms) How long Profinity waits between connection attempts, in milliseconds. Profinity keeps trying when the device is down at start and after a connection is lost, as described in Connections and reconnecting. Between 0 and 600000. The default is 2000. Auto Connect Connects to the PLC automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default.

docs.title: Point map
docs.text:
The point map lists the PLC tags to read. Each row becomes one tag.

Column Description Name The name of the tag, published under the component's Points tags. Use a unique name for each row. PLC tag The tag name in the PLC. For ControlLogix, CompactLogix and Micro800 this is the Logix tag name. For PLC-5 and SLC it is the file and element, for example N7:0. Data type How the value is read: Boolean, Word, SignedWord, Dword (the default), SignedDword or Real. Writable Allows Profinity to write the PLC tag from the Profinity tag. Off by default. Unit An optional unit label for the tag.

The data types map to the element size in the PLC, and to the type of the Profinity tag.

Data type Size Profinity tag Boolean 1 byte Boolean Word / SignedWord 2 bytes (unsigned / signed) Integer Dword / SignedDword 4 bytes (unsigned / signed) Integer Real 4 bytes (floating point) Number

Choose a data type that matches the PLC tag's type, otherwise the value is misread. Each row reads one element of the size given for its data type.

Writing to a PLC

A write can change the controlled process, so turn Writable on only for tags that must be set from Profinity.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The component dashboard shows the connection STATUS, whether the PLC is CONNECTED, and the number of values read (RECEIVED) and values written (SENT). Use the Connect / Disconnect menu action to start or stop polling manually. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

Polled values behave like any other tag, so they can be shown on a dashboard, logged, watched by a rule, or read by a script.

docs.title: If a point shows bad quality
docs.text: If a point cannot be read, its tag is marked as bad quality. The usual causes are a PLC tag name that does not exist in the PLC, a Data type that does not match the PLC tag's type, a CIP path that does not lead to the CPU, and a PLC kind that does not match the controller. Check these before reading the Log for the reason. The Log records the first failed read of an outage as a warning, repeat failures in the same outage at debug level, and the first success afterwards at information level, as described in Connections and reconnecting. The first success is the first poll in which every point reads correctly.

docs.title: Modbus
docs.text:
The Modbus Device component is a Modbus master. It connects to one Modbus slave over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) or over a serial line using Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) framing, and polls the coils and registers you list in its point map, publishing each one as a Profinity tag. Modbus is used for industrial devices and distributed input/output (I/O). Profinity acts as a Modbus master only, and it does not act as a Modbus slave or server.

flowchart LR
    Slave["Modbus slave"]
    subgraph Profinity
        Component["Modbus Device"] --> Tags
    end
    Slave --> Component
The Modbus Device component in Profinity polls the coils and registers in its point map from one Modbus slave and publishes each as a Profinity tag

Licence required

The Modbus plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add a Modbus Device to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. Add one component for each slave you want to read. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

docs.title: Communications settings
docs.text:
Which settings apply depends on the Connection Mode.

Setting Applies to Description Name Both The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Connection Mode Both TCP (the default) or RTU. Host TCP The IP address of the slave. Required. The default is 127.0.0.1. Port TCP The TCP port. Between 1 and 65535. The default is 502. Serial Port RTU The serial port the slave is connected to. Required for RTU. Baud Rate RTU The serial baud rate. The default is 9600. Parity RTU The serial parity. The default is None. Data Bits RTU 7 or 8. The default is 8. Stop Bits RTU The number of stop bits. The default is One. Unit ID Both The Modbus unit (slave) address. Between 0 and 255. The default is 1. Poll interval (ms) Both How often the point map is read, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 600000. The default is 1000. Request timeout (ms) Both How long Profinity waits for the slave to answer a request, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 60000. The default is 1000. Reconnect delay (ms) Both How long Profinity waits between connection attempts, in milliseconds. Profinity keeps trying when the device is down at start and after a connection is lost, as described in Connections and reconnecting. Between 0 and 600000. The default is 2000. Auto Connect Both Connects automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default.

Match the serial settings to those configured on the slave. If they differ, the slave does not answer.

docs.title: Point map
docs.text:
The point map lists the coils and registers to read. Each row becomes one tag.

Column Description Name The name of the tag, published under the component's Points tags. Use a unique name for each row. Table The Modbus table to read: Coil, DiscreteInput, HoldingRegister (the default) or InputRegister. Address The zero-based protocol address. Register 40001 in a manufacturer's manual is address 0 of the holding registers when the manual uses one-based numbering. Data type How the value is decoded: Boolean, Word (the default), SignedWord, Dword, SignedDword or Real. Scale A factor that reads are multiplied by. Writes are divided by the same factor. The default is 1. Writable Allows Profinity to write the value from the tag. Off by default. Unit An optional unit label for the tag.

Registers are read as big-endian values. Word and SignedWord use one register, and Dword, SignedDword and Real use two consecutive registers starting at the address, with the first register holding the high word. The component has no word-swap option, so a device that sends the low word first returns wrong 32-bit values. Real is a 32-bit floating point value.

The Scale suits devices that report fixed-point values: a temperature held as tenths of a degree uses a scale of 0.1.

A Coil or DiscreteInput row always reads a single on/off bit, and its Data type is not used. A Boolean row on a HoldingRegister or InputRegister table reads one register and is true when the register is not zero.

Only the HoldingRegister and Coil tables can be written. DiscreteInput and InputRegister points are always read-only, even if Writable is on.

Writing to a device

Leave Writable off for any point that Profinity should only monitor, because a write changes the device.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The component dashboard shows the connection STATUS (Connected or Disconnected), whether the device is CONNECTED, and the number of values read (RECEIVED) and values written (SENT). Use the Connect / Disconnect menu action to start or stop polling manually. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

Polled values behave like any other tag, so they can be shown on a dashboard, logged, watched by a rule, or read by a script.

docs.title: If a point shows bad quality
docs.text: If a point cannot be read, its tag is marked as bad quality. The usual causes are an address that is one higher or lower than the device manual states, a Unit ID that differs from the slave, serial settings that differ from the slave, and a Data type that does not match the register. Check these before reading the Log for the reason. The Log records the first failed read of an outage as a warning, repeat failures in the same outage at debug level, and the first success afterwards at information level, as described in Connections and reconnecting. The first success is the first poll in which every point reads correctly.

docs.title: OPC UA certificates
docs.text:
The OPC UA Client and the OPC UA Server keep their application certificates in the opcua_pki folder inside the Profinity data folder of the account that runs Profinity, in the own, trusted, issuer and rejected sub-folders. On Windows the folder is %LocalAppData%\Prohelion\Profinity\opcua_pki, on macOS it is ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity/opcua_pki, and on Linux it is ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity/opcua_pki. The folder follows the home folder of the account that runs Profinity, not the PROFINITY_HOME setting or the /var/lib/prohelion/profinity data folder, so in Docker it sits inside the container rather than in the data volume, and the certificates are created again if the container is recreated. For a Windows service that runs as LocalSystem, the folder is under C:\Windows\SysWOW64\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Prohelion\Profinity on 64-bit Windows.

To trust a certificate explicitly, rather than trusting all, place it in trusted. Certificates that are refused are placed in rejected, so a connection that fails on a certificate leaves the refused certificate there to move into trusted once you have confirmed it.

The Trust all server certificates setting of the OPC UA Client and the Trust all client certificates setting of the OPC UA Server skip certificate validation instead, and are described on the OPC UA Client and OPC UA Server pages.

docs.title: OPC UA Client
docs.text:
The OPC UA Client connects to a remote Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) server and polls the nodes you list into Profinity tags. Use it to bring values from a programmable logic controller (PLC), a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system or another OPC UA server into Profinity. Add one client for each server you want to read. The OPC UA plugin also provides the OPC UA Server, and the two components can be used on their own or together.

For a Siemens S7-1200 or S7-1500, the OPC UA Client against the PLC's built-in OPC UA server lets you read symbolic tags by name, which the S7 component cannot do.

flowchart LR
    Source["Remote OPC UA server"] --> Client["OPC UA Client"] --> Tags
The OPC UA Client polls nodes from a remote OPC UA server into Profinity tags

Licence required

The OPC UA plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add the client to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Endpoint URL The address of the server. Required, and must start with opc.tcp://. The default is opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840. Use security When off (the default), the client connects without message security. Turn it on to connect to an endpoint that uses security (message signing or encryption) when the server offers one. Username An optional user name. Leave it empty to connect anonymously. Password The password for the user name. It is stored encrypted. Trust all server certificates Skips validation of the server's certificate. Off by default. Turn it on only when connecting to a trusted endpoint that uses a self-signed certificate. Poll interval (ms) How often the node map is read, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 600000. The default is 1000. Request timeout (ms) How long Profinity waits for the server to answer a request, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 60000. The default is 5000. Reconnect delay (ms) How long Profinity waits between connection attempts, in milliseconds. Profinity keeps trying when the device is down at start and after a connection is lost, as described in Connections and reconnecting. Between 0 and 600000. The default is 2000. Auto Connect Connects to the server automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default.

Trusting certificates

Trust all server certificates removes the check that proves you are talking to the server you intended. Use it only on a trusted network, and where you can, place the server's certificate in the trusted folder instead, as described in OPC UA certificates.

docs.title: Point map
docs.text:
The point map lists the OPC UA nodes to read. Each row becomes one tag.

Column Description Name The name of the tag, published under the component's Points tags. Use a unique name for each row. NodeId The OPC UA NodeId of the node, for example ns=2;s=Temp. Writable Allows Profinity to write the node from the tag. Off by default, so every node is read-only unless you turn this on. Unit An optional unit label for the tag.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The component has a dashboard showing its STATUS, the number of values read (RECEIVED) and values written (SENT), and whether it is CONNECTED to the server. The client has a Connect / Disconnect menu action. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

Values polled by the client behave like any other tag, so they can be shown on a dashboard, logged, watched by a rule, or read by a script.

To check that the client works, look for the status Connected, CONNECTED true, and tags under the component's Points tags with Good quality and a changing value.

docs.title: If a point shows bad quality
docs.text: Each point's tag is created as soon as its row exists and shows Unavailable quality until the first poll reads it. After that a successful read gives Good quality, and a node that cannot be read is marked as Bad quality. The usual causes are a NodeId that the server does not have, an Endpoint URL that does not start with opc.tcp:// or cannot be reached, and a server certificate in the rejected folder, so check these before reading the Log for the reason. The Log records the first failed read of an outage as a warning, repeat failures in the same outage at debug level, and the first success afterwards at information level, as described in Connections and reconnecting. The first success is the first poll in which every point reads correctly. To move a refused certificate into trusted, refer to OPC UA certificates.

docs.title: OPC UA Server
docs.text:
The OPC UA Server listens for Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) clients and exposes this profile's tag tree to them as a read-only address space.
