Use it to let third-party OPC UA clients, such as a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) or historian system, read the live values held in this Profinity profile. The OPC UA plugin also provides the OPC UA Client, and the two components can be used on their own or together.

flowchart LR
    Tags --> Server["OPC UA Server"] --> Consumer["Third-party OPC UA client"]
The OPC UA Server exposes the Profinity tag tree to third-party OPC UA clients as a read-only address space

The server exposes the readable scalar tags in the profile's tag tree.

Licence required

The OPC UA plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add the server to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Bind URL The endpoint address that the server listens on, and the address clients connect to. Required, and must start with opc.tcp://. The default is opc.tcp://127.0.0.1:4840/Profinity, which accepts clients on this computer only. Auto Connect Starts the server automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default. Trust all client certificates Skips validation of connecting clients' certificates. Off by default. Turn it on only on a trusted network.

For where the server keeps its certificates and how to trust one explicitly, refer to OPC UA certificates.

docs.title: What the server exposes
docs.text: The server publishes the readable scalar values in the profile's tag tree. Each tag appears as a node with the NodeId ns=2;s= followed by the tag's full tag ID, which is the tag's tag tree path. Clients cannot write to the address space, so the server cannot be used to change values in Profinity. The server accepts anonymous connections without message security only. The address space is built once when the server starts, from the tags that are readable at that moment, so tags added to the profile after the server starts do not appear until the server is restarted. A tag with no sample or a null value reads as BadNoData to the client.

docs.title: Listening address
docs.text:
With the default Bind URL, the server listens on the loopback address 127.0.0.1 only, so only clients on the Profinity computer can connect. The server uses no security policy and accepts anonymous clients, so allow other computers only on a network you trust. To accept remote clients, replace the host in the Bind URL with the IP address or host name of the Profinity computer that those clients can reach, for example opc.tcp://192.168.1.20:4840/Profinity. An IP address listens on that address only, and a host name listens on every address of the computer. When the address changes, Profinity replaces the server certificate if it does not name the new address.

A Bind URL with a host of 0.0.0.0 or localhost is treated in the same way as the default and listens on 127.0.0.1 only.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The component has a dashboard showing its STATUS, whether it is LISTENING, and the number of client requests RECEIVED and responses SENT since the server last started listening. To check that the server works, look for the status Listening and LISTENING true, then connect a client to the Bind URL, browse Objects > Profinity (the Profinity folder, NodeId ns=2;s=Profinity), and read a tag at ns=2;s= followed by its full tag ID. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

docs.title: S7
docs.text:
The S7 PLC component is an S7comm (Siemens S7 communication) client for Siemens programmable logic controllers (PLCs). It connects to one PLC and polls the addresses you list in its point map, publishing each one as a Profinity tag. It supports S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 and S7-1500 controllers.

flowchart LR
    PLC["Siemens PLC"]
    subgraph Profinity
        Component["S7 PLC"] --> Tags
    end
    PLC --> Component
The S7 PLC component in Profinity polls the addresses in its point map from one Siemens PLC and publishes each as a Profinity tag

Licence required

The S7 plugin is not part of the standard installation, and it requires the Industrial Protocols licensed component group. Refer to Industrial Protocols for how to obtain, install, and licence it.

Add an S7 PLC to your Profile from the Industrial Protocols group in the component catalogue, as described in Adding Components to Your Profile. Add one component for each PLC you want to read. The settings below can be changed later from the component's Change Settings menu action.

You specify the memory area and byte offset of each value, and symbolic tag names are not supported. For symbolic access to an S7-1200 or S7-1500, use the OPC UA Client against the PLC's OPC UA server.

Prepare the PLC

S7-1200 and S7-1500 PLCs must have Put/Get access enabled before they answer, and data blocks must not use optimised block access, because optimised blocks cannot be read by absolute address. Both are changed in the PLC's project, in the Siemens engineering software (TIA Portal), by whoever maintains the PLC program.

docs.title: Communications settings
docs.text:
Setting Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique within the profile. Host The IP address of the PLC. Required. The default is 127.0.0.1. Port The TCP port. Between 1 and 65535. The default is 102. Rack The rack number of the PLC. Between 0 and 7. The default is 0. Slot The slot number of the CPU (central processing unit). Between 0 and 31. The default is 1. CPU type The PLC family: S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200 (the default) or S7-1500. Poll interval (ms) How often the point map is read, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 600000. The default is 1000. Request timeout (ms) How long Profinity waits for the PLC to answer a request, in milliseconds. Between 50 and 60000. The default is 1000. Reconnect delay (ms) How long Profinity waits between connection attempts, in milliseconds. Profinity keeps trying when the device is down at start and after a connection is lost, as described in Connections and reconnecting. Between 0 and 600000. The default is 2000. Auto Connect Connects to the PLC automatically when the profile is loaded. Off by default.

The usual rack and slot is 0 and 1 for S7-1200 and S7-1500 controllers, and 0 and 2 for most S7-300 controllers. Confirm the values in the PLC's hardware configuration.

docs.title: Point map
docs.text:
The point map lists the PLC addresses to read. Each row becomes one tag.

Column Description Name The name of the tag, published under the component's Points tags. Use a unique name for each row. Area The memory area: DataBlock (the default), Memory (M), Input (I) or Output (Q). DB number The data block number. Used only when the area is DataBlock, and ignored otherwise. The default is 1. Offset The byte offset within the selected area. Data type How the value is read: Boolean, Word (the default), SignedWord, Dword, SignedDword or Real. Writable Allows Profinity to write the PLC value from the tag. Off by default. Unit An optional unit label for the tag.

The data types map to the width of the value in the PLC, and to the type of the Profinity tag.

Data type Size Profinity tag Boolean 1 bit (bit 0 of the byte) Boolean Word / SignedWord 2 bytes (unsigned / signed) Integer Dword / SignedDword 4 bytes (unsigned / signed) Integer Real 4 bytes (floating point) Number

A Boolean point always reads bit 0 of the byte at its offset, because the point map has no bit number, so the PLC program must place the value you need in bit 0 of a byte. A Boolean point at data block 1, offset 10 reads the address DB1.DBX10.0. Other types are read as, for example, DB1.DBW10 (word) or DB1.DBD10 (double word or real). For the Memory, Input and Output areas, a word at offset 10 is MW10, IW10 and QW10. Siemens tools set to German show the input and output areas as E and A rather than I and Q.

Writing to a PLC

A write can change the controlled process, so turn Writable on only for values that must be set from Profinity.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The component dashboard shows the connection STATUS, whether the PLC is CONNECTED, and the number of values read (RECEIVED) and values written (SENT). Use the Connect / Disconnect menu action to start or stop polling manually. Viewing the dashboard requires the Security administration permission, described under Roles and Permissions.

Polled values behave like any other tag, so they can be shown on a dashboard, logged, watched by a rule, or read by a script.

docs.title: If a point shows bad quality
docs.text: If a point cannot be read, its tag is marked as bad quality. The usual causes are Put/Get access disabled on the PLC, a data block that uses optimised block access, a wrong Rack or Slot, and a DB number or Offset that the PLC does not have. Check these before reading the Log for the reason. The Log records the first failed read of an outage as a warning, repeat failures in the same outage at debug level, and the first success afterwards at information level, as described in Connections and reconnecting. The first success is the first poll in which every point reads correctly.

docs.title: Loggers
docs.text:
A logger writes data out of Profinity for later retrieval, whereas a publisher pushes data to a receiver that is listening now. InfluxDB v2 and v3 are historians, not loggers, because Profinity can read their data back. The table compares the six loggers, and each component name links to its page. Rotation, archive, and SFTP settings that the file loggers share are on File logger rotation, archive, and SFTP settings.

Component Direction Where the data goes Selects data by Auto Connect default Licence CAN File Logger Out The local file system of the machine running Profinity, as native CAN bus messages The CAN bus, not tag collections On Included in every edition CAN SFTP Logger Out A remote SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) server, as native CAN bus messages The CAN bus, not tag collections On Included in every edition TAG File Logger Out The local file system of the machine running Profinity, as comma-separated values (CSV) or JSON Lines Tag collections On Included in every edition TAG SFTP Logger Out A remote SFTP server, as CSV or JSON Lines Tag collections On Included in every edition InfluxDB v1 Logger Out An InfluxDB v1 server, which Profinity sends the data to Tag collections On Included in every edition Prometheus Logger Out Served by Profinity, which Prometheus calls to request the latest values Tag collections On Included in every edition

To push data to a broker or a web service, refer to the Publishers and subscribers components.

docs.title: CAN file and SFTP loggers
docs.text:
The CAN File Logger and the CAN SFTP Logger record native CAN bus messages to a file, which the CAN File Logger stores on the local file system of the machine running Profinity and the CAN SFTP Logger transmits to a remote SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) server. Each is added to a Profile as its own component under Loggers and is included in every edition. Profinity can also log and replay messages from a CAN bus network.

flowchart LR
    Source["CAN bus messages"] --> File["CAN File Logger"] --> Files["Local log files"]
    Source --> Sftp["CAN SFTP Logger"] --> Server["SFTP server"]
The CAN File Logger records CAN bus messages to log files on the local file system, and the CAN SFTP Logger transmits them to an SFTP server

Both loggers have Auto Connect, which is on by default, so a logger begins logging when the Profile loads and needs no further action. They record the bus, so they do not use tag collections. Both loggers also have Update Interval (Seconds), which defaults to 10 and accepts values from 1 to 86400, and sets the seconds between background updates. Their File Format setting chooses the layout of the text file, which always uses a .txt extension. Prohelion, the default, writes a line for every packet with a Sent or Received column, and Tritium writes the same fields without that column.

The CAN File Logger has no destination setting. It creates its files under the Profinity CAN bus log directory (can_bus_logs/), in a folder named after the Profile and the component. Refer to the artefacts directory for where that directory sits on each platform. The CAN SFTP Logger needs the remote server settings described in File logger rotation, archive, and SFTP settings, which also covers rotating, archiving, and compressing the log files.

docs.title: Download the logged files
docs.text:
Once a log file has been created, select the link on the Logger Dashboard to download it from Profinity. A CAN File Logger shows this link as FILE LOGS REPOSITORY.

Download Log File

To take the same data further, refer to How to configure data logging.

docs.title: File logger rotation, archive, and SFTP settings
docs.text: The CAN file and SFTP loggers and the Tag file and SFTP loggers share the settings on this page for rotating, archiving, and compressing log files, and for connecting to an SFTP server.

docs.title: SFTP settings
docs.text:
The CAN SFTP Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger send each completed log file to the remote server and need the following settings.

Setting Default Purpose Remote Host None The name or address of the SFTP server. Required. Remote Port 22 The port of the SFTP server, from 1 to 65535. Remote server username None The account used to sign in. Required. Remote server password None The password for that account. Required, and stored encrypted. Remote Directory None The directory the files are uploaded to, relative to the home directory of the user on the server, so it must not start with /. For example, enter home/sftp/upload and not /home/sftp/upload. Required.

If a transfer fails, Profinity writes an error to the Profinity system logs (refer to Logs). The CAN SFTP Logger writes "Failed to transfer archived file via SFTP" and the TAG SFTP Logger writes "Failed to transfer archived TAG log via SFTP", each followed by the file name and the reason. A connection or login failure also logs "Failed to connect to the SFTP server to test the connection" and "Failed to transfer the file to the SFTP server". Check the host, port, credentials, and remote directory.

docs.title: Archive, compression, and rotation
docs.text:
Rotation closes the current log file and starts a new one, and the Rotate By setting selects No Rotation, Time or File Size. Rotate By defaults to No Rotation, so a logger writes one growing file until rotation is switched on.

Setting Purpose Rotate By No Rotation (the default), Time or File Size. Rotation Interval (Sec) Shown when Rotate By is Time. The seconds between rotations. When it is not set, it follows Update Interval (Seconds), or is 600 seconds when neither is set. Rotate MB Shown when Rotate By is File Size. The size in megabytes at which the file rotates, 0 or greater. Archive the Logs Moves rotated log files into an archive folder beneath the log folder, so no archive directory needs to be provided. Compress Logs Shown when Archive the Logs is on. Compresses archived log files into .zip files. Limit Number of Archive Files Shown when Archive the Logs is on. Enables a limit on the number of log files retained in the archive. Archive File Limit Shown when Limit Number of Archive Files is on, and must be greater than 0. Sets the maximum number of log files retained in the archive, and applies to the remote files for the SFTP loggers.

The CAN SFTP Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger always archive, because files are archived before they are uploaded, and they therefore do not show Archive the Logs.

docs.title: InfluxDB v1 Logger
docs.text:
The InfluxDB v1 Logger sends the values of the tags in selected tag collections to an InfluxDB v1 server. A logger only writes data out. The InfluxDB v2 and v3 components are historians, which also let the data be read back, and they are documented in the Historians section.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Profinity["Profinity"]
        Collections["Tag collections"] --> V1["InfluxDB v1 Logger"]
    end
    V1 --> Influx["InfluxDB v1 server"]
The InfluxDB v1 Logger pushes the selected tag collections to an InfluxDB v1 server

InfluxDB dashboard showing pack voltage and pack current logged by Profinity

InfluxDB both stores and visualises data. InfluxDB v1, v2 and v3 are separate products with different APIs, authentication methods and configuration requirements, and using the wrong component type results in connection failures. Profinity provides a separate component for each InfluxDB version, so the version of InfluxDB in use must be known before a component is added to a profile. The v2 and v3 components are registered as the InfluxDB v2 Historian and the InfluxDB v3 Historian, which write data in the same way and additionally allow it to be read back through the APIs, and they are documented in InfluxDB historians. The Loggers page compares this logger with the others.

docs.title: Add the logger
docs.text:
InfluxDB v1 uses username and password authentication and the concept of databases and retention policies. To log data to InfluxDB v1, install InfluxDB v1 and confirm that it is running, then add an InfluxDB v1 Logger to the profile. Enter the InfluxDB Database, add at least one tag collection under Collections, and set the other settings as needed.

Setting Default Purpose InfluxDB Database None The InfluxDB database that the data is stored in. Required. InfluxDB Username Blank The username for InfluxDB authentication. Leave blank for unsecured connections. InfluxDB Password Blank The password for InfluxDB authentication. Leave blank for unsecured connections. InfluxDB Retention Policy autogen The InfluxDB retention policy used when writing data. Influx Server URL http://localhost:8086/ The endpoint URL that InfluxDB is running on. Dashboard URL Blank The URL of the InfluxDB dashboard. Optional, and leaving it blank shows no dashboard link. InfluxDB Health Check On Performs a health check on the connection at regular intervals. Turn it off for InfluxDB Cloud. Collections None The tag collections whose tags are logged. At least one collection must be configured before the component starts. Update Interval (Seconds) 10 The interval, in seconds, at which log data is sent, from 1 to 86400. Logging mode Snapshot Sets what is sent on each interval: Snapshot, On Change or Everything. Refer to Logging modes. Auto Connect On Starts the logger when the profile is loaded.

The Logging mode setting applies to this logger, the InfluxDB v2 Historian, the InfluxDB v3 Historian and the other collection-based loggers, and nothing is logged until at least one tag collection is selected in Collections. Logging modes defines the three modes, Snapshot (the default), On Change and Everything.

Every sample is written with its quality in a quality field. A Good sample also has a value field, and a Stale sample keeps its last value with quality Stale. A tag that is Unavailable or Bad is written as a gap, with a quality field and no value, so a chart can show the gap instead of an invented reading. Only tags that hold a number are written, and a query for readings should ask for the value field.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
Each sample is stored as one point in a measurement named after the profile. For example, a motor speed signal on a component called Inverter is stored like this:

Part Example Meaning Tag component Inverter The component that owns the tag. Tag message Status The CAN message the signal belongs to. Tag signal Speed The signal name. Tag full_tag_id Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed The tag's path when the sample was written. Field value 23.4 The reading. Field quality Good The quality of the reading.

In InfluxDB line protocol, that point is:

MyProfile,profile=MyProfile,component=Inverter,message=Status,signal=Speed,full_tag_id=Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed value=23.4,quality="Good" 1792315200000000000

The component, message and signal tags identify the tag in the history. A CAN signal is stored under its component, message and signal names from its DBC file, and a component property is stored with the message _Property_ and its dotted name as the signal, for example Settings_Name. Any other tag is stored with the message _TagPath_, and its place inside its component, joined with underscores, as the signal. Characters other than letters and digits in these names are replaced with underscores.

InfluxDB Cloud does not support the InfluxDB Health Check API, and InfluxDB Health Check is on by default, so set it to off when InfluxDB Cloud is used to store the data.

docs.title: If data does not arrive
docs.text:
When these settings are correct, data flows into InfluxDB v1. If it does not, check the Profinity system logs for more details, as described in Logs. If the logger cannot reach InfluxDB, it shows Error, writes the reason to the system logs once, and retries every 5 seconds until the problem clears.

For the steps to set up logging and to send data to InfluxDB Cloud, refer to How to configure data logging and How to log data to the cloud (InfluxDB).

docs.title: Prometheus Logger
docs.text:
The Prometheus Logger serves the values of the tags in selected tag collections to Prometheus. A logger only writes data out.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Profinity["Profinity"]
        Collections["Tag collections"] --> Prom["Prometheus Logger"]
    end
    Prometheus["Prometheus server"] --> Prom
The Prometheus Logger serves the selected tag collections to a Prometheus server that calls Profinity to request the latest values

Prometheus logging works differently from InfluxDB logging. InfluxDB expects its data to be pushed to it, whereas Prometheus treats Profinity as a source of data and calls it to request the latest values. Prometheus stores data only and has no graphing capability out of the box, so it is usually coupled with a tool such as Grafana for visualisation.

Adding a Prometheus Logger to Profinity is all that is required on the Profinity side to set up Prometheus logging. The Collections setting selects the tag collections that are served, and at least one collection must be selected before the component starts. The following connection values can also be set.

Setting Default Purpose Data endpoint URL metrics/ The URL path, within the hostname and port, that the Prometheus data is served on. Server Hostname localhost The host name or IP address that Profinity's Prometheus endpoint answers to. With localhost, only a scraper on the same computer can read it. To let a scraper on another computer connect, enter the computer's host name or IP address, or + to answer on every address. On Windows, listening on anything other than localhost needs a URL reservation, for example netsh http add urlacl url=http://+:7065/metrics user=DOMAIN\user, or running Profinity with administrator rights. Server Port 7065 The port that the endpoint runs on, from 1 to 65535. Dashboard URL Blank The full URL of the Prometheus dashboard. Optional, and leaving it blank shows no dashboard link. Update Interval (Seconds) 10 The interval, in seconds, between samples, from 1 to 86400. Auto Connect On Starts the logger automatically when the profile is loaded.

A tag that is not Good quality is reported as NaN.

Once the Prometheus Logger is active, Prometheus can call Profinity on this URL to receive data. With all settings left at their defaults, for example, the data is served at:

http://localhost:7065/metrics

Configuring Prometheus to receive and display this data is covered in the Prometheus documentation.

docs.title: What Prometheus receives
docs.text:
Each tag in the selected collections is served as one gauge. The name is the profile, component, message and signal joined with underscores, and the labels identify the tag. For example, a motor speed signal on a component called Inverter is served like this:

# HELP MyProfile_Inverter_Status_Speed Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed
# TYPE MyProfile_Inverter_Status_Speed gauge
MyProfile_Inverter_Status_Speed{profile="MyProfile",component="Inverter",transmitter="",message="Status",signal="Speed",full_tag_id="Inverter_DBC_Status_Speed"} 23.4

The message and signal labels come from the tag itself. A CAN signal uses its message and signal names from its DBC file, a component property uses the message _Property_, and any other tag uses the message _TagPath_ with its place inside its component as the signal. Characters other than letters and digits in names and labels are replaced with underscores, which is why the full_tag_id label shows underscores where the tag's path has slashes. The value is the latest reading, or NaN when the tag is not Good quality.

docs.title: If Prometheus shows no data
docs.text:
If the logger cannot open its Prometheus endpoint (for example the port is in use), it shows Error, writes the reason to the Profinity system logs (refer to Logs) once, and retries every 5 seconds until the problem clears. If Prometheus shows no data, check that the logger is running, that the scraper is configured with the same hostname, port and endpoint path, and that at least one collection with tags is selected.

For the steps to set up logging, refer to How to configure data logging.

docs.title: Tag file and SFTP loggers
docs.text:
The TAG File Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger write the values of the tags in selected tag collections to a file as comma-separated values (CSV) or JSON Lines. The TAG File Logger writes the file to the local file system of the machine running Profinity, and the TAG SFTP Logger transmits it to a remote SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) server. Each is added to a Profile as its own component under Loggers and is included in every edition. A logger only writes data out for later retrieval, so history that Profinity must read back belongs in a historian.

flowchart LR
    Source["Tag collections"] --> File["TAG File Logger"] --> Files["Local log files"]
    Source --> Sftp["TAG SFTP Logger"] --> Server["SFTP server"]
The TAG File Logger writes the values in tag collections to log files on the local file system, and the TAG SFTP Logger transmits them to an SFTP server

Both loggers have Auto Connect, which is on by default, so a logger begins logging when the Profile loads and needs no further action. The TAG File Logger has no destination setting. It creates its files under the Profinity tag log directory (tag_logs/), in a folder named after the Profile and the component. Refer to the artefacts directory for where that directory sits on each platform. The TAG SFTP Logger needs the remote server settings described in File logger rotation, archive, and SFTP settings, which also covers rotating, archiving, and compressing the log files.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Both loggers log the values of the tags in the collections selected in Collections, and every sample is written with its quality: a Stale tag keeps its last value, and a tag that is Unavailable or Bad is written with its quality and an empty value. A logger with no collection selected does not start, and its status stays off, so a collection has to exist and be selected before the logger can be started.

Setting Purpose Collections The tag collections whose member values are logged. At least one collection must be configured before the logger starts. Update Interval (Seconds) The interval, in seconds, between writes. The default is 10, and the value must be between 1 and 86400. With Snapshot this is how often the current value of each member is written, and with On Change or Everything it is how often pending changes or samples are flushed. Logging mode Chooses between Snapshot, On Change and Everything. Refer to Logging modes for what each mode writes. The default is Snapshot. File Format CSV writes one row per sample, with the header Recv time,TagId,ValueType,Value,UtcTimestamp,Quality,Reason,Message, and the file uses a .txt extension. JSON Lines writes one JSON object per line, and the file uses a .jsonl extension. The default is CSV. In the CSV header, Recv time is the local time the line was written and UtcTimestamp is the timestamp carried by the tag sample, so the two can differ.

Logging modes describes how the modes behave across all collection-based components.

docs.title: What a logged line looks like
docs.text:
Each sample is one line. For example, a motor speed tag is written like this in CSV:

Recv time,TagId,ValueType,Value,UtcTimestamp,Quality,Reason,Message
2026-10-18T09:15:02.1234567+10:00,Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed,Double,23.4,2026-10-18T09:15:02.0000000Z,Good,ok,

and like this in JSON Lines, where the t field is the time the line was written:

{"t":"2026-10-18T09:15:02.1234567+10:00","tagId":"Inverter/DBC/Status/Speed","valueType":"Double","value":23.4,"utcTimestamp":"2026-10-18T09:15:02.0000000Z","quality":"Good","reason":"ok","message":null}

A Stale sample keeps its last value, and a tag that is Unavailable or Bad is written with its quality and an empty value, so the file shows the gap.

docs.title: Download the logged files
docs.text:
Once a log file has been created, select the link on the Logger Dashboard to download it from Profinity. A TAG File Logger shows this link as TAG LOGS REPOSITORY.

To take the same data further, refer to How to log data to the cloud (InfluxDB) and How to configure data logging.

docs.title: Elmar Solar MPPT
docs.text: Profinity monitors the Elmar Solar Maximum Power Point Tracker (MPPT) Series A and B, which use the CAN database (DBC) file described in the Elmar MPPT DBC documentation. Elmar Solar makes MPPTs that optimise the output of solar arrays. The Elmar range distributed by Prohelion consists of the Elmar 3A MPPT, the Elmar Race MPPT and the Elmar Best MPPT, described in the Solar Charge Controllers by Elmar documentation.

docs.title: Add the MPPT to a profile
docs.text:
To monitor an Elmar Solar MPPT, add an Elmar Solar MPPT tracker to the Profile. Profinity prompts for the following information about the device, and the Change Settings button on the MPPT dashboard changes these details later.

Parameter Description Default Name The name of the component. Must be unique. The component name Milliseconds Valid The timeout of the device, from 1 to 60000, or -1 if the device should never time out. If the network receives no traffic from this device within this many milliseconds, Profinity treats the connection as lost. 5000 Base Address The CAN address of the MPPT, as described in the Elmar MPPT DBC. 0x300

Once the MPPT is added to the Profile, the Elmar Solar MPPT dashboard is available in the sidebar. The dashboard displays input and output voltage graphs, error status indicators and, under the MORE DETAILS banner, temperature readings.

Elmar Solar MPPT

The raw CAN data from an Elmar Solar MPPT can also be viewed in the DBC view, which opens from the Messages and Signals button in the top right corner of the dashboard.

docs.title: MPPT data
docs.text:
The top row of the MPPT dashboard presents a summary of the following information, from left to right.

Cell Meaning INPUT VOLTAGE The voltage produced by the connected solar array, in volts. INPUT CURRENT The current delivered by the connected solar array, in amps. OUTPUT VOLTAGE The output voltage of the MPPT, in volts. OUTPUT CURRENT The output current of the MPPT, in amps.

Below the summary are two time-series graphs depicting the input voltage and output power of the MPPT. Hovering the cursor over a graph shows the data in greater resolution.

The MPPT EVENTS panel at the lower left of the window shows status indicators for MPPT events, and the colour of each indicator matches its type.

Type Colour Indicators Error Red Low array power, hardware overvoltage, hardware overcurrent, metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) overheat, 12 V undervoltage, battery low and battery full Limit Amber Input current minimum and maximum, output voltage maximum, duty cycle minimum and maximum, and MOSFET temperature Limit Green The local and global MPPT limits

The events correspond to the Status message of the Elmar MPPT DBC, which carries the error and limit flags, the mode, and the CAN receive and transmit error counters. The datasheets of each product are linked from the Solar Charge Controllers by Elmar documentation.

The right-hand side depicts a simplified flowchart of the MPPT state, which is either Standby or On according to the Mode signal of the Status message, and the grey box marks the current state. Expanding the MORE DETAILS banner shows the input, output, and power readings, the MOSFET, controller, and power connector temperatures, and the auxiliary 12 V and 3 V supply and battery-side output voltages. The state of a connected battery is described in the BMU section.

docs.title: Motor controllers
docs.text:
Profinity monitors Prohelion WaveSculptor22 and WaveSculptor200 motor controllers over CAN.

  • WaveSculptor motor controller: add a WaveSculptor to a Profile and set its name, timeout, and base address.
  • WaveSculptor dashboard: read the bus data, limit indicators and error indicators.
  • Update WaveSculptor configuration and firmware: run wsConfig and flash the firmware from a Windows desktop instance.

docs.title: Update WaveSculptor configuration and firmware
docs.text: Configure a WaveSculptor and flash its firmware from the Firmware Utilities tab in the component settings.

docs.title: Updating the WaveSculptor configuration
docs.text:
WaveSculptor configuration tools run on Windows only

The WaveSculptor configuration and firmware tools (Setup and Config, wsConfig and Update Firmware) are available only on Windows, and only to the user of the Profinity desktop application. A Docker, Linux, or macOS installation has no Setup and Config button, so the WaveSculptor must be connected to a Windows desktop instance for the duration of the update.

The Tritium wsConfig program performs the configuration. Profinity launches it from the Setup and Config button on the Firmware Utilities tab in the settings, and wsConfig also sets the CAN bus data rate and base address of the WaveSculptor. The factory default rate for all Prohelion devices is 500 kbit/s, and the CAN adapter in the Profile must be set to the same rate as the WaveSculptor.

A CAN to Ethernet bridge is required

The configuration tools need a Prohelion or Tritium CAN to Ethernet Bridge on the same CAN bus as the WaveSculptor and the same local network as the PC. Where no bridge is available, pairing the Virtual CAN Adapter with another CAN adapter creates a virtual one. A physical bridge accepts only one TCP connection at a time, as covered under Multiple TCP clients on one bridge.

Setup and Config runs three steps in order, and stops if one fails.

  1. Check Suitable Available Network: Profinity checks that a suitable network is available.
  2. Set Active: Profinity sets the WaveSculptor as the active device over a TCP connection.
  3. Run WaveSculptor Config: Profinity launches wsConfig.

Configure a WaveSculptor

If the sequence stops at step 1, no suitable network is available, so check that the bridge and the PC are on the same local network. If it stops at step 2, check that no other client holds the bridge's single TCP connection. If wsConfig does not open, the sequence has stopped before step 3, and the Profinity log records that the operation did not run successfully.

The PhasorSense, ParamExtract, and ImExtract tools and the procedure for setting up a motor are covered in the configuration software documentation.

docs.title: Flashing the WaveSculptor firmware
docs.text: Once the configuration has been updated, the Update Firmware button on the Firmware Utilities tab in the settings flashes the firmware. It needs the same Windows desktop instance and the same CAN to Ethernet bridge or Virtual CAN Adapter as the configuration tool, but sets the WaveSculptor active over UDP rather than TCP, so it does not use the bridge's single TCP connection.

docs.title: WaveSculptor motor controller
docs.text:
The WaveSculptor dashboard monitors a Prohelion WaveSculptor22 motor controller and appears as a tab in the sidebar once the controller is added to the Profile. The dashboard decodes the controller with the message and signal names of the WaveSculptor22 DBC file.

The WaveSculptor communicates only over CAN and takes its low-voltage supply from the CAN cable. A CAN adapter connected to a powered CAN bus is therefore required before the dashboard shows any data.

flowchart LR
    WaveSculptor --> Adapter["CAN adapter"] --> Dashboard["WaveSculptor dashboard"]
The WaveSculptor sends CAN messages through a CAN adapter, and the WaveSculptor dashboard in the Profile decodes them

The WaveSculptor22 component monitors both the WaveSculptor22 and the WaveSculptor200. The two controllers send the same CAN messages with the same signals, and the WaveSculptor200 DBC file matches the one the component uses, so add the WaveSculptor22 component whichever controller you have.

Profinity requests the settings below when the WaveSculptor is added, and the Change Settings button at the top-right of the dashboard changes them later.

Parameter Description Name The name of the component. Must be unique. Milliseconds Valid The timeout of the device, which defaults to 5000. Enter -1 if the device should never time out. If no traffic is received from the device within this time, Profinity treats the connection as lost. Base Address The CAN base address of the WaveSculptor, which defaults to 0x400 and must match the address programmed into the controller. Every WaveSculptor on the same CAN bus requires a different base address, as described in CAN Bus and Low Voltage.

If the dashboard shows no data, check that the CAN adapter status is green, that the Base Address matches the address programmed into the controller, and that the adapter and the WaveSculptor use the same CAN bit rate (500 kbit/s by default).

The WaveSculptor dashboard page describes the data, limit indicators and error indicators. To configure the controller or flash its firmware, refer to Update WaveSculptor configuration and firmware.

docs.title: WaveSculptor dashboard
docs.text:
The WaveSculptor dashboard decodes the CAN messages of a WaveSculptor and appears as a tab in the sidebar once the controller is added to the Profile.

Prohelion WaveSculptor

docs.title: WaveSculptor data
docs.text:
The top row of the dashboard summarises the bus voltage, bus current, bus power, digital signal processor (DSP), motor and heatsink temperatures, motor speed in RPM and vehicle speed in MPS (metres per second). A negative bus current or bus power indicates power flowing out of the WaveSculptor, for example during regenerative braking. Profinity calculates BUS POWER as the product of bus voltage and bus current. MOTOR TEMP reads correctly only when a motor temperature sensor is connected and configured, and MPS depends on the tyre diameter entered in the WaveSculptor configuration.

Below the summary are time-series graphs of bus power and velocity, followed by a CONTROLLER LIMITS panel (amber) and a CONTROLLER ERRORS panel (red). An indicator lights when the matching bit of the Status message is set. Only one control loop limits the motor torque at any one time, so a single limit indicator is lit, and MOTOR CURRENT or VELOCITY lighting means the setpoint has been reached during normal operation.

Limit indicator Meaning OUTPUT VOLTAGE PWM There is not enough bus voltage to produce more current and more torque. MOTOR CURRENT The motor current setpoint is being regulated. VELOCITY The velocity setpoint has been reached. BUS CURRENT The bus current setpoint is limiting any further increase in motor torque. BUS VOLTAGE UPPER Regenerative torque is limited by the maximum bus voltage setpoint. BUS VOLTAGE LOWER Drive torque is limited by the minimum bus voltage setpoint. IPM OR MOTOR TEMP A temperature limit is reducing the motor torque. IPM is the intelligent power module. Error indicator Meaning HARDWARE OVER CURRENT The hardware over current comparator tripped, even if only for an instant. SOFTWARE OVER CURRENT The measured current exceeded the limit in the calibration configuration. DC BUS OVER VOLTAGE The bus voltage exceeded the over voltage limit in the calibration configuration. WATCHDOG RESET The watchdog reset the controller. This is a warning rather than a fault and stays set until the next power cycle. CONFIG READ The stored configuration could not be read at start-up, so default values are in use. 15v UNDER VOLTAGE The internal 15 V rail has dropped too low. DESATURATION FAULT On the WaveSculptor22 this indicates an under voltage of the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) driver. MOTOR OVERSPEED The motor speed exceeded the configured maximum by 15%.

Each limit and error is described in more detail on the Observation page of the configuration software manual. The MORE DETAILS banner reveals the internal controller state, which is useful for debugging and not needed for general use. The state includes the low-voltage rails, phase currents, direct-quadrature (D-Q) reference frame vectors, slip speed, odometer, serial number and CAN error counts. Signals that the default dashboard does not display, such as the motor hall sequence error, can be bound to a lamp in a custom dashboard.

docs.title: Publishers and Subscribers
docs.text:
The Publishers & Subscribers category holds the components that move tag values between Profinity and other systems while both ends are running. A publisher pushes the current values of one or more profile tag collections to a receiver that is listening now. A subscriber brings data from an external source into the profile tag tree as ordinary read-only tags, which can then be shown on a dashboard, logged, used in a rule or read by a script.

Component Direction Connects to Use it when MQTT Publisher Out of Profinity A Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) broker, in JSON or Sparkplug B format Other systems already subscribe to a broker for your data. Webhook Publisher Out of Profinity An HTTP or HTTPS address, with an HTTP POST and a JSON payload The consumer is an ordinary web service rather than a broker. MQTT Subscriber Into Profinity A Sparkplug B namespace on an MQTT broker The data comes from an external edge node, gateway, or industrial IoT platform.

All three components have Auto Connect on by default. The data format and the retry behaviour differ.

Component Selects data by Data format Retries MQTT Publisher Tag collections JSON, a flat object of tag key to numeric value, or Sparkplug B Keeps trying to connect every 5 seconds Webhook Publisher Tag collections A JSON array of samples, in one POST for each publish When the destination returns a status other than a success code, cannot be reached, or takes longer than 10 seconds to respond, makes up to three attempts in total, and if all three fail the batch is not retried further MQTT Subscriber Topic filter Sparkplug B metrics, scalar types only, written as read-only tags Keeps trying to connect every 5 seconds

All three components require the Data Relay licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the components are unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Choosing between a publisher, a logger and a Tag Relay
docs.text:
A publisher sits in this category rather than with the loggers because a publisher pushes to a receiver that is listening now, whereas a logger writes to a file or database for later retrieval. To share tags between two Profinity instances, use Tag Relay instead, which has its own snapshot format and does not use Sparkplug.

The two publishers share the same trigger modes, either on a fixed interval or whenever a member tag's value changes, and neither starts until at least one collection is selected and every selected collection exists in the profile.

docs.title: MQTT Publisher
docs.text:
The MQTT Publisher sends the current values of one or more profile tag collections to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) broker, either on a fixed interval or whenever a member tag's value changes. Any system subscribed to the broker receives the data as it is published.

It sits in the Publishers & Subscribers category rather than Loggers because a publisher pushes to a subscriber that is listening now, whereas a logger writes to a file or database for later retrieval. To bring data from an external MQTT or Sparkplug source into Profinity instead, use the MQTT Subscriber.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Publishing["Publishing instance"]
        Tags --> Collections["Tag collections"] --> Publisher["MQTT Publisher"]
    end
    subgraph Server["MQTT server"]
        Broker["MQTT broker"]
    end
    subgraph Receiving["Receiving instance"]
        Subscriber["Subscriber"]
    end
    Publisher --> Broker --> Subscriber
The MQTT Publisher in the publishing instance sends tag collections to the broker on an MQTT server, on an interval or when a value changes, and the broker delivers them to every subscriber in the receiving instance

Licence required

The MQTT Publisher requires the Data Relay licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. See Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Profinity does not run a broker, so you need one first: a self-hosted broker such as Mosquitto or HiveMQ, or a managed cloud MQTT service. These steps publish one collection as JSON.

  1. Add an MQTT Publisher to your profile from the Publishers & Subscribers category.
  2. Enter the broker address in Server URL, for example mqtt://broker.example.com:1883.
  3. Enter a Device ID that no other client on the broker uses.
  4. Leave Payload as JSON and enter a Destination Topic, for example profinity/site1/tags.
  5. Under Collections, add a collection and choose it by name, then save.

The publisher does not start until at least one collection is selected and every selected collection exists in the profile. With Auto Connect on, which is the default, it starts when the profile loads, and its status shows On while it is running. Subscribe to the topic on your broker to see the data arrive, in the form shown under Payload formats.

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text: Setting Required Purpose Server URL Yes The broker's connection URL, for example mqtt://broker.example.com:1883. The accepted schemes are mqtt, mqtts, http and https. Use mqtts:// to enable Transport Layer Security (TLS) and mqtt:// for an unencrypted connection. The port is taken from the URL, and when the URL has no port the publisher uses 1883 for mqtt:// and 8883 for mqtts://. Trust all server certificates No Disables TLS server certificate validation for this connection. Enable only when connecting to a trusted broker using a self-signed certificate. Username / Password No Credentials for broker authentication, when the broker requires them. The password is stored encrypted and can be left empty for username-only authentication. Device ID Yes The MQTT client ID this publisher connects with, which must be unique among the clients connected to the broker. It is also used as the Sparkplug Edge Node ID when that field is left empty. Payload No JSON publishes a flat object to the destination topic, and Sparkplug B publishes node birth, data, and death messages on Sparkplug topics. Defaults to JSON. See Payload formats. Destination Topic Yes, for JSON The topic the flat JSON payload is published to, for example profinity/site1/tags. Shown only when Payload is JSON. A save without it fails with "You must provide a destination topic."

docs.title: Sparkplug settings
docs.text:
Shown only when Payload is Sparkplug B:

Setting Required Purpose Group ID Yes The Sparkplug group ID used in the topic path. A save without it fails with "You must provide a Sparkplug Group ID." Edge Node ID No The Sparkplug edge node ID. Defaults to Device ID when left empty.

docs.title: Publishing settings
docs.text: Setting Default Purpose Collections None The tag collections to publish. Add one or more, and choose each by name in the Collection field. An empty entry fails validation with "You must select a collection." Auto Connect On Starts the publisher automatically when the profile is loaded. Logging mode Snapshot Chooses between Snapshot, On Change and Everything. Refer to Logging modes for what each mode publishes. Update Interval (Seconds) 10 From 1 to 86400 seconds. In Snapshot mode this is how often a full publish runs, and in On Change and Everything modes it is how often accumulated changes are sent.

docs.title: Payload formats
docs.text:
JSON publishes a flat object of tag key to numeric value, with no timestamp, quality, or metadata alongside it. Each key is the tag path with every character other than a letter or digit replaced by an underscore, so Vehicles/Car1/Speed becomes the key Vehicles_Car1_Speed:

{
  "Vehicles_Car1_Speed": 87.4
}

A sample is included only when it has good quality and holds a finite number. The payload has no place for quality, so a tag that is stale, lost or not numeric does not appear in it.

Sparkplug B follows the Sparkplug topic and payload convention. The publisher sends a birth message (NBIRTH) on connect, data messages (NDATA) on each publish, and a death message (NDEATH) that the broker delivers if the connection drops unexpectedly. Topics take the form spBv1.0/{group}/NDATA/{edgeNode}. The publisher also subscribes to the node command topic and republishes its birth message when a Sparkplug-aware platform requests a rebirth. Sparkplug B is available on the MQTT Publisher only, not on the Webhook Publisher.

docs.title: Status and troubleshooting
docs.text:
The MQTT Publisher shows On while it is running, Off when it is stopped, and Error when the connection to the broker fails or a publish fails. The status returns to On after the next successful publish.

The publisher keeps trying to connect every 5 seconds. A broker that is down when the publisher starts, or that goes away later, leaves the publisher in Error until the broker is back, and you do not need to restart the publisher. A rejected login is treated the same way, so fixing the credentials needs no restart either. The log records the reason once for each outage.

If the status shows Error, check the Logs for the underlying message, then confirm that:

  • The Server URL scheme and port match the broker.
  • The Username and Password are accepted.
  • No other client on the broker uses the same Device ID.
  • Trust all server certificates is on, if the broker has a self-signed certificate.

Changed in Profinity 2.3: the component was renamed from MQTT Logger, and existing MQTT Logger configurations keep working unchanged.

Rule actions can also send a one-off MQTT message or webhook, and need the Tag Rule Actions licensed feature. For a plain HTTP receiver, use the Webhook Publisher.

docs.title: MQTT Subscriber
docs.text:
The MQTT Subscriber connects to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) broker, subscribes to a Sparkplug B namespace, and writes the incoming metrics into the profile tag tree as read-only tags. It is the inbound counterpart to the MQTT Publisher, which only sends, and it sits in the Publishers & Subscribers category.

Use it to bring the data of an external Sparkplug edge node, or of a supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) or industrial IoT platform, into Profinity as ordinary tags. The tags can be shown on a dashboard, logged, used in a rule, or read by a script.

flowchart LR
    Broker["MQTT broker"] --> Subscriber["MQTT Subscriber"] --> Tags["Read-only tags"]
The MQTT Subscriber receives Sparkplug metrics from an MQTT broker and writes them into the profile tag tree as read-only tags

The MQTT Subscriber is for an external Sparkplug B source, such as a third-party edge device, gateway, or platform like Ignition. To share tags between two Profinity instances, use Tag Relay, which has its own snapshot format and does not use Sparkplug.

Licence required

The MQTT Subscriber requires the Data Relay licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Add an MQTT Subscriber to your profile from the Publishers & Subscribers category, then configure its settings. The subscriber does not start unless Server URL, Topic filter, Host ID and Tag path prefix are all set.

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text: Setting Required Purpose Server URL Yes The broker's connection URL, for example mqtt://broker.example.com or mqtts://broker.example.com. The accepted schemes are mqtt and mqtts, and mqtts:// enables Transport Layer Security (TLS). Broker port No The broker's port, from 1 to 65535. Defaults to 1883. A port written in the Server URL takes precedence. With an mqtts:// URL and no port in the URL, leaving Broker port at 1883 connects on 8883, and any other value is used as entered. Auto Connect No Connects to the broker when the profile is loaded. On by default. With it off, the subscriber waits until you switch it on with Connect. Trust all server certificates No Disables TLS server certificate validation. Enable only when connecting to a trusted broker that uses a self-signed certificate. Username / Password No Credentials for broker authentication, when the broker requires them. The password is stored encrypted. Client ID No The MQTT client ID. Leave blank to generate one.

docs.title: Sparkplug settings
docs.text: Setting Required Purpose Topic filter Yes The Sparkplug topic filter to subscribe to. Defaults to spBv1.0/#, the whole Sparkplug B namespace. Narrow it to one group, for example spBv1.0/Plant1/#, to subscribe to only that group. Host ID Yes The name this subscriber announces as a Sparkplug primary host application, for example Profinity. It is published on spBv1.0/STATE/{hostId}. It must not contain +, # or /.

docs.title: Tags settings
docs.text: Setting Required Purpose Tag path prefix Yes The profile subtree that subscribed metrics are written under, for example External/Ignition. The subscriber owns this subtree, so no other component or script should create tags beneath it. Refer to Tag tree path for the path rules.

docs.title: Where tags appear
docs.text:
An incoming metric is written to a path built from the Tag path prefix and the Sparkplug group, edge node, device, and metric names:

{prefix}/{groupId}/{edgeNodeId}/{deviceId}/{metric segments}

For example, with the prefix External, group Plant1, edge node Node1, device Pump and metric Temp/Out, the tag path is External/Plant1/Node1/Pump/Temp/Out. The device segment is omitted for a node-level metric, which arrives in NBIRTH and NDATA messages, and is present for a device-level metric, which arrives in DBIRTH and DDATA messages. A metric name that contains / adds further segments beneath the device.

Subscribed tags are read-only

A tag the MQTT Subscriber creates cannot be written to from a dashboard, a script or any other source, and the write is rejected. The only thing that updates one of these tags is the next Sparkplug message for that metric.

To react to an incoming value, use a Run On Tag Change script watching the tag, which reads the new sample the same way it would for any other tag change and is not given the raw MQTT payload. Refer to Script Types for the script types.

If an incoming metric's path is already occupied by something that is not one of this subscriber's own tags, such as an existing device tag, a Tag Relay mirror, a script register or a derived tag, that one metric is skipped and a warning is written to the log. The rest of the message is still applied.

docs.title: Messages applied and ignored
docs.text: The subscriber applies NBIRTH, NDATA, NDEATH, DBIRTH, DDATA and DDEATH messages, so it handles both node-level and device-level publishers. It ignores STATE, NCMD and DCMD messages as data, even under the default spBv1.0/# filter, so a command or state message is never written to a tag.

docs.title: Host state
docs.text: While connected, the subscriber publishes a retained message {"online": true, ...} to spBv1.0/STATE/{hostId}. It publishes {"online": false, ...} on a graceful stop or, if the connection drops unexpectedly, through the broker's Last Will. The retained message stays on the broker while the subscriber is offline, so a Sparkplug-aware consumer can see the last known state.

docs.title: Sequence gaps and metric death
docs.text:
When a message arrives out of sequence, the subscriber requests a rebirth from the edge node and does not apply the out-of-sequence values as current values.

When a metric dies, or a later birth message omits a metric that was known before, the tag is kept and its quality is set to Stale. History and dashboard bindings against that tag path keep working and show the value as no longer live. Refer to Tags for how data quality is shown.

docs.title: Data types and malformed payloads
docs.text: The subscriber supports scalar metric types only: boolean, string, the integer widths, float, double, and DateTime. Dataset, template, bytes, and property-set values are skipped. A metric that arrives by alias with no earlier birth message is also skipped, because its name is not known. A payload that cannot be decoded is logged and dropped, and the subscriber stays connected.

docs.title: Reconnection
docs.text: The subscriber keeps trying to connect every 5 seconds, both when the broker is down at start and after a lost connection. It stays in Error until the broker is back, and the log records the reason once for each outage.

docs.title: Status and troubleshooting
docs.text:
The MQTT Subscriber shows On while it is connected to the broker, Error while it is running but not connected, and Off when it is stopped. While it is in Error, it retries as described under Reconnection.

If the status shows Error, check the Logs for the underlying message, then confirm that the Server URL scheme and Broker port match the broker, and that the Username and Password are accepted. If the component stays Off, confirm that Server URL, Topic filter, Host ID and Tag path prefix are all set, because the subscriber does not start without them. If the component is On but no tags appear, check that the Topic filter covers the group you expect.

Use the MQTT Publisher or Webhook Publisher to send data out, and Tag Relays to share tags between Profinity instances.

docs.title: Webhook Publisher
docs.text:
The Webhook Publisher pushes the current values of one or more profile tag collections to an HTTP or HTTPS address with an HTTP POST, either on a fixed interval or whenever a member tag's value changes. It uses the same trigger modes as the MQTT Publisher. Use it when the consumer is an ordinary web service rather than an MQTT broker.

It sits in the Publishers & Subscribers category rather than Loggers because a publisher pushes to a receiver that is listening now, whereas a logger writes to a file or database for later retrieval.

flowchart LR
    Tags --> Collections["Tag collections"] --> Publisher["Webhook Publisher"] --> Endpoint["HTTP endpoint"]
The Webhook Publisher sends tag collections to an HTTP or HTTPS endpoint with a POST, on an interval or when a value changes

Licence required

The Webhook Publisher requires the Data Relay licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
These steps publish one collection to a web service with no authentication.

  1. Add a Webhook Publisher to your profile from the Publishers & Subscribers category.
  2. Enter the address of the receiver in Destination URL.
  3. Under Collections, add a collection and choose it by name, then save.

The publisher does not start until at least one collection is selected and every selected collection exists in the profile. With Auto Connect on, which is the default, it starts when the profile loads.

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text: Setting Required Purpose Destination URL Yes The HTTP or HTTPS address the publisher POSTs to on each publish. The URL is stored encrypted and masked on screen, because webhook URLs often embed an access token. A save without it fails with "You must provide a webhook destination URL." Authentication No None, Bearer token, API key header or Basic auth. Defaults to None. Refer to Authentication. Selecting a mode shows its credential fields, and each field is required for that mode.

docs.title: Publishing settings
docs.text: Setting Default Purpose Collections None The tag collections to publish. Add one or more, and choose each by name in the Collection field. An empty entry fails validation with "You must select a collection." Logging mode Snapshot Chooses between Snapshot, On Change and Everything. Refer to Logging modes for what each mode publishes. Update Interval (Seconds) 10 From 1 to 86400 seconds. In Snapshot mode this is how often a full publish runs, and in On Change and Everything modes it is how often accumulated changes are sent. Auto Connect On Starts the publisher automatically when the profile is loaded.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
The Webhook Publisher adds the selected credential as a header on every request.

Mode Fields Behaviour None None No authentication header is added. Bearer token Bearer token Adds Authorization: Bearer <token>. API key header API key header name, API key header value Adds a header with the configured name and value, for example X-Api-Key: <value>. Basic auth Basic auth username, Basic auth password Adds Authorization: Basic <base64(username:password)>.

Whichever mode you choose, the credential is stored encrypted and masked on screen.

Destination addresses are not restricted

Anyone who can edit the profile can point a Webhook Publisher at any address the Profinity server can reach, including internal services. Restrict profile editing accordingly.

docs.title: Payload format
docs.text:
Each publish sends one POST containing a JSON array of the samples in that batch, never one POST per sample. Each entry has the same fields that GET /api/v2/Tags/Sample/{path} returns for a tag sample, limited to fullTagId, utcTimestamp, quality and value. The API's reason, message and metadata fields are not sent.

[
  {
    "fullTagId": "Vehicles/Car1/Speed",
    "utcTimestamp": "2026-09-24T04:12:03Z",
    "quality": "Good",
    "value": 87.4
  }
]

Each entry reports the quality the tag had when the sample was taken. A Stale entry carries its last value, and an entry for a tag that is Unavailable or Bad has quality and no value. Only tags that hold a finite number are included.

docs.title: Delivery health
docs.text:
When the destination returns a status other than a success code, cannot be reached, or takes longer than 10 seconds to respond, the publisher makes up to three attempts in total, waiting 1 second before the second attempt and 2 seconds before the third. The attempt count, timeout and waits cannot be changed in Profinity 2.3. If all three attempts fail, the batch is not retried further and the publisher reports Error until a later publish succeeds.

The publisher shows On while it is running, Off when it is stopped, and Error after a failed delivery. It also exposes two tags for a dashboard or rule:

Tag Meaning LastDeliverySuccess true when the most recent delivery succeeded, and false otherwise. LastDeliveryError Empty when healthy. After a failed delivery it reads "Webhook delivery failed - see log for details."

If the status shows Error, check the Logs for the underlying message, then confirm that:

  • The Destination URL is correct.
  • The receiver accepts the selected Authentication. A 401 or 403 response points to a wrong credential.
  • The receiver returns a success status.
  • The receiver presents a certificate that the Profinity server trusts, for an HTTPS destination. The Webhook Publisher has no option to skip certificate validation.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text: Use the MQTT Publisher to publish to a broker, or the MQTT Subscriber to bring external data in. A rule action can also send a one-off webhook or MQTT message, and needs the Tag Rule Actions licensed feature.

docs.title: Tag Relays
docs.text:
Tag Relays let one Profinity instance show live tags from other instances, so a head office can watch many sites from one place. Each site, vehicle, or installation runs a Tag Relay Sender, which publishes the tags you choose, and a central instance runs a Tag Relay Receiver, which shows them alongside its own. Dashboards, alerts, and rules on the central instance work on the relayed tags as they do on local ones.

Sender and receiver roles, with per-site tag prefixes on the receiving instance

docs.title: How the components fit together
docs.text:
Component Runs on Role Default protocol Auto Connect Tag Relay Sender The site instance that owns the tags Exports a snapshot of the tags in selected collections at a fixed interval, over HTTPS or MQTT. HTTPS On by default Tag Relay Receiver The central instance Mounts the incoming tags as read-only tags under a prefix that identifies the sending site. MQTT On by default, with the MQTT protocol

A receiving instance can ingest many senders, because each tag is mounted beneath the receiver's own prefix followed by the sender's prefix. A sender with the prefix Vehicle12 relayed to a receiver with the prefix Fleet appears at Fleet/Vehicle12/..., so give each sender a distinct Sender tag path prefix. Relayed tags are read-only on the receiver, although local collections, rules, alerts, dashboards, and scripts on the receiver can use them in the same way as any other tag. The Tag tree path page describes how paths are built.

Tag Relay works between Profinity instances only and uses its own snapshot format, so it does not use Sparkplug. If the other end is a third-party Sparkplug B source, use the MQTT Subscriber instead.

Both components are added to a profile from the Tag Relays category.

Licence required

Both components require the Data Relay licensed feature on the instance they run on, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Refer to Licensing to check whether it is available.

To set up a first relay, refer to Set up a tag relay. The Tag Relay page covers the concept, collision rules and known limitations.

docs.title: Set up a tag relay
docs.text:
This page sets up a first Tag Relay, so that tags on a sending Profinity instance appear on a receiving instance. Both components require the Data Relay licensed feature on the instance they run on, and the HTTPS protocol needs a user with the Receive external tags permission on the receiving instance.

  1. On the sending instance, create a tag collection that holds the tags to share, as described in Collections.
  2. On the receiving instance, add a Tag Relay Receiver, choose the protocol and set a unique Receiver tag path prefix.
  3. For HTTPS, create a user on the receiving instance with the Receive external tags permission, and note a JSON Web Token (JWT) for that user.
  4. On the sending instance, add a Tag Relay Sender, choose the same protocol, select the collection, and enter the receiver's address (HTTPS) or the broker and snapshot topic (MQTT).
  5. For HTTPS, enter the token as the Bearer token.
  6. If Auto Connect is off, select Start Sender.
  7. Wait for one Snapshot interval (seconds), then confirm that the tags appear under the receiver's prefix in Tag Explorer.

If the tags do not appear, refer to the troubleshooting sections on the sender and receiver pages.

docs.title: Tag Relay Receiver
docs.text:
The Tag Relay Receiver ingests the snapshots published by one or more Tag Relay Senders and mounts the incoming tags in the local tag tree as read-only tags beneath a prefix that identifies where they came from. It sits in the Tag Relays category. Once relayed tags are mounted they behave like any other tag, so they can be browsed in Tag Explorer, placed in collections, shown on a dashboard, logged, and used in rules and scripts. The Tag Relay page covers the concept, collision rules and limitations.

Sender and receiver roles, with per-site tag prefixes on the receiving instance

Licence required

The Tag Relay Receiver requires the Data Relay licensed feature.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Add a Tag Relay Receiver to your profile from the Tag Relays category, choose the protocol and set a Receiver tag path prefix. Set up a tag relay describes how to set up a first relay end to end.

docs.title: Tag Relay settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Protocol MQTT subscribes to a broker topic and applies each snapshot it receives. HTTPS uses the local relay API on this instance, so this component makes no outbound connection. Defaults to MQTT. Receiver tag path prefix Required. The profile subtree that every ingest batch is applied under, so it must be unique to this receiver. A prefix supplied by the sender is appended beneath it, so a receiver prefix of Fleet and a sender prefix of Vehicle12 give tags at Fleet/Vehicle12/.... Refer to Tag tree path.

docs.title: MQTT settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Auto Connect With the MQTT protocol, connects to the broker when the profile is loaded. On by default. With it off, the receiver waits until you switch it on with Connect. MQTT broker URL The broker's connection URL. Use an mqtts:// scheme to enable Transport Layer Security (TLS). Required when the protocol is MQTT. MQTT broker port The broker's port. Defaults to 1883. A port written in the broker URL takes precedence, and with an mqtts:// URL that has no port, leaving this at 1883 connects on 8883. Trust all server certificates Disables TLS server certificate validation. Enable only when connecting to a trusted broker that uses a self-signed certificate. MQTT username / MQTT password Credentials for broker authentication, when the broker requires them. The password is stored encrypted. MQTT client id Optional MQTT client ID. Leave blank to generate one, and give each client on the broker a different ID. MQTT subscribe topic The topic carrying the JSON snapshots, for example profinity/relay/site1. Required when the protocol is MQTT, and it must match the sender's MQTT snapshot topic.

docs.title: Receiving over HTTPS
docs.text:
When the protocol is HTTPS the sender posts directly to this instance, using a JSON Web Token (JWT) for a user with the Receive external tags permission (or Admin). Create a service account on this instance with that permission and give its token to the sender. Refer to Roles and permissions for how to grant the permission. The Tag Relay Receiver component supplies the receiver prefix and only displays the receiving state. An instance accepts a relay post for only one Tag Relay Receiver set to HTTPS, so add a single HTTPS receiver per instance. Integrators can find the route in the Endpoint Reference.

Relayed tags are read-only

A tag created by the receiver cannot be written to from a dashboard, a script or any other source, and the only thing that updates it is the next snapshot from the sender. A path already occupied by a tag that relay does not own, such as a local device tag, causes the whole batch to be rejected, which is explained in Collision rules.

docs.title: Monitoring the receiver
docs.text: The component shows On while it is receiving and Off when it is stopped, and its dashboard shows its status and the total number of messages received. The status reflects whether the receiver is running and not whether the broker connection is established.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If no tags appear, check the Logs first. A receiver set to MQTT that has no MQTT broker URL or MQTT subscribe topic does not start and logs the reason. A receiver that shows On but receives nothing usually has a broker connection problem, which the log reports as a disconnection or failed reconnect (the receiver keeps retrying, every 5 seconds), or a MQTT subscribe topic that differs from the sender's MQTT snapshot topic.

If snapshots arrive but the tags do not update, a path in the batch is already occupied by a tag that relay does not own, and the whole batch is rejected. The log of an MQTT receiver then shows an ingest conflict warning, and a sender using HTTPS receives a 409 response. Change the Receiver tag path prefix or the sender's Sender tag path prefix so that the relayed tags mount in an empty subtree.

Over HTTPS, a 401 or 403 response at the sender means the token is missing, invalid, or belongs to a user without the Receive external tags permission, and a 409 response can also mean that more than one Tag Relay Receiver set to HTTPS is active on this instance.

docs.title: Tag Relay Sender
docs.text:
The Tag Relay Sender exports the tags that belong to the collections you select and sends them, as a full snapshot at a fixed interval, to a remote Profinity instance running a Tag Relay Receiver. It sits in the Tag Relays category. The position of each tag in the exported tree is its tag tree path, and the Tag Relay page covers the concept of sender and receiver roles.

Sender and receiver roles, with per-site tag prefixes on the receiving instance

Licence required

The Tag Relay Sender requires the Data Relay licensed feature.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Add a Tag Relay Sender to your profile from the Tag Relays category, choose the protocol, and select the collections to export. Only the member tags of the selected collections are sent, so create the collections first, as described in Collections. The sender does not start until at least one collection is selected and every selected collection exists in the profile. Set up a tag relay describes how to set up a first relay end to end.

docs.title: Tag Relay settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Protocol HTTPS posts the snapshot to the remote instance's relay API, and MQTT publishes it as a JSON payload on a broker. Defaults to HTTPS. Sender tag path prefix Optional. Prepended as outer path segments on the exported tree, and placed beneath the receiver's own Receiver tag path prefix. A sender prefix of Vehicle12 relayed to a receiver prefix of Fleet appears at Fleet/Vehicle12/.... Exclude relay-managed nodes Excludes tags that were themselves received from another Tag Relay, so that mirrored data is not sent on again in a loop. Enabled by default. Snapshot interval (seconds) How often a snapshot is published or posted, from 5 to 86400 seconds. Defaults to 60. Each snapshot carries every tag in the selected collections, so a short interval with a large collection produces a large payload. Auto Connect Starts sending automatically when the profile is loaded. Enabled by default. Collections The profile tag collections to export. Add one or more.

docs.title: HTTPS settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose Remote base URL The remote Profinity base URL, for example https://receiver:443/. Required when the protocol is HTTPS. Bearer token A JSON Web Token (JWT) for a user on the remote instance with the Receive external tags permission (or Admin). Use the token of a service account created on the receiving instance for this, so the relay keeps working without anyone signing in again. Required to start the sender when the protocol is HTTPS, and stored encrypted. Trust all server certificates Disables Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificate validation. Enable only when connecting to a trusted receiver that uses a self-signed certificate.

docs.title: MQTT settings
docs.text: Setting Purpose MQTT broker URL The broker's connection URL. Use an mqtts:// scheme to enable TLS. Required when the protocol is MQTT. MQTT broker port The broker's port. Defaults to 1883. A port written in the broker URL takes precedence, and with an mqtts:// URL that has no port, leaving this at 1883 connects on 8883. Trust all server certificates Disables TLS server certificate validation. Enable only when connecting to a trusted broker that uses a self-signed certificate. MQTT username / MQTT password Credentials for broker authentication, when the broker requires them. The password is stored encrypted. MQTT client id Optional MQTT client ID. Leave blank to generate one, and give each client on the broker a different ID. MQTT snapshot topic The topic the UTF-8 JSON snapshot is published on, for example profinity/relay/site1. Required to start the sender when the protocol is MQTT, and the receiver must subscribe to the same topic.

docs.title: Running the sender
docs.text: The component shows On while it is running and Off when it is stopped. Start Sender and Stop Sender actions, and a toggle combining the two, are available on the component, and the component's dashboard shows its status and the total number of messages sent. The status reflects whether the sender is running and not whether the last snapshot was delivered, so a sender that shows On can still be failing to deliver. The total number of messages sent increases only when a snapshot is delivered.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the sender shows Error, it is running but cannot reach its broker, so it retries every second and the log records the reason once. If the sender does not start at all, check the Logs. The sender refuses to start, and logs the reason, when no collection is selected, when a selected collection does not exist, when the HTTPS protocol is missing the Remote base URL or Bearer token, or when the MQTT protocol is missing the MQTT broker URL or MQTT snapshot topic.

If the sender shows On but the total number of messages sent stays at zero, the log holds a warning for each failed snapshot. Over HTTPS the warning carries the response code from the receiver:

  • 401 or 403 points to a missing or invalid token, or a user without the Receive external tags permission.
  • 409 means the receiver rejected the batch because of a collision with a tag that relay does not own.
  • 400 means the receiver rejected the request, which includes a request body over 5 MB.

Over MQTT, the sender retries a lost broker connection every second and logs each failed connection, so check the broker URL, port, credentials, and TLS settings.

If the sender delivers but nothing appears on the receiver, confirm that the receiver uses the same protocol and, for MQTT, subscribes to the same topic as the MQTT snapshot topic.

To grant the Receive external tags permission that the HTTPS receiver needs, refer to Roles and permissions.

docs.title: Customising Profinity
docs.text:
Profinity can be tailored to a deployment without application code. Dashboards show the system in the terms operators use, a theme applies branding, a hosted web application runs alongside Profinity, and white-label mobile builds let an original equipment manufacturer (OEM) ship a branded app.

  • Dashboards builds operator interfaces that show live data from Profinity tags in the visual dashboard editor, with YAML behind it as a fallback.
  • Themes and branding applies branding and theme customisation from a theme.yaml file.
  • Hosting custom applications serves a custom web application from Profinity's integrated web server, with Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) certificates.
