                    content: "<p>Summary details</p>"
          - group:
              width: "60%"
              direction: "vertical"
              items:
                - chart:
                    type: "line"
                    value:
                      labels: ["00:00", "06:00", "12:00", "18:00"]
                      datasets:
                        - label: "Pressure Trend"
                          data: [1010, 1012, 1015, 1013]

docs.title: Panel component
docs.text:
A panel is a titled container within a panels grid that holds related content and data visualisations.

Panel component displaying a titled container with organised content

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use a panel for one titled section of data inside a panels grid. Use a Group when the components need no title or panel frame.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Not used by the web interface class string No None Style variant of the panel body. sunken is the only variant that Profinity defines, and it suits charts and state diagrams. The variant applies to the panel body and not to the whole panel title string Yes None Title text in the panel header, at the top of the panel menu object No None When present, the panel header shows a static menu icon. The icon is not interactive and the menu items are not displayed, so a panel menu does not provide navigation, actions, or dialogs. width string No None Width in CSS format, for example 100px, 50% or auto, applied to the panel height string No None Height in CSS format, for example 100px, 50vh or auto, applied to the body area of the panel minHeight string No None Minimum height of the panel body in CSS format. The body grows to fit its content and never shrinks below this value, and the value never stretches the panel to fill space items array Yes None Components displayed in the body of the panel: a chart, lamps, state diagram, group, readouts, table, html, redirect, or caption. Place any other component inside a group

A panel with a menu shows a static menu icon in its header, and clicking the icon does nothing. Use the Titlebar menu or an Action component for navigation and actions.

docs.title: Basic example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    title: "Temperature Sensors"
                    height: "auto"
                    items:
                      - readouts:
                          items:
                            - readout:
                                label: "Sensor 1"
                                value: 22.5
                                unit: "°C"
                                precision: 1
                            - readout:
                                label: "Sensor 2"
                                value: 24.2
                                unit: "°C"
                                precision: 1

docs.title: Height variations
docs.text:
Panels support different height configurations for flexible layouts.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    title: "Fixed Height Panel"
                    height: "200px"
                    items:
                      - chart:
                          type: "line"
                          value:
                            labels: ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar"]
                            datasets:
                              - label: "Data"
                                data: [10, 20, 30]
                - panel:
                    title: "Viewport Height Panel"
                    height: "50vh"
                    items:
                      - table:
                          tableHeaders:
                            - header:
                                accessorKey: name
                                value: Name
                          value: []
                - panel:
                    title: "Auto Height Panel"
                    height: "auto"
                    items:
                      - readouts:
                          items:
                            - readout:
                                label: "Value"
                                value: 42

docs.title: Width example
docs.text:
Panels also support explicit width values to control horizontal sizing within layouts.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    title: "Half Width Panel"
                    width: "50%"
                    height: "auto"
                    items:
                      - readouts:
                          items:
                            - readout:
                                label: "Value"
                                value: 42
                - panel:
                    title: "Fixed Width Panel"
                    width: "480px"
                    height: "auto"
                    items:
                      - html:
                          content: "<p>Fixed width content area</p>"

docs.title: Complex nested structures
docs.text:
Panels can contain complex nested component structures, in which a group holds the components that the panel does not accept directly.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    title: "Motor Controller Overview"
                    height: "auto"
                    items:
                      - group:
                          direction: "horizontal"
                          items:
                            - icon:
                                image: nav_motorcontrollers_active.svg
                            - readouts:
                                items:
                                  - readout:
                                      label: "Bus Voltage"
                                      precision: 1
                                      bind:
                                        - target: value
                                          source: 'DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage'
                                  - readout:
                                      label: "Bus Current"
                                      precision: 1
                                      bind:
                                        - target: value
                                          source: 'DBC/BusMeasurement/BusCurrent'
                      - chart:
                          type: "line"
                          legend: false
                          refreshInterval: 1000
                          bind:
                            - target: value
                              source: 'DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage'
                              seriesMode: timeSeries
                              timeRangeStart: "-5m"
                              timeRangeStop: "0m"
                      - lamps:
                          items:
                            - lampgroup:
                                items:
                                  - lamp:
                                      color: "green"
                                      label: "Online"
                                      value: 1
                                      bind:
                                        - target: enabled
                                          source: 'DBC/Status/Online'
                                          toType: boolean
                                  - lamp:
                                      color: "red"
                                      label: "Error"
                                      value: 1
                                      bind:
                                        - target: enabled
                                          source: 'DBC/Status/Error'
                                          toType: boolean

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    class: "sunken"
                    title: "System Status"
                    height: "60vh"
                    minHeight: "200px"
                    items:
                      - group:
                          direction: "vertical"
                          items:
                            - lamps:
                                items:
                                  - lampgroup:
                                      items:
                                        - lamp:
                                            color: "green"
                                            label: "Online"
                                            value: 1
                                            bind:
                                              - target: enabled
                                                source: 'DBC/Status/Online'
                                                toType: boolean
                            - readouts:
                                items:
                                  - readout:
                                      label: "Temperature"
                                      bind:
                                        - target: value
                                          source: 'DBC/Temperature/Value'
                            - chart:
                                type: "line"
                                bind:
                                  - target: value
                                    source: 'DBC/Temperature/Value'
                                    seriesMode: timeSeries
                                    timeRangeStart: "-5m"
                                    timeRangeStop: "0m"

docs.title: Panels component
docs.text:
A panels component is a grid that lays out several panel containers, where each panel holds its own content and data visualisations. The panels sit side by side and wrap onto the next line when the row has no room left.

Panels component showing a grid layout of multiple panel containers

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use panels to divide a section of a dashboard into several titled areas that each show a different data view. Use a Row or a Group when the components need no titles or panel frames.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Not used by the web interface class string No None CSS class added to the panel grid, for use with a profile style sheet height string No None Height in CSS format, applied directly to the grid and overriding any height the grid would otherwise take minHeight string No None Minimum height in CSS format. The grid grows to fit its content and never shrinks below this value, and the value never stretches the grid to fill space items array Yes None Array of objects that each contain a single panel. The grid displays the panels in the order listed

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - panels:
              items:
                - panel:
                    title: "System Status"
                    items:
                      - lamps:
                          items:
                            - lampgroup:
                                items:
                                  - lamp:
                                      color: "green"
                                      label: "CPU"
                                      value: 1
                                      enabled: true
                - panel:
                    title: "Performance"
                    items:
                      - chart:
                          type: "bar"
                          value:
                            labels: ["CPU", "Memory", "Disk"]
                            datasets:
                              - label: "Usage %"
                                data: [45, 67, 23]

docs.title: Pill component
docs.text:
A pill is a compact status display that shows several related values, arranged in groups, beside a central icon, which suits component status and key metrics.

Pill component showing status display with icon and grouped readouts

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use a pill for component status and key metrics, where several related values sit beside one icon. Use Readouts when the values need no icon or grouping.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Not used by the web interface class string No None CSS class added to the pill element title string No None Heading at the top of the pill, before the icon and groups icon object No None Icon shown at the left of the pill. When omitted, the icon area is left empty items array Yes None Array of pill groups, laid out horizontally in order

docs.title: Icon parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Required Default Description image string No None Icon name such as BatteryCharging, an icon filename such as nav_battery_active.svg, or an image filename from the /Profile/Images directory. See Icon for the icon names recess boolean No false When true, the icon is displayed in a recessed frame at a larger size value number No None State of the icon between 0 and 1. The value only affects icons that change with state, and has no visible effect on an icon drawn from image bind array No None Data binding for the icon. Only the value target is handled

docs.title: Pill group parameters
docs.text:
Each item in the pill's items must contain a pillgroup object with:

Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Not used by the web interface class string No None Not used by the web interface items array Yes None Array of value items

docs.title: Pill item parameters
docs.text:
Each item in the pill group's items must contain a value object, which is a pill item, with:

Parameter Type Required Default Description label string No None Caption shown beside the value. The caption can be bound with the label target value number or string No None Static value. When no data is available, the pill shows -- and the item is displayed as stale unit string No None Unit appended after a numeric value. The unit can be bound with the unit target precision number No None Number of decimal places for numeric values dotColor string No None Shows a status dot beside the value. Use success, warning or error for the dashboard theme colours, or any CSS colour value. Give the item a label as well, because colour alone does not state the status. The dot is not shown when hyperlink is set hyperlink string No None When set, the value is displayed as a link. A path that starts with Profile/ resolves against the Profinity server openHyperLinkInNewWindow boolean No false When true and hyperlink is set, the link opens in a new browser tab. The parameter has no effect without hyperlink enabled boolean No true Not used by the web interface, because pill items are always displayed normally visible boolean No true Not used by the web interface, because pill items are always displayed bind array No None Data binding for the item. The value, label and unit targets are handled, and enabled and visible bindings are ignored

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - pill:
              title: MOTOR CONTROLLER
              icon:
                image: nav_motorcontrollers_active.svg
                recess: false
                value: 0
              items:
                - pillgroup:
                    items:
                      - value:
                          label: BUS VOLTAGE
                          unit: V
                          precision: 1
                          bind:
                            - target: value
                              source: 'DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage'
                      - value:
                          label: BUS CURRENT
                          unit: A
                          precision: 1
                          bind:
                            - target: value
                              source: 'DBC/BusMeasurement/BusCurrent'
                - pillgroup:
                    items:
                      - value:
                          label: DSP TEMP
                          unit: °C
                          precision: 1
                          dotColor: warning
                          bind:
                            - target: value
                              source: 'DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp'
                      - value:
                          label: DOCUMENTATION
                          value: Open
                          hyperlink: https://www.prohelion.com
                          openHyperLinkInNewWindow: true

docs.title: Row component
docs.text:
A row is a layout container that holds several components and arranges them vertically or horizontally, which makes rows the fundamental building blocks of dashboard layout.

Row layout container organising multiple components in a dashboard

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use a row to divide a dashboard into logical sections and to control the direction in which the components of a section are laid out. A row stacks its items vertically unless direction is set to horizontal, so set direction: horizontal to place items side by side. Use a Group when a set of related components needs a shared width, because a row takes a height and not a width.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Set as the id attribute of the row element class string No None CSS class added to the row, alongside the horizontal or vertical layout class direction string No vertical Layout direction, vertical or horizontal. Items are stacked from top to bottom unless the value is horizontal height string No None Height in CSS format, for example 100px, 50vh or auto, applied directly to the row minHeight string No None Minimum height in CSS format. The row grows to fit its content and never shrinks below this value, and the value never stretches the row to fill space distributeChildren boolean No false When the row holds several stacked Panels grids, shares the height of the row evenly between them instead of letting each grid size to its own content. The setting has no effect unless a height or minHeight is set on the row itself, because a height on a parent of the row does not count items array No None Components displayed in the row

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        id: "status-row"
        class: "status-container"
        direction: "horizontal"
        height: "auto"
        items:
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: "green"
                          label: "Online"
                          value: 1
                          enabled: true
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "Temperature"
                    value: 25.5
                    unit: "°C"

docs.title: Titlebar component
docs.text:
The titlebar is the header bar of a dashboard, with a status lamp and a toolbar of menu items that provide dashboard identification, status information, navigation, component-specific actions and settings dialogs.

Dashboard titlebar component showing a status lamp and a menu toolbar

docs.title: When to use
docs.text: Use the titlebar for dashboard identification, a status indicator, navigation links, component-specific actions and settings dialogs. The menu of a titlebar can hold a modal item that opens a dialog.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Required Default Description id string No None Not used by the web interface class string No None CSS class added to the titlebar element lamp object No None Status lamp shown in the left group of the titlebar. Refer to Lamp menu object No None Menu whose items are shown as icons in the toolbar at the right of the titlebar. showTitlebar boolean No true When false, the titlebar background, the hamburger menu button and the lamp are hidden, and the toolbar remains visible on a transparent background showActions boolean No true When false, the toolbar of menu items is hidden

When both showTitlebar and showActions are false, the titlebar is not displayed and takes no space.

docs.title: Menu items in the titlebar
docs.text:
The titlebar displays every item of its menu as an icon, without the item caption, and each item type behaves as follows.

Item type Behaviour in the titlebar menuitem Icon link that navigates to the navigate target when clicked. A lamp on the item is displayed beside the icon action Icon button that runs the action when clicked toggle Switch that runs the action when clicked modal Icon that opens a dialog when clicked: a settings dialog, an editor, the Change Password dialog, the Two-Factor Authentication dialog or the Profinity AI chat. logo Displayed in the same way as a menuitem, as an icon link to the navigate target submenu Icon that expands its child items inline in the toolbar when clicked. The location parameter is not used

A titlebar menu usually contains menuitem, action, toggle and modal items. The logo and submenu types suit the side menu, which displays menuitem, modal, logo and submenu entries and does not display action or toggle entries.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
dashboard:
  items:
    - titlebar:
        lamp:
          color: grey
          value: 1
          label: Prohelion BMU
          enabled: true
          bind:
            - target: color
              source: /Prohelion BMU/Properties/StatusColourText
              toType: string
        menu:
          items:
            - menuitem:
                image: nav_custom_active.svg
                imageAlt: Messages and Signals
                navigate: dbc?view=messages&componentIdFilter=Prohelion+BMU
            - modal:
                id: default
                image: dash_config.svg
                imageAlt: Change Settings
                settings:
                  update: true
                  reload: true
                  urlSettings: /api/v2/ActiveProfile/Component/Prohelion%20BMU/settings

docs.title: Data binding
docs.text:
Data binding connects a dashboard component to a tag. A tag is a named value in Profinity, such as a CAN signal, a component property or a derived value, and you can browse every tag in the Tag Explorer. When the tag changes, the component updates, so a dashboard shows live information without any code to fetch it. This page covers how a binding names a tag, which tags a dashboard can use, and the binding modes. Refer to the binding settings reference for the settings of a binding, and to Transform and Map Values for scaling, type conversion and text mapping.

flowchart LR
    Tag --> Binding --> Component
A binding connects a tag to a dashboard component, and the component updates when the tag changes

A binding can show the latest value of a tag, plot its recent history, or read its values back from the data log. The tag is the same in each case, and only the binding settings differ. Whatever the origin of the value, Profinity presents it as a tag with an address, a value, a quality flag and a timestamp, so one binding works the same way for all of them.

docs.title: Understanding tags
docs.text: A binding names a tag by its tag path, which is a list of names separated by /, in the same tree that the Tag Explorer displays. To bind a component, open the Tag Explorer, find the tag, and copy its path into the source of the binding. The visual editor does this for you, because its Binding section lets you choose the tag from the tree, as described in Dashboard Visual Editor. Refer to Tags for how Profinity builds and maintains the tag tree.

docs.title: Binding source paths
docs.text:
The source of a binding is a tag path, and it takes one of two forms:

Form Example Meaning Relative DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage A tag of the component that owns the dashboard Absolute /Prohelion BMU/DBC/PackStateOfCharge/SOCPercent A tag of a named component, which can be a different component

A path without a leading / is relative to the component that owns the dashboard, and the common branches are DBC/..., Properties/... and Firmware/.... Profinity resolves a relative path under the owning component when the dashboard loads. A relative path makes a dashboard reusable, because the dashboard does not contain the name of a component, which allows it to be renamed or applied to another component with the same tags. A component dashboard needs a leading / to bind to a tag in a different component.

A dashboard that has no owning component, such as a profile home dashboard, names the component in full, either with a leading /, which is the form the visual editor writes, or without it, as in Prohelion BMU/Properties/StatusColourText in the example profile that ships with Profinity. If a component is mounted at a nested location in the tag tree, an absolute path includes that location, as described in Tag Tree Path.

Dashboards from earlier versions

Dashboards written before Profinity 2.3 may use dots instead of slashes, as in {COMPONENT_NAME}.BusMeasurement.BusVoltage and {COMPONENT_NAME}.[Property].Status, the {COMPONENT_NAME} placeholder for the owning component, or the [TimeSeries] prefix on a source, as in [TimeSeries].{COMPONENT_NAME}.BusMeasurement.BusCurrent. These dashboards continue to work. New dashboards use the slash form shown on this page, a relative path in place of the placeholder, and seriesMode: timeSeries in place of the prefix.

docs.title: Tags you can bind to
docs.text:
A binding can use any tag in the tree. The branch that a tag sits under shows where its value comes from, and these are the tags that dashboards use most often.

A component that reads Controller Area Network (CAN) bus messages publishes each signal in its DBC (CAN database) file as a tag, in the form DBC/<Message>/<Signal>. DBC tags suit real-time data, sensor readings and status indicators that the DBC file defines.

  • DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage is the tag for a signal (BusVoltage) of a CAN message (BusMeasurement).
  • DBC/Status/LimitBusCurrent is the tag for a limit flag signal (LimitBusCurrent, set when the bus current setpoint is limiting the motor torque) of a CAN message (Status).
  • /Prohelion BMU/DBC/PackStateOfCharge/SOCPercent is the tag for a signal of a named component.

The Properties/ branch holds the tags that a component calculates or holds in addition to its DBC signals. Which tags exist depends on the component, so find them in the Tag Explorer. Property tags suit component status, calculated values and data structures that the component defines in code.

  • Properties/StatusColourText is the status colour of the component.
  • Properties/BusPower is the bus power, in watts, that the WaveSculptor22 component calculates as the product of the BusVoltage and BusCurrent signals. The WaveSculptor22 does not transmit it as a signal.
  • Properties/PackData/BatteryMilliVolts is the battery voltage data of a Prohelion Battery Management Unit (BMU) component, where nested names are separated by /.

A derived tag is a tag whose value Profinity computes from an expression or a script, and a dashboard binds to it exactly as it binds to any other tag. Use a derived tag when a dashboard needs a value that no device reports, such as a calculated power or a combined status, so that the calculation lives in one place instead of in every dashboard. Derived tags suit calculated values that several dashboards, rules, or the API also use.

docs.title: Binding modes
docs.text: The mode of a binding decides what the dashboard reads from the tag. The source is a tag path in every mode. The default mode, seriesMode: instant with store: local, shows only the latest value of the tag. Readouts, lamps, and most other components use it, and it is the setting to leave unchanged unless a chart needs history.

docs.title: Time series
docs.text:
A chart plots history when its binding sets seriesMode. The value timeSeries plots the recent values of the tag over the window set by timeRangeStart and timeRangeStop, timeSeriesDelta plots the change between successive values, and instant, the default, shows only the latest value.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - chart:
              type: line
              bind:
                - target: value
                  source: DBC/VelocityMeasurement/VehicleVelocity
                  seriesMode: timeSeries
                  timeRangeStart: "-5m"
                  timeRangeStop: "0m"

A series binding that sets timeRangeStop but omits timeRangeStart starts its window 10 minutes before the stop time, which is the same length of history that the visual editor sets when it adds a series. A binding that sets neither shows only the latest value, so set both timeRangeStart and timeRangeStop on a series binding to state the history that the chart shows. Time values use a relative form, where -5m is five minutes before now and 0m is now. Time series bindings suit charts, trends and the live history of any numeric tag.

docs.title: Logged data
docs.text:
Set store: logged to read the values of a tag back from the data log instead of the live values. A logged binding names a time range and, optionally, how to aggregate the data:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - chart:
              type: line
              bind:
                - target: value
                  source: DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage
                  store: logged
                  timeRangeStart: "-1h"
                  timeRangeStop: "0m"
                  aggregationWindow: "1m"
                  aggregationFunction: mean

Logged data requires data logging to be configured and enabled for the profile, as described in How to Configure Data Logging, and a logged binding returns no data while logging is not available. The aggregationWindow groups the data into intervals of the given length (for example 10s or 1m), and the aggregationFunction decides which value represents each interval. Logged bindings suit historical analysis over periods longer than the live window.

Tags covers the Tag Explorer, Derived Tags and Create collections, rules, and bindings from tags, which adds tags to a dashboard from the Tag Explorer. Binding Settings Reference lists every binding setting, Conditional Styling shows how visible, enabled and color bindings change the look of a component, and the annotated Motor Controller Dashboard Example shows a complete dashboard.

docs.title: Binding settings reference
docs.text:
A binding is an object in the bind list of a component, and a bind list can hold several bindings, one for each property that the data drives. This page is a lookup table of every binding setting, and each group links to the page that explains it.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "DSP Temperature"
                    unit: "°C"
                    bind:
                      - target: "value"
                        source: "DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp"

docs.title: Source and target
docs.text:
The schema requires only source, and every other setting is optional. The target is optional in the schema, but it names the property that the value updates, so set it on every binding that is meant to change what a component shows.

Setting Type Description source string The tag path of the tag to bind (for example DBC/BusMeasurement/BusVoltage or Properties/StatusColourText). Refer to Binding source paths target string The component property to update (for example value, label, enabled, visible, color). Each component accepts a fixed set of targets, and a binding with any other target is ignored. Refer to Conditional styling for the targets and Component Reference for the targets of each component

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
These settings change the value before the component shows it, and Transform and map values shows each one in use.

Setting Type Description toType string Data type conversion (number, string, boolean or string\|number) gain number Multiplicative scaling factor, applied before offset offset number Additive offset, applied after gain invert boolean Flips a boolean or 0/1 value mapToText object Text mapping configuration. Refer to Text mapping

docs.title: Mode
docs.text:
These settings decide whether the binding reads the latest value, recent history or the data log, and Binding modes explains them.

Setting Type Description seriesMode string instant (the default), timeSeries, or timeSeriesDelta. A chart plots a series of samples when this is timeSeries or timeSeriesDelta store string local (the default) for live values, or logged for values read from the data log timeRangeStart string Start of the time window for a logged or time series binding, relative to now (for example -10m). When timeRangeStop is set and this is omitted, the window starts 10 minutes before the stop time timeRangeStop string End of the time window, where 0m is now aggregationWindow string Length of each aggregation interval for logged data (for example 1m) aggregationFunction string How each interval is reduced for logged data: max (the default), mean, min, last, first, sum, or count

docs.title: Chart only
docs.text:
Setting Type Description stackScale boolean Gives this series its own Y axis seriesType string line, bar, or scatter, overriding the chart type for this series

Component Reference describes the chart and the other components, and the Motor Controller Dashboard Example shows a complete dashboard.

docs.title: Conditional styling
docs.text:
Conditional styling lets a dashboard component change its appearance, visibility, and behaviour with the current value of a tag, so that a dashboard follows the state of the system and gives users immediate visual feedback without any user action. It uses data binding: the same bind list as every other dashboard component, where the target of a binding names the component property that the data drives and a value mapping turns a number or boolean into a colour name or label.

Each component accepts only a fixed set of targets, and a binding with a target that the component does not support is ignored.

Target Effect Components visible Hides the component when the value is false (0 or false). Not supported on lamps, rows, groups, or panels. Readout, Tab, Accordion, Footer enabled Greys the component out when the value is false, but keeps it on screen Readout, Lamp, Tab, Action, Toggle color Sets the colour. A lamp accepts red, green, amber, grey, on, off, disabled, or unknown. A caption accepts red, green, amber, or grey Lamp, Caption label Replaces the label text Readout, Lamp, Pill value classes Adds CSS class names to the component Action, Toggle tooltip Sets the tooltip text Action

The Readout, Lamp, Caption, Tab, Accordion, Footer, and Action definitions in the Component Reference and the dashboard schema list the targets for each component.

docs.title: Show or hide a component
docs.text:
Binding the visible target shows or hides a component with a data value. This suits a detail readout that matters only while a limit is active, a tab or accordion that is hidden when its data is not available, or advanced readouts that appear once a condition is met. The visible target removes the component from view, whereas the enabled target leaves it on screen in a greyed state, so that users can see that the item exists while a component is offline.

The following readout always shows the bus current, and it appears only while the controller reports that the bus current limit is active, because the visible binding follows the DBC/Status/LimitBusCurrent tag. When the tag value is 0 the readout is hidden, and when it is 1 the readout is shown.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "BUS CURRENT (LIMITED)"
                    unit: "A"
                    precision: 1
                    value: 0
                    bind:
                      - target: value
                        source: DBC/BusMeasurement/BusCurrent
                      - target: visible
                        source: DBC/Status/LimitBusCurrent
                        toType: boolean

A visible binding only changes the display when it receives a value. If the tag stops updating, a readout, accordion or footer keeps its last visibility state, so a readout that should have disappeared stays on screen, whereas a tab is hidden because the tab treats a missing value as false. To hide a lamp, place it in an accordion that has a visible binding.

docs.title: Change colour or label
docs.text:
Binding a lamp color or a label changes how a component looks with a data value, for example a lamp that changes colour when a status flag is set, or a text label such as "Online" or "Offline" in place of a number. The classes target of an action or toggle applies the bound string value as a CSS class name in the same way.

The following lamp is green while the LimitBusCurrent flag is 0 and amber while it is 1. The partition list alternates a label and a threshold, so a value below 1 takes the first colour and a value of 1 or more takes the second.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: green
                          label: "BUS CURRENT LIMIT"
                          value: 1
                          bind:
                            - target: color
                              source: DBC/Status/LimitBusCurrent
                              mapToText:
                                partition: ["green", 1, "amber"]
                                bias: right

A partition with more thresholds styles a value by range, which suits status indicators and alerts. The following lamp is green below 60, amber from 60 up to (but not including) 80, and red from 80 upward. With bias: right, a value equal to a threshold takes the label after that threshold, and with bias: left it takes the label before it.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: green
                          label: "DSP TEMP"
                          value: 1
                          bind:
                            - target: color
                              source: DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp
                              mapToText:
                                partition: ["green", 60, "amber", 80, "red"]
                                bias: right

Do not rely on colour alone to convey a status, because some users cannot tell red from green. A second binding on the same lamp can change the label with the same partition, so that the text states the condition as well as the colour:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: green
                          label: "DSP TEMP"
                          value: 1
                          bind:
                            - target: color
                              source: DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp
                              mapToText:
                                partition: ["green", 60, "amber", 80, "red"]
                                bias: right
                            - target: label
                              source: DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp
                              mapToText:
                                partition: ["DSP TEMP NORMAL", 60, "DSP TEMP HIGH", 80, "DSP TEMP CRITICAL"]
                                bias: right

Data Binding describes the binding settings used here, Component Reference lists the targets of each component, and the annotated Motor Controller Dashboard Example shows bound lamps in a complete dashboard.

docs.title: Transform and map values
docs.text: Binding settings can transform the value, convert its type, and map it to text. This page covers type conversion with toType, scaling with gain and offset, inversion with invert, and text mapping with mapToText. Refer to the binding settings reference for the full list of binding settings.

docs.title: Type conversion
docs.text:
Use toType to convert data types. Each component already applies the conversion that suits each of its targets (for example, a lamp enabled target is always read as a boolean), so toType is optional for most bindings and is shown in these examples for clarity:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "DSP Temperature"
                    unit: "°C"
                    bind:
                      - target: "value"
                        source: "DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp"
                        toType: "number"
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: "amber"
                          value: 1
                          label: "Bus Current Limit"
                          bind:
                            - target: "enabled"
                              source: "DBC/Status/LimitBusCurrent"
                              toType: "boolean"

docs.title: Scaling and offset
docs.text:
Apply mathematical transformations with gain and offset:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "Battery Voltage"
                    unit: "V"
                    bind:
                      - target: "value"
                        source: "Properties/PackData/BatteryMilliVolts"
                        gain: 0.001
                        offset: 0

The readout in the next example shows a raw value that is a temperature in tenths of a kelvin. The gain of 0.1 converts the raw value to kelvin first, and the offset of -273.15 is then added to give degrees Celsius, so a raw value of 2981.5 shows as 25.0 with the precision of 1. The tag DBC/Example/RawTemperature is a placeholder for a tag of your own.

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "Temperature"
                    value: 0
                    unit: "°C"
                    precision: 1
                    bind:
                      - target: "value"
                        source: "DBC/Example/RawTemperature"
                        gain: 0.1
                        offset: -273.15
                        toType: "number"

To invert a boolean or numerical value, set invert: true:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - lamps:
              items:
                - lampgroup:
                    items:
                      - lamp:
                          color: "green"
                          value: 1
                          label: "Configuration Read OK"
                          bind:
                            - target: "enabled"
                              source: "DBC/Status/ErrorConfigRead"
                              invert: true

docs.title: Text mapping
docs.text:
Map values to display text using boolean or partition-based mapping. A boolean mapping gives one text for a true value and another for a false value:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "Status"
                    bind:
                      - target: "label"
                        source: "DBC/Status/ErrorConfigRead"
                        toType: "boolean"
                        mapToText:
                          trueValue: "Fault"
                          falseValue: "OK"

A partition-based mapping gives a text for each range of a number:

dashboard:
  items:
    - row:
        items:
          - readouts:
              items:
                - readout:
                    label: "Temperature Status"
                    bind:
                      - target: "label"
                        source: "DBC/DspBoardTempMeasurement/DspBoardTemp"
                        toType: "number"
                        mapToText:
                          partition: ["Cold", 0, "Normal", 25, "Hot"]
                          bias: "right"

The partition array defines ranges in the form [label1, threshold1, label2, threshold2, label3], so that a value below threshold1 takes label1, a value from threshold1 up to threshold2 takes label2, and any higher value takes label3. The bias is required, and it is either left or right: with left a value equal to a threshold takes the label before that threshold, and with right it takes the label after it. The text that results can drive a label target, or a lamp color target when the labels are colour names.

Conditional Styling uses text mapping to drive lamp colours and labels, and the Motor Controller Dashboard Example shows a complete dashboard.

docs.title: Hosting custom applications
docs.text:
As well as hosting the REST APIs and the Swagger interface, Profinity includes an integrated web server that hosts a custom application built on those APIs in any modern web technology. Frameworks such as ReactJS and Angular work, as do traditional HTML and JavaScript.

The Extensions Web server needs a licence that includes the Profinity Server feature and is disabled by default, so enable it in System Configuration first, as described in Extensions Web. The application is then placed in the webroot folder of the artefacts directory:

{Artifacts}/webroot

When a browser requests the server without a URL path, Profinity serves the index.html file from this folder, so with the default ports an application is opened at http://<host>:19080/, where <host> is the name or address of the Profinity machine.

docs.title: Production configuration and HTTPS
docs.text:
The Profinity web server supports Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security (SSL/TLS) certificates for production environments. A certificate comes from either the Windows Certificate Store or a certificate file with its password, and the certificate file option works on Windows, macOS, and Linux. When a certificate comes from the Windows Certificate Store, Windows Cert Store, Windows Cert Store Location, and Windows Cert Store Subject must all be provided, and Profinity validates that the named store and certificate exist.

Setting Effect Cert File The certificate file. Cert File Password The password for the certificate file. Cert Key File Optional. IP Port for Http The HTTP port. The default is 19080. IP Port for Https The HTTPS port. The default is 19443. Redirect all Http traffic to Https Forces all HTTP traffic to the HTTPS interface. Enable Swagger on API Publishes the Swagger interface on this server. This setting is on the Extensions Web tab.

These settings are on the Extensions Web tab. The Web tab has its own copy of the same settings for the Profinity web interface, with default ports 18080 and 18443.

Saving the configuration with Redirect all Http traffic to Https enabled while HTTPS is disabled is rejected with the message "You can only redirect traffic if Https is enabled". Turn off Enable Swagger on API in a production environment that does not need it.

An application hosted here calls the same APIs that Profinity itself uses, and the Profinity Web tab describes the HTTPS certificate options in full.

docs.title: Themes and branding
docs.text:
Profinity 2.3 applies theme and branding settings from a theme.yaml file in the themes folder of the artefacts directory, and the web client shows the colours, logos, and application title from that file in place of the defaults.

Download the example theme

Unzip the file into the themes folder of the artefacts directory.

Themes need a licence, and distributing a themed Profinity needs an agreement

Themes and branding are included in the Desktop licence and above, and an unlicensed instance keeps its theme.yaml file but shows the default Profinity appearance. You can change the theme for your own use with a licensed instance. To distribute a themed Profinity, for example as an original equipment manufacturer (OEM), you need a licence agreement with Prohelion, so contact Prohelion to arrange it before you ship.

docs.title: Where the theme is defined
docs.text:
The theme is a file-based setting, so there is no administration screen for it. Edit themes/theme.yaml on the Profinity host, and put logos and icons in the assets sub-folder. Profinity applies the file when it starts and again whenever the file changes. A missing file leaves the built-in defaults in place, and a file with errors is reported in the Profinity log and also falls back to the defaults. The file holds a version plus three optional groups.

Group Keys What they set app title The application title shown by the web client. colors navBackground, navForeground, primary, secondary, success, warning, error Navigation fill and foreground, the accent, the secondary colour, and the success, warning, and error colours used by status and charts. assets logo, loginLogo, favicon The main logo, the logo on the sign-in page, and the browser tab icon.

Each asset is a single file name that must exist in themes/assets with one of the extensions .svg, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, or .ico.

Colours are hex values in the six-digit form such as "#E07A3F", and the three-digit form such as "#abc" is expanded to "#AABBCC". The eight-digit form with transparency, such as "#E07A3F80", is also accepted, but the lighter and darker shades Profinity calculates from it are solid. A value that is not a valid colour is reported in the log and the theme falls back to the defaults. A key you leave out keeps that built-in colour.

navForeground colours the text and the icons on navigation surfaces, including the title bar and dialog bars that use the navigation colour. primary colours accent controls such as focus rings, links, and selection. success, warning, and error colour the status lamps, badges, and chart series that already use those colours. Information banners stay the built-in blue.

The lighter wash, the brighter fill, the darker text colour, and the text drawn on a solid status fill are calculated from the colour you set, so they are not keys in theme.yaml. Profinity checks that the theme stays readable, and logs a warning in the Profinity log when text would fall below a contrast ratio of 4.5:1, the usual minimum for readable text. This happens when navForeground is too close to navBackground, or when a primary, success, warning, or error colour is too pale to read against white. The theme is still applied, and choosing a darker or higher-contrast colour clears the warning.

docs.title: Example theme.yaml
docs.text:
This example rebrands Profinity for a fictional OEM. Place it at themes/theme.yaml, and put acme-logo.svg, acme-login.svg, and acme-favicon.svg in themes/assets. Every group and key is optional, so include only what you want to override.

version: "2.3"

app:
  title: Acme Monitor

colors:
  navBackground: "#0F5257"
  navForeground: "#FFFFFF"
  primary: "#E07A3F"
  secondary: "#4F6D7A"
  success: "#4CAF7A"
  warning: "#E9B44C"
  error: "#D1495B"

assets:
  logo: acme-logo.svg
  loginLogo: acme-login.svg
  favicon: acme-favicon.svg

A dashboard with the example theme applied

An OEM build can combine custom themes with hidden catalogue entries, as described in Components and Plugins, and the settings that control the rest of the system are in System Configuration. Integrators can read the theme through the API.

docs.title: Developing with Profinity
docs.text:
When configuration is not enough, Profinity can be extended with code. A script runs inside Profinity, a Custom Component allows a developer to create a new component from files, a compiled plugin adds a new component type, and the Profinity SDK develops and packages all three.

Core components, plugins, and the data flowing in and out of the tag tree
  • Scripting automates tasks and creates custom operations in C#, Python or Lua. A script can react to a tag, a CAN message, a rule or a schedule, run continuously as a service, and write results back to tags.
  • Custom Components covers the four ways to create a custom component, from a Dashboard Component through to a compiled C# plugin, and then the files that make a Custom Component, using an optional DBC (CAN database) file, a dashboard, scripts, actions, and settings maps. Using one in a profile is covered on Using a Custom Component under Components.
  • Profinity SDK covers the developer kit Prohelion provides to approved developers, with frameworks for plugins, Custom Components, and scripts.
    • Developing Plugins covers a compiled plugin, built on the same framework as Prohelion's own components. An administrator installs it in Components & Plugins.
    • Component Pack CLI covers the profinity-component-pack tool for validating, packing, and installing Custom Component bundles.
    • Test a script outside Profinity covers profinity-script, which creates a script and runs it before the file is copied into a profile.

Scripting requires a Desktop, Server or Enterprise licence, and an unlicensed instance cannot add or run scripts. Refer to Licensing.

docs.title: Choosing between a script, a Custom Component and a plugin
docs.text: A script suits logic that runs inside an existing profile, such as reacting to a tag change, answering a CAN message or running on a schedule. Custom Components sets out the four ways to create a custom component: a Dashboard Component for a screen of existing tags, a Custom Component built from files, that same component packed for other installations, and a compiled C# plugin when files and scripts are not enough.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text: To make a first Custom Component, follow Make your first Custom Component. To call Profinity from another system rather than run code inside it, refer to Integrating to Profinity. For dashboards, theming, and hosting, refer to Customising Profinity. Rule actions that run scripts are covered in Actions.

docs.title: Custom Components
docs.text:
Profinity provides four ways to create a custom component, from a simple dashboard through to a compiled C# plugin: a Dashboard Component bound only to tags that already exist, a Custom Component built from files and scripts in a profile, that same Custom Component packed so another installation can add it by name, and a full plugin written in C#, compiled against the Profinity SDK and installed through Components & Plugins. Once any of them is in a profile, it is monitored, graphed, logged, and used by rules and scripts in the same way as a built-in component.

A Dashboard Component is enough when the page only needs existing tags. A Custom Component is enough when the behaviour can be described with files, and a packed Custom Component is that same component made installable on another system. A dynamic-link library (DLL) plugin is used when files and scripts are not enough.

flowchart LR
    DC["Dashboard Component"] ~~~ CC["Custom Component"] ~~~ Pack["Packed Custom Component"] ~~~ Plugin["C# plugin"]
The four ways to create a custom component

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Dashboard Component Custom Component Packed Custom Component C# plugin Built from Dashboard YAML Files and scripts in a profile The same files, plus component_metadata.yaml An assembly compiled by the author Typical use A screen of existing tags A new component in one profile The same component on other installations When files and scripts are not enough DBC, scripts, and maps None Optional Optional As the assembly implements them

To make a first Custom Component, follow Make your first Custom Component. This section is the reference for a Custom Component: the files that make one up, including component_metadata.yaml which names a pack. Packing that folder is done with the Component Pack CLI in the SDK. Refer to How to create a Custom Component to attach optional files, and to Using a Custom Component for the component once it is there. For the dashboard itself, refer to the Dashboard visual editor. A DLL plugin is covered on Developing Plugins.

  • Custom Component files lists every file, which ones a pack requires, and which upload field holds each one.
  • DBC, dashboard, and rules covers the CAN database, the component page, and tag rules.
  • Settings covers settings_map.yaml, the extra fields on the settings dialog.
  • Main script covers the service that publishes the component's tags.
  • Menu actions covers actions.yaml, including Connect / Disconnect.
  • Firmware maps covers firmware_map.yaml, the firmware fields on the component.
  • Firmware actions covers firmware.yaml, which names the load, save, and other firmware scripts.
  • Component metadata covers component_metadata.yaml, which names the pack in the catalogue.
  • Component Pack CLI covers the profinity-component-pack commands that pack and install that folder.

docs.title: Component metadata
docs.text:
component_metadata.yaml names a Custom Component in the catalogue and binds the files in the folder. It is written in the component folder; it is not an upload on the settings dialog. A pack also needs settings_map.yaml, firmware_map.yaml, and actions.yaml. Refer to Custom Component files. The Component Pack CLI in the Profinity SDK validates that folder and writes the bundle.

Key Meaning version Document stamp. Set it to "2.3" name Catalogue name. It must be usable as a folder name, or validation fails with Component name is not a valid folder name description Catalogue description author Author. A .nupkg requires a non-empty author pluginVersion Semantic version. A .nupkg requires one requiredSdkVersion SDK version the pack needs, such as ">=1.0.0" componentType CustomComponent componentGroup Catalogue group. The sample uses Custom allowMultiple true lets a profile hold more than one instance mainScript Path of the main script, relative to the component folder dbcFile DBC file name dashboardFile Dashboard file name rebaseDbc Same as Rebase DBC on the component rebaseAddress Same as Rebase Address on the component deviceIdFilter Device identifier, as a hex value such as 0x1000 
version: "2.3"
name: Hello
description: First Custom Component tutorial
author: Prohelion
pluginVersion: 1.0.0
requiredSdkVersion: ">=1.0.0"
componentGroup: Custom
componentType: CustomComponent
allowMultiple: true
mainScript: scripts/hello.py
dbcFile: hello.dbc
dashboardFile: hello.yaml

That file is the metadata from the Hello component pack. After an administrator uploads the bundle under ADMIN > Components & Plugins, ADD COMPONENT lists the name from this file. Refer to Install and manage plugins for the upload screen, and to Using a Custom Component for the instance that results. A compiled plugin is a different bundle. Refer to Developing Plugins.

docs.title: DBC, dashboard, and rules
docs.text: A Custom Component can decode CAN traffic, show a page, and raise alerts from its tags, using an optional DBC file, dashboard, and rules file. Which upload field holds each file is on Custom Component files.

docs.title: DBC file
docs.text: With a DBC file, the component menu includes Messages and Signals and Edit DBC File, so the device's CAN traffic can be read as named messages and signals, and the dashboard can bind those signals. The component runs with Upload DBC File (Optional) left empty, and Rebase DBC and Rebase Address shift the loaded message identifiers onto the base address the device actually uses. Edit DBC File opens the DBC editor once a file is set, and a saved change is picked up automatically. The viewer is documented in CAN bus DBC.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard YAML is the page the operator opens, and Profinity writes a starter file named after the component when Upload Dashboard (Optional) is left empty, which the dashboard editor then replaces. Layout, elements, and the visual editor are in the Profinity dashboard development guide.

A binding that reads a CAN signal uses the DBC names, and a binding that reads a value the main script published uses a tag path. A relative path has no leading /, and Profinity resolves it against the component's place in the tag tree, so the binding follows the component if Tag tree path changes. An absolute path begins with / and names some other place in the tree. Use a relative path in place of the {COMPONENT_NAME} placeholder. Refer to Data binding and Tag tree paths and dashboard binds.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text: Rules YAML file is an optional Tag rules document for this component, evaluated when this component's tags change, and alerts raised from those rules appear in Alerts Log. A tag rule can also run an action when a condition fires, which is not a menu action: menu entries are declared in actions.yaml. Refer to Menu actions.

docs.title: Custom Component files
docs.text:
Each file on a Custom Component is optional while the component lives in one profile, and a pack requires four of them: component_metadata.yaml, settings_map.yaml, firmware_map.yaml, and actions.yaml.

Custom Component settings with pack files and scripts

Settings for an authored component are arranged as Settings, Pack files, Scripts, and Security, with Pack files grouping the uploads into Device, Presentation, Behaviour, Maps, and Firmware, DBC Settings holding Rebase DBC and Rebase Address, and Scripts holding Main Script (Optional) and Auto Start Main Script. component_metadata.yaml is not an upload, and it is written in the component folder when the component is packed. None of these files is required for the component to run in a profile, and if no dashboard is uploaded Profinity writes a starter dashboard named after the component.

File Upload field Required to pack Role DBC (.dbc) Upload DBC File (Optional) No CAN message and signal database for Messages and Signals, and for dashboard bindings that read CAN signals Dashboard (.yaml) Upload Dashboard (Optional) No The component page Rules YAML Rules YAML file (Optional) No Rules evaluated when this component's tags change actions.yaml Actions YAML file (Optional) Yes Menu actions: a button, a service toggle, or Connect / Disconnect for the main script Main script (.cs, .py, or .lua) Main Script (Optional) on Scripts No Long-running service that publishes tags settings_map.yaml Settings Map YAML file (Optional) Yes Extra settings fields shown on the component firmware_map.yaml Firmware Map YAML file (Optional) Yes Firmware settings fields shown on the component firmware.yaml Firmware Actions YAML file (Optional) No Scripts for load, save, and any further firmware actions component_metadata.yaml Written in the component folder Yes Catalogue name, description, and which files the pack binds

Every Profinity YAML document in that set carries version: "2.3", and a component can mix script languages because Profinity runs each script from its file extension: .cs, .py, or .lua. profinity-component-pack validate and pack stop with Missing required file: followed by the file name when any of the four pack files is absent, but the component still runs in a profile without those files. The keys are on Component metadata, and the pack commands are on Component Pack CLI.

An instance added from a pack hides Pack files and Scripts, so the operator then edits Name, Tag tree path, menu placement, and the fields from settings_map.yaml. Refer to Using a Custom Component.

docs.title: Firmware actions
docs.text:
The firmware page of a Custom Component shows LOAD SETTINGS, SAVE SETTINGS, and any extra buttons the author declares, and firmware.yaml names the scripts behind those buttons. The fields they read and write come from firmware_map.yaml. Refer to Firmware maps.

version: "2.3"
loadScript: scripts/load_firmware.py
saveScript: scripts/save_firmware.py
actions:
  - id: updateFirmware
    displayName: Update firmware
    icon: Update
    script: scripts/update_firmware.py
    uploadFileType: Firmware
    uploadFileExtension: .bin

scripts/load_firmware.py, scripts/save_firmware.py, and scripts/update_firmware.py are paths inside the component folder.

The upload field is Firmware Actions YAML file (Optional), under Pack files and Firmware, and on the Scripts tab Firmware scripts lists the paths from this file. Until the file is attached, that note reads: "Load, save, and flash scripts are named in firmware.yaml under Pack files → Firmware. Attach that file to see the script paths here." Refer to Custom Component files. The buttons are on the Firmware Utilities tab, in the Firmware group, and they are shown to an operator with Allow firmware actions. Refer to Roles and permissions.

Key Button the operator gets loadScript LOAD SETTINGS. Runs once and, on success, marks the firmware as loaded saveScript SAVE SETTINGS. Runs once actions One button per entry. The label is displayName in capitals

LOAD SETTINGS and SAVE SETTINGS are fixed labels, and either key can be omitted. A path is relative to the component folder and must end in .cs, .py, or .lua, and a different extension fails with firmware.loadScript must reference a .cs, .py, or .lua script., or firmware.saveScript for the save script.

docs.title: Extra buttons
docs.text:
Each entry under actions needs an id, a displayName, and a script, and displayName: Update firmware is shown as UPDATE FIRMWARE. The older key name is still accepted in place of displayName, and icon follows the same rules as a menu action icon. An action that does not ask for a file asks the operator to confirm before it runs: "This writes a firmware binary to the device and cannot be undone. Continue only if you intend to flash."

Key Meaning id Identifier for the entry. The validation message names this id displayName Words on the button, shown in capitals script Path of the script, relative to the component folder, ending in .cs, .py, or .lua icon Icon on the button. When omitted, the button uses the custom icon uploadFileType Asks the operator to choose a file before the button runs. The usual firmware flash uses Firmware uploadFileExtension Required with uploadFileType. The extension the chosen file must have, such as .bin requiresFirmwareLoaded true hides the button until LOAD SETTINGS has succeeded requiresActiveDevice true shows the button only when the component status is on, idle, warning, or error

The usual firmware flash uses Firmware with .bin. uploadFileType also accepts Certificate, Collections, Content, Dashboard, DBC, DerivedTags, FirmwareSettings, Images, MenuLayout, Models, ProfileDashboard, Rules, Script, SettingsMap, and Styles.

Problem Message Missing id Each firmware action requires a non-empty 'id'. Missing displayName Firmware action '<id>' requires a non-empty 'displayName' (or legacy 'name'). Missing script Firmware action '<id>' requires a 'script' path. Unrecognised uploadFileType Firmware action '<id>' has unsupported uploadFileType '<type>'. uploadFileType without uploadFileExtension Firmware action '<id>' requires uploadFileExtension when uploadFileType is set.

profinity-component-pack validate reports the same messages. Refer to Component Pack CLI.

The load script opens the device with Profinity.ComponentSettings, such as a COM port and a baud rate, and writes each firmware field with Profinity.FirmwareSettings, and the save script reads those fields and sends them to the device. Only an entry under actions receives Profinity.Action, including the uploaded file and progress. Refer to Component and firmware settings and Action context.

docs.title: Firmware maps
docs.text:
firmware_map.yaml adds the firmware tabs on a Custom Component, using the same sections, categories, and fields as Settings, so a section is a tab, a category is a group on that tab, and a field is a control. The upload field is Firmware Map YAML file (Optional), the file must contain at least one field, and a map with no fields fails with Settings map contains no field definitions., which profinity-component-pack validate reports as Failed to parse firmware_map.yaml: followed by the same message. Refer to Custom Component files. The scripts that load and save the values are named in firmware.yaml. Refer to Firmware actions.

An older file that uses a flat config map instead of sections is still read, and those fields are shown on a Firmware Settings tab, in a group named Firmware.

docs.title: Index and scale
docs.text:
index is the device parameter address, which a load script and a save script use when they read or write that field on the device, and it is written on the field next to type and scale. scale multiplies the number shown on the firmware page, and min and max are checked against that number, so write them in the units the operator is typing. The other field keys are on Settings.

This is a complete map for a battery management unit.

version: "2.3"
sections:
  - id: bms
    displayName: BMS Settings
    categories:
      - id: cell
        displayName: Cell Limits
        fields:
          balanceUp:
            name: Balance Up
            type: UINT16
            default: 4100
            units: V
            scale: 0.001
            min: 0
            max: 4.4
            index: 0x35
          cellBalancingVoltage:
            name: Balance Down
            type: UINT16
            default: 4050
            units: V
            scale: 0.001
            min: 0
            max: 4.4
            index: 0x36
      - id: shunt
        displayName: Current Shunt
        fields:
          currentShuntRating:
            name: Current Shunt Rating
            type: UINT16
            default: 500
            units: A
            min: 2
            max: 1999
            index: 0x50
          shuntRatedAt:
            name: Current Shunt Rated @
            type: LIST
            default: 2
            values:
              "2": 50mv
              "4": 100mv

That file adds a BMS Settings tab. Cell Limits heads Balance Up and Balance Down. Current Shunt heads Current Shunt Rating and Current Shunt Rated @. Balance Up opens as 4.1 V, because 4100 multiplied by 0.001 is 4.1, and a value above 4.4 is rejected. index: 0x35 is the slot the load and save scripts send on the bus for Balance Up. Current Shunt Rated @ has no index, so it is not a device parameter: it is a companion list that only exists in the UI.

A save stores the number on screen

scale changes the number drawn on the firmware page. A save stores that on-screen number. After the operator saves Balance Up in the example above, the stored value is 4.1, not 4100.

A script reads a saved value with Profinity.FirmwareSettings and the field identifier, such as balanceUp, a load script writes those values after it reads the device, and a save script reads them and sends them to the device. Refer to Component and firmware settings.

docs.title: Make your first Custom Component
docs.text:
This tutorial adds a Custom Component named Hello.

Download the Hello component pack

Unzip the pack, then attach the files in the steps that follow. The pack includes a DBC file so this path can bind a CAN signal. It also includes firmware files so the component can show an Output Limit field. A Custom Component does not need a DBC file or firmware files. At the end the component publishes a count tag, lists a Temperature message, shows those values on its page, has Connect / Disconnect in the menu, and shows an Output Limit firmware field. The path takes about 20 minutes.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Profinity 2.3 running, with an active profile.
  • A Desktop, Server, or Enterprise licence, which includes Custom Plugins and Scripting. Refer to Licensing.
  • The Modify components, View tags, View firmware, Modify firmware, and Allow firmware actions permissions. Refer to Roles and permissions.
  • Scripting enabled on the Application Config tab of System Configuration.

Scripts run with application permissions

A script runs inside Profinity with the same operating system permissions as the application, so review any script before running it.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text:
To add the component:

  1. Select ADD COMPONENT in the side menu.
  2. Select Custom Component.
  3. Enter Hello as the Name.
  4. Select ADD COMPONENT.

The component appears in the side menu and opens its starter dashboard.

docs.title: Add a DBC file
docs.text:
A DBC file names the CAN messages the component can decode. This example uses a DBC file. A Custom Component does not need one.

  1. Create a file named hello.dbc that contains this DBC:

    VERSION ""

NS_ :

BS_:

BU_: Sensor

BO_ 256 Temperature: 8 Sensor
 SG_ Value : 0|16@1+ (0.1,0) [0|150] "C" Vector__XXX

    The file describes one message named Temperature with one signal named Value.

  2. On the Hello dashboard, select the three bar icon at the top right to open the settings.

  3. Select the Pack files tab.
  4. Set Upload DBC File (Optional) to hello.dbc.
  5. Select SAVE.

The component menu includes Messages and Signals and Edit DBC File.

docs.title: Add the main script
docs.text:
A main script is a long-running service that publishes tags for the component.

  1. Create a file named scripts/hello.py that contains this Python:

    import time

_run_count = 0

def on_start():
    global _run_count
    _run_count = 0
    return True

def run():
    global _run_count
    while not Profinity.ScriptCancelled:
        _run_count = _run_count + 1
        Profinity.Tags.SetValue("count", _run_count)
        time.sleep(1)
    return True

    The script publishes a tag named count under the component once a second.

  2. Open the settings from the three bar icon.

  3. Select the Scripts tab.
  4. Set Main Script (Optional) to scripts/hello.py.
  5. Turn on Auto Start Main Script.
  6. Select SAVE.

Profinity starts the main script because Auto Start Main Script is on. Select TAG UTILITIES in the side menu to open the Tag Explorer, expand Hello, and find count. The value increases once a second.

docs.title: Add a dashboard
docs.text:
The dashboard is the component's page. This file binds count from the main script and DBC/Temperature/Value from the DBC file.

  1. Create a file named hello.yaml that contains this dashboard:

    version: "2.3"
dashboard:
    items:
        - row:
            direction: vertical
            items:
            - group:
                class: statscontainer
                items:
                    - pill:
                        icon:
                            image: IbmWatsonKnowledgeStudio
                        items:
                        - pillgroup:
                            items:
                            - value:
                                label: COUNT
                                precision: 0
                                bind:
                                  - target: value
                                    source: count
                            - value:
                                label: TEMPERATURE
                                precision: 1
                                bind:
                                  - target: value
                                    source: DBC/Temperature/Value

  2. Open the settings from the three bar icon.

  3. Select the Pack files tab.
  4. Set Upload Dashboard (Optional) to hello.yaml.
  5. Select SAVE.

The Hello page shows COUNT updating once a second. TEMPERATURE stays empty until a CAN frame for that message arrives.

docs.title: Add menu actions
docs.text:
actions.yaml adds items to the component menu. This file adds Connect / Disconnect for the main script.

  1. Create a file named actions.yaml that contains this YAML:

    version: "2.3"
menuActions:
  - id: connect
    displayName: Connect / Disconnect
    icon: Start
    kind: mainScriptToggle

  2. Open the settings from the three bar icon.

  3. Select the Pack files tab.
  4. Set Actions YAML file (Optional) to actions.yaml.
  5. Select SAVE.

The Hello menu includes Connect / Disconnect.

docs.title: Add firmware
docs.text:
A firmware map adds firmware fields on the component. The load and save scripts are named in firmware.yaml. Refer to Firmware actions. This example uses a firmware map and firmware scripts. A Custom Component does not need them.

  1. Create a file named firmware_map.yaml that contains this YAML:

    version: "2.3"
sections:
  - id: limits
    displayName: Limits
    categories:
      - id: output
        displayName: Output
        fields:
          outputLimit:
            name: Output Limit
            type: UINT16
            default: 100
            units: "%"
            min: 0
            max: 100
            index: 0x10

  2. Create a file named scripts/load_firmware.py that contains this Python:

    Profinity.FirmwareSettings.SetValue("outputLimit", 80)
print("Firmware settings loaded")

  3. Create a file named scripts/save_firmware.py that contains this Python:

    value = Profinity.FirmwareSettings.GetValue("outputLimit")
print(value)

  4. Copy the scripts folder into the Hello folder under components in the active profile. The profile sits in the profiles folder of the artefacts directory.

  5. Create a file named firmware.yaml that contains this YAML:

    version: "2.3"
loadScript: scripts/load_firmware.py
saveScript: scripts/save_firmware.py

  6. Open the settings from the three bar icon.

  7. Select the Pack files tab.
  8. Set Firmware Map YAML file (Optional) to firmware_map.yaml.
  9. Set Firmware Actions YAML file (Optional) to firmware.yaml.
  10. Select SAVE.

The settings show a Limits tab with Output Limit at 100. On Firmware Utilities, select LOAD SETTINGS. Output Limit changes to 80.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Change the dashboard in the visual editor, as described in How to create a custom dashboard.
  • Replay CAN traffic so TEMPERATURE shows a value, as described in How to replay CAN bus logs.
  • Write component_metadata.yaml and pack the folder so another installation can add it by name. The file is described in Component metadata, and the commands are on Component Pack CLI. The downloaded pack already includes settings_map.yaml and component_metadata.yaml.

docs.title: Main script
docs.text:
A Custom Component needs a main script when live values come from the script rather than from a DBC file, or when the script publishes extra tags beside the DBC signals. Main Script is a service script in C#, Python, or Lua, and it keeps running until Disconnect or until the component shuts down. Auto Start Main Script starts it when the profile loads, and with auto start left off the operator starts and stops it from Connect / Disconnect, which is a mainScriptToggle entry in actions.yaml. Refer to Menu actions.

The script creates branches and leaves under the component in the tag tree, publishes with SetValue, ClearValue, and MarkStale, and the dashboard binds those paths directly.
