On Disconnect the current values are cleared and marked stale, and the branches stay in place so the dashboard bindings remain valid. Refer to Tags for the tag calls, and to Profinity Scripting for the service lifecycle.

The upload field is Main Script (Optional) on the Scripts tab. Refer to Custom Component files.

docs.title: Menu actions
docs.text:
actions.yaml adds items to the menu of a Custom Component, each of which is a button that runs a script once, a toggle that starts and stops a service, or Connect / Disconnect for the main script.

version: "2.3"
menuActions:
  - id: connect
    displayName: Connect / Disconnect
    icon: Start
    kind: mainScriptToggle
  - id: zero
    displayName: Zero Calibration
    icon: Play
    kind: button
    script: scripts/calibrate_zero.py

The upload field is Actions YAML file (Optional). Refer to Custom Component files.

kind What the operator gets button Runs script once when the menu item is chosen toggle Starts and stops a service script, and publishes that running state on the component mainScriptToggle Connect / Disconnect for Main Script. The script is the Main Script field on the Scripts tab

Refer to Main script for the service behind mainScriptToggle.

Field Required Meaning id Yes Unique name for the entry displayName Yes Label on the menu item. The older key name is still accepted kind Yes button, toggle, or mainScriptToggle script For button and toggle A path relative to the component folder, such as scripts/calibrate.cs. A path that leaves the component folder is rejected icon No A Carbon icon name, such as Play or BatteryCharging. A Profinity name such as Start is still accepted. A file name such as icons/logo.svg is a custom icon. An omitted icon is shown as Custom iconPath No An image in the component folder, used instead of icon

An entry with an unsupported kind, or a button or toggle without a script, fails validation, and the message names the entry, for example Menu action 'zero' has unsupported kind. profinity-component-pack validate runs the same check. Refer to Component Pack CLI.

A tag rule can also run an action when a condition fires, which is not this file. Refer to DBC, dashboard, and rules.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: settings_map.yaml adds extra fields to the settings dialog of a Custom Component, with each section drawn as a tab, each category as a headed group on that tab, and each field as a control in that group. The upload field is Settings Map YAML file (Optional). Refer to Custom Component files. The file must contain at least one field, and a map with no fields fails with Settings map contains no field definitions., which profinity-component-pack validate reports as Failed to parse settings_map.yaml: followed by the same message. A script reads a saved value with Profinity.ComponentSettings and the field identifier, such as comPort. Refer to Component and firmware settings. Firmware fields use this same layout in firmware_map.yaml. Refer to Firmware maps.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The file starts with version: "2.3", then a sections list. Sections, categories, and fields are drawn in the order they appear in the file. displayName is the heading the operator sees. The older key label is still accepted.

This is a complete map for a serial device that can also publish on CAN.

version: "2.3"
sections:
  - id: comms
    displayName: Communications
    categories:
      - id: serial
        displayName: Serial Settings
        fields:
          comPort:
            name: COM Port
            type: STRING
            default: COM1
            required: true
            description: Serial port the device is connected to.
          baudRate:
            name: Baud Rate
            type: LIST
            default: "9600"
            values:
              "4800": "4800"
              "9600": "9600"
              "57600": "57600"
      - id: canExport
        displayName: CAN Export
        fields:
          publishTelemetryToCan:
            name: Publish Telemetry To CAN
            type: BOOL
            default: false
          canExportMessageId:
            name: CAN Export Message ID
            type: UINT32
            default: 1280
            dependsOn:
              publishTelemetryToCan: true

COM1 is an example port name. Replace it with the port on the machine that runs Profinity. That file adds a Communications tab. Serial Settings heads COM Port and Baud Rate. CAN Export heads Publish Telemetry To CAN and CAN Export Message ID. CAN Export Message ID is shown only while Publish Telemetry To CAN is ticked.

Key On a section On a category id Identifier for the tab Identifier for the group displayName Tab name. label is still accepted Group heading. label is still accepted categories The groups on the tab fields The controls in the group

An older file that uses a flat config map instead of sections is still read. Those fields are shown on a Configuration Settings tab, in a group named Settings.

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
The key under fields, such as comPort, is the identifier a script passes to GetValue. name is the label on the control. When name is omitted, the identifier is used as the label.

Key Meaning name Label on the control description Help text shown with the field type Which control is drawn. The type names are in the field types table default Value shown until the operator saves another values Choices for a LIST field. The text on the right is what the list shows, and that text is what is saved required true means the field must have a value readOnly true means the value is visible and the operator cannot change it min, max Smallest and largest numbers the field accepts. Write them in the units the operator is typing units Unit printed beside a number scale Multiplies the number shown on a firmware field. A save stores that on-screen number index Firmware maps only. Device parameter address the load and save scripts use dependsOn The field is shown when every named field has the given value. The name is another field identifier in this file gridSpanX How many columns the control spans. 2 draws it across two columns gridSpanY How many rows the control spans requiresFeature The field is shown only when the licence includes this feature

For a LIST field, set default to one of the texts on the right. The baud rate in the example does this with "9600". A script then reads that same text. When the two sides differ, for example "1": NMEA, the list shows NMEA and GetValue returns NMEA after the operator picks that row.

units is shown for V, mV, A, Ah, W, Wh, Ms, Seconds, °C, kb/s, %, Ohms, Ohm, J, kPa, RH %, and Bitfield. Any other text is ignored.

scale applies to firmware fields. It multiplies the number the firmware page shows. min and max are checked against that number, so write them in the units the operator is typing.

balanceUp:
  name: Balance Up
  type: UINT16
  default: 4100
  units: V
  scale: 0.001
  min: 0
  max: 4.4
  index: 0x35

Balance Up opens as 4.1 V, because 4100 multiplied by 0.001 is 4.1. A value above 4.4 is rejected. 4100 is the stored default, and 4.4 is the largest number the operator can type. index: 0x35 is the device parameter address, as described on Firmware maps.

A save stores the number on screen

scale changes the number drawn on the firmware page. A save stores that on-screen number. After the operator saves the example above, the stored value is 4.1, not 4100.

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
type Control STRING Text box. An omitted or unrecognised type is also a text box BOOL, BOOLEAN Tick box LIST Drop-down of the values entries UINT8, UINT16, UINT32, UINT64, INT8, INT16, INT32, INT64, FLOAT, DOUBLE, DECIMAL, NUMBER Number HEX, HEXVALUE Hexadecimal number IPADDRESS IP address PASSWORD Masked text EMAIL Email address INFORMATION Text only, with no value to edit

The calls a script uses to read these values are on Component and firmware settings. The service that uses them is on Main script.

docs.title: Profinity SDK
docs.text:
Prohelion provides the Profinity SDK to approved developers. The kit includes worked examples and documentation that goes further than these pages. These pages explain what the SDK can do. For a copy of the SDK, or for more information, contact Prohelion.

The SDK is the set of frameworks for extending Profinity with code that is written outside a running instance, then installed into Profinity. It covers plugins, Custom Components, and scripts.

The SDK is an add-on to the Desktop, Server, or Enterprise edition. Refer to Licensing.

docs.title: Plugin framework
docs.text: The plugin framework is the same one Prohelion uses for its own components. A plugin adds a compiled component that Profinity does not ship: a settings screen, a status, tags, and actions. Once an administrator installs it, a profile uses it in the same way as a built-in component. Refer to Developing Plugins.

docs.title: Custom Component framework
docs.text: The Custom Component framework describes a device with files: a dashboard, scripts, actions, and an optional CAN database and settings maps, with no compiling. The kit includes the tool that checks those files and packs them into a bundle for a profile. Refer to Custom Components and Component Pack CLI.

docs.title: Script framework
docs.text: The script framework runs automation inside a profile, in C#, Python, or Lua. A script can react to a tag, a CAN message, a rule, or a schedule, run as a service, and write results back to tags. The kit includes the tool that creates a script from a template and runs it against a simulated Profinity, before the finished script is copied into a profile. Refer to Test a script outside Profinity. What a script can do inside a profile is on Scripting.

docs.title: Component Pack CLI
docs.text: The profinity-component-pack command-line tool ships as part of the Profinity SDK developer kit, not with the engine install itself. It validates Custom Components file bundles (YAML, scripts, and maps), packs them as a .zip or a .nupkg, and installs that package into a profile. It does not handle DLL plugins, which are installed through Components & Plugins (refer to Developing Plugins). component_metadata.yaml names the pack in the catalogue and binds the files in the folder. Refer to Component metadata. The tool runs from the kit's profinity-component-pack subfolder.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
profinity-component-pack validate --component-dir <path>
profinity-component-pack pack --component-dir <path> --output bundle.zip
profinity-component-pack install --package bundle.zip --profinity-dir <Artifacts> --profile <name> --engine-dir <engine-bin>

<Artifacts> is the Artefacts directory, and <engine-bin> is the bin folder of the Profinity engine install.

Command Purpose validate Checks the component folder and reports the first problem found pack Creates a bundle for distribution, as a .zip or a .nupkg according to the extension of --output install Extracts the bundle into the components folder of the named profile, at {profinity-dir}/profiles/{profile}/components Flag Used by Required Meaning --component-dir validate, pack Yes The component folder --output pack Yes The bundle to write, which must end in .zip or .nupkg --package or --zip install Yes The bundle to install, ending in .zip or .nupkg. The two flags are aliases and cannot be combined --profinity-dir install Yes The Artifacts directory --engine-dir install Yes The engine bin folder, used to validate the bundle against the installed SDK version --profile install Yes The name of the profile to install into

Each flag takes one value and may be given once. The first positional argument can replace --component-dir (or --package for install), and the second positional argument can replace --output for pack.

docs.title: What validation requires
docs.text: validate and pack require component_metadata.yaml, settings_map.yaml, firmware_map.yaml and actions.yaml in the component folder, and report Missing required file: followed by the name when one is absent. The name in component_metadata.yaml must be usable as a folder name (Component name is not a valid folder name otherwise), and a .nupkg also needs a valid semantic pluginVersion and a non-empty author. Messages from actions.yaml that name a menu entry, such as an unsupported kind, are described on Menu actions.

docs.title: When to use the tool
docs.text: Use the tool when the same Custom Component is installed on more than one system, for example from a continuous integration (CI) pipeline that produces versioned bundles for field engineers, so that an administrator uploads one .nupkg in Components & Plugins instead of copying files into each profile by hand. A DLL plugin is packed as described on Developing Plugins, and a dashboard-only component can be copied through profile administration without a pack step. Custom Components compares Custom Components with Dashboard Components and DLL plugins.

docs.title: Developing Plugins
docs.text:
A plugin adds a component type that Profinity does not ship. It is compiled with the Profinity SDK, and an administrator installs it through Components & Plugins. Installing, enabling, and removing a plugin is covered on Components & Plugins.

A plugin is separate from a Custom Component, which is a bundle of files and scripts and needs no compiling. A plugin is the choice when the component needs compiled code. Custom Components compares the two.

docs.title: What the framework provides
docs.text:
The plugin framework is the same one Prohelion uses for its own components. A component built on it can:

  • Show a settings screen, a status, and a status message.
  • Publish tags that a profile can graph, log, and use in rules and scripts.
  • Offer actions on the component.
  • Connect to a device, broker, or server, show an error when the other end is down, and connect again when it appears. Refer to Connections and reconnecting.

The kit Prohelion sends to approved developers includes examples of this framework, and documentation that goes further than this page. For a copy of the SDK, or for more information, contact Prohelion.

Uploading a plugin needs the Modify plugins permission, described in Roles and Permissions, and the Custom Plugins feature. That feature is available from the Desktop edition upwards, and not when unlicensed. Refer to Licensing.

docs.title: Test a script outside Profinity
docs.text:
profinity-script creates a script on a developer machine and runs it against a simulated Profinity, before the script file is copied into a profile. The tool ships in the Profinity SDK, in the kit's profinity-script folder, and not with the Profinity install. On Windows the program is profinity-script.exe. The same kit contains profinity-component-pack and the Profinity.Sdk package. The package on its own does not create or run a script. The SDK is licensed separately. Refer to Licensing. For a copy of the SDK, contact Prohelion.

The simulator does not start Profinity and does not need a CAN bus. It calls the script the way Profinity does, and the script calls the same Profinity object. Once the script is in a profile it needs the Scripting feature, which a Desktop, Server, or Enterprise licence includes. Refer to Scripting.

A C# project in a generated folder references Profinity.Sdk. Add the kit folder that contains that package as a local NuGet source, so the editor can complete Profinity types. profinity-script sim compiles and runs the script itself. If a project still references Profinity.Component.Sdk, change that reference to Profinity.Sdk.

docs.title: Create a runnable script
docs.text:
Python and Lua need only profinity-script. Run the following commands from the kit's profinity-script folder. With no arguments, profinity-script runs sim in the current directory.

  1. Create a runnable Python script.

    profinity-script new runnable --language python

    The command writes a folder named runnable and prints its path. --language accepts python, lua, or csharp, and it defaults to python.

  2. Change into that folder.

    cd runnable

  3. Run the simulator.

    profinity-script sim

    The command prints ran and exits with no error message. That line is what script.py writes with Profinity.Console.WriteLine.

    ran

profinity-script sim runnable, run from the profinity-script folder, does the same thing without changing directory. profinity-script new with no template name prints the template names and exits with no error message.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
new copies one example folder. The folder contains sim.yaml and the script. The table is in the order profinity-script new prints.

Template Languages What the simulator runs runnable Python, Lua, and C# The script file. Python and Lua run it from the top, and C# calls Run. A scheduled script uses this mode. tag-change Python, Lua, and C# on_tag_change with the sample in sim.yaml. The example stores the value and prints nothing. receiver Python, Lua, and C# receive with one CAN packet. service Python, Lua, and C# on_start, then run, then on_stop. firmware-load Python A runnable script that sends a CAN packet and waits for the reply under onSend. rule-context Python on_alert with the rule id in sim.yaml. prompt Python A runnable script whose confirm prompt is answered from sim.yaml.

If on_start returns false, the simulator stops and does not call run or on_stop. If run returns false, the cycle loop stops and on_stop still runs. serviceCycles in sim.yaml is how many times run is called, and the default is 1. The simulator does not call on_pause or on_continue. The function or method for each mode is the one Profinity calls. Refer to Script types.

docs.title: The scenario file
docs.text:
sim.yaml sits next to the script. profinity-script sim reads it, runs the script, and prints the lines the script writes to the console. A script that only stores a tag or a setting prints nothing. The run has still worked when the command exits with no error message. Add Profinity.Console.WriteLine to see a stored value. The command does not print tags, settings, notifications, or CAN frames on its own.

The runnable example is this file:

version: "2.3"
script: script.py
mode: runnable
componentName: sim

A script that waits for a CAN reply names that reply under onSend. matchId is the id the script sends, and replyId is the id it receives. Both are decimal numbers: 256 is CAN id 0x100. The reply packet carries replyId and no data bytes. A wait uses the timeout the script passes, and a reply that is not listed does not arrive. Sending and receiving are on CAN bus.

version: "2.3"
script: script.py
mode: runnable
componentName: sim
onSend:
  - matchId: 256
    replyId: 257
Key Default Meaning version Write "2.3". script The script file name in this folder. mode runnable runnable, tagChange, receiver, service, or alert. tag-change is accepted for tagChange. rule and rule-context are accepted for alert. componentName sim The name of the simulated component. A script that looks up its component by name uses this value. tagId tag The tag id passed to a tag-change script, and the trigger tag on an alert, when the file omits the key. tagValue The sample value, in quotes, such as "12.5". steps A list of tag-change samples. Each item sets tagId, tagValue, or both. When the list is present, the simulator delivers the list and does not also deliver the single pair. A step that omits one of them uses the value at the top of the file. canId 0 The CAN id of the packet passed to a receiver script, as a decimal number. The packet has no data bytes. serviceCycles 1 How many times run is called after on_start returns true. promptConfirm true or false. This answers the first confirm prompt. With no value, a confirm prompt returns false. promptInput Text that answers the first input prompt. With no value, the prompt returns the default the script passed. ruleId rule The rule id and the rule name passed to an alert script. The level is warning and the transition is raised. componentFields Field identifiers that ComponentSettings can read and write. firmwareFields Field identifiers that FirmwareSettings can read and write. onSend Replies to packets the script sends. Each item has matchId and replyId.

A tag-change sample has quality Good, and its timestamp is the time of the run. Any other file in the folder is copied next to the script, so the script can load a sibling file. sim.yaml itself is not copied.

List every field identifier the script reads or writes under componentFields or firmwareFields. Without that entry, SetValue reports an unknown field. Refer to Component and firmware settings.

docs.title: Limits of the simulator
docs.text: The simulator covers the Profinity object the script calls, and the call Profinity makes into the script. It has no DBC database and no tag history. A DBC call fails with DBC lookup is not loaded in the Profinity script simulator. A tag-history call fails with Timeseries sources are not available in the Profinity script simulator. Profinity.Action is not set. A script that reads an action context is checked in a profile. Refer to Action context. Live hardware stays in Profinity.

docs.title: Copy the script into a profile
docs.text: When the console lines are right, copy the script file into the profile. Leave sim.yaml on the developer machine. Profinity runs the copied file. A script component is added as described in How to write your first script. A script that belongs to a Custom Component goes in that component, under the name the component already uses. Review the script before it is enabled. A script in a profile runs with the same operating system permissions as Profinity. Refer to Scripting.

docs.title: When the command fails
docs.text:
A failure prints one message on the error stream and exits with code 1. A C# script that does not compile prints the compiler messages there.

Message What to change No sim.yaml in followed by a path Run sim from the folder new created, or pass that folder. No python example for firmware-load, or the same sentence with another language and template That template does not ship in that language. firmware-load, rule-context, and prompt are Python only. Unknown sim mode followed by the mode Set mode to runnable, tagChange, receiver, service, or alert. Tag-change script must define an on_tag_change(tagId, sample) function Define the function that mode calls. Receiver, alert, and service scripts use the same form of message for receive, on_alert, and on_start. C# script has no public followed by an interface name Add a public class with a constructor that takes no arguments, implementing the interface for that mode. Refer to Script types.

docs.title: Profinity Scripting
docs.text:
Profinity scripting automates tasks, processes CAN messages and creates custom operations in C#, Python or Lua.

Licence required

Scripting requires the Scripting licensed feature, included in the Desktop, Server, and Enterprise editions. An unlicensed instance cannot add or run scripts. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

Rule actions, scripts, and Tag Relay, all built in

docs.title: Scripts run with the permissions of Profinity
docs.text:
Profinity scripts execute with the same security permissions as Profinity itself

Because Profinity Scripting runs inside the Profinity engine, any script executes with the same operating system security permissions as Profinity itself, so an administrator must review what each script does before it is enabled.

To keep the Profinity environment secure, scripting is disabled until it is explicitly enabled. To enable Profinity Scripting, open Application Config and turn on Enable Scripting.

Profinity System Configuration

docs.title: Script types
docs.text: Profinity has five script types, which between them cover seven values of the Script Mode setting: Run On Demand, Run On Receipt of CAN Message, Run On Tag Change, Run On Alert, Run On Time Interval, Run On CRON Schedule and Run as Service. Run Scripts cover manual and scheduled operations (the Run On Demand, Run On Time Interval and Run On CRON Schedule modes), Receive Scripts handle incoming CAN messages, Service Scripts run continuously, Tag Change Scripts react when a watched tag changes, and Rule Scripts handle a rule firing. The Script Types page describes each mode and when to use it. Refer to Rule Scripts and Actions.

docs.title: Supported languages
docs.text: A script can be written in C#, Python or Lua, and each language supports the same set of script types (Run, Receive, Service, Tag Change and Rule Script). C# suits complex, type-safe operations, Python suits data handling and quick edits, and Lua suits lightweight scripts. Refer to Supported Languages for the comparison.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Profinity provides five built-in operations to every script through the Profinity object: CAN Bus for CAN communication, DBC for Message and Signal handling, State for data that survives between runs, Console for output and logging, and Tags for reading and writing tag values. Scripts that belong to a Custom Component can also read and write Component and firmware settings. A script that a Custom Component runs from a firmware action also receives an action context, with the action name, any uploaded file, and progress reporting. The Supported Operations page describes each in more detail.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: Writing and testing a script on a developer machine, before it is copied into a profile, is covered on Test a script outside Profinity. Supported Languages helps with choosing a language, Script Types with choosing a script style, and Supported Operations lists what a script can do. A first script is built in How to Write Your First Script.

docs.title: Script examples
docs.text:
This page holds worked script examples that read a DBC signal, send a CAN message and persist script state. To add a script component and run a first script, refer to How to write your first script. Scripting needs a Desktop, Server, or Enterprise licence. Refer to Licensing.

Scripts run with application permissions

A script runs inside Profinity with the same operating system permissions as the application, so review any script before running it. Refer to the Scripting overview for the security context and behaviour.

The following examples use the Example Profile, so load it and replay example_log.csv as described in the Quick Start Guide to give them data. Use names from your own DBC and profile in other profiles: Component, Message and Signal are case-sensitive, and a name that does not exist raises an error. Confirm the names in the DBC viewer in Profinity. Refer to DBC.

docs.title: Reading a DBC signal value
Sending a CAN message
docs.text:
Payload data can be built from a byte array (in C#) or set as typed properties on CanBusPacket (for example Int32Pos0 and Int32Pos1) when the layout matches your frames. The CanBusPacket type is available to C# scripts without an extra using statement, and Python scripts import it from Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus. A sent message goes onto the connected CAN bus, so use IDs that are safe for the devices on that bus.

C#Python 
// Method 1: Byte array
var packetBytes = new CanBusPacket(0x123, new byte[] { 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04 });
Profinity.CAN.Send(packetBytes);

// Method 2: Property-based (common when filling structured data)
var packetProps = new CanBusPacket(0x100)
{
    Int32Pos0 = 100,
    Int32Pos1 = 200
};
Profinity.CAN.Send(packetProps);

from Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus import CanBusPacket

# Property-based (common when filling structured data)
packet_props = CanBusPacket(0x100)
packet_props.Int32Pos0 = 100
packet_props.Int32Pos1 = 200
Profinity.CAN.Send(packet_props)

docs.title: Persisting script state
Supported operations
docs.text:
The following operations are available to every script, regardless of the language used, through the Profinity object.

  • CAN bus communication: scripts can send CAN packets and read the latest received packets. Refer to CAN Bus for examples and usage.
  • DBC message and signal information: scripts can read signal values from the loaded DBC files by component, message, and signal name, with the raw CAN data converted to physical values. Refer to DBC for examples and usage.
  • State management: Profinity provides two state stores. State keeps data for a single script between its runs, and GlobalState shares data across multiple scripts. Refer to State for examples and usage.
  • Tags: scripts can read tag values, publish values to tags, and attach metadata to the tags they publish. Refer to Tags for examples and usage.
  • Console output: scripts in all three languages can write information and error messages to the Profinity log. Refer to Console for examples and usage.

A script started by a firmware action also receives an action context: the action name, any uploaded file, the invoker, and progress reporting. Refer to Action context.

docs.title: Component and firmware settings
docs.text: A script on a Custom Component reads settings_map.yaml with Profinity.ComponentSettings and firmware_map.yaml with Profinity.FirmwareSettings. firmware.yaml names the scripts that load and save those firmware values. Refer to Component and firmware settings for the methods, which script reads or writes each value, and an example.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Each operation has its own page. The Profinity SDK page describes how to write and test a script offline, and Profinity offers a starting template for each script type when you create a script. The Profinity repository on GitHub also holds further C# and Python examples. The language references are on Supported Languages.

docs.title: Action context
docs.text:
Profinity.Action is set for the duration of a script that a Custom Component runs from a firmware action. The object carries the action name, any file the operator uploaded, the user who started the action, and a way for the script to report progress. When the script returns, Profinity clears Profinity.Action.

A firmware action is an entry under actions in firmware.yaml. Refer to Firmware actions.

The load script and the save script (loadScript and saveScript) do not receive this object. On a menu button, a scheduled run, a service, a tag change, a CAN receive, and a rule script, Profinity.Action is null (None in Python, nil in Lua). A script checks for null before it reads the object.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
Property Meaning Name The action's display name from firmware.yaml Group The action group. Firmware actions use Firmware FileName The profile-relative name of the uploaded file, or null when the action takes no file FilePath The absolute path of that file after Profinity has resolved it, or null InvokedByUsername The user who started the action InvokedByJti The session identifier of that user Variables A string dictionary. When a file was uploaded it contains fileName and filePath, with the same values as FileName and FilePath

GetVariable(key) returns the value for that key, or null when the key is missing or empty.

docs.title: Reporting progress
docs.text:
ReportProgress(progress) takes a number from 0.0 to 1.0, and Profinity limits the value to that range. The firmware action shows that fraction as its percentage complete.

C#PythonLua 
if (Profinity.Action != null)
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine(Profinity.Action.Name);
    string path = Profinity.Action.FilePath;
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine(path);
    Profinity.Action.ReportProgress(1.0);
}

if Profinity.Action is not None:
    print(Profinity.Action.Name)
    print(Profinity.Action.FilePath)
    Profinity.Action.ReportProgress(1.0)

if Profinity.Action ~= nil then
    print(Profinity.Action.Name)
    print(Profinity.Action.FilePath)
    Profinity.Action:ReportProgress(1.0)
end

The rule firing passed to OnAlert or on_alert is a separate object. Refer to Rule scripts.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text: The CAN bus operations let a script work with Controller Area Network (CAN) traffic: send CAN packets, read the latest received packets, and look packets up by CAN ID. They are reached through two script variables. Profinity.CAN is the script's own CAN client, which suits waiting for and buffering the packets one script cares about, and Profinity.CANBus is the shared cache of the latest packet for every CAN ID that the Profinity engine has seen. For real-time packet reception, Receive Scripts run automatically when matching CAN packets are received.

docs.title: Sending CAN packets
docs.text:
The following examples create a CAN packet and transmit it to the bus. A packet is created from its CAN ID and then filled using the typed data properties such as Int32Pos0 and Int32Pos1, and in C# a packet can also be created directly from a byte array.

C#PythonLua 
// Create a packet with CAN ID 0x100 and fill it using typed properties
var packet = new CanBusPacket(0x100)
{
    Int32Pos0 = 100,
    Int32Pos1 = 200
};
bool sent = Profinity.CAN.Send(packet);

// Or create a packet from a byte array and send it through the CAN bus service
var bytePacket = new CanBusPacket(0x123, new byte[] { 0x01, 0x02, 0x03, 0x04 });
int packetsSent = Profinity.CANBus.SendMessage(bytePacket);

from Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus import CanBusPacket

# Create a packet with CAN ID 0x100 and fill it using typed properties
packet = CanBusPacket(0x100)
packet.Int32Pos0 = 100
packet.Int32Pos1 = 200
sent = Profinity.CAN.Send(packet)

-- Create a packet with CAN ID 0x100 and fill it using typed properties
local packet = CanBusPacket(0x100)
packet.Int32Pos0 = 100
packet.Int32Pos1 = 200
local sent = Profinity.CAN:Send(packet)

Profinity.CAN.Send() returns true when the packet was sent. Profinity.CANBus.SendMessage() returns the number of interfaces the packet was sent on (one for each CAN adapter the packet went out on, so more than one when several CAN adapters are configured).

docs.title: Accessing latest received packets
docs.text:
Profinity maintains a cache of the latest received CAN packets, from which a script can read the most recent packet or query packets by CAN ID. Profinity.CAN.LatestValidPacketReceivedByID() returns the latest packet for a CAN ID only while it is still valid (a packet is expired once it is older than the script's Milliseconds Valid setting, which defaults to 5000 and accepts -1 to 60000, where -1 means packets never expire and 0 means no packet is ever valid; a script saved earlier with 0 now sees no valid packets until it is changed to -1 or a window). The method returns null (None in Python, nil in Lua) when no valid packet exists. Milliseconds Valid is shown only in Run On Receipt of CAN Message mode.

C#PythonLua 
// Get the latest valid packet for a specific CAN ID
CanBusPacket validPacket = Profinity.CAN.LatestValidPacketReceivedByID(0x123);

// Get the most recently received packet (any CAN ID) from the CAN bus service
CanBusPacket latestPacket = Profinity.CANBus.LatestCanBusPacketReceived;

// Get the latest packet for a specific CAN ID from the CAN bus service
CanBusPacket packetById = Profinity.CANBus.LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x123);

// Or access the dictionary of latest packets keyed by CAN ID
if (Profinity.CANBus.LatestCanBusPacketsReceived.TryGetValue(0x123, out CanBusPacket packet))
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Latest packet for 0x123: {packet.CanIdAsHex}");
}

# Get the latest valid packet for a specific CAN ID
valid_packet = Profinity.CAN.LatestValidPacketReceivedByID(0x123)

# Get the most recently received packet (any CAN ID) from the CAN bus service
latest_packet = Profinity.CANBus.LatestCanBusPacketReceived

# Get the latest packet for a specific CAN ID from the CAN bus service
packet_by_id = Profinity.CANBus.LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x123)

if packet_by_id is not None:
    print(f"Latest packet for 0x123: {packet_by_id.CanIdAsHex}")

-- Get the latest valid packet for a specific CAN ID
local validPacket = Profinity.CAN:LatestValidPacketReceivedByID(0x123)

-- Get the most recently received packet (any CAN ID) from the CAN bus service
local latestPacket = Profinity.CANBus.LatestCanBusPacketReceived

-- Get the latest packet for a specific CAN ID from the CAN bus service
local packetById = Profinity.CANBus:LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x123)

if packetById ~= nil then
    print('Latest packet for 0x123: ' .. packetById.CanIdAsHex)
end

docs.title: Receiving CAN packets in real-time
docs.text:
For real-time CAN packet reception, use Receive Scripts. Receive scripts automatically execute when matching CAN packets are received, which suits real-time monitoring and processing.

C#PythonLua 
using System;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus;

public class MyReceiverScript : ProfinityScript, IProfinityReceiverScript
{
    public void Receive(CanBusPacket canPacket)
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Received packet: {canPacket.CanIdAsHex}");
        // Process the packet in real-time
    }
}

def receive(canPacket):
    print(f"Received packet: {canPacket.CanIdAsHex}")
    # Process the packet in real-time

function receive(canPacket)
    print('Received packet: ' .. canPacket.CanIdAsHex)
    -- Process the packet in real-time
end

docs.title: Complete example
docs.text:
The following example sends a packet and then checks for a response.

C#PythonLua 
using System;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus;

public class CanExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityRunnableScript
{
    public bool Run()
    {
        // Send a request packet
        var requestPacket = new CanBusPacket(0x100, new byte[] { 0x01, 0x02 });
        int sent = Profinity.CANBus.SendMessage(requestPacket);
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Sent on {sent} interface(s)");

        // Wait a bit for response
        System.Threading.Thread.Sleep(100);

        // Check for response packet
        CanBusPacket response = Profinity.CANBus.LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x101);
        if (response != null)
        {
            Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Received response: {response.CanIdAsHex}");
            return true;
        }

        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("No response received");
        return false;
    }
}

import time
from Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus import CanBusPacket

# Send a request packet
request_packet = CanBusPacket(0x100)
request_packet.BytePos0 = 0x01
request_packet.BytePos1 = 0x02
sent = Profinity.CANBus.SendMessage(request_packet)
print(f"Sent on {sent} interface(s)")

# Wait a bit for response
time.sleep(0.1)

# Check for response packet
response = Profinity.CANBus.LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x101)
if response is not None:
    print(f"Received response: {response.CanIdAsHex}")
else:
    print("No response received")

-- Send a request packet
local requestPacket = CanBusPacket(0x100)
requestPacket.BytePos0 = 0x01
requestPacket.BytePos1 = 0x02
local sent = Profinity.CANBus:SendMessage(requestPacket)
print('Sent on ' .. tostring(sent) .. ' interface(s)')

-- Wait a bit for response
sleep(0.1)

-- Check for response packet
local response = Profinity.CANBus:LatestReceivedCanBusPacketById(0x101)
if response ~= nil then
    print('Received response: ' .. response.CanIdAsHex)
else
    print('No response received')
end

docs.title: Notes on receiving and sending
docs.text: Receive Scripts are the better choice for real-time packet reception than polling LatestCanBusPacketReceived. The LatestCanBusPacketsReceived dictionary stores only the most recent packet for each CAN ID, so an older packet is overwritten by a newer one. A script should check for null, None or nil before it reads packet properties, because no packet may exist for a given CAN ID. The SendMessage() return value is the number of interfaces the packet was sent on, which helps when debugging a multi-adapter configuration.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
Console output is available in every script and writes to two streams. Standard output reaches the Profinity log at the Info level only when the script's Log Script Output setting is on, and the setting is off by default, so a script whose print() output does not appear in the log needs that setting switched on. Error output and script exceptions always reach the Profinity log at the Error level, whatever the setting.

Each language writes to the console in its own way. In C# the console is Profinity.Console. In Python, print() writes standard output and print(..., file=sys.stderr) writes error output. In Lua, print(...) writes standard output and the stderr(...) global writes error output.

docs.title: Example usage
docs.text:
The examples below show standard output and error stream usage in each language.

C#PythonLua 
// Write normal program output
Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Starting script execution...");

try
{
    // Perform some operation
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Operation completed successfully");
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // Write error to error stream
    Profinity.Console.Error.WriteLine($"Error occurred: {ex.Message}");
}

import sys

# Write normal program output
print("Starting script execution...")

try:
    # Perform some operation
    print("Operation completed successfully")
except Exception as ex:
    # Write error to error stream
    print(f"Error occurred: {ex}", file=sys.stderr)

-- Write normal program output
print('Starting script execution...')

local ok, err = pcall(function()
    -- Perform some operation
    print('Operation completed successfully')
end)

if not ok then
    -- Write error to error stream
    stderr('Error occurred: ' .. tostring(err))
end

The standard output stream is for normal program output and the error stream is for error messages and warnings. Output is held in memory, so a script should limit how much it writes.

docs.title: DBC
docs.text:
The DBC functionality in Profinity provides tools for reading signals defined in the CAN bus database (DBC) files that are loaded by the components in a profile. These files define the structure of CAN messages, including signals, message IDs, and data formats. A script does not load or parse a DBC file itself, because the DBC file is loaded by the component that owns it, and the script looks up that component's signals by name through Profinity.DBC. The DBC viewer shows the Component, Message, and Signal names that a script needs to track.

A script can look up a signal definition from a component's loaded DBC file by component, message, and signal name, read signal properties such as the unit, minimum, maximum, and comment, and read the current physical value of a signal, converted from the latest raw CAN data using the signal's factor and offset.

docs.title: The GetDbcSignal method
docs.text: The GetDbcSignal method retrieves a signal definition from a component's loaded DBC file using the component name, message name and signal name.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
C#PythonLua 
DbcSignal signal = Profinity.DBC.GetDbcSignal(string component, string message, string signal);

signal = Profinity.DBC.GetDbcSignal(component, message, signal)

local signal = Profinity.DBC:GetDbcSignal(component, message, signal)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text: Parameter Meaning component The name of the component in the profile that owns the DBC file message The name of the CAN message containing the signal signal The name of the signal to retrieve

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: Returns a DbcSignal object containing the signal definition. The method throws an ArgumentException when the component, message, or signal cannot be found, so a script that could reference a missing name wraps the call in try/catch (C#), try/except (Python) or pcall (Lua).

docs.title: Value property
docs.text:
The most important property of the returned DbcSignal object is the Value property, which returns the current physical value of the signal, or NaN (not a number) when no valid value is available, for example when no packet has been received for the message yet or the last packet is older than the DBC validity period.

C#PythonLua 
try
{
    // Get a signal definition
    var signal = Profinity.DBC.GetDbcSignal("ECU", "EngineData", "EngineSpeed");

    // Get the current physical value of the signal
    double currentValue = signal.Value;
    if (double.IsNaN(currentValue))
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("No valid value for EngineSpeed yet");
    }
    else
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Current engine speed: {currentValue} {signal.Unit}");
    }
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Error reading DBC signal: {ex.Message}");
}

import math

try:
    # Get a signal definition
    signal = Profinity.DBC.GetDbcSignal("ECU", "EngineData", "EngineSpeed")

    # Get the current physical value of the signal
    current_value = signal.Value
    if math.isnan(current_value):
        print("No valid value for EngineSpeed yet")
    else:
        print(f"Current engine speed: {current_value} {signal.Unit}")
except Exception as ex:
    print(f"Error reading DBC signal: {ex}")

local ok, signal = pcall(function()
    return Profinity.DBC:GetDbcSignal('ECU', 'EngineData', 'EngineSpeed')
end)

if ok then
    local currentValue = signal.Value
    -- NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself
    if currentValue ~= currentValue then
        print('No valid value for EngineSpeed yet')
    else
        print('Current engine speed: ' .. tostring(currentValue) .. ' ' .. tostring(signal.Unit))
    end
else
    print('Error reading DBC signal: ' .. tostring(signal))
end

docs.title: Names and conversion
docs.text: GetDbcSignal throws an ArgumentException (Component not found: followed by the name, when the component is the one that does not match) if any of the parameters do not match the profile or the DBC file. The Value property converts the raw CAN data to the physical value using the signal's factor and offset, and returns NaN when the device is not valid or no current packet is available.

docs.title: Component and firmware settings
docs.text:
A script on a Custom Component reads and writes two sets of saved values. Profinity.ComponentSettings uses the field identifiers in settings_map.yaml. Profinity.FirmwareSettings uses the field identifiers in firmware_map.yaml. firmware.yaml names the scripts that load and save firmware.

The layout of settings_map.yaml is on Settings. The layout of firmware_map.yaml is on Firmware maps. firmware.yaml is on Firmware actions. A firmware action script also receives Action context.

docs.title: Which script reads which values
docs.text:
Each Custom Component script uses one or both objects.

Script Values Main script ComponentSettings toggle in actions.yaml ComponentSettings button in actions.yaml ComponentSettings loadScript in firmware.yaml Reads ComponentSettings, writes FirmwareSettings saveScript in firmware.yaml Reads FirmwareSettings and ComponentSettings An entry under actions in firmware.yaml Either object, and Profinity.Action is set

When each script runs is on Script types.

A load script opens the device with the values in ComponentSettings, such as a COM port and a baud rate, then calls FirmwareSettings.SetValue once for each field it read from the device. Those values are what the firmware page shows after a successful load. A save script reads the same fields with FirmwareSettings.GetValue and sends them to the device. Profinity.Action is set only for an entry under actions.

A load or save script reports success the same way as a Run script. In C#, Run() returns true or false. In Python and Lua the file runs from the top, and the script reports failure by raising an error. Refer to Run scripts.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
ComponentSettings and FirmwareSettings have the same methods. Pass the field identifier from the map, such as comPort or nmeaGgaRate. GetValue also accepts the prefixed form returned in metadata, such as SETTINGS.comPort. C#, Python and Lua call the methods with a dot.

Method What it returns GetValue(fieldId) The saved value, or null in C#, None in Python and nil in Lua when the field is missing or empty TryGetValue(fieldId, out value) Whether the field exists. In C# the value is an out argument SetValue(fieldId, value) Nothing. Saves the value, or fails with one of the messages below TrySetValue(fieldId, value, out errorMessage) Whether the save succeeded. The error message is an out argument in C# GetMetadata(fieldId) A dictionary of the field definition, or an empty dictionary when the field identifier is unknown GetAllMetadata() A dictionary of every field, keyed by field identifier, or an empty dictionary when the component has no map GetMapDefinition() The map's field definitions, or null when the component has no map

GetMetadata is the dictionary a script reads by key. GetMapDefinition returns the same definitions as objects.

Entry Meaning id Field identifier, including a SETTINGS. or FIRMWARE. prefix label Name shown on the settings or firmware page description Help text from the map, or null type Resolved type: StringValue, NumberValue, BooleanValue, HexValue, ListValues, IPAddressValue, PasswordValue, EmailValue or InformationValue readOnly Whether the operator can edit the field required Whether the field must have a value

A STRING field in the map is StringValue, a BOOL field is BooleanValue, a LIST field is ListValues, and a numeric field such as UINT8 or UINT32 is NumberValue.

docs.title: Saved values
docs.text:
GetValue returns the value last saved for that field. For a LIST field, that value is the text shown for the row the operator chose. Refer to Settings. Convert a numeric field before using it as an integer: in Python, int(str(value)) accepts both a number and text. SetValue stores the value the script passes.

ComponentSettings also reads the component's own settings by property name. DBCFilename is the uploaded DBC file, and RebaseAddress is the rebase address. Setting RebaseAddress to a value that is not a number fails.

Failure Message Unknown field on ComponentSettings Unknown component settings field id. Unknown field on FirmwareSettings Unknown firmware field id. FirmwareSettings when the component has no firmware map Firmware settings are not available on this component. Either object when the script has no host component This script has no host component - ComponentSettings is only available to a component-scoped script. The firmware message uses FirmwareSettings in that sentence

profinity-script sim runs the script on a simulated component. List the field identifiers under componentFields and firmwareFields in sim.yaml so SetValue can save them, and GetValue returns a value only after one has been saved. The rest of that file is on Test a script outside Profinity. Without those entries, SetValue reports an unknown field.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The example is a firmware load script. comPort is a field in settings_map.yaml, and nmeaGgaRate is a field in firmware_map.yaml, both from the G-STAR IV sample. A script uses the field identifiers from its own map files. A save script reads nmeaGgaRate with GetValue instead of writing it.

C#PythonLua 
using System;

public class LoadFirmwareExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityRunnableScript
{
    public bool Run()
    {
        object port = Profinity.ComponentSettings.GetValue("comPort");
        if (port == null)
        {
            Profinity.Console.WriteLine("COM port is not set");
            return false;
        }

        Profinity.FirmwareSettings.SetValue("nmeaGgaRate", 1);
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Firmware load wrote nmeaGgaRate");
        return true;
    }
}

port = Profinity.ComponentSettings.GetValue("comPort")
if port is None:
    print("COM port is not set")
    raise SystemExit(1)

Profinity.FirmwareSettings.SetValue("nmeaGgaRate", 1)
print("Firmware load wrote nmeaGgaRate")

local port = Profinity.ComponentSettings.GetValue("comPort")
if port == nil then
    print("COM port is not set")
    error("COM port is not set")
end

Profinity.FirmwareSettings.SetValue("nmeaGgaRate", 1)
print("Firmware load wrote nmeaGgaRate")

The settings map layout is on Settings, the firmware map layout is on Firmware maps, and firmware.yaml is on Firmware actions. How to choose a script shape is on Script types.

docs.title: State
docs.text: Scripts in Profinity run and then stop, so information that must survive between invocations of a script, or be shared between different scripts, needs to be held in state. Profinity provides two key-value stores for this, with examples below in C#, Python and Lua. State holds values that persist between runs of the same script, so a script that runs several times finds the values it stored on the earlier runs. GlobalState holds values that every script can read and change, which allows scripts to pass data to each other. Either store accepts any object type as a value, and each individual call is thread-safe, so several scripts can use the stores at the same time.

docs.title: Storing state values
docs.text:
The examples below save data to both the local and global state stores, using different value types.

C#PythonLua 
// Store a value that persists between runs of this script
Profinity.State.Set("scriptRunCount", 42);

// Store a value that can be shared with other scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("totalScriptsRun", "Shared data");

// Store complex objects
Profinity.State.Set("lastRunConfig", new { Name = "Local", Value = 100 });
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedConfig", new { Name = "Global", Value = 200 });

# Store a value that persists between runs of this script
Profinity.State.Set("scriptRunCount", 42)

# Store a value that can be shared with other scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("totalScriptsRun", "Shared data")

# Store complex objects
Profinity.State.Set("lastRunConfig", {"Name": "Local", "Value": 100})
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedConfig", {"Name": "Global", "Value": 200})

-- Store a value that persists between runs of this script
Profinity.State:Set('scriptRunCount', 42)

-- Store a value that can be shared with other scripts
Profinity.GlobalState:Set('totalScriptsRun', 'Shared data')

docs.title: Retrieving state values
docs.text:
Any stored key can be retrieved from both the local and global state stores, and a key that does not exist returns null.

C#PythonLua 
// Retrieve state from previous runs of this script
object runCount = Profinity.State.Get("scriptRunCount");

// Retrieve state shared by other scripts
object totalRuns = Profinity.GlobalState.Get("totalScriptsRun");

// Retrieve and test for a specific type, because Get returns object
if (Profinity.State.Get("scriptRunCount") is int lastRunValue)
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine($"Previous value: {lastRunValue}");
}
object sharedConfig = Profinity.GlobalState.Get("sharedConfig");

# Retrieve state from previous runs of this script
run_count = Profinity.State.Get("scriptRunCount")

# Retrieve state shared by other scripts
total_runs = Profinity.GlobalState.Get("totalScriptsRun")

# Retrieve and use values
last_run_config = Profinity.State.Get("lastRunConfig")
shared_config = Profinity.GlobalState.Get("sharedConfig")

-- Retrieve state from previous runs of this script
local runCount = Profinity.State:Get('scriptRunCount')

-- Retrieve state shared by other scripts
local totalRuns = Profinity.GlobalState:Get('totalScriptsRun')

print('Run count: ' .. tostring(runCount))
print('Total runs: ' .. tostring(totalRuns))

docs.title: More complete examples
docs.text:
The examples below show both State and GlobalState in typical scenarios, including a run counter and shared configuration. The C# and Python versions are shown, and Lua uses the Profinity.State:Get and Profinity.State:Set calls from the examples above for the same pattern.

C#Python 
// Store configuration that persists between runs of this script
Profinity.State.Set("scriptConfig", new {
    Timeout = 5000,
    RetryCount = 3,
    LogLevel = "Debug"
});

// Store configuration that can be shared with other scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedConfig", new {
    MaxConnections = 100,
    DefaultTimeout = 10000
});

// Track number of times this script has run
int runCount = Profinity.State.Get("runCount") is int previousCount ? previousCount : 0;
Profinity.State.Set("runCount", runCount + 1);

// Share data between scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedData", new {
    LastRunTime = DateTime.Now,
    TotalProcessed = 1000
});

from datetime import datetime

# Store configuration that persists between runs of this script
Profinity.State.Set("scriptConfig", {
    "Timeout": 5000,
    "RetryCount": 3,
    "LogLevel": "Debug"
})

# Store configuration that can be shared with other scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedConfig", {
    "MaxConnections": 100,
    "DefaultTimeout": 10000
})

# Track number of times this script has run
run_count = Profinity.State.Get("runCount")
if run_count is None:
    run_count = 0
Profinity.State.Set("runCount", run_count + 1)

# Share data between scripts
Profinity.GlobalState.Set("sharedData", {
    "LastRunTime": datetime.now(),
    "TotalProcessed": 1000
})

docs.title: Thread safety and limits
docs.text:
Each store has three methods: Get(key), Set(key, value) and Clear(), which removes every value in the store. The individual calls are thread-safe, but a sequence of calls is not atomic, so a read followed by a write, such as the run counter in the examples above, can lose an update when two scripts run it at the same time on the same GlobalState key. Neither store survives a Profinity restart, and both keep their values in memory, so a script should store only the data it needs.

Get returns null for a key that has not been set, so every Get should be checked for null. Name each key for its purpose, store one value type under each key, and prefix the keys written to GlobalState with the script name so that two scripts do not overwrite each other.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
The Tags object lets a script read tag values, publish values to tags, and describe the tags it publishes. It is provided automatically in every script, in every script mode, and works the same way in C#, Python and Lua.

Access to tags varies by language:

  • C#: Profinity.Tags.SetValue(...)
  • Python: Profinity.Tags.SetValue(...)
  • Lua: Profinity.Tags:SetValue(...) (note the colon)

docs.title: Tag paths
docs.text:
Paths passed to Profinity.Tags can address any tag in the tag tree. How a path is written decides where it starts:

Path Starts at Example (script on a component named Inverter) No leading / The script's host component SpeedKmh is the tag Inverter/SpeedKmh. Leading / The root of the tag tree /Battery/Voltage is the tag Battery/Voltage, on another component.

A leading / means the same as it does in dashboards and rules: the root of the tag tree. A relative path that has several segments, such as Battery/Voltage or position/latitude, is still placed under the host component, so Battery/Voltage on Inverter is Inverter/Battery/Voltage. A relative path that already starts with the host component's name is used as it is, so Inverter/SpeedKmh and SpeedKmh are the same tag.

Use a relative path for a script's own component, which keeps the script working if the component is renamed or copied, and a leading / to read or write tags that belong to other components. If the component is mounted in a folder using a Tag tree path, a relative path still starts at the component, and a path with a leading / starts at the root of the whole tree, so it includes that folder.

Paths are not a security boundary

Resolving relative paths under the host component is for convenience. It is not a sandbox or an authorisation check, and a script can reach any tag in the tree, so treat scripts as trusted code that runs inside the Profinity engine.

Tag ids passed to a Tag Change script are full tag ids. To use one with Profinity.Tags, add a leading /, for example Profinity.Tags.GetSample("/" + tagId), and to compare one, match on the end of the id, as the examples there do.

A script can read the current sample for a tag, including its quality and timestamp, publish a value to a tag (creating the tag path if it does not exist), clear a value or mark a tag stale, attach catalogue metadata to a tag, and browse the tag catalogue.

docs.title: Reading tag values
docs.text:
GetSample returns a sample for the tag. If the tag cannot be found, the sample has a Quality of Unavailable rather than throwing, so check the quality before using the value. ReadSample returns true and fills in the sample only when the tag exists.

A sample has these properties:

Property Description Value The scalar reading, or null when unavailable. Enumeration values are returned as their name. Quality Good, Unavailable, Stale or Bad. UtcTimestamp The source timestamp in UTC. Reason A machine-readable reason for the quality. Message Optional detail for errors and diagnostics. C#PythonLua 
var sample = Profinity.Tags.GetSample("SpeedKmh");

if (sample.Quality == TagQuality.Good)
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Speed is " + sample.Value + " at " + sample.UtcTimestamp);
}
else
{
    Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Speed unavailable: " + sample.Reason);
}

sample = Profinity.Tags.GetSample("SpeedKmh")

if str(sample.Quality) == "Good":
    print("Speed is " + str(sample.Value) + " at " + str(sample.UtcTimestamp))
else:
    print("Speed unavailable: " + str(sample.Reason))

local sample = Profinity.Tags:GetSample('SpeedKmh')

if tostring(sample.Quality) == 'Good' then
    print('Speed is ' .. tostring(sample.Value) .. ' at ' .. tostring(sample.UtcTimestamp))
else
    print('Speed unavailable: ' .. tostring(sample.Reason))
end

To read a tag on another component, start the path with /:

C#PythonLua 
var voltage = Profinity.Tags.GetSample("/Battery/Voltage");

voltage = Profinity.Tags.GetSample("/Battery/Voltage")

local voltage = Profinity.Tags:GetSample('/Battery/Voltage')

docs.title: Writing tag values
docs.text:
SetValue publishes a value to a tag. It creates the tag path first if it does not exist, and returns true when the write succeeds. Values must be scalar (a number, string, or true/false value). Other types are rejected.

SetValue also accepts a quality as a third argument. ClearValue sets the value to null, and MarkStale flags the existing value as stale without changing it.

C#PythonLua 
// Publish a value
Profinity.Tags.SetValue("SpeedKmh", 88.5);

// Publish a value with an explicit quality
Profinity.Tags.SetValue("SpeedKmh", 88.5, TagQuality.Stale);

// Remove the value, or mark it as out of date
Profinity.Tags.ClearValue("SpeedKmh");
Profinity.Tags.MarkStale("SpeedKmh");

# Publish a value
Profinity.Tags.SetValue("SpeedKmh", 88.5)

# Remove the value, or mark it as out of date
Profinity.Tags.ClearValue("SpeedKmh")
Profinity.Tags.MarkStale("SpeedKmh")

-- Publish a value
Profinity.Tags:SetValue('SpeedKmh', 88.5)

-- Remove the value, or mark it as out of date
Profinity.Tags:ClearValue('SpeedKmh')
Profinity.Tags:MarkStale('SpeedKmh')

A script can trigger itself

A script that writes a tag it is also watching in a Tag Change script can trigger itself, so it should watch the source tag and publish to a different tag.

docs.title: Creating tags and adding metadata
docs.text:
EnsurePath creates a writable tag path without writing a value, and can attach catalogue metadata at the same time. SetMeta adds or updates metadata on an existing tag, either one key at a time or as a dictionary. Each returns true on success.

C#PythonLua 
Profinity.Tags.EnsurePath("SpeedKmh", new Dictionary<string, object> { { "unit", "km/h" } });
Profinity.Tags.SetMeta("SpeedKmh", "description", "Vehicle speed in kilometres per hour");

Profinity.Tags.EnsurePath("SpeedKmh", {"unit": "km/h"})
Profinity.Tags.SetMeta("SpeedKmh", "description", "Vehicle speed in kilometres per hour")

Profinity.Tags:EnsurePath('SpeedKmh')
Profinity.Tags:SetMeta('SpeedKmh', 'description', 'Vehicle speed in kilometres per hour')

docs.title: Browsing the tag catalogue
docs.text: GetCatalog returns the tag tree as a nested JSON object, and GetFlatCatalog returns it as a flat JSON array of tags. Both take an optional includeLeafSamples argument. Pass true to include each leaf tag's current sample, which is more expensive on large trees.

docs.title: Method summary
docs.text:
Method Purpose GetSample(path) Returns the current sample, with Unavailable quality if the tag does not exist. ReadSample(path, out sample) Returns true and the sample only when the tag exists. SetValue(path, value [, quality]) Publishes a value, creating the path if needed. ClearValue(path) Sets the value to null. MarkStale(path) Flags the current value as stale. EnsurePath(path [, meta]) Creates a writable tag path, optionally with metadata. SetMeta(path, key, value) or SetMeta(path, meta) Adds or updates catalogue metadata. GetCatalog([includeLeafSamples]) Returns the tag tree as nested JSON. GetFlatCatalog([includeLeafSamples]) Returns the tag tree as a flat JSON array.

For related pages, refer to Derived tags and State.

docs.title: Script types
docs.text:
Profinity supports seven script modes, each with its own trigger and execution context: Run On Demand, Run On Receipt of CAN Message, Run On Tag Change, Run On Alert, Run On Time Interval, Run On CRON Schedule and Run as Service. The Script Mode setting selects the mode. This page explains the differences between the modes and when to use each one. A Custom Component main script is a service script, and a firmware load, save, or action script runs once.

Script Mode Selection and Configuration in the Profinity UI

docs.title: Choosing a mode
docs.text:
Script type Mode Use it for Run Script Run On Demand Short jobs that need little state, such as one-time operations, testing, and troubleshooting. The operator starts the script. Run Script Run On Time Interval Work that starts at a fixed interval, for example every 5 minutes or every hour. Run Script Run On CRON Schedule Time-of-day, weekly, and monthly work. The script starts from a Quartz cron expression. Receive Script Run On Receipt of CAN Message Answering a packet with a reply message. The script runs each time a matching CAN packet arrives. Service Script Run as Service Continuous monitoring and other work that runs for a long time. The script implements a full lifecycle (start, stop, pause, and continue). Tag Change Script Run On Tag Change Computed tags, reacting to another component's output and chained automation without polling. The script runs each time a watched tag changes. Rule Script Run On Alert Notifications and side effects beyond the built-in rule actions. The script runs when a rule names it as an action.

A Run Script is not the right choice for continuous monitoring or real-time responses, and a Service Script is not the right choice for one-off or manual tasks. A Receive, Tag Change or Rule Script handler should return quickly, because a new event that arrives while it is still running is handled according to Trigger Overlap.

docs.title: Custom Component scripts
docs.text:
A Custom Component script is a file named on the component. Script Mode applies to a script component.

Script Runs as Main script Service scripts, started by Auto Start Main Script or Connect / Disconnect toggle in actions.yaml Service script button in actions.yaml Once, when the operator chooses the menu item loadScript in firmware.yaml Once, when firmware is loaded saveScript in firmware.yaml Once, when firmware is saved An entry under actions in firmware.yaml Once, with an action context

Profinity.Action is set only for an entry under actions. Which values each script reads or writes is on Component and firmware settings. The settings map layout is on Settings, the firmware map layout is on Firmware maps, and firmware.yaml is on Firmware actions. The action object is on Action context.

docs.title: Script settings
docs.text:
Each script component has the following settings. The schedule, receive, and tag change settings appear only for the mode that uses them.

Setting Applies to Meaning Script Mode All The mode the script runs in Auto Start Script All Starts the script when Profinity starts. Off by default Log Script Output All Writes the script's console output to the script log. Off by default Trigger Overlap Run On Receipt of CAN Message, Run On Tag Change, Run On Alert What happens to an event that arrives while the handler is still running. Drop (the default) discards it, and Queue keeps a short backlog and runs it afterwards Queue Depth Trigger Overlap set to Queue How many events may wait, from 1 to 100, with a default of 8. Further events are dropped Time Interval and Time Interval Unit Run On Time Interval How often the script runs, in seconds, minutes, hours, or days Cron Schedule Run On CRON Schedule The Quartz cron expression that decides when the script runs Maximum Run Time (seconds) All The time one run may take before it is cancelled. Blank means no limit. Trigger handlers stop only when the script checks Profinity.ScriptCancelled Base Address, Address Range and Milliseconds Valid Run On Receipt of CAN Message The CAN addresses the script receives, in hexadecimal, and how long traffic from the device counts as valid. Milliseconds Valid defaults to 5000 and accepts -1 to 60000, where -1 means traffic never expires Tag Paths and Collections Run On Tag Change The tags and tag collections that trigger the script

docs.title: Keeping scripts healthy
docs.text:
A script runs inside the Profinity engine, so a loop, lock, or open connection that is never released slows every other component. A script should be reviewed whenever Profinity performs badly while that script is running.

Scripts run inside Profinity

Inefficient code, leaked memory or leaked resources run inside the Profinity engine and affect it directly.

Keep each script short, release anything it opens when the script stops, and set Maximum Run Time (seconds) on any script that could stall. A Tag Change, Receive, or Rule Script handler stops at Maximum Run Time (seconds) only when the script checks Profinity.ScriptCancelled, so a long handler should check it regularly. A script that fails should write the failure to the Profinity Logs, with Log Script Output switched on while the script is being developed, so that a failed scheduled run can be traced afterwards. For event-driven scripts, use Queue with a small Queue Depth when no event may be lost and Drop when only the newest state matters.

State follows the same rule. Use State for values that belong to one script, and use GlobalState only for values that several scripts share, and remove a value once nothing needs it. Refer to State for how each scope behaves.

docs.title: Receive scripts
docs.text: Receive scripts handle incoming CAN (Controller Area Network) messages in real time. A script in Run On Receipt of CAN Message mode runs automatically when a matching CAN packet is received, and gets the packet as an argument, which suits CAN bus monitoring, protocol implementation and any case where an immediate response to a CAN message is needed. The script implements a Receive method (C#) or a receive function (Python and Lua).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Three settings decide which packets reach the script.

Setting Meaning Base Address The base CAN address of the device, entered in hexadecimal. Address Range The range of packet addresses the device sends, entered in hexadecimal. Milliseconds Valid How long traffic from the device counts as valid before the connection is assumed lost. The default is 5000 and the range is -1 to 60000, where -1 means traffic never expires.

Receive Script Editor

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The example is the minimum implementation of a Receive script in each supported language. It implements the Receive handler, reads the CAN ID of the incoming packet in hexadecimal format with CanIdAsHex, and writes it to the Profinity console.

C#PythonLua 
using System;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.CANBus;

public class CSharpReceiveExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityReceiverScript
{
    public void Receive(CanBusPacket canPacket)
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("CSharp CanBusId Received : " + canPacket.CanIdAsHex);
    }
}

def receive(canPacket):
    print("Python CanPacket Id Received : " + canPacket.CanIdAsHex)

function receive(canPacket)
    print('Lua CanPacket Id Received : ' .. canPacket.CanIdAsHex)
end

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
Receive scripts run synchronously for each matching CAN packet, which on a busy bus can mean many invocations per second. The Receive or receive handler should stay short and avoid blocking calls such as time.sleep in Python, Thread.Sleep in C#, long calculations, locks, and slow input or output, because a slow handler delays other work.

The Trigger Overlap setting decides what happens to a packet that arrives while the handler is still running.

Trigger Overlap Effect Drop (default) Discards the packet. Queue Keeps a short backlog of up to Queue Depth packets (a default of 8, from 1 to 100) and runs them afterwards. This is the setting the shipped receive templates recommend.

Heavier processing belongs in a Service Script, with the handler passing a small amount of data to a queue.

docs.title: Rule scripts
docs.text:
Licence required

A script set to Run On Alert needs both the Scripting and Tag Rule Actions licensed features, so the Server or Enterprise edition. A Desktop licence can add the script, but a rule does not run it. An unlicensed instance cannot add or run scripts. Refer to Licensing.

A rule script is a script component with Script Mode set to Run On Alert. There is no separate rule script component to add, and the rule passes its firing context directly as a parameter to the method the script implements.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Enable scripting in Application Config first, because every script trigger requires it. Then add a CSharp Script, Python Script or Lua Script component (or use an existing one), set Script Mode to Run On Alert, and name that component in the actions list of a rule, in the same way any other rule action is referenced by component name. The rule below calls a script component named PackTempScript when the pack temperature passes 45:

version: "2.3"
rules:
  scope:
    prefix: Vehicles/Car1
  rules:
    - rule:
        id: pack_temperature_high
        level: Warning
        scope:
          prefix: Battery/PackTemperature
        expression: tag.Value > 45
        actions:
          - action: PackTempScript

docs.title: The alert context
docs.text: When the rule fires, Profinity calls the script's alert method once, passing the firing context as a parameter. This is the same context every other rule action receives (refer to Actions): the rule id, name and level, the edge that fired, the triggering tag, and TriggeredTags, which holds every tag in the rule's scope that is currently true. The context object has the properties RuleId, RuleName, RuleDisplayName, RuleDescription, RuleLevel, Transition, TriggerTagId, Value, Quality, MetaType, Message, ExpandedMessage and TriggeredTags, with the same names in C#, Python and Lua. RuleLevel is one of Trace, Debug, Info, Warning, Error or Fatal (refer to Alert levels). Transition is one of EnteredTrue, EnteredFalse, EnteredStep or ExitedStep. Each row in TriggeredTags has TagId, Value, Quality and MetaType.

docs.title: Example
Behaviour
docs.text:
Running the script by hand does not call this method

The Run Script action on a component menu, and the Run On Demand and scheduled paths, do not call OnAlert or on_alert. Only a rule firing does, so the alert method is tested by driving the rule's condition true.

Run On Alert has no start and stop lifecycle, because a rule invokes the script and the script does not sit watching. Between firings its status reads Not Run or Run N times, and the status shows Running while OnAlert or on_alert is executing. The component's menu in this mode is Edit Script only.

docs.title: Trigger overlap
docs.text:
If the alert method is still running when the rule fires again, Trigger Overlap decides what happens. It is the same setting that Run On Tag Change and Run On Receipt of CAN Message use:

Trigger Overlap Effect Drop (default) Discards the new firing while the current one is still running. Queue Holds a bounded backlog, up to Queue Depth (1 to 100, default 8), and runs it once the current firing completes.

The alert method should stay fast, because a slow script under Queue builds a backlog and under Drop silently misses firings.

For the other script modes, refer to Script types. For the scripting overview and a worked first script, refer to Profinity Scripting and How to Write Your First Script.

docs.title: Run scripts
docs.text:
Run scripts are the general-purpose script type: they run when an operator starts them or on a schedule, which suits data collection, testing, and system configuration. A Run script can use the CAN bus, DBC, State, Console, and Tags operations, can write to the console, and can stop early when it checks Profinity.ScriptCancelled.

A Custom Component firmware load script, firmware save script, menu button and firmware action also run once. Refer to Custom Component scripts.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A Run script has three modes, chosen with Script Mode.

Script Mode Behaviour Run On Demand Runs the script when an operator selects Run Script from the script component's menu. Cancel Script stops a run that is still going. Run On Time Interval Runs the script automatically at a fixed interval set with Time Interval and Time Interval Unit. Run On CRON Schedule Runs the script from a Quartz cron expression entered in Cron Schedule.

The scheduled modes use these settings.

Setting Description Time Interval The interval between runs in Run On Time Interval mode, for example every 5 minutes or every hour. Time Interval Unit The unit of the interval: Seconds, Minutes, Hours, or Days. Cron Schedule A Quartz cron expression for Run On CRON Schedule mode. Auto Start Script When on, a scheduled script starts by itself. Otherwise it is started with Start Scheduled Script and stopped with Stop Scheduled Script.

A Quartz expression has six or seven fields that start with seconds, which differs from a standard five-field cron expression, so 0 0 6 ? * MON-FRI runs the script at 06:00 on every weekday.

Run Script Editor

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The example shows the basic structure of a Run script in each supported language. It writes two messages to the console, one fixed and one taken from Profinity.Message, and reports success. The interfaces used by the C# sample are available to a script by default, so the sample needs no using line for them.

C#PythonLua 
using System;

public class CSharpRunExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityRunnableScript
{
    public bool Run()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("This is a CSharp Message!");
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine(Profinity.Message);
        return true;
    }
}

def RunMe():
    print('This is a Python message!')
    print(Profinity.Message)

RunMe()

function RunMe()
    print('This is a Lua message!')
    print(Profinity.Message)
end

RunMe()

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
In C# the Run() method returns a boolean, where true reports success and false reports failure. Python and Lua Run scripts have no return value: the script file runs from the top, so the sample defines a function and then calls it. A Python or Lua script reports failure by raising an error (or, in Python, by calling sys.exit() with a non-zero exit code, where sys.exit(0) is treated as success).
