Python scripts run on IronPython with Python 3 syntax, as described on Supported Languages.

docs.title: Service scripts
docs.text:
Service scripts are designed for continuous, long-running operations that keep state and respond to system events. They have a full lifecycle of start, stop, pause, and continue, which suits monitoring, continuous data logging and other work that must run reliably for extended periods. An operator controls a service from the script component's menu with Start Service, Pause Service, Continue Service and Stop Service, and the component shows its status as Running, Paused, or Stopped.

A Custom Component main script is a service script. Auto Start Main Script, or Connect / Disconnect, starts and stops it, and the script reads settings_map.yaml through Component and firmware settings.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Description Auto Start Script When on, the service starts by itself. Maximum Run Time (seconds) Cancels a run that takes too long. Service Script Editor

docs.title: Which lifecycle methods are required
docs.text: Only OnStart() (C#) or on_start (Python and Lua) is required. In C#, OnStop, OnPause, OnContinue and Run are virtual, so a service overrides the ones it needs, and in Python and Lua the other functions (on_stop, on_pause, on_continue and run) are used only when the file defines them. The on_stop() function or OnStop() method is called both when the service is stopped by hand and when Profinity shuts down.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Each example implements the start, stop, pause, and continue methods, although only the start method is required, and a Run() or run() that loops until Profinity.ScriptCancelled is set. In C#, extend ProfinityBaseService, which makes only OnStart mandatory, because a class that extends ProfinityScript and implements IProfinityServiceScript directly must implement all five methods. The loop sleeps between iterations with time.sleep (Python), Thread.Sleep (C#) or sleep (Lua), and the Python version declares global for the shared run counter. These match Profinity's built-in Python, C# and Lua service templates, which show both single-step and loop-style run patterns.

C#PythonLua 
using System;
using System.Threading;

public class CSharpServiceTest : ProfinityBaseService
{
    private int _runCount = 0;

    public override bool OnStart()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Started CSharp Service");
        _runCount = 0;
        return true;
    }

    public override bool OnStop()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Stopped CSharp Service");
        return true;
    }

    public override bool OnPause()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Paused CSharp Service");
        return true;
    }

    public override bool OnContinue()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Continue CSharp Service");
        return true;
    }

    public override bool Run()
    {
        while (!Profinity.ScriptCancelled)
        {
            _runCount++;
            Profinity.Console.WriteLine("Run #" + _runCount);
            Thread.Sleep(100);
        }
        return true;
    }
}

import time

_run_count = 0

def on_start():
    global _run_count
    print("Python Service Started!")
    _run_count = 0
    return True

def on_stop():
    print("Python Service Stopped!")
    return True

def on_pause():
    print("Python Service Paused!")
    return True

def on_continue():
    print("Python Service Continued!")
    return True

def run():
    global _run_count
    while not Profinity.ScriptCancelled:
        _run_count += 1
        print(f"Run #{_run_count}")
        time.sleep(0.1)
    return True

local run_count = 0

function on_start()
    print('Started Lua Service')
    run_count = 0
    return true
end

function on_stop()
    print('Stopped Lua Service')
    return true
end

function on_pause()
    print('Paused Lua Service')
    return true
end

function on_continue()
    print('Continue Lua Service')
    return true
end

function run()
    while not Profinity.ScriptCancelled do
        run_count = run_count + 1
        print('Run #' .. run_count)
        -- sleep(seconds) is clamped to 30 seconds per call, so a longer wait
        -- is expressed as repeated calls rather than one large value
        sleep(0.1)
    end
    return true
end

docs.title: Cooperative cancellation
docs.text: Long-running work in Run() or run() should observe Profinity.ScriptCancelled, which becomes true when the service is stopped, paused, or when Profinity is shutting down, so that loops exit and release resources promptly. A run() function with its own while loop tests not Profinity.ScriptCancelled (or !Profinity.ScriptCancelled in C#) in the loop condition, and may break out before slow steps. When the service is paused, cancellation is signalled so an inner loop can finish, and when the service continues Profinity calls run() again. In Python the service body uses import time for time.sleep, in C# Thread.Sleep needs using System.Threading;, and in Lua the sleep(seconds) global is limited to 30 seconds per call, so a longer wait is written as repeated calls.

docs.title: Python module-level variables
docs.text: The lifecycle functions are separate functions. A counter or other mutable value kept in a module-level name and assigned inside those functions is treated by Python as a local variable unless each function that assigns to it declares global _my_var. Leaving out global is a common mistake when state is reset in on_start and updated in run().

docs.title: Tag change scripts
docs.text:
A Tag Change script runs each time the value of a watched tag changes. It suits reacting to another component's output, computing values that need more than a single expression, and chaining automation, without polling the tag on a timer.

A script becomes a Tag Change script by setting its Script Mode to Run On Tag Change. It implements the OnTagChange method (C#) or the on_tag_change function (Python and Lua), which receives the tag's id and a sample holding the new value, quality, and timestamp. The script can read and write other tags with Tags and keep earlier values between calls with State.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Enable scripting in Application Config first, as every script type requires it. Then add a CSharp Script, Python Script or Lua Script component, set Script Mode to Run On Tag Change, and choose the tags to watch in the Tag Change Settings category:

Setting Description Tag Paths Explicit full tag paths to watch. Collections Tag Collections to watch. Members are resolved from the collections file.

The script watches the union of the two lists, and at least one tag path or collection is required.

docs.title: The method and its arguments
docs.text:
Profinity calls the method once for each tag that changes, passing:

Argument Description tagId The id of the tag that changed. sample The new reading: Value, Quality (Good, Unavailable, Stale or Bad), UtcTimestamp, Reason and Message. C#PythonLua 
using Profinity.Sdk.Abstractions.Scripting;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.Tags;

public class CSharpTagChangeExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityTagChangeScript
{
    public void OnTagChange(string tagId, DataTagSample sample)
    {
        object previous = Profinity.State.Get(tagId);
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("CSharp Tag Change : " + tagId + " = " + sample.Value + " (was " + previous + ")");
        Profinity.State.Set(tagId, sample.Value);
    }
}

def on_tag_change(tagId, sample):
    previous = Profinity.State.Get(tagId)
    print("Python Tag Change : " + str(tagId) + " = " + str(sample.Value) + " (was " + str(previous) + ")")
    Profinity.State.Set(tagId, sample.Value)

function on_tag_change(tagId, sample)
    local previous = Profinity.State:Get(tagId)
    print('Lua Tag Change : ' .. tostring(tagId) .. ' = ' .. tostring(sample.Value) .. ' (was ' .. tostring(previous) .. ')')
    Profinity.State:Set(tagId, sample.Value)
end

The full files CSharpTagChangeTemplate.cs, PythonTagChangeTemplate.py and LuaTagChangeTemplate.lua are built into Profinity as the templates it offers when you create a script of that type.

One call per tag

The sample argument is only the tag that changed. Reading any other tag returns its live value at that moment, not the value published together with this change. A frame, a payload or several tags written as one update are already separate changes before the method runs, so sibling tags are not guaranteed to be consistent with each other.

To read the tag that fired, including its quality and timestamp, pass its id back to Profinity.Tags with a leading /, which is the root of the tag tree: Profinity.Tags.GetSample("/" + tagId) in C# and Python, or Profinity.Tags:GetSample('/' .. tagId) in Lua. Without the /, the id would be treated as relative to the script's host component.

docs.title: Publishing a computed tag
docs.text:
A common use is computing one tag from another. This example, which follows the CSharpDerivedTagTemplate.cs, PythonDerivedTagTemplate.py and LuaDerivedTagTemplate.lua templates built into Profinity, converts a speed in miles per hour into kilometres per hour whenever the source tag changes, and publishes the result with Profinity.Tags.SetValue. Refer to Derived tags for when to choose this over an expression-based derived tag.

C#PythonLua 
using Profinity.Sdk.Abstractions.Scripting;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.Tags;

public class CSharpDerivedTagExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityTagChangeScript
{
    private const string SourceTagPath = "SpeedMph";
    private const string PublishedTagPath = "SpeedKmh";

    public void OnTagChange(string tagId, DataTagSample sample)
    {
        if (!tagId.EndsWith(SourceTagPath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        {
            return;
        }

        double speedKmh = Convert.ToDouble(sample.Value) * 1.60934;
        Profinity.Tags.SetValue(PublishedTagPath, speedKmh);
    }
}

SOURCE_TAG_PATH = "SpeedMph"
PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH = "SpeedKmh"

def on_tag_change(tagId, sample):
    if not str(tagId).lower().endswith(SOURCE_TAG_PATH.lower()):
        return

    speed_kmh = float(sample.Value) * 1.60934
    Profinity.Tags.SetValue(PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH, speed_kmh)

local SOURCE_TAG_PATH = 'SpeedMph'
local PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH = 'SpeedKmh'

function on_tag_change(tagId, sample)
    if not tostring(tagId):lower():find(SOURCE_TAG_PATH:lower() .. '$') then
        return
    end

    local speedKmh = tonumber(sample.Value) * 1.60934
    Profinity.Tags:SetValue(PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH, speedKmh)
end

Paths without a leading / are relative to the script's host component, so this script is meant to run on the component that owns both tags. To publish to a tag on another component, start the path with /, as described in Tag paths. Reading the published tag never re-runs the script. It returns the last value the script wrote.

docs.title: Behaviour
docs.text:
Running the script by hand does not call this method

Run On Demand and scheduled runs do not call OnTagChange or on_tag_change. Only a change to a watched tag does, so test by changing the tag.

The method runs when a watched tag's value changes. Writing the same value again does not call it, and neither does a change of quality alone, such as a tag going stale while it keeps its last value.

docs.title: Trigger overlap
docs.text:
If the method is still running when another change arrives, Trigger Overlap decides what happens. It is the same setting used by Run On Alert and Run On Receipt of CAN Message:

Trigger Overlap Effect Drop (default) Discards the new change while the current one is still running. Queue Holds a bounded backlog, up to Queue Depth (1 to 100), and runs it once the current call completes.

Keep the method fast. A slow script under Queue builds a backlog, and under Drop silently misses changes. Store previous values in State rather than recomputing them. If a run must be bounded, set Maximum Run Time (seconds). The handler stops only when the script checks Profinity.ScriptCancelled.

For the other script modes, refer to Script types, and for a worked first script, refer to How to Write Your First Script.

docs.title: Supported Languages
docs.text:
Profinity scripting supports three languages: C#, Python (through IronPython) and Lua (through NLua). Each language runs on .NET, the Microsoft software framework Profinity is written in, so scripts can use .NET libraries directly. Each language supports the same script types (Run, Receive, Service, Tag Change and Rule Script, the last being a script set to Run On Alert mode) and the same host operations, exposed through the Profinity script variable, so the choice of language is a matter of preference and background.

Language Typing and style Main limits C# Statically typed classes with full .NET access More verbose, and needs some .NET knowledge Python Procedural functions with Python 3 syntax Runs on IronPython, so libraries that need compiled CPython extensions cannot be used Lua Procedural functions with a small syntax Smaller standard library, and fewer third-party packages

Functionality beyond what Profinity Scripting provides is available by calling the Profinity APIs from separate tools.

docs.title: C# scripting
docs.text: C# is a statically typed, object-oriented language. C# scripts in Profinity are classes that inherit from a base class or implement a specific interface, and they have full access to the .NET framework. Because Profinity is itself written in C#, C# gives the deepest integration with Profinity types and suits large automation projects and performance-critical work. See the C# Language Reference and the .NET API Documentation.

docs.title: Python scripting
docs.text:
Python scripts in Profinity use a procedural style, with functions that Profinity calls at defined points. Profinity runs them through IronPython, a .NET implementation of Python, so a Python script can also call .NET libraries directly. IronPython is not the standard CPython interpreter, so Python packages that depend on compiled CPython extensions, such as numpy, cannot be imported, whereas the Python standard library modules that IronPython provides and .NET types can.

Profinity runs IronPython with Python 3 compatibility enabled, so all Python scripts use Python 3 syntax, including:

  • print() as a function, not a statement
  • f-strings, such as f"Value: {value}"
  • / for true division and // for floor division
  • Unicode literals
  • Absolute imports

See the IronPython Documentation and the Python Language Reference.

docs.title: Lua scripting
docs.text:
Lua scripts in Profinity use a procedural style, with functions that Profinity calls at defined points, such as receive() for a Receive script or on_start() for a Service script. Profinity embeds the Lua 5.4 runtime through NLua, and a Lua script can call .NET types directly, including the same Profinity script variable that C# and Python scripts use. The General Purpose Input/Output (GPIO) and serial port types GpioController, PinMode, PinValue, SerialPort, Parity, StopBits and Handshake are available as globals without any import.

Profinity also registers four Lua host functions:

Function What it does print(...) Writes its arguments to the script output stream stderr(...) Writes its arguments to the script error stream, the Lua equivalent of Python's sys.stderr sleep(seconds) Pauses the script for the given number of seconds. Each call is limited to 30 seconds, so a loop that needs to wait longer calls sleep() again CanBusPacket(address) Creates a new CAN packet for the given CAN address, for use with the operations described in CAN Bus

Lua scripts follow Lua syntax, including these points that differ from Python and C#:

  • Native Lua tables use 1-based indexing, whereas .NET collections such as TriggeredTags keep their own 0-based indexing.
  • nil takes the place of null or None.
  • Strings are joined with .. rather than +.
  • Blocks are written as function name(...) ... end rather than with indentation or braces.

See the Lua 5.4 Reference Manual and the NLua Documentation.

docs.title: Getting started with Profinity
docs.text:
These pages take a new Profinity 2.3 user from a first install to live data on a dashboard. Work through them in order, or go straight to the page you need.

  • Quick start guide: install Profinity, apply a licence, load an example profile, replay a CAN log, edit your first dashboard, and look at rules and alerts.
  • Create a user: create a user, set an initial password, and assign roles.
  • Profiles: how a profile organises configuration, components, dashboards, and settings for a setup.
  • How to add a component to your profile: add hardware devices and protocol adapters from the dashboard interface.
  • Profinity dashboard development guide: see component data on the built-in dashboards, and build your own.
  • Logs: read the timestamped log entries when you troubleshoot.

To install on a specific platform, refer to Installation.

docs.title: Create a user
docs.text:
Create a user account for each person who signs in to Profinity, and give it the roles that match their job. You need the Security administration permission and the Profinity Server licensed feature, which the Server and Enterprise editions include. Without the feature there are no user accounts or roles: a Desktop installation runs as a single built-in admin user, and Users & Groups shows that user and group administration requires a Server licence. Licensing lists what each edition includes.

  1. In the side menu, select ADMIN, then Users & Groups.
  2. Select + Add user.
  3. Enter a username and an initial password for local sign-in.
  4. Under Assigned roles, choose one or more roles, then save.

The Add user panel

Profinity creates the account and its login details, and the new user can sign in with the username and initial password. If you are not sure which roles to assign, read the next section first.

docs.title: Choose roles
docs.text:
A role is a named set of permissions, and a person can hold more than one. A user can only do what their roles allow, so give each person the smallest set that lets them do their job. A good starting point is three roles:

Role For people who Typical access Viewer Watch the system but never change it View data, tags, alerts, and dashboards Operator Run a vehicle, bench, or pack each day Everything a Viewer can do, plus running component actions and controlling charging Engineer Set up and tune a system Everything an Operator can do, plus changing profiles, components, dashboards, and firmware

The default Administrators role includes every permission, so assigning it gives that person the access of every other role. Keep it for the few people who manage the installation. Roles and permissions explains how to create these roles and lists every permission, and Manage users covers password resets and service accounts.

docs.title: Profinity profiles
docs.text:
A profile is the core mechanism that Profinity uses to maintain the configuration of your system. Any component that you add to your system becomes associated with the active profile, and the configuration for each device is retained after Profinity is shut down. Profinity keeps track of your profiles and loads the most recently used one each time you start Profinity.

Each profile keeps its own set of components, dashboards, and settings.

docs.title: Managing profiles
docs.text:
Profiles are managed from the ADMIN section of Profinity. Selecting ADMIN in the side menu and then the Profile pill lists every profile. ACTIVATE on a row makes that profile the active profile, which is useful when working with different system configurations or testing different setups. Add profile creates a new profile, and Upload Profile Pack imports a profile from another Profinity instance. Each row can also be viewed, edited, or deleted. How to Create a New Profile gives the steps for creating one.

The Profinity profile list (ADMIN, then Profile), where the active profile is marked ACTIVE

Profiles in the Administration section covers creating and managing profiles in full.

docs.title: Quick start guide
docs.text: This guide takes you from a fresh installation to a running system in six steps: installing Profinity, applying a licence if one has been issued, loading the example profile, replaying example CAN logs, editing your first dashboard, and looking at the rules and alerts. To install Profinity on Linux or macOS instead, refer to Install Profinity on Linux and macOS, and for Docker deployments, refer to Install Profinity with Docker.

docs.title: Step 1: Install Profinity on Windows
docs.text:
Follow Install Profinity on Windows to install Profinity with the Setup Wizard. After installation, launch Profinity from the Start menu, which opens the Profinity homepage. The Windows desktop application signs in automatically with a built-in account, so no sign-in is needed to complete this guide. Installations that run Profinity as a web service, such as Docker and Linux, and a Windows installation that holds a Server licence, create an admin user with the password password and require a new password at the first sign-in.

Change the default password

On Docker and Linux installations, and on any installation where you sign in as the default admin user, change the password at the first sign-in, so that the system is not left running with publicly documented credentials. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then the Change My Password pill.

docs.title: Step 2: Apply a licence
docs.text:
You do not need a licence to complete the rest of this guide, because an unlicensed Desktop installation runs for personal, non-commercial use and other installations start a 14-day local trial. When Prohelion has issued a commercial or evaluation licence, apply it now:

  1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then the License pill.
  2. Copy the Fingerprint and send it to Prohelion, which returns a signed license.yaml file for this installation.
  3. Select Update license file and choose the license.yaml file, then check that State reads Valid.

The License pill needs the Security administration permission. For Docker, Linux services, installations with no network access, and what to do when a licence is rejected, refer to Applying a Licence. For what each edition includes, refer to Licensing.

docs.title: Step 3: Load the example profile
docs.text:
Profinity includes an Example Profile, which is installed automatically and holds pre-configured components, a dashboard, styling, and images that show how a profile fits together. To load the Example Profile:

  1. Select ADMIN in the side menu.
  2. Select the Profile pill.
  3. Select ACTIVATE on the Example Profile row in the list to make it the active profile.

The Example Profile includes the following pre-configured components:

  • Prohelion 12v
  • Prohelion BMU (Battery Management Unit)
  • Three Elmar Solar Maximum Power Point Tracker (MPPT) devices (6A0, 6B0 and 6C0)
  • Two Prohelion WaveSculptor 22 Motor Controllers (Left and Right)

It also includes the following dashboard content:

  • A home dashboard file with status displays, data visualisations and component monitoring, which the home page uses only after Custom Home Dashboard is enabled in the profile settings
  • Custom styling and images used by the dashboards
  • Data bindings that connect dashboard elements to component data

For more information about profiles, refer to Profinity Profiles.

docs.title: Step 4: Run the example CAN log
docs.text:
The Example Profile works best with data flowing through the system. Profinity includes an Example Log (example_log.csv) that you can replay to simulate CAN bus traffic. To replay the Example Log:

  1. Select CAN UTILITIES in the side menu.
  2. Select CAN LOG REPLAY.
  3. Select example_log.csv from the list of available log files, then select Play to start the replay.

The log replays CAN bus messages, and data flows through the dashboards in the Example Profile. The playback controls pause, resume, and move to a new position in the log. Refer to How to Replay CAN Bus Logs for the steps and Log / Replay CAN bus Messages for the full reference.

docs.title: Step 5: Edit your first dashboard
docs.text:
With the Example Profile running with data, an existing dashboard is the quickest way to learn how dashboards work. With the Example Profile active, the home page is still the standard home page, because the profile's home dashboard is switched off, so start from a component dashboard. To view and edit a dashboard's source:

  1. Select a component in the side menu, for example Prohelion BMU or Prohelion WaveSculptor 22 - Left.
  2. Select the pencil (Edit Dashboard) icon in the menu at the right of the dashboard title bar, which opens the dashboard editor in DESIGN mode, the visual editor.
  3. Select the YAML tab to see the dashboard's source.

The pencil icon needs the Modify dashboards permission. The editor shows the full structure of the dashboard, how each component is configured and how data bindings and styling apply, and it edits visually in DESIGN mode or as text in the YAML tab. The same pencil icon opens the home dashboard once Custom Home Dashboard is enabled, as described in How to Create a Profile Dashboard. Every dashboard in Profinity is built with the same dashboard system, so the source of an existing dashboard shows the format that a new dashboard uses.

docs.title: Make your first edit
docs.text:
To make a simple change:

  1. Find a text element or label in the dashboard.
  2. Change the text content by selecting the dashboard element and modifying it in the inspector.
  3. Select SAVE, then close the editor.

The edit appears on the dashboard behind the editor, because DESIGN is an outline and not a live preview. For more detailed information on creating and editing dashboards, refer to:

  • Dashboard Development Guide, the full guide to dashboard development
  • Core Elements, which covers dashboard structure
  • Data Binding, which connects data to your dashboard
  • Component Reference, which lists the available dashboard components

docs.title: Step 6: Look at the rules and alerts
docs.text:
With data flowing, Profinity's rules watch your tags and raise alerts when something needs attention. Rules are defined in the profile, and the alerts they raise appear in the Alerts Log and as indicators across the UI. To view the rules:

  1. Select TAG UTILITIES in the side menu.
  2. Select RULES & ACTIONS to open the rules editor.
  3. Expand the rule groups for the Example Profile's battery components.

The Example Profile includes battery management system (BMS) alert rules for the Prohelion 12v and the Prohelion BMU, arranged in groups such as Cell limits (cell over voltage, under voltage and over temperature) and Critical status flags (for example communications timeouts and emergency stop). Open a rule to see the tags it watches, its condition, its level and its description. To find what would make a rule fire, note the condition it uses, then find the tag it watches in Tag Explorer.

The RULES & ACTIONS entry needs the View tag rules permission, and saving changes needs Modify tag rules. A signed-in admin user holds both. Actions that send an email, Slack message, webhook, or MQTT message need the Tag Rule Actions feature, as described in Rule Actions.

To view the alerts:

  1. Select ALL ALERTS in the side menu to open the Alerts Log.
  2. On the Active tab, see any alerts currently firing.
  3. Select the History tab to see earlier alerts, newest first.
  4. Select an alert to Acknowledge it, or Silence it for a set number of minutes.

Alerts also show as a yellow triangle on dashboard widgets bound to the affected tag, and on the matching leaf in Tag Explorer. The web client refreshes these every four seconds, so they appear and clear as the data changes. For more detail, refer to:

  • Alerts Log, which covers alert levels, indicators, acknowledging, and silencing
  • Rule Actions, which covers what happens when a rule fires
  • Tag Expressions, which covers writing rule conditions
  • Tags, which explains how tags, collections, rules, and alerts fit together

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
From here, the following pages cover the usual next tasks:

  • How to add a component to your profile adds further components.
  • Profinity dashboard development guide builds your own dashboard.
  • Log / Replay CAN bus Messages sets up CAN bus logging.
  • Create a user creates additional users, which needs the Profinity Server feature.
  • Tags creates rules and alerts for your system.

Before you create users, read the Choose roles section of Create a user, which explains how to decide what access each person needs.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
• The Dashboard Troubleshooting Guide covers common issues.
  • The Dashboard FAQ answers frequently asked questions.
  • Contact Prohelion through the Feedback pill on the ADMIN page.

docs.title: How to guides
docs.text: These guides cover common Profinity 2.3 jobs, such as connecting a CAN bus adapter, building a dashboard and logging data. Most guides list what they need first, then the steps, and link to the reference page for the feature they use. Start with the Quick Start Guide if Profinity is not yet installed.

docs.title: Build and style dashboards
docs.text:
• How to Create a Custom Dashboard: builds a first dashboard for a Custom Component.
  • How to create a profile dashboard: replaces the default home page with a custom dashboard, built in the visual editor or uploaded as a YAML file, and removes it again.
  • How to Add Images to Your Dashboard: uses custom images in dashboard components.
  • How to style your dashboard: adds a profile.css stylesheet and applies its classes to dashboard groups and readouts.
  • How to view dashboard source: opens the YAML source of a component or profile dashboard to copy or learn from.
  • How to debug dashboard issues: lists the cause and fix for a dashboard that does not load, a readout with no data, a missing image or a style with no effect.

docs.title: Add components and connect devices
docs.text:
• How to Add a Component to Your Profile: configures a component and adds it to the active profile.
  • How to create a Custom Component: adds a Custom Component to the profile and attaches optional files.
  • How to Connect to CAN Bus: connects Profinity to a CAN bus network.
  • How to send and receive CAN bus messages: views CAN traffic, and sends a CAN packet once or on a schedule.
  • How to replay CAN bus logs: replays recorded CAN bus messages from a log file for testing without live CAN hardware.

docs.title: Log and publish data
docs.text:
• How to Configure Data Logging: sets up logging and publishing to files, InfluxDB, Prometheus, Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) or a webhook.
  • How to log data to the cloud (InfluxDB): logs tag values to InfluxDB Cloud or a self-hosted InfluxDB with the InfluxDB v2 Historian, and describes the data it writes.

docs.title: Configure and deploy
docs.text:
• How to Create a New Profile: sets up a profile for a separate site or configuration.
  • Environment variables: sets a configuration value from an environment variable.
  • How to set up Profinity as a kiosk application: configures Kiosk Mode and starts a fullscreen browser on Windows, Linux, or macOS.

docs.title: Extend Profinity
docs.text:
• How to Connect Profinity to AI: connects an AI tool to the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.
  • Make your first Custom Component: adds a Custom Component with a DBC file, dashboard, main script, menu actions, and firmware.
  • How to write your first script: enables scripting, adds a script component, and runs a first script. Script examples shows a DBC signal, a CAN message, and script state.

docs.title: Tags, rules, and plugins
docs.text:
These Profinity 2.3 features have no separate guide, and the reference pages describe them in full.

  • Tag Collections: groups tags for logging and publishing.
  • Derived Tags: calculates a new tag from existing tags with an expression.
  • Rules and Actions: runs an action when a rule raises an alert.
  • AI Skills: generates dashboards, rules, and scripts with an AI tool.
  • Developing Plugins: extends Profinity with a plugin.

docs.title: More help
docs.text:
• Prohelion Profinity 2.3: the documentation home page.
  • Dashboard FAQ: answers to frequently asked dashboard questions.

docs.title: How to add a component to your profile
docs.text:
Add a component to the active profile from the sidebar or homepage to monitor a CAN bus device, then check its status and connect it. You need Profinity V2 installed and running, a loaded profile, and the Modify components permission, which allows components to be added (Roles and Permissions). Some component types also need a licence that includes the feature behind them, because a component type that is not licensed shows as unavailable, such as a historian. Licensing lists which features each edition includes.

Add a protocol adapter first. A protocol adapter allows Profinity to receive data from external systems, and without incoming data Profinity is limited in what it is able to show and do. For CAN bus networks, the supported adapters, including the Prohelion and Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridges, are described in CAN Bus Adapters, and a step-by-step procedure is given in How to Connect to CAN Bus. For industrial systems, Profinity also supports BACnet, EtherNet/IP, Modbus, OPC UA, and S7, described in Industrial protocols.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text:
The ADD COMPONENT page groups the component types by category. The filter options are on the left-hand side of the page, and the COMPONENT TYPES filter limits the list to one category:

  • Adapters, including the CAN Bus Adapters, which are also shown at the top of the screen when discovered
  • Battery Management Systems, Chargers & Power Supplies, Motor Controllers and MPPTs for devices such as a Battery Management Unit (BMU), a motor controller or a Maximum Power Point Tracker (MPPT)
  • Custom Component to create a new component
  • Loggers (CAN File, TAG File, InfluxDB v1 and Prometheus)
  • Historians (InfluxDB v2, InfluxDB v3 and TAG SQL)
  • Publishers & Subscribers (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) and Webhook)
  • Scripts, for scripts that run inside Profinity

To add a component:

  1. Select ADD COMPONENT on the homepage or at the bottom of the sidebar. The homepage tile is not shown when the home screen has Add Component turned off. A page opens that lists every component type that can be added, including hardware devices, data loggers and custom scripts. Some CAN bus adapters in Profinity can be auto-discovered, and a discovered adapter that is available in your configuration is shown at the top of the screen.
  2. Select the type to add. Profinity prompts for a Component Name, which must be unique in the profile, a CAN ID or address where the device needs one, the setting that starts the component automatically, and any settings specific to that component type. The properties required differ for each component.
  3. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog, which reads SAVE when the settings of an existing component are being changed. The component's icon appears in the sidebar.

Add a new component to the profile

Example of defining component properties

The start setting is Auto Connect on every component that connects to a broker, device, server, or database. With it on, the component connects when the profile loads. With it off, the component waits until you switch it on with its Connect or Start action, and it stays off until you do.

Hovering the mouse over a component icon in the sidebar presents a list of all devices associated with the current profile that match that component type. You can change the properties later by opening the Change Settings menu from the component's dashboard. More information about specific component properties and how to correctly configure each component is in the dedicated component sections.

Multiple components of the same type can be added to a profile, but each must have a unique name. A device that listens on a range of CAN addresses must not use a range that overlaps the range of another such device in the profile, because Profinity refuses the component otherwise. Some component types can be added to a profile only once. If the profile already has a component with the same name as the one being added, a digit is added to the new component name to keep the component names in the profile unique.

docs.title: Check the component status
docs.text:
Each component has a coloured indicator on its icon that displays the operational status of the device.

Colour Status Meaning Green On The device is available, sending valid data and is in a valid state Amber Warning The device is available, but is either not sending data or is in a warning state Red Error The device is in an error state Grey Idle The device is idle Outlined, no fill Off The device can be contacted but is switched off Empty (white) N/A The device is not available or cannot be contacted

A red indicator means an error state, so check the logs. A component that stays red, or shows an outlined or empty lamp, after it is added usually has an adapter that is not connected or a CAN bus that is not delivering data. The troubleshooting section of How to Connect to CAN Bus covers the usual causes and fixes.

docs.title: Connect the component
docs.text:
A component that holds a connection, such as an adapter, shows a Connect button on its dashboard. A component that starts automatically needs no click. To connect the component:

  1. Click the component in the sidebar.
  2. Click Connect.
  3. Wait for the status to turn green, then confirm that data is appearing.

docs.title: Remove a component
docs.text:
If a component is no longer required, you can remove it:

  1. Open the component settings, which is the three bar icon at the top right of the component dashboard.
  2. Select DELETE COMPONENT at the bottom of the settings dialog, then confirm in the Delete component dialog. If rules use the component as an action, those actions are removed from the affected rules.

A dashboard showing the three bar settings icon (top right)

docs.title: How to add images to your dashboard
docs.text: Add custom images to your dashboards by placing them in the images folder of the profile directory, which Profinity serves at /Profile/Images. You need access to the images folder of your profile's directory, image files in a supported format (SVG, PNG, JPG, WEBP, or GIF), and a dashboard to edit.

docs.title: Place the image file
docs.text:
Each profile has its own directory, which is profiles/<profile name> inside the artefacts directory, so the images for a profile named Example Profile are in <artefacts directory>/profiles/Example Profile/images. The artefacts directory is:

  • %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity on Windows
  • ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity on macOS
  • /var/lib/prohelion/profinity on Linux
  • On Docker, the path inside the container named by PROFINITY_HOME, so on Docker the image must be copied into the mounted volume that holds that directory

To place the file:

  1. Open the images folder of the profile directory. If the folder does not exist, create it, using the lowercase name, because Linux and Docker file systems are case-sensitive and Profinity serves only the lowercase folder (refer to Store dashboard files in a profile).
  2. Copy the image file into the folder.
<profile name>/
└── images/
    ├── company-logo.svg
    ├── device-icon.png
    └── custom-banner.jpg

Profinity serves the folder of the active profile when a browser requests a file, so a new image does not need a restart.

docs.title: Reference the image in a component
docs.text:
In an Icon component, or the icon of a pill component, set image to the filename only:

icon:
  image: device-icon.png  # Use filename only

In an HTML component, reference the file by its full path, which uses the capitalised URL form /Profile/Images:

html:
  content: |
    <img src="/Profile/Images/custom-banner.jpg" alt="Banner" />

In an Image component, which shows an interactive image, set image to the filename only:

image:
  image: device-diagram.png  # Use filename only

docs.title: Check the image
docs.text:
Save the dashboard, and the image appears in it. If the image area stays empty, one of these causes applies:

  • The filename in the dashboard differs from the file in the images folder, because the match is case-sensitive.
  • The file format is not one of SVG, PNG, JPG, WEBP, or GIF.
  • The file is in a folder other than the active profile's images folder.

Correct the name, convert the file or move it, and save again.

docs.title: Image format recommendations
docs.text:
• SVG is best for icons and logos, because it scales without loss of quality and has a smaller file size.
  • PNG suits images with transparency.
  • JPG suits photographs.
  • WEBP suits photographs and images with transparency at a smaller file size.
  • GIF suits animated images. A GIF copied into the images folder is served and displays in a dashboard, but the image library in the visual editor lists and uploads only SVG, PNG, JPG, and WEBP files, so place GIF files in the folder by hand.

docs.title: How to configure data logging
docs.text: Set up data logging or publishing to send CAN bus messages or tag values to files, InfluxDB, Prometheus, a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) broker, or a webhook. Choose a destination in the table, add the component, then follow the section for that destination.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An active profile with components configured
  • Access to the destination: a file system or an SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) server, InfluxDB, Prometheus, an MQTT broker, or a webhook receiver
  • The Modify components permission, which allows loggers and publishers to be added
  • The licensed feature for the destination, which is Historians for the InfluxDB v2 and v3 Historians (Desktop, Server, and Enterprise editions) and Data Relay for the MQTT Publisher and Webhook Publisher (Server and Enterprise editions). The file and SFTP loggers, the InfluxDB v1 Logger and the Prometheus Logger are available in every edition. Refer to Licensing

docs.title: Choose a destination
docs.text:
Destination Component Category What it needs A file on the local file system CAN File Logger (native CAN bus messages), TAG File Logger (tag values) Loggers No licensed feature A file on an SFTP server CAN SFTP Logger, TAG SFTP Logger Loggers No licensed feature InfluxDB v1 InfluxDB v1 Logger Loggers No licensed feature InfluxDB v2 or v3 InfluxDB v2 Historian, InfluxDB v3 Historian Historians Historians Prometheus Prometheus Logger Loggers No licensed feature An MQTT broker MQTT Publisher Publishers & Subscribers Data Relay An HTTP(S) URL Webhook Publisher Publishers & Subscribers Data Relay

The TAG loggers log the values of the tags in selected tag collections. The Loggers and Historians write to a queryable store for later, disconnected retrieval, and the Historians can additionally be read back through the APIs. The MQTT Publisher and Webhook Publisher push to a receiver that is listening at that moment. InfluxDB V1, V2 and V3 are separate, incompatible products, so the component must match the installed InfluxDB version.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text:
1. Select ADD COMPONENT in the side menu (or on the home page).
  2. Select the logger or publisher type from the table in Choose a destination.
  3. Enter its settings as described in the section for the destination.

A component whose licensed feature is missing shows as unavailable.

docs.title: Configure a file or SFTP logger
docs.text:
The CAN File Logger writes native CAN bus messages to the local file system and needs no destination setting, because it creates its files under the Profinity CAN bus log directory (can_bus_logs/) in a folder named after the profile and the component. The TAG File Logger writes tag values the same way, under the Profinity tag log directory (tag_logs/). The CAN SFTP Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger transmit the files to a server.

  1. For the CAN SFTP Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger, set Remote Host, Remote Port, Remote server username, Remote server password and Remote Directory. The remote directory is relative to the home directory of the user on the SFTP server, so it must not start with /.
  2. Set the Update Interval (Seconds).
  3. For the TAG File Logger and TAG SFTP Logger, also set:
    1. The Logging mode (On Change, Snapshot or Everything).
    2. The File Format (CSV or JSON Lines).
  4. Set Rotate By to No Rotation, Time or File Size, which determines when the current log file is closed and a new one created. Then set Rotation Interval (Sec) for time-based rotation or Rotate MB for size-based rotation.
  5. File loggers can generate large files. To manage them:
    1. Enable Archive the Logs to move rotated log files into an archive folder beneath the log folder. The CAN SFTP Logger and the TAG SFTP Logger always archive, so they do not show this setting.
    2. Optional: Enable Compress Logs to compress rotated logs.
    3. Enable Limit Number of Archive Files and set the Archive File Limit to the number of log files to retain.
  6. For the TAG File Logger and TAG SFTP Logger, select the tag collections to log in Collections. At least one collection must be configured before the logger starts, and only the tags in those collections are written. Adding a collection row works in the same way as for InfluxDB, which is described in the InfluxDB section.
  7. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog, which reads SAVE when the settings of an existing component are being changed.

docs.title: Configure an InfluxDB logger or historian
docs.text:
1. Add the InfluxDB v1 Logger, InfluxDB v2 Historian or InfluxDB v3 Historian for the InfluxDB version in use.
  2. Enter the connection settings:
    1. Influx Server URL: the endpoint InfluxDB is running on.
    2. InfluxDB Database for V1, InfluxDB Bucket and InfluxDB Organisation for V2, or InfluxDB Database for V3.
    3. InfluxDB Username and InfluxDB Password for V1, or InfluxDB Token for V2 and V3.
  3. Set the Update Interval (Seconds) and the Logging mode (Snapshot, On Change or Everything).
  4. In Collections, add a row for each tag collection to log and select the collection in that row. The logger starts only when at least one collection is configured and logs only the tags that belong to the selected collections.
  5. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog, which reads SAVE when the settings of an existing component are being changed.

How to Log Data to the Cloud (InfluxDB) works through the InfluxDB v2 Historian with InfluxDB Cloud.

docs.title: Configure a Prometheus logger
docs.text:
Prometheus collects data from Profinity rather than receiving it, so no destination is configured.

  1. Add a Prometheus Logger component.
  2. Set the Data endpoint URL, Server Hostname and Server Port. The defaults serve data at http://localhost:7065/metrics.
  3. In Collections, select the tag collections to serve, which works in the same way as for InfluxDB.
  4. Configure the Prometheus server to collect from that URL.

docs.title: Configure an MQTT Publisher or Webhook Publisher
docs.text: Refer to MQTT Publisher and Webhook Publisher for the full setting reference, including the Sparkplug B settings.

docs.title: MQTT Publisher
docs.text:
1. Set Name and configure the broker connection:
    1. Server URL: the MQTT broker address, using mqtts:// for Transport Layer Security (TLS).
    2. Username and Password: if required.
    3. Device ID: the MQTT client ID.
  2. Choose the Payload, which is JSON or Sparkplug B. For a JSON payload, set the Destination Topic, which is the topic the messages are published to.
  3. Choose the Logging mode (Snapshot, On Change or Everything).
  4. Select which tag collections to publish.
  5. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog.

docs.title: Webhook Publisher
docs.text:
1. Set Name and configure the destination:
    1. Destination URL: the HTTP(S) endpoint to POST to.
    2. Authentication: None, Bearer token, API key header, or Basic auth.
  2. Choose the Logging mode (Snapshot, On Change or Everything).
  3. Select which tag collections to publish.
  4. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog.

docs.title: Start the logger or publisher
docs.text: Make sure the logger or publisher is added to the active profile. The Auto Connect setting, which is on by default, starts the component when the profile is loaded, so with it off the component does not start when the profile loads. Check the component's status in the component list.

docs.title: Check that data is flowing
docs.text:
• For file logging, look in the log folder on the machine running Profinity (can_bus_logs/ for a CAN File Logger, tag_logs/ for a TAG File Logger), or in the remote directory on the SFTP server, for new log files.
  • For InfluxDB or Prometheus, query the database, or the Prometheus server, to confirm that data is arriving, and check the status of the logger or historian component.
  • For MQTT or a webhook, subscribe to the configured MQTT topic, or check the webhook receiver's own logs, to see published messages, and check the publisher's status for connection information.

docs.title: No data is logged
docs.text: A logger or publisher that writes nothing is usually not running, or has no tag collection to log. Check that the component is active and, for a TAG logger, InfluxDB, Prometheus, or a publisher, that at least one tag collection is selected, because those components start only when a collection is configured. Also check that the components that feed the tags are receiving data.

docs.title: A connection error appears
docs.text: A connection error means the destination cannot be reached or does not accept the credentials. Check the network connectivity to the destination and the credentials, and for InfluxDB confirm that the component type matches the installed InfluxDB version, because using the wrong component type results in connection failures. The Profinity logs record connection errors.

docs.title: Data is missing
docs.text: Gaps in logged data usually come from a logging interval that is too long for the data or from a component that stopped receiving data. Check the logging interval, because a shorter interval gives more granular data, and check that the component that supplies the data is receiving it.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• File and Tag Loggers: full file and tag logger configuration
  • InfluxDB and Prometheus Logging: InfluxDB and Prometheus logging setup

docs.title: How to connect Profinity to AI tools like Claude or ChatGPT
docs.text:
Connect Profinity to AI tools and large language models (LLMs) using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server integration. Three stages make the connection: enabling the MCP server, creating a service account token, and adding the server to the AI tool.

Profinity also has built-in AI

Profinity includes its own AI assistant, AI Chat, which answers questions about your live components, tags, and alerts without any external AI tool. To use it, an administrator only needs to enter an API key (token) from Claude, OpenAI, or OpenRouter, or the address of a local model, in Profinity AI settings. Connect an external AI tool when you want to use Profinity data from that tool instead.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity 2.3 installed and running
  • A licence that includes the AI feature, which the MCP server needs, and the Profinity Server feature, which Users & Groups needs for the service account. Both are included in the Server and Enterprise editions. On other editions the Enable MCP Server setting is unavailable. Refer to Licensing
  • Administrator access to the Profinity AI Settings and to user management
  • An AI tool or LLM client that supports MCP over Streamable HTTP with a custom Authorization header, because the Profinity MCP server authenticates every request with a JSON Web Token (JWT) bearer token
  • Familiarity with how your AI tool adds an MCP server

docs.title: Enable the MCP server
docs.text:
1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then System Configuration.
  2. Find the Profinity AI category, and its MCP Server field group.
  3. Enable Enable MCP Server.
  4. Select Save.

Enabling or disabling the MCP server takes effect only after Profinity restarts, and Profinity shows a "Restarting, please wait..." message and refreshes the settings once the engine is running again.

The MCP server is then available at http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Ai/Mcp (using the default Profinity web server port). It uses Streamable HTTP transport, not Server-Sent Events (SSE), so there is no /sse path.

docs.title: Create a service account and get a token
docs.text:
Every call to the MCP server requires a JWT bearer token for a user with the MCP integration permission. Each tool also checks its own permission before returning data: View tags for the tag tools and View alerts for the alert tools. A tag or alert the user cannot view is omitted from the response.

  1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then Users & Groups, and select + Add user.
  2. Enter a name (for example "mcp-service"), and enable Service account.
  3. Assign a role that includes MCP integration, View tags and View alerts, and save the user.
  4. Select the user's row, open the User Actions tab and select Generate Token.
  5. Copy the token and store it in a secrets manager, because a service account token does not expire and stays valid until an administrator generates a new one or disables the account (refer to Service Accounts).

Get a token from the API

A script can instead authenticate with the service account username and password through the Profinity API, which puts the password on the command line:

curl -X POST http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Users/Authenticate \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"username":"mcp-service","password":"your-password"}'

docs.title: Configure your AI tool
docs.text:
A Profinity MCP client needs three things: the Streamable HTTP endpoint http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Ai/Mcp, the HTTP transport, and an Authorization: Bearer <token> header sent on every request. A tool on another machine replaces localhost with the address of the Profinity server, and the Profinity web server port must be reachable from that machine. Each AI tool enters these values in its own way, and the following example shows the common JSON form.

Examples that use Ollama are on the Prohelion GitHub page.

A client that reads an mcpServers JSON file with type, url and headers fields, the form used by tools such as Claude Code and Cursor, takes this entry, which is added to the AI tool's MCP server configuration with the name profinity:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "profinity": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Ai/Mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE"
      }
    }
  }
}

Replace YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE with the token from the previous section and restart the AI tool.

Claude Code can add the same server from its command line:

claude mcp add --transport http profinity http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Ai/Mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE"

A client that cannot send a custom Authorization header, including a connector that supports only OAuth sign-in, cannot connect to the Profinity MCP server, because the server rejects an unauthenticated request.

docs.title: Verify the connection
docs.text: In the AI tool, ask "What components are in my active profile?", and a list of component names confirms the connection. Tag values and alerts are available in the same way.

docs.title: What the AI tool can do
docs.text:
Once connected, the AI tool can use the ten read-only MCP tools to discover components and search the tag tree, read current tag values and tag history, and review active alerts and alert history. Refer to MCP Server for every tool and its parameters. The MCP server does not expose any tool that changes Profinity data, so changes such as generating dashboards or scripts are made in your AI tool and applied separately (refer to AI Skills).

Example questions to ask once the connection works:

  • "What components are in my active profile?"
  • "Show me the current battery voltage from the BMU"
  • "Which alerts have been raised in the last hour?"
  • "Plot the motor controller temperature over the last 24 hours"

docs.title: Build Profinity content with AI Skills
docs.text: The MCP server lets an AI tool read data from Profinity, while AI Skills lets an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or ChatGPT build Profinity dashboards, rules, collections, scripts, plugins, derived tags, and example apps. AI Skills reads live data through the MCP server and the live schema through the Profinity REST API, and asks for approval before it saves any change to your instance. To add the skills to your AI tool, refer to Install AI Skills.

docs.title: The connection fails
docs.text: If the AI tool reports that the connection failed, the MCP server is disabled, Profinity has not finished restarting, the web server port is not reachable from the AI tool, or the endpoint path is wrong. Confirm that Enable MCP Server is on, that Profinity has restarted, and that the URL ends in /api/v2/Ai/Mcp, and check the Profinity logs for MCP connection issues. If the web server runs on another machine, make sure its port is allowed through the firewall.

docs.title: Enable MCP Server is unavailable
docs.text: The Enable MCP Server setting needs the AI licensed feature, so on an edition without it the setting cannot be used. Refer to Licensing.

docs.title: No data is returned
docs.text: If the AI tool connects but returns nothing, there may be no active components or profile, or the token's user lacks the View tags or View alerts permission. Make sure a profile with components is active and that the user's role includes the permission for the data requested.

docs.title: Authentication errors
docs.text: An authentication error means the token is incomplete, or its user lacks the MCP integration permission. Check that the token was copied completely and that the user's role includes MCP integration.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• AI Chat: the built-in chat assistant, which uses the same MCP server
  • AI Skills: skills that let an AI coding assistant build Profinity dashboards, rules, and scripts
  • Install AI Skills: add the skills to your AI tool
  • Scripting: Profinity scripting
  • APIs: REST API documentation

docs.title: How to connect to CAN bus
docs.text: Connect Profinity to your CAN bus network using a supported adapter. The work has two halves: preparing and cabling the adapter, and adding the adapter to the profile, setting it up, connecting it and checking that messages arrive.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Profinity V2 installed
  • A supported CAN bus adapter (Peak USB, SocketCAN, SocketCANd, Ewert Energy CANdapter, or a Prohelion or Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridge)
  • Adapter drivers installed, where the adapter needs them
  • The Modify components permission, which allows components to be added (Roles and Permissions)

docs.title: Peak USB adapters
docs.text:
1. Install the Peak drivers before starting Profinity.
  2. Use the Peak tools to verify that the adapter is working.
  3. On Windows, confirm that the adapter appears in Device Manager.

docs.title: SocketCAN
docs.text:
The SocketCAN adapter is not available on Windows, and it needs SocketCAN enabled in the kernel.

  1. For remote SocketCAN, install socketcand and allow UDP port 42000 through the firewall, because SocketCANd adapters are discovered on that port.
  2. Confirm that the CAN interfaces are available.
  3. Set the bit rate of the interface in the operating system, because Profinity does not set it, for example sudo ip link set can0 up type can bitrate 500000 on Linux.

The CAN Bus Adapters page gives the details of each adapter.

docs.title: CAN to Ethernet bridges
docs.text:
1. Power the bridge with 9 to 30 V DC on pin 9 of the DB9 connector (13.8 V nominal), because the bridge takes its power from the CAN connector.
  2. Allow UDP and TCP port 4876 through the firewall, which the Profinity installer does automatically.
  3. Place the PC and the bridge on the same subnet, ideally with a static IP address on the bridge (refer to Supported Network Setups).

docs.title: Cable the adapter
docs.text:
1. If you use a USB adapter, plug it into the computer's USB port.
  2. If you use an Ethernet bridge, connect it to the network, or directly to the PC, with an Ethernet cable. Press the reset button if the bridge has previously been on another network.
  3. If you use SocketCAN, configure the CAN interface as described in SocketCAN.
  4. Connect the adapter to the CAN bus network, which must be terminated with a 120 ohm resistor at each end because the CAN to Ethernet bridge does not terminate the bus.
  5. Confirm that the physical connections are secure.

docs.title: Add the adapter in Profinity
docs.text:
1. Select ADD COMPONENT in the side menu, and look for the adapter among the discovered adapters, which are shown at the top of the screen. If the adapter is listed, click it to add it.
  2. If the adapter is not listed, select CAN Bus Adapter or the specific adapter type, and enter the adapter details.
  3. Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog to add the adapter to the profile.

A manually added adapter asks for the following:

  • Name: a unique name for the adapter
  • Type: the adapter type
  • Network Protocol, Tritium Protocol Version, IP Address and Bus Number: for a Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridge, select UDP or TCP, select V1 or V2 to match the bridge, enter the IP address of the bridge (TCP only) and enter the bus number of the bridge
  • Network Adapter: the network interface, for the Virtual CAN to Ethernet Bridge
  • PCAN Channel ID and PCAN BaudRate: for a Peak adapter
  • Candapter COM Port and Candapter BaudRate: for an Ewert Energy CANdapter
  • Bus Name: the CAN interface, for SocketCAN

docs.title: Set the adapter up and connect it
docs.text:
1. Click the adapter in the sidebar, open Change Settings (top right of the adapter dashboard), and save the adapter settings.
  2. Click Connect on the adapter dashboard, and wait for the adapter to connect.
  3. Check that the status indicator turns green, as defined in the colour table in Adding Components to Your Profile. An adapter that is connected but sees no traffic shows amber, and a red indicator means a connection error, so check the logs.
  4. Select CAN UTILITIES in the side menu, then SEND & RECEIVED CAN (a user who holds only the View CAN data permission sees RECEIVED CAN instead), and confirm that messages appear in the CAN Activity panel. How to Send and Receive CAN Bus Messages describes the panel.

The adapter settings are:

  • Auto Connect: enable to connect the adapter when the profile loads.
  • Allow Loopback Traffic: enable where needed, which applies to Tritium adapters in UDP mode only.
  • The bit rate, where the adapter has one: the PCAN BaudRate and Candapter BaudRate settings default to 500 kbit/s and must match the network. A CAN to Ethernet bridge holds its bit rate (default 500 kbit/s) in the bridge firmware settings, as described in CAN Bridge Configuration.

docs.title: The adapter is not discovered
docs.text: An adapter that does not appear at the top of the ADD COMPONENT screen is usually unpowered, disconnected, in a different subnet or blocked by a firewall, or its driver is missing. Check that the adapter is powered and connected, that the drivers are installed, and that the firewall allows UDP and TCP port 4876 for bridges and UDP port 42000 for SocketCANd. Most bridge problems come from the PC and the bridge being in different subnets (refer to the Quickstart). For a bridge over WiFi, check that the router passes broadcast UDP, and for a bridge across subnets add it manually over TCP, because Auto Discovery relies on UDP heartbeats.

docs.title: No data arrives
docs.text: An adapter that is green or amber with an empty CAN Activity panel usually has a bit rate that does not match the network, a loose or broken connection, or devices on the bus that are not powered. Confirm that the bit rate matches every device on the bus, check the physical CAN bus connections, make sure the devices are powered, and look at the adapter status for errors.

docs.title: The connection fails
docs.text: A red indicator after Connect means the adapter is held by another application, or the bridge refuses the connection. Check the adapter logs in Profinity, and confirm that no other application is using the adapter and, for a bridge in TCP mode, that no other client holds the single TCP connection that a bridge accepts. A bridge that was rapidly connected and disconnected rejects TCP connections temporarily, so wait 30 seconds to a minute (refer to Common Problems and Solutions), and restart Profinity if the connection still fails.

docs.title: Related pages
docs.text:
• Virtual CAN Adapter: using virtual adapters
  • CAN to Ethernet Bridge documentation: the bridge user manual, datasheet, and troubleshooting

docs.title: How to create a Custom Component
docs.text: For a first Custom Component, follow Make your first Custom Component. You can create a new component in the active profile by adding a Custom Component. A Custom Component needs only a name, and every file attached to it is optional. When no dashboard is uploaded, Profinity writes a starter dashboard named after the component, which is then built out in the Dashboard visual editor. The files that can be attached are described in Custom Components, and the finished component is described in Using a Custom Component.

docs.title: Add the component
docs.text:
Adding a component needs the Modify components permission.

  1. Select ADD COMPONENT in the side menu (or on the home page).
  2. Select Custom Component.
  3. Enter a Name that is unique in the profile, and save.

The component appears in the side menu and is ready to use with its starter dashboard.

docs.title: Attach pack files
docs.text:
Open the component settings and use the Pack files tab. Every field on the tab is optional, so leave a field empty when that file is not needed. The format of each YAML file is defined in Custom Component files.

Section Field Use it for Device Upload DBC File (Optional) A .dbc file describing the device's CAN messages Presentation Upload Dashboard (Optional) A finished dashboard YAML file Behaviour Actions YAML file (Optional) actions.yaml, for menu actions Behaviour Rules YAML file (Optional) Rules for this component's tags Maps Settings Map YAML file (Optional) Extra settings fields Maps Firmware Map YAML file (Optional) Firmware settings fields Firmware Firmware Actions YAML file (Optional) firmware.yaml, naming the load and save scripts

With Upload Dashboard (Optional) empty, Profinity writes the starter dashboard and the dashboard editor opens on that file.

docs.title: Add a main script
docs.text:
A main script is optional. On the Scripts tab, set Main Script (Optional) to a .cs, .py, or .lua file in the component folder. Auto Start Main Script starts that service when the profile loads. Leave auto start off when the operator should start it from the menu, and add a mainScriptToggle entry to actions.yaml so Connect / Disconnect appears. Refer to Menu actions for that entry, and to Main script for the service.

A main script runs without a DBC file, and the tags it publishes can be read by dashboard bindings.

docs.title: Describe CAN messages with a DBC file
docs.text:
A DBC file is needed only when Profinity should decode the CAN messages the device sends, so they can be viewed in Messages and Signals or read by CAN-signal bindings. Once a DBC file is set in Upload DBC File (Optional), the component menu includes Edit DBC File and, after the file parses, Messages and Signals.

A minimal DBC file that describes one message with one signal shows what the viewer and the bindings read. The message below is named Temperature and carries one signal named Value, so after the file is attached, Messages and Signals lists Temperature with its signal Value, and a dashboard binding reads it with the source DBC/Temperature/Value.

VERSION ""

NS_ :

BS_:

BU_: Sensor

BO_ 256 Temperature: 8 Sensor
 SG_ Value : 0|16@1+ (0.1,0) [0|150] "C" Vector__XXX

If the device's CAN identifiers use a different base address than the DBC was written for, enable Rebase DBC and set Rebase Address.

docs.title: Check the component
docs.text:
1. Confirm the component is in the side menu and opens its dashboard.
  2. If a main script was set, connect it and confirm the tags the script publishes are updating on the dashboard.
  3. If a DBC file was attached, open Messages and Signals and confirm the expected messages are arriving.

CAN log replay can supply recorded traffic while a DBC file and the dashboard are being checked.

Next, refer to How to create a custom dashboard to build the dashboard for the component, and to the Dashboard Development Guide for the full dashboard reference.

docs.title: How to create a custom dashboard
docs.text:
Create your first custom dashboard using the Visual Editor. No YAML knowledge is needed for the visual steps, and each step also shows its YAML equivalent.

A custom dashboard can belong to either of two component types:

  • A Dashboard Component has no DBC file, so it shows tags that other components already publish, such as a battery management system (BMS), a motor controller, or an industrial protocol client.
  • A Custom Component has its own DBC file, so it shows the signals that the DBC file decodes from the CAN bus.

Both start from the same template dashboard and use the same editor, so the steps on this page apply to either type. Only the tag paths differ, as described in Add your first data binding.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• One of the following components in your profile:
    • A Dashboard Component (refer to Add a Dashboard Component), plus at least one other component that publishes the tags to show
    • A Custom Component (refer to How to create a Custom Component) with a DBC file attached, because a signal has a tag to bind only when a DBC file is attached
  • The Modify dashboards permission, which allows dashboards to be edited

To practise without a device, load the Example Profile and replay example_log.csv, as described in the Quick Start Guide. Add a Dashboard Component and bind to a tag such as /Prohelion BMU/DBC/PackStateOfCharge/SOCPercent.

docs.title: Open the dashboard editor
docs.text:
1. Navigate to your Dashboard Component or Custom Component in the sidebar.
  2. Select the pencil (Edit Dashboard) icon in the menu at the right of the dashboard title bar. The editor opens in DESIGN mode, the Visual Editor, with a "CUSTOM DASHBOARD" starter dashboard.

docs.title: Add your first data binding
docs.text:
1. In the dashboard tree, select the value element labelled CUSTOM DASHBOARD.
  2. In the Inspector, change the label to TEMPERATURE.
  3. In the Binding section, add a binding for the value property and choose the tag for the temperature.

As an alternative, select the YAML tab and replace the static label with a data binding. The source path depends on the component type that owns the dashboard.

Dashboard ComponentCustom Component 
- value:
    label: TEMPERATURE
    precision: 1
    bind:
      - target: value
        source: /My Device/DBC/Temperature/Value

A Dashboard Component has no DBC, so a relative path finds no tag. Start the source with / and the name of the component that publishes the tag, and replace My Device, Temperature, and Value with the component, message, and signal names in your profile.

- value:
    label: TEMPERATURE
    precision: 1
    bind:
      - target: value
        source: DBC/Temperature/Value

A source that starts with DBC/ is relative to the Custom Component that owns the dashboard, so replace Temperature and Value with the message and signal names from its DBC file. To show a tag from another component, use an absolute path that starts with /.

Refer to Data Binding.

docs.title: Add more components
docs.text:
1. In the dashboard tree, select the pill group that holds the value.
  2. Select Add, and choose Value (in pill) in the Add component window.
  3. Set its label to PRESSURE in the Inspector and bind it to the pressure tag in the Binding section.

As an alternative, add additional readouts in the YAML tab. This example uses the relative paths of a Custom Component; in a Dashboard Component, start each source with / and the component name, as in the previous section.

- pillgroup:
    items:
      - value:
          label: TEMPERATURE
          precision: 1
          bind:
            - target: value
              source: DBC/Temperature/Value
      - value:
          label: PRESSURE
          precision: 2
          bind:
            - target: value
              source: DBC/Pressure/Value

docs.title: Validate and save
docs.text:
1. Fix anything listed under Schema validation issues. The editor checks the dashboard against the schema as you work, and SAVE is blocked while any entry remains.
  2. Select SAVE when the list is empty.
  3. Close the editor to see the result on the dashboard behind it, because DESIGN is an outline and not a live preview.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Dashboard Visual Editor: the editor in full
  • Dashboard Development Guide: the full reference for dashboards
  • Core Elements: more complex layouts
  • Component Reference: available components
  • Motor Controller Dashboard Example: a complete dashboard, section by section

docs.title: How to create a new profile
docs.text:
Create a new profile to manage different configurations for different setups or locations. You create a profile by adding one, or by importing a Profile Pack from another Profinity instance. You need Profinity V2 installed and running, and the Modify profiles permission, which allows profiles to be added and switched (Roles and Permissions).

  1. In the side menu, select ADMIN, then the Profile pill. The profile list opens.
  2. Click Add profile.
  3. Enter a unique Profile Name that identifies the site or purpose, for example "Production Site" or "Test Rig".
  4. Optional: Add a description.
  5. Save the profile.
  6. In the list, click ACTIVATE on the row of the new profile. It becomes the active profile immediately, without restarting Profinity.

To import a Profile Pack from another Profinity instance instead, use Upload Profile Pack. Each profile keeps its own components, so a component added to one profile does not appear in another, and ACTIVATE on any row switches to that profile.

With the new profile active, add components to it as described in How to add a component to your profile, and configure their settings. A profile can also have its own home dashboard, which How to Create a Profile Dashboard describes. Changes to the profile, such as components added to it, are saved with the profile.

Refer to Profiles for the full profile reference, including renaming, Profile Packs and Kiosk Mode, and to Profile Dashboard for profile dashboard configuration.

docs.title: How to create a profile dashboard
docs.text:
Replace the default Profinity home page with a custom dashboard for your profile. Build the dashboard in the dashboard visual editor, or upload an existing dashboard YAML file instead. The Profile Dashboard page is the full reference for profile dashboards.

Before you start, you need:

  • An active profile in Profinity.
  • The Modify profiles permission, which allows profile settings to be changed (refer to Roles and Permissions).
  • The Modify dashboards permission, which allows dashboards to be edited.
  • Optional: an existing dashboard YAML file to upload, if you are not starting from the starter dashboard.

docs.title: Turn on the custom home dashboard
docs.text:
1. Select ADMIN in the side menu.
  2. Select the Profile pill.
  3. Select the name of your profile in the list to open its settings.
  4. Enable the Custom Home Dashboard option.
  5. Leave the Dashboard YAML file (Optional) field empty and save the profile settings.

Profinity creates a starter dashboard from the built-in template.

docs.title: Build the dashboard in the visual editor
docs.text:
1. Go to the home page (select the home icon or refresh).
  2. Select the pencil (Edit Dashboard) icon in the menu at the right of the dashboard title bar.
  3. In DESIGN mode, add rows, groups, and widgets, set their properties and bind tags. Refer to Dashboard Visual Editor for the steps.
  4. Resolve anything listed under Schema validation issues, then select SAVE.

Close the editor to see the result, because DESIGN is an outline and not a live preview. The custom dashboard now replaces the default home page, and it stays in place whenever this profile is the active profile.

docs.title: Upload a YAML file
docs.text:
You can upload a dashboard YAML file that already exists instead of building a new one, for example one written outside the editor or shared from another profile.

  1. Open the profile settings and enable the Custom Home Dashboard option.
  2. In the Dashboard YAML file (Optional) field, select your dashboard YAML file. It must have the .yaml extension.
  3. Save the profile settings.

An uploaded dashboard opens in the visual editor like any other, so you can change it there. The YAML tab shows the source, which you can copy as a backup. The editor does not save a dashboard that fails schema validation, and an invalid dashboard does not load.

docs.title: Remove a profile dashboard
docs.text:
To revert to the default home page:

  1. Open the profile settings.
  2. Disable the Custom Home Dashboard option.
  3. Save the profile settings.

Removing the dashboard deletes its file

Saving the profile with Custom Home Dashboard disabled deletes the dashboard YAML file from the profile's dashboards folder and clears the dashboard file setting, so the file cannot be recovered from Profinity afterwards. Download or copy the dashboard YAML before saving the profile if it is needed again. If the file cannot be deleted, for example because of a file permission problem, the dashboard file setting is not cleared and the error is written to the log.

For more on dashboards, refer to the Dashboard Development Guide.

docs.title: How to debug dashboard issues
docs.text: A dashboard problem usually shows itself in one of four ways: the dashboard does not load, a readout shows no data, an image is missing, or a style has no effect. Each is covered below with its usual cause and fix. This guide needs access to the dashboard editor and a dashboard that shows the problem.

docs.title: The dashboard does not load
docs.text:
A dashboard that fails to load, or that cannot be saved, has a validation error, because Profinity does not load an invalid dashboard. A dashboard whose saved layout no longer matches the schema shows the message "This dashboard no longer matches the schema" with the buttons Reset from Template and View Logs.

Warning

Reset from Template replaces the dashboard with the latest template and loses every customisation, so use it only when the dashboard is not needed.
