Otherwise, open Edit Dashboard from the title bar to repair the file.

In the dashboard editor, read the Schema validation issues list, which names each problem, and correct each entry. The usual causes are a missing colon, wrong indentation, an invalid property name, or a required property that is absent. SAVE is blocked while any entry remains, so save once the list is empty, then close the editor, because the dashboard behind it shows the result.

docs.title: A readout shows no data
docs.text:
A readout that stays empty has a binding that does not match a tag, a component that is not running, or no data arriving. Start with the binding, because it is the most common cause:

bind:
  - target: value
    source: DBC/Message/Signal

Find the tag in the Tag Explorer and compare its path with the source character for character, for example Prohelion BMU/DBC/PackStateOfCharge/SOCPercent in the Example Profile. Confirm that the component name in the path is correct and that the tag has a current value and a good quality flag. If the tag is correct, check the component's status indicator in the sidebar. A green indicator means the component is active, and anything else means it is not receiving CAN data, in which case the fault is the CAN bus connection and How to Connect to CAN Bus applies.

To separate a binding fault from a data fault, replace the binding temporarily with a static value:

- readouts:
    items:
      - readout:
          label: "TEST"
          value: 42.5

A readout that shows 42.5 displays correctly, so the fault is in the binding or the data. Adding the binding back one element at a time shows which element fails.

docs.title: An image does not appear
docs.text:
An image that does not appear is missing from the profile's images folder, has a filename that differs from the one in the dashboard, or is in a format Profinity does not support. File names are case-sensitive, so Logo.png and logo.png are different files, and an image in an HTML component needs its full path:

<img src="/Profile/Images/logo.png" />

How to Add Images to Your Dashboard gives the location of the folder and lists the supported formats.

docs.title: A style has no effect
docs.text: A style that does not apply is usually a stylesheet that is not loaded, or a class name that differs from the CSS. The web interface loads only profile.css from the profile's styles folder, and any other stylesheet must be imported from it, because Profinity removes a link element from an HTML component. The class named in the dashboard must also match the one in the CSS exactly, and a class on a readout item has no effect, so it goes on the readouts element. Refer to How to Style Your Dashboard.

docs.title: When the cause is still unclear
docs.text:
The Profinity logs record dashboard errors, including data binding errors and missing component or tag errors. Open ADMIN, then Logs, and read the entries from the time the dashboard was opened.

Comparing the dashboard with a working one also locates the difference quickly. Open the working dashboard's source as described in How to View Dashboard Source, compare its structure and formatting with the faulty one, and copy the working pattern.

For more, refer to the Troubleshooting Guide, the Dashboard FAQ and the Dashboard Development Guide, which has schema validation information.

docs.title: How to log data to the cloud (InfluxDB)
docs.text:
Configure Profinity to log CAN bus data to InfluxDB for cloud-based data analytics and visualisation. The steps use InfluxDB Cloud and the InfluxDB v2 Historian, the typical cloud setup. The InfluxDB v1 Logger, which is available in every edition, and the InfluxDB v3 Historian take different connection settings, which are listed in InfluxDB and Prometheus Logging.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity 2.3 installed and running.
  • A licence that includes the Historians feature, which the InfluxDB v2 Historian needs (Desktop, Server, and Enterprise editions, not an unlicensed instance). Refer to Licensing.
  • An InfluxDB instance (cloud or self-hosted), with its version known, because InfluxDB V1, V2 and V3 are separate, incompatible products and Profinity provides a separate component for each.
  • An InfluxDB bucket (V2) or database (V1 and V3) created and accessible.
  • Network access to your InfluxDB server.
  • The Modify components permission (refer to Roles and Permissions), which allows loggers and historians to be added.

docs.title: Set up InfluxDB
docs.text:
To use InfluxDB Cloud:

  1. Sign up for InfluxDB Cloud.
  2. Create a new organisation.
  3. Create a new bucket for your data.
  4. Generate an API token with write permissions.
  5. Note the organisation name, bucket name, API token and the InfluxDB URL shown in your account.

To use a self-hosted InfluxDB:

  1. Install InfluxDB on your server.
  2. Start the InfluxDB service.
  3. Create a bucket and generate an API token, for example:
influx bucket create --name my-profinity-data
influx auth create --org my-org --all-access

docs.title: Add the InfluxDB v2 Historian component
docs.text:
1. Select ADD COMPONENT in the side menu (or on the home page).
  2. Select the InfluxDB v2 Historian (under Historians).

docs.title: Configure the InfluxDB connection
docs.text:
1. Enter a component name, for example "InfluxDB Cloud Logger".
  2. Enter the Influx Server URL. For a cloud instance this is the URL shown in your InfluxDB Cloud account, for example https://us-east-1-1.aws.cloud2.influxdata.com. For a self-hosted instance it is http://your-server:8086.
  3. Enter the InfluxDB Organisation name.
  4. Enter the InfluxDB Bucket name.
  5. Enter the InfluxDB Token.
  6. For InfluxDB Cloud, set InfluxDB Health Check to false, because InfluxDB Cloud does not support the health check API.

docs.title: Configure the logging interval and mode
docs.text:
1. Set the Update Interval (Seconds), for example 1 to 5 seconds. A shorter interval gives more granular data but uses more bandwidth, and a longer interval uses less bandwidth but gives coarser data.
  2. Set the Logging mode to Snapshot to send the current value of every tag on each interval, On Change to send the changes recorded during the interval, or Everything to send every sample that arrives, including unchanged values.
  3. In Collections, add a row for each tag collection to log and select the collection in that row. The historian starts only when at least one collection is configured, and it logs only the tags that belong to the selected collections.

docs.title: Save and start the historian
docs.text: Select ADD COMPONENT at the bottom of the dialog to add the historian to the active profile. The button reads SAVE when you change the settings of an existing component. The historian starts when the profile is loaded if Auto Connect is on, which is the default.

docs.title: Verify data logging
docs.text:
1. Check the status of the historian component for connection errors.
  2. Log in to the InfluxDB web interface and open Data Explorer.
  3. Query your data, which should return points when data is arriving: 
    from(bucket: "my-profinity-data")
  |> range(start: -1h)
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r["_measurement"] == "Your_Profile_Name")
  4. If no data arrives, check the Profinity logs for connection errors.

docs.title: Data structure in InfluxDB
docs.text:
Profinity writes one point per tag sample, with this structure:

  • Measurement: the active profile name, with spaces and any character other than a letter or digit replaced by an underscore, so Example Profile becomes Example_Profile.
  • Tags:
    • profile: the same formatted profile name.
    • transmitter: currently always empty in Profinity 2.3.
    • component: the first segment of the full tag path, which is the component, formatted in the same way as the profile name.
    • message: the DBC message name for a DBC signal tag.
    • signal: the DBC signal name, or the dotted property path.
    • full_tag_id: the full tag path, unaltered.
  • Fields: a single numeric field named value.
  • Timestamp: the sample timestamp in UTC, written with nanosecond precision.

An example data point follows. The values are illustrative, and the component, message and signal names depend on the profile and DBC file.

measurement: "Example_Profile"
tags:
  profile: "Example_Profile"
  transmitter: ""
  component: "Prohelion_BMU"
  message: "Pack_Status"
  signal: "PackVoltage"
  full_tag_id: "Prohelion BMU/DBC/Pack_Status/PackVoltage"
fields:
  value: 400.5
timestamp: 2024-01-17T10:30:00Z

Tags other than DBC signals and component properties, such as relayed or registered tags, are written with the tag path after the component in signal, joined with dots, because they have no DBC message name.

To read the data back, filter on the measurement, the value field and the tags. Tags are indexed, so filter on component, message and signal in queries where possible, for example:

from(bucket: "my-profinity-data")
  |> range(start: -1h)
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r["_measurement"] == "Example_Profile")
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r["_field"] == "value")
  |> filter(fn: (r) => r["component"] == "Prohelion_BMU" and r["signal"] == "PackVoltage")

docs.title: The connection fails
docs.text: A historian that reports a connection failure has a URL that cannot be reached, a token that is not accepted, or an organisation name that does not match. Verify that the Influx Server URL is correct and reachable and that the firewall allows the connection. Verify that the API token is correct and has write permissions, and that the organisation name matches. For InfluxDB Cloud, confirm that InfluxDB Health Check is set to false. Testing network connectivity from the Profinity machine to the URL separates a network fault from a credential fault.

docs.title: No data arrives
docs.text: A historian that connects but writes nothing is usually stopped, has no tags selected, or has no incoming data. Verify that the historian is active, that at least one collection is selected in Collections and that the collection contains tags, that the components are receiving data, that the logging interval is set, and that the token has write permission in InfluxDB.

docs.title: Authentication errors
docs.text:
An authentication error means the token or the organisation is wrong. Verify that the API token is correct and has write permissions, and that the organisation name matches the one in InfluxDB.

For more, refer to How to Configure Data Logging, the general data logging guide, and the official InfluxDB documentation.

docs.title: How to replay CAN bus logs
docs.text:
Replay recorded CAN bus messages to test dashboards, rules, and custom components without live CAN bus data, or to debug a component configuration against a recording. The CAN Data Log Replayer replays log files that were recorded earlier in Profinity. For how to record a log, refer to Log / replay CAN bus messages.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity V2 installed and running.
  • A recorded CAN bus log file from a File Logger or an SSH File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) logger, or the example_log.csv supplied with Profinity. Logs from InfluxDB or Prometheus cannot be replayed, so use a File or SFTP logger to record logs for later replay.
  • The Replay CAN logs permission (refer to Roles and Permissions), which provides the CAN LOG REPLAY side-menu entry and also turns on View CAN data.
  • A profile whose components match the recording. example_log.csv carries the CAN traffic of the Example Profile's components, so load the Example Profile first (refer to the Quick Start Guide), because only components whose CAN addresses match the logged messages receive data.
  • Optional for testing: a CAN bus adapter connected.

docs.title: Replay a log
docs.text:
Replay mixes with live traffic

Replayed messages are processed by Profinity as if they had been received from the bus, so tags, dashboards, rules, and alerts react to them alongside any live traffic from a connected adapter. Disconnect the adapter, or isolate the live hardware from the bus, before replaying a log, or the live and replayed values compete.

The replayer lists only the can_bus_logs/replay/ folder in the artefacts directory, which sits in a different place on each platform. To replay a log:

  1. Select CAN UTILITIES in the side menu, then CAN LOG REPLAY. This opens the CAN Data Log Replayer and lists the available log files.
  2. If the log file is not listed, for example a file recorded earlier or on another Profinity instance, copy it into the can_bus_logs/replay/ folder, or use the Upload CAN Log files control and select the file. The file then appears in the list.
  3. Select the log file in the list and select Play to start the replay. Replayed messages appear in the CAN Activity panel, components receive them, dashboards update, and the slider shows the position in the log.

An uploaded file must have a .csv or .txt extension, otherwise the upload is refused with "Your file must have an extension of .txt or .csv". The upload is also refused if a log with the same name already exists, so delete the existing log first or rename the new one.

CAN Data Log Replayer

docs.title: Control the replay
docs.text: While a replay plays, the position slider moves to a different point in the log. You can drag the slider at any time, including during playback. Releasing the handle during playback jumps to that point and continues playing, and while the replay is paused or stopped it sets the position that Play resumes from. Pause suspends the replay so that it can be resumed later, and Play resumes it. Stop ends the replay, and Loop replays the log continuously. The trashcan icon deletes a log file from the list, which is separate from controlling a replay.

docs.title: If nothing happens
docs.text:
Only a CAN message log recorded by a File or SFTP logger can be replayed, so an uploaded file of another kind does not play. If the CAN LOG REPLAY entry is missing from the side menu, the signed-in user lacks the Replay CAN logs permission. If the replay runs but the dashboards stay empty, no component in the active profile listens to the replayed CAN IDs, so load the profile that the log was recorded against. Recorded tag values are replayed separately with TAG LOG REPLAY, described in Replay a tag log.

To check a Custom Component against its DBC file with recorded messages, refer to How to Create a Custom Component.

docs.title: How to send and receive CAN bus messages
docs.text:
Send and receive CAN bus messages using Profinity's built-in CAN tools. Receiving shows the traffic on the bus, and sending transmits a packet once or on a schedule. The Send / receive CAN bus messages page is the full CAN utilities reference.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity V2 installed and running.
  • A CAN bus adapter connected and active. To set one up, refer to Connect to CAN Bus.
  • A role that includes the View CAN data permission to receive and view CAN messages, and Send CAN messages to send them.
  • An active profile with the adapter configured.

docs.title: Check user permissions
docs.text:
On a Server or Enterprise installation:

  1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then Users & Groups.
  2. Select your user account.
  3. Check that one of the Assigned roles includes View CAN data, which allows CAN messages to be received and viewed. To send messages, check that an assigned role includes Send CAN messages, which also includes View CAN data.
  4. Change the roles if needed and select Save.

Changing a user's roles revokes their active sessions, so the user must sign in again for the change to take effect. A Desktop installation runs as a built-in user that holds every permission, so it needs no change (refer to Licensing).

docs.title: Receive CAN messages
docs.text:
Select CAN UTILITIES in the side menu, then SEND & RECEIVED CAN. This opens the CAN Activity window showing all CAN messages currently on the network. A user who holds only View CAN data sees RECEIVED CAN instead and cannot send. The CAN Activity panel shows these columns:

Column Contents CAN ID The message identifier Data The message data bytes Direction Incoming or outgoing Count The number of times the message was seen Time The timestamp of the last message

Two toggle icons change the view. Spaced data breaks the data into individual hex bytes and is on by default. Heatmap highlights frequently changing bytes in warmer colours and relatively constant bytes in cooler colours, and is also on by default. Select a column header to sort by that column, use the filters to show specific CAN IDs or data patterns, and select a message to see its details.

docs.title: Send a CAN packet
docs.text:
A sent packet can command connected hardware

A packet sent from Profinity goes on to the live CAN bus and is acted on by every connected device, so a packet can start a motor controller, open a contactor or change a device setting. Check what is connected to the bus and what the packet's CAN ID and data mean before sending it, and be especially careful with a scheduled packet, which keeps sending until it is deleted.

A packet can be sent once, or saved so that Profinity adds it to the Scheduled CAN Packets list and continues to send it in the background. To send a packet:

  1. Select the + icon in the Scheduled CAN Packets list at the bottom of the screen. To start from a received packet instead, double-click it or select it in the CAN Activity panel, then select the Open in Schedule Editor + icon at the top of the page. This opens the packet editor.
  2. Enter the CAN ID (hex or decimal), and select the Endian byte order (little endian by default). The schedule editor reference explains why little endian is the default.
  3. Choose the Data Format, which is Bytes, Int16, Int32, Floats or Raw Data, and enter the values. The raw data updates automatically as the values change. For example, in Bytes the values 0x01, 0x02 and 0x03 go in bytes 0 to 2, and in Int16 the values 1234 and 5678 go in Int16[0] and Int16[1] and are converted to bytes automatically.
  4. Set the Interval [ms] to choose how often the packet is sent, for example 100 ms sends it 10 times per second. The value is a whole number from 1 to 4,294,967,295. Leave it blank, or enter 0, to send the packet once only, and the primary button then reads SEND instead of START.
  5. Select Save to add the packet to the scheduled list. The packet appears in the scheduled packets panel and, if an interval is set, starts sending at once.
  6. To send a packet manually at any time, including a packet that is not set up on a schedule, select it in the Scheduled CAN Packets list and select the Send arrow button, or press the Space key. The packet is sent immediately.
  7. Check the CAN Activity panel, where the sent message appears with an outgoing direction, and confirm that the CAN ID and data match your configuration.

docs.title: Manage scheduled packets
docs.text:
The Scheduled CAN Packets list at the bottom of the screen shows every scheduled packet. A scheduled packet is saved with the profile, so if you change profile or restart Profinity the saved packets are not lost, and they are restored. A packet with an interval starts sending when it is saved, and it keeps sending after the user signs out, so logging off does not stop it. Packets do not start automatically after a profile change or a restart of Profinity, and you need to restart them manually.

To stop a packet, select it in the scheduled packets panel and delete it by selecting Delete or pressing the Delete key, which removes it from the schedule. To change a packet, select it, select Edit or double-click it, modify the settings and select Save. Sending a packet manually before scheduling it, and checking that the CAN ID, data format and CAN bus bit rate match what the network expects, avoids sending unexpected traffic to a live bus.

docs.title: A packet does not send
docs.text: A scheduled packet that never appears in the CAN Activity panel has usually met one of four conditions: the adapter is not connected (its status indicator is not green), the signed-in user lacks the Send CAN messages permission, the CAN ID is not valid, or no interval is set, in which case the packet waits for a manual send. Work through them in that order, then select the packet and select the Send arrow to confirm it transmits before relying on the schedule.

docs.title: A packet does not appear in the activity panel
docs.text: A packet that was sent but is missing from the CAN Activity panel is usually hidden by a filter, or the adapter is not receiving traffic back, or the CAN bus bit rate does not match the network. Clear the filters, check that the adapter is receiving traffic, and check the bit rate.

docs.title: The data is wrong
docs.text: Data that differs from what was entered usually has the wrong byte order or the wrong data format. Check that the Endian setting matches your system, check the conversion between bytes and integers, and review the raw data to confirm the values.

docs.title: How to set up Profinity as a kiosk application
docs.text:
Configure Profinity to run as a kiosk application that launches in fullscreen mode when the display starts. Two parts are involved: Kiosk Mode in Profinity, which signs the display in automatically as a chosen user, and the browser and operating system setup, which opens Profinity fullscreen. The Kiosk Mode page is the full reference, including how to choose the kiosk user and manage its token.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity 2.3 installed as a service or in Docker with automatic start enabled, and running, because the browser fails to connect if Profinity is not already running (refer to Running as a Service).
  • Administrator access to the system.
  • A profile configured and ready to display, and the Modify profiles permission to change its settings. Profiles describes the profile settings, including Kiosk Mode.
  • An enabled user to act as the kiosk user, holding only the permissions the display needs (refer to Choosing the Kiosk User).
  • A licence that includes the Profinity Server feature, to create that user. Kiosk Mode is available in every edition, but the kiosk user must be a user account, and user accounts are created in Users & Groups, which needs the Profinity Server feature (Server and Enterprise editions). Without it there are no user accounts, so a Desktop installation has no user to select (refer to Licensing).

docs.title: Configure Kiosk Mode in Profinity
docs.text:
Kiosk Mode is configured per profile, and it authenticates the browser automatically as the configured kiosk user so that no login page is shown.

  1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then Profile.
  2. Select or create the profile to display, and open its profile settings.
  3. Enable Kiosk Mode.
  4. Select a Kiosk Mode User from the dropdown. All enabled users are listed, so choose one with minimal permissions.
  5. Save the profile settings.
  6. Ensure this profile is the active profile, because Kiosk Mode applies only to the active profile.

docs.title: Configure the browser for fullscreen display
docs.text:
Start Profinity before the browser

The browser fails to connect if Profinity is not already running, so Profinity must start automatically as a service or in Docker, and the browser must start after it, allowing time for Profinity to finish starting.

The browser's own --kiosk switch provides the fullscreen display, and Profinity does not read query parameters that request fullscreen. The steps for each operating system follow, and each uses http://localhost:18080, the default Profinity web address.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
The example assumes that Google Chrome is installed.

  1. Create a desktop shortcut for the browser.
  2. Right-click the shortcut and select Properties.

  3. In Target, add --kiosk http://localhost:18080, for example:

    "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --kiosk http://localhost:18080

  4. Press Win + R, type shell:startup, and copy the shortcut to the startup folder that opens.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
1. Create a systemd service with sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/profinity-kiosk.service and add the following unit:

    [Unit]
Description=Profinity Kiosk Mode
After=graphical.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=your-username
ExecStart=/usr/bin/chromium-browser --kiosk --noerrdialogs http://localhost:18080
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=graphical.target

  2. Enable the service with sudo systemctl enable profinity-kiosk.service.

  3. Start the service with sudo systemctl start profinity-kiosk.service.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
1. Open Automator and create a new Application.
  2. Add a Run Shell Script action and enter the script /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome --kiosk http://localhost:18080.
  3. Save it as an application.
  4. Open System Settings (System Preferences on older versions of macOS), select Users & Groups, then Login Items, and add the kiosk application.

docs.title: Hide the side menu
docs.text: Profinity pages that are rendered from a dashboard accept the noMenu=true query parameter, which hides the side menu so that only the dashboard is shown. Append it to the address of the dashboard page that the browser opens, as ?noMenu=true after the page path (or &noMenu=true where the address already has a query string). Profinity does not read query parameters that select a profile, so the profile that is shown is always the active profile.

docs.title: Lock down the display
docs.text:
The browser's --kiosk switch fills the screen but does not disable operating system shortcuts such as Alt+F4 or Ctrl+Alt+Del. Lock the system down with the operating system's own facilities, for example Windows Group Policy, hide the taskbar and system tray, and configure the system to restart the browser when it exits (the Linux unit above does this with Restart=always).

Anyone at the display inherits the kiosk user's permissions

Confirm that the kiosk user holds only the permissions the display needs, for example a read-only role built from view permissions only, because anyone at the display inherits them.

A kiosk session expires under the normal token expiry policy, so a display that runs for months without attention can use a kiosk user marked as a service account, as described in Kiosk Mode. A chart that polls for data at a fixed interval is set in the dashboard, as described in Charts.

docs.title: Test Kiosk Mode
docs.text:
1. Restart the system.
  2. Confirm that Profinity starts automatically.
  3. Confirm that the browser opens fullscreen, loads the correct profile and signs in automatically without the login page.

docs.title: The browser does not start
docs.text: A browser that does not open after a restart usually starts before Profinity or before the display is ready. Check the startup order and service dependencies so that the browser starts after Profinity. To run Profinity as a service, refer to Running as a Service.

docs.title: The login page is shown
docs.text: A login page that appears instead of the dashboard means Kiosk Mode is off for the active profile, or the kiosk user is missing or disabled. Verify that Kiosk Mode is enabled for the active profile and that a valid kiosk user is selected. Refer to Kiosk Mode for the other causes.

docs.title: The wrong profile is shown
docs.text: Kiosk Mode shows the active profile only, so make the intended profile the active profile.

docs.title: The display or performance is poor
docs.text: A blank, cropped, or slow display usually comes from the display resolution settings or a dashboard that is too complex for the machine. Check the display configuration and resolution settings, and monitor system resources and simplify the dashboard.

docs.title: How to style your dashboard
docs.text:
Apply custom CSS styling to your dashboard elements for branding and visual customisation. The web interface loads one stylesheet from the profile, profile.css, so a first style needs that one file.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity V2 installed.
  • A dashboard to style.
  • Basic CSS knowledge.
  • Access to the styles folder of the profile directory, which is <artefacts directory>/profiles/<profile name>/styles.

The artefacts directory is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity on macOS and /var/lib/prohelion/profinity on Linux. On Docker it is the path inside the container named by PROFINITY_HOME, so on Docker the file must be created in the mounted volume that holds that directory. The folder is named styles in lowercase on disk, and /Profile/Styles is only its URL path (refer to Store dashboard files in a profile).

docs.title: Create the stylesheet
docs.text:
1. Create the styles folder in the profile directory if it does not exist.

  2. Create a file named profile.css in it and add the rules for your dashboard:

    .custom-panel {
    background-color: #f0f0f0;
    border: 2px solid #007bff;
    border-radius: 8px;
    padding: 1rem;
}

.custom-readout {
    font-size: 1.2em;
    color: #333;
    font-weight: bold;
}

docs.title: Split the styles across files
docs.text:
A large set of styles can be kept in further files in the same folder, for example custom-dashboard.css, which profile.css loads with a CSS @import rule. The web interface loads only profile.css, and the HTML sanitiser removes link elements from the content of an HTML component. A stylesheet therefore cannot be linked from the dashboard and must be imported from profile.css:

/* /Profile/Styles/profile.css */
@import url("custom-dashboard.css");

docs.title: Apply the classes
docs.text:
Use the class property on a group or readouts element in a dashboard. A class on an individual readout item is not used by the web interface, so the class that styles the readouts goes on the readouts element that holds them (refer to Readouts). Other components list which of them accept class.

- group:
    class: "custom-panel"
    items:
      - readouts:
          class: "custom-readout"
          items:
            - readout:
                label: "Temperature"

docs.title: Check the styling
docs.text:
Save the dashboard, close the editor and reload the page, because the web interface loads profile.css when the page opens. If a class has no effect, the stylesheet is not named profile.css or is not imported from it, or the class name in the dashboard differs from the CSS in spelling or case, or the class is on an element that does not use it, such as a readout item. Correct the file or the dashboard and reload the page.

For more, refer to Conditional Styling, which styles elements from data values.

docs.title: How to view dashboard source
docs.text:
Open the YAML source of an existing dashboard to learn from examples and modify them. The Quick Start Guide introduces the same task with the Example Profile.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity V2 installed and running.
  • Access to a dashboard (component or profile dashboard).
  • The Modify dashboards permission, which shows the pencil icon that opens the dashboard editor.

docs.title: Open a component dashboard's source
docs.text:
1. Select the component in the sidebar.
  2. Select the pencil (Edit Dashboard) icon in the menu at the right of the dashboard title bar. This opens the dashboard editor in DESIGN mode.
  3. Select the YAML tab to see the complete dashboard configuration.

docs.title: Open a profile dashboard's source
docs.text:
A profile dashboard replaces the standard home page when Custom Home Dashboard is enabled in the profile settings. To find the setting, select ADMIN in the side menu, then Profile, and select the profile. How to Create a Profile Dashboard describes enabling the option.

With the option enabled:

  1. Go to the home page.
  2. Select the pencil (Edit Dashboard) icon in the menu at the right of the dashboard title bar.
  3. Select the YAML tab.

docs.title: Copy and reuse a dashboard
docs.text:
1. In the YAML tab, select all of the YAML.
  2. Copy it with Ctrl+C or Cmd+C.
  3. Paste it into a text editor to save it, or paste it into a new dashboard, component, or profile to use it as a template.
  4. Modify the pasted source to suit the new dashboard, then save it as the new dashboard.

Reading the YAML shows how components are organised, how data bindings are configured, how layout elements nest and how styling is applied. Copying a simple dashboard first and adding complexity in small, tested changes keeps a faulty change easy to find.

For more, refer to the Dashboard Development Guide, the Motor Controller Dashboard Example and the Component Reference.

docs.title: How to write your first script
docs.text:
Create your first Profinity script to automate tasks and interact with your CAN bus system. This guide adds a script component, writes a run script that prints a message, runs it and finds the output.

Before you start, you need:

  • Profinity 2.3 installed and running.
  • A Desktop, Server, or Enterprise licence. An unlicensed instance cannot add or run scripts. Refer to Licensing.
  • An active profile with components configured.
  • Basic understanding of C# or Python. Profinity scripting uses IronPython for Python, which limits the Python syntax available, and also supports Lua. Refer to Supported Languages.
  • Scripting enabled in Profinity configuration, as in the first step below.

Scripts run with application permissions

A script runs inside Profinity with the same operating system permissions as the application, so review any script before running it. Refer to the Scripting overview for the security context and behaviour.

docs.title: Enable scripting
docs.text:
1. Select ADMIN in the side menu and open the System Configuration pill. Refer to System Configuration for detail.
  2. Find the Optional Capabilities section.
  3. Enable Enable Scripting.
  4. Select Save.

docs.title: Add a script component and set its mode
docs.text:
A script is a component in your profile, and the language is set by which script component you add. For a first script use a run script, whose type is set by the Script Mode of the script component. The main types are Run scripts, which run on demand or on a schedule (time interval or cron), Receive scripts, which run when selected CAN messages are received, and Service scripts, which are long-running background services with lifecycle control. Tag Change and Alert modes also exist, and Script Types describes them.

  1. Select ADD COMPONENT. Refer to Adding Components to Your Profile.
  2. Select the CSharp Script, Python Script or Lua Script component. This opens the script component settings and the script editor together.
  3. Set the component name, and add a description if wanted.
  4. Set Script Mode to Run On Demand, which runs the script manually from the UI. Run On Time Interval runs it at a fixed interval, for example every few minutes, and Run On CRON Schedule runs it on a Quartz cron expression.
  5. Optional: enable Auto Start Script to start the script automatically when Profinity starts, and enable Log Script Output, which is off by default, so that the script's output appears in the Profinity log.

docs.title: Write the script
docs.text: Use the same patterns as in Run Scripts. C# implements IProfinityRunnableScript with a Run() method, and Python defines functions and calls them from the top level, with no import profinity because the Profinity host object is provided. In C#, use Profinity.Console.WriteLine for output, and in Python use print(). Refer to Console.

docs.title: C
docs.text:
using System;

public class MyFirstRunScript : ProfinityScript, IProfinityRunnableScript
{
    public bool Run()
    {
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine("This is my first Profinity script.");
        Profinity.Console.WriteLine(Profinity.Message);
        return true;
    }
}

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
def main():
    print("This is my first Profinity script.")
    print(Profinity.Message)


main()

docs.title: Run the script
docs.text:
Select Save to save the script and the component settings, which are saved together. The script component appears in your profile. Run the script from the script component's menu by selecting Run Script (available when Script Mode is Run On Demand), and use Cancel Script to stop a script that is still running.

With Log Script Output enabled, the output appears in the Profinity log (select ADMIN, then Logs) at the Info level as Script <script file name>: This is my first Profinity script., followed by a line for Profinity.Message. Compile errors and script errors are always written to the log, whether or not Log Script Output is on, so review the error message, fix the script, and run it again. A script with a time interval or cron schedule runs according to the schedule that was set.

For more examples, refer to Script examples.

docs.title: The script does not run
docs.text: A script that does not run usually has scripting disabled or a component language that does not match the source. Confirm that scripting is enabled in System Configuration and that the script component's language matches the language of the source.

docs.title: The DBC signal is null or missing
docs.text: A signal that returns nothing or raises an error has a component, message, or signal name that does not match the DBC, because the names are case-sensitive. Check the names against the DBC viewer. The Script examples page shows a script that reads a DBC signal.

docs.title: A syntax error appears
docs.text: Fix compile errors (C#) or IronPython and Python 3 syntax errors (Python) before running, and add one API (DBC, CAN bus or state) at a time so that a fault is easy to find. The Script examples page shows each API in turn.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Script examples: reading a DBC signal, sending a CAN message, and persisting script state.
  • Scripting Overview: security, enabling scripting, and next steps.
  • Supported Languages: C#, Python and Lua.
  • Script Types: run, receive, service, interval, cron, tag change and alert modes.
  • Script Operations: CAN bus, DBC, state, and console.

docs.title: Installing Profinity
docs.text: Choose the installation method that matches your platform, then complete the setup pages that apply to your deployment.

docs.title: Choose an installation method
docs.text:
• Install Profinity on Windows: the Setup Wizard installer, for the desktop application or browser access.
  • Install Profinity on Linux and macOS: the bootstrap installer, with update, data location, and sign-in.
  • Install Profinity from an archive on Linux and macOS: a downloaded archive, started with the profinity.sh script.
  • Install Profinity with Docker: run Profinity in containers with Docker Compose, expose CAN devices, and prepare for production.
  • Install Profinity with the Docker one-line installer: install in Docker with a single script.

docs.title: After you install
docs.text:
• Apply a licence: apply a licence file and check that it has taken effect.
  • Upgrade from Profinity 2.2: back up, install 2.3, and check the licence, roles, dashboards, and integrations in order.
  • Update the Profinity Docker image: move a Docker installation to a newer image, by hand or with Watchtower.
  • Environment variables: set configuration and profile values from the environment on each platform, with the placeholder syntax and the variables Profinity reads.
  • Artefacts directory: where Profinity keeps configuration, profiles, plugins, and logs.
  • Run Profinity as a service: start automatically on Linux, macOS, or Windows, with a page for each system.
  • Security guide: the controls to put in place for a production deployment.
  • Migration from V1 to V2: the differences between the two generations, and the clean installation that moving requires.

docs.title: Apply a licence
docs.text:
A new Profinity installation runs without a licence file. An unlicensed Desktop installation is limited to personal, non-commercial use, and other installations start a one-time 14-day local trial with the Server features, as described in Licensing. A commercial or evaluation licence from Prohelion removes those limits, and you apply it after installation in the same way on every platform.

You need three things:

  • The Security administration permission, which is needed to view or change the License page. On a Windows desktop installation the built-in account holds it.
  • The licence file, named license.yaml, which Prohelion signs for one installation and returns after receiving its fingerprint.
  • Access to the machine that runs Profinity, or to its artefacts directory, when the instance has no network access.

docs.title: Apply a licence from the License page
docs.text:
1. Select ADMIN in the side menu, then License.
  2. Copy the Fingerprint with the copy button beside it, and send it to Prohelion through the usual sales or support channel. The fingerprint identifies this installation and is the only information Prohelion needs to issue a licence.
  3. When Prohelion returns the license.yaml file, return to the License page, select Update license file, and choose the file.
  4. Restart Profinity if the licence adds features, in particular a Server licence, because the address the web interface listens on is set when Profinity starts.

Profinity checks the file's signature, its expiry, and that its fingerprint matches this installation before it applies the file. If any check fails, the upload is rejected and the existing licence, if there is one, stays in effect. The fingerprint and the returned file can travel by any route, such as email from another computer, a USB drive, or a secure file copy, so the machine that runs Profinity does not need internet access.

docs.title: Apply a licence without the web interface
docs.text:
For Docker, Linux services, and scripted deployments, copy the file into the artefacts directory instead.

  1. Copy license.yaml into the license folder of the artefacts directory, so that the file ends up at license/license.yaml.
  2. On Docker, place it in the mounted volume that holds the artefacts directory, so that it survives the container being recreated.
  3. Restart Profinity if the licence adds features, or if the License page still shows the previous state.

The licence must belong to the installation's own fingerprint, in the same way as one uploaded from the page. To read the fingerprint without the web interface, open the License page from a browser on the same machine, or refer to the machine fingerprint.

docs.title: Check that the licence has taken effect
docs.text:
Open ADMIN, then License, and check these three things:

  • State reads Valid, or Expiring when 30 days or fewer remain before the licence expires.
  • Expires, Customer, and Edition match the licence that Prohelion issued.
  • The Licensed features and Licensed component groups tables show the expected entries as licensed and available.

If the page still shows the previous state after you copied the file into the folder, restart Profinity and check again. Removing licensed features restarts Profinity automatically.

docs.title: If the licence is rejected
docs.text:
What the page or message shows Likely cause What to do The upload is rejected The file's signature, expiry, or fingerprint did not pass validation. A file issued for a different machine is rejected with the message "License is not valid for this instance." and is not saved Check that the file is the unchanged license.yaml that Prohelion returned, and that it has not expired WrongInstance as the State after a license.yaml is copied into the license folder The file was issued for a different machine Send Prohelion the fingerprint shown on this installation, and apply the file that is issued for it Expired The licence's expiry date has passed Ask Prohelion for a renewal, and apply it in the same way

A rejected upload never replaces a working licence, so it is safe to retry. For editions, features, and the 14-day local trial, refer to Licensing.

docs.title: Artefacts directory
docs.text: Profinity stores its writable data, such as configuration, profiles, plugins, and logs, in a single artefacts directory, which is separate from the install directory that holds the program files. The path matters when you upgrade from 2.2, deploy on Linux as a service, or mount Docker volumes.

docs.title: Default locations
docs.text:
Platform Default artefacts path Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity Linux (2.3 and later) /var/lib/prohelion/profinity

On Linux, Profinity 2.2 stored data in ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity. From 2.3 the default is /var/lib/prohelion/profinity, and Profinity moves existing data there automatically on first start unless PROFINITY_HOME is set.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
Everything under the root uses the same layout on every platform, and the subfolders use lowercase names on every platform because Linux file systems are case-sensitive.

Subfolder Contents config/ config.yaml, security.yaml, plugins.yaml, custom.yaml profiles/ Profile and component YAML, dashboards, scripts plugins/ User-installed DLL plugin folders logs/ File logs when enabled can_bus_logs/ CAN bus logs, with replay/ and archive/ beneath it tag_logs/ Tag logs license/, certificates/, themes/, webroot/ Licence file, generated and uploaded certificates, themes, and web content

The Linux installer pre-creates only config/, profiles/, plugins/, and logs/, and Profinity creates the other folders on demand. Earlier releases used capitalised names (Config, Config.yaml, Profiles, Logs), and the first start of 2.3 renames them to the lowercase forms. This documentation uses the lowercase names throughout.

docs.title: Move the directory with PROFINITY_HOME
docs.text:
Set the environment variable PROFINITY_HOME to the full path of the artefacts root to run several Profinity instances on one host, to use a staging or test layout outside the default path, or to match a non-standard mount root in a Docker or custom image. Give each instance its own PROFINITY_HOME and its own HTTP and HTTPS ports. For example, in a Linux shell:

export PROFINITY_HOME=/var/lib/prohelion-staging/profinity

docs.title: Automatic migration on startup
docs.text:
On the first start after you upgrade to 2.3, Profinity copies data from the older locations below into the artefacts directory, renames Config, Profiles, and Logs to lowercase, and removes an old folder once every file is present at the new location. A locked or offline file does not stop Profinity from starting, and migration resumes from where it stopped on the next restart. The Windows desktop application shows a progress window during migration, and on every host the ADMIN > Logs page lists a message for each file that moved.

Platform Older locations that Profinity migrates Windows and macOS ~/Documents/Prohelion/Profinity, ~/Prohelion/Profinity, and the same folder under the application-data location with the other casing (prohelion/profinity) Linux ~/Documents/Prohelion/Profinity, ~/Prohelion/Profinity, ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity (the 2.2 location), /var/lib/Prohelion/Profinity, and /var/lib/profinity/Prohelion/Profinity

Migration does not run when PROFINITY_HOME is set

When PROFINITY_HOME is set, Profinity does not copy data from the older locations, so a custom root is never filled from the default install. Copy any data you need into the custom root yourself, including for Docker deployments that set PROFINITY_HOME. The rename of capitalised folders (Config, Profiles, Logs) to lowercase still runs under any root.

docs.title: Back up and restore
docs.text: Back up the artefacts directory before every upgrade, and keep config/ (including security.yaml), profiles/, license/, and certificates/ in every backup. Stop Profinity before you copy or restore the folders, restore by replacing those folders, and start Profinity again.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The profile is empty after an upgrade: migration did not find your data. Check ADMIN > Logs for migration messages, and if PROFINITY_HOME is set, copy the old data across yourself or unset the variable.
  • Linux reports a permission error: the account that runs Profinity does not own the artefacts directory. Give it ownership with chown on the artefacts tree, because /var/lib needs root to create the folder, which is then handed to the service user.
  • Two instances share one configuration: give each its own PROFINITY_HOME and its own HTTP and HTTPS ports.

The Linux service layout and launcher are described in Run Profinity as a Linux service, and Docker volume mounts in Install Profinity with Docker.

docs.title: Install Profinity with Docker
docs.text:
Run Profinity in a Docker container on most devices that can run Docker, including macOS and Linux machines and single-board computers such as the Raspberry Pi and BeagleBone Black. Prohelion publishes the Profinity image for linux/amd64, linux/arm64, and linux/arm/v7, and Docker pulls the variant that matches the host processor.

A container binds all network interfaces, so other machines can reach it. Opening the web interface from another machine, and creating user accounts and roles, need the Profinity Server licensed feature, which the Server and Enterprise editions include.

A new installation in docker starts a one-time 14-day local trial with the Server features and then drops to the unlicensed feature set, so apply a licence file under ADMIN > License before the trial ends, as described in Apply a licence. To upgrade a 2.2 container, read Upgrade from Profinity 2.2 first.

You need Docker on the target device, on an x86-64, 64-bit ARM, or 32-bit ARM (ARMv7) processor, and Docker Compose, which Docker Desktop includes and which is available as a plugin on Linux. You also need a suitable CAN adapter for the target device.

To install with a single script instead of a compose file, refer to Install Profinity with the Docker one-line installer. To move an existing installation to a newer image, refer to Update the Profinity Docker image.

docs.title: Install with Docker Compose
docs.text:
1. On the target device, create a new empty directory.

  2. In the new directory, create a file named docker-compose.yml with these contents:

    services:
  profinity:
      image: prohelion/profinity:latest
      restart: always
      #On linux hosts you can run in host mode to enable autodiscovery
      #network_mode: host
      ports:
        - 18080:18080
        - 18443:18443
        - 4876:4876
      # PROFINITY_HOME must match the container-side mount path below, otherwise the
      # security keys and profiles are written to the container's writable layer and are
      # lost when the image is updated
      environment:
        - PROFINITY_HOME=/app/Prohelion
      volumes:
        - $HOME/Prohelion:/app/Prohelion:rw

  3. Make sure the host directory mounted at PROFINITY_HOME is writable by the app user, because the container runs as that non-root user.

  4. In the directory that holds the compose file, run docker compose up -d.
  5. Open http://localhost:18080 on the local machine, or http://[your IP address]:18080 from another machine.

The sign-in page opens, as described under Sign in.

The compose file publishes three ports:

Port Purpose 18080 HTTP web interface 18443 HTTPS web interface 4876 Tritium CAN to Ethernet bridge, an IANA-assigned port that the bridge protocol uses for both UDP and TCP and that is not configurable

Docker publishes a port as TCP unless the mapping ends in /udp, so add - 4876:4876/udp when a Tritium adapter is reached through the published ports. On Linux hosts, use host networking (network_mode: host) where multicast adapter discovery or Profinity Mobile server discovery is required, because UDP broadcasts do not leave a Docker bridge network.

The artefacts directory inside the container is whatever PROFINITY_HOME names. With the mount above, the configuration is in /app/Prohelion/config, the profiles in /app/Prohelion/profiles, and the logs in /app/Prohelion/logs, which appear on the host under $HOME/Prohelion. The one-line installer uses PROFINITY_HOME=/var/lib/prohelion/profinity mounted from a local data directory, which is also the default artefacts path on Linux. Either path is valid, provided that the environment variable and the mount destination match.

Set PROFINITY_HOME to your mount path

If PROFINITY_HOME does not name the container path of your mounted volume, Profinity writes its configuration and profiles inside the container, and they are lost when the image is replaced. Compose files written for 2.2 that mount /root/Prohelion/Profinity/... need their mounts moved to the new PROFINITY_HOME path, because the automatic migration from legacy operating system locations is skipped whenever PROFINITY_HOME is set. The sub-folders beneath the artefacts directory use lowercase names (config, profiles, logs), and Linux file systems are case-sensitive, so mounts must target those names. Refer to Artefacts directory.

To check where Profinity stores its files, open a shell in the running container with docker compose exec profinity bash, and run ls -la /app/Prohelion/.

docs.title: Start and stop Profinity
docs.text:
Run these commands from the directory that holds the docker-compose.yml file. Docker Compose, not Profinity, starts the container on boot, and the restart: always line in the compose file restarts the container whenever Docker starts, so configure Docker to start on boot.

Command Effect docker compose up Starts Profinity in the foreground docker compose up -d Starts Profinity in the background (detached mode) docker compose stop Stops the containers and keeps them, so docker compose start can restart them docker compose down Stops the containers and removes them, so you run docker compose up again to recreate them docker compose logs -f Follows the log output

Refer to the Docker Compose reference for more commands.

docs.title: Sign in
docs.text:
The container serves HTTP with the default credentials below, so follow the Security guide to enable HTTPS before you expose it beyond a trusted network. The browser opens the Profinity sign-in page.

Profinity sign-in page

A fresh installation has only the administrator user active. Sign in with the username admin and the password password, and Profinity asks for a new password at the first sign-in. Choose one as described in the Security guide. After you sign in, the Profinity homepage appears.

Profinity homepage

docs.title: Expose devices to the container
docs.text: Docker does not expose all devices to containers. Expose additional devices to Docker so that SocketCAN can be accessed natively, and use network_mode: host on Linux so that components that use UDP broadcasting can be discovered. Refer to the Docker Compose documentation for how to expose these devices.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The profile and configuration are back to their defaults after an image update: PROFINITY_HOME did not match the container-side mount path, so the data was written to the container and lost when it was replaced. Set the variable to the mount path and restore the files from your backup.
  • Profinity fails to start with a permission error on the mounted directory: the app user cannot write to it, so change the ownership or permissions of the host directory.
  • A Tritium adapter is not found: publish port 4876 for UDP as well as TCP, or use host networking.
  • The host's SocketCAN interfaces are not visible inside the container: expose them to Docker, as described under Expose devices to the container.

docs.title: Run Profinity in production
docs.text: For production environments, and deployments that run many Profinity instances, configure Profinity with environment variables so that one compose file can serve every instance. The compose files, .env files, and environment-specific deployment examples are in Environment variables.

docs.title: Install Profinity with the Docker one-line installer
docs.text:
Install Profinity on a Docker host with a single script instead of writing a compose file yourself. To write the compose file yourself, and for the Docker, CAN adapter, licence, and PROFINITY_HOME requirements that apply to both methods, refer to Install Profinity with Docker.

Prohelion provides three helper scripts for Docker hosts. install-docker.sh creates ~/profinity-docker, or the folder named by --dir, writes a compose file, pulls the image, and starts Profinity. The --image option, or the PROFINITY_DOCKER_IMAGE variable, selects a different image than the default prohelion/profinity:latest. Afterwards, ~/profinity-docker/profinity.sh runs docker compose up -d and waits for the HTTP port to answer, and ~/profinity-docker/update.sh runs docker compose pull and docker compose up -d.

  1. Download the installer from the Profinity release on GitHub, with its checksum. install-docker.sh writes profinity.sh and update.sh itself, so it is the only file you need.

    curl -fsSL -o install-docker.sh https://github.com/Prohelion/Profinity/releases/latest/download/install-docker.sh
curl -fsSL -o install-docker.sh.sha256 https://github.com/Prohelion/Profinity/releases/latest/download/install-docker.sh.sha256

  2. Verify the checksum and run the installer:

    sha256sum -c install-docker.sh.sha256 && bash install-docker.sh --dir ~/profinity-docker

    On macOS, use shasum -a 256 -c install-docker.sh.sha256 in place of sha256sum -c.

To open the web interface and sign in, refer to Sign in. To update the installation, run ~/profinity-docker/update.sh, or refer to Update the Profinity Docker image.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Profinity substitutes environment variables into its configuration file (config.yaml) and into profile files, so one set of files can serve development, staging, and production, keep sensitive values out of the files, and let you change a setting without editing a file. A variable has an effect only where a ${VARIABLE_NAME} placeholder in one of those files references it. To set a variable on Windows, Linux, macOS, or Docker, refer to Set a variable.

docs.title: Placeholder syntax
docs.text:
A placeholder uses the form ${VARIABLE_NAME}. Profinity also supports Docker-style default values with ${VARIABLE_NAME:-default}, where it uses the value of the variable when it is set and non-empty, and the text after :- otherwise.

# Variable without a default: must be set
httpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS}

# Variable with a default: uses 18080 if HTTP_PORT is not set
httpPort: ${HTTP_PORT:-18080}

# Variable with an empty default: uses an empty string if the variable is not set
token: ${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN:-}

A name uses only letters, numbers and underscores, and must not start with a number. So ${PROFILE_NAME}, ${BMU1_BASE_ADDRESS} and ${_UNDERSCORE_VAR} are valid, while ${VAR-WITH-DASH}, ${VAR WITH SPACES} and ${VAR.WITH.DOTS} are not. Profinity looks the name up exactly as written, so ${Profile_Name} and ${profile_name} are different variables on Linux and macOS, where names are case-sensitive, and the same variable on Windows, where they are not.

A missing variable stops the file from loading

A configuration or profile file that references an undefined or empty variable with no default fails to load, and Profinity writes the names of the undefined variables to the log. Define every variable that has no default before starting Profinity, or give it a default.

docs.title: In the configuration file
docs.text:
This config.yaml takes the active profile, the web server address and port, the log settings and the scripting switch from environment variables:

version: "2.3"
activeProfile: ${PROFILE_NAME:-Docker Profile}

appSettings:
  profinityServer:
    httpAddress: ${HTTP_ADDRESS:-0.0.0.0}
    httpPort: ${HTTP_PORT:-18080}
  logs:
    logLevel: ${LOG_LEVEL:-Info}
    rollsizeMB: ${LOG_ROLLSIZE:-10}
    retainedLogs: ${RETAINED_LOGS:-10}
  scripts:
    enabled: ${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-false}

docs.title: In a profile file
docs.text:
This profile.yaml takes the connection settings of an InfluxDB v2 historian from environment variables, so the token never appears in the file:

description: ${PROFILE_DESCRIPTION}
version: "2.3"
kioskModeEnabled: false
useCustomProfileDashboard: false
components:
- component:
    token: ${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN}
    organisation: ${INFLUXDB_ORG}
    bucket: ${INFLUXDB_BUCKET}
    url: ${INFLUXDB_URL}
    healthCheck: true
    intervalSec: 10
    logType: Snapshot
    autoStart: false
    type: InfluxDbHistorianV2
    id: InfluxDbLoggerV21
    tagTreeParentPath: /
    name: InfluxDbLogger

The same syntax works for any component setting in a profile file.

docs.title: Set a variable
docs.text: Set the variable in the environment of the process that starts Profinity.

docs.title: Change a setting from an environment variable
docs.text:
This example moves the Profinity web server to port 8080, and the same steps apply to any other setting. config.yaml is in the config folder of the artefacts directory.

  1. In config.yaml, replace the port with a placeholder that has a default: httpPort: ${HTTP_PORT:-18080}.
  2. Set HTTP_PORT to 8080 in the environment of the process that starts Profinity, as described in Windows, Linux and macOS, or Docker.
  3. Restart Profinity.

Open http://localhost:8080 in a browser, and the Profinity sign-in page loads on the new port. If Profinity does not start, confirm that the variable is set in the environment of the process that starts Profinity, and read the Profinity logs. In Docker, publish the same port number on the host and in the container.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
In a command prompt, run set PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile, and in PowerShell, run $env:PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile". Either form lasts only for that window. To set a variable permanently:

  1. Open System Properties, then Advanced, then Environment Variables.
  2. Add the variable under User or System variables.
  3. Restart Profinity.

When Profinity runs as a Windows service, add the variable as a System variable, because a user variable is not visible to a service that runs as another account. Restart the service, not only the application, so that it reads the new value.

docs.title: Linux and macOS
docs.text: In a shell, run export PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile" to set a variable for that session, or add the same line to a shell profile file such as ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile or ~/.zshrc for an interactive run. A service does not read those files. For the Linux systemd service, add Environment= lines to the [Service] section of /etc/systemd/system/profinity.service, for example Environment=PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile", then run sudo systemctl daemon-reload and restart the service. Refer to Run Profinity as a Linux service.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
Set variables in a .env file next to the compose file, in the environment section of the compose file, or with docker run -e:

PROFILE_NAME=Production Profile
HTTP_PORT=8080

docker run -e PROFILE_NAME="Production Profile" \
           -e HTTP_PORT="8080" \
           prohelion/profinity:latest

Docker Compose substitutes variables into the compose file as well, so the same variable can set the published port and the setting inside the container:

services:
  profinity:
    image: prohelion/profinity:latest
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "${HTTP_PORT:-18080}:${HTTP_PORT:-18080}"
      - "${HTTPS_PORT:-18443}:${HTTPS_PORT:-18443}"
      - "4876:4876"
    environment:
      # The artefacts directory inside the container, which must match the volume below
      - PROFINITY_HOME=/app/Prohelion

      - HTTP_ADDRESS=${HTTP_ADDRESS:-0.0.0.0}
      - HTTP_PORT=${HTTP_PORT:-18080}
      - LOG_LEVEL=${LOG_LEVEL:-Info}
      - ENABLE_SCRIPTING=${ENABLE_SCRIPTING:-false}
      - PROFILE_NAME=${PROFILE_NAME:-Docker Profile}
    volumes:
      - ./profiles:/app/Prohelion/profiles
      - ./config:/app/Prohelion/config

With HTTP_PORT=8080, host port 8080 maps to container port 8080, which matches a config.yaml that listens on ${HTTP_PORT}. The Profinity image declares only ports 18080 and 18443, but Docker publishes any port the container listens on.

Keep the config.yaml and profile files that hold placeholders in the mounted volume folders that map to /app/Prohelion/config and /app/Prohelion/profiles. PROFINITY_HOME must match the container-side mount path, as described in Install Profinity with Docker. Docker Compose reads a .env file in the same folder as the compose file automatically, and to keep one file per environment, name it explicitly:

docker compose --env-file .env.production up
docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file .env.production up

Docker documents env files and compose file overrides in detail.

docs.title: Variables Profinity reads
docs.text:
Besides the variables that your own files reference, Profinity and its install scripts read these variables.

Variable Read by Effect PROFINITY_HOME Profinity, profinity.sh Sets the artefacts directory and turns off automatic migration from older locations PROFINITY_INSTALL_ROOT profinity.sh, update.sh Overrides the install root, which otherwise is the folder that holds the script DOTNET_ROOT profinity.sh Sets the .NET install root for the portable edition PROFINITY_DOTNET_INSTALL_URL profinity.sh Overrides the address that the portable edition downloads the .NET installer from PROFINITY_FILES_BASE install.sh, update.sh Overrides the file server that releases are downloaded from PROFINITY_DOCKER_IMAGE install-docker.sh Sets the Docker image that the one-line Docker installer uses

The Profiles page covers the profile format, and System configuration covers the other settings in config.yaml.

docs.title: Install Profinity from an archive
docs.text:
Install Profinity from a downloaded archive when you are trying it, running it interactively, or installing without root or systemd. To install on a Linux server or embedded device, or on any host where Profinity should start on boot, use the bootstrap installer instead. Profinity does not need Prohelion hardware to run.

An archive installation needs no installer. To have Profinity start on boot, configure the extracted files as a service by following Run Profinity as a service.

A separate archive is published for each supported host architecture. Select the archive that matches the host operating system and CPU architecture.

Host Archive Format .NET runtime Linux, x86_64 / amd64 Profinity-Linux-x64.tar.gz tar.gz Bundled, so no separate install is needed Linux, ARM64 (aarch64, 64-bit ARM) Profinity-Linux-arm64.tar.gz tar.gz Bundled, so no separate install is needed Linux, 32-bit ARM (ARMv6 / ARMv7) Profinity-Linux-arm.tar.gz tar.gz Bundled. The host also needs the system ICU (International Components for Unicode) library macOS (any architecture), or any other unsupported architecture Profinity-Portable.zip zip Not bundled. Needs the .NET 10 ASP.NET Core runtime, which profinity.sh installs automatically if it is missing

The Linux archives are self-contained. The macOS and portable archive needs the .NET 10 ASP.NET Core runtime, which profinity.sh downloads and verifies the first time Profinity starts, if the host has internet access. To install the runtime yourself, or to prepare a host without internet access, download it from Microsoft.

Download ASP.NET Core 10

  1. Download the archive that matches the host.

  2. Create a destination folder and extract the archive into it, because the archives have no wrapping top-level folder.

    For a Linux .tar.gz archive, substitute the file name for your architecture:

    mkdir profinity && tar -xzf Profinity-Linux-x64.tar.gz -C profinity

    For the macOS and portable .zip archive:

    mkdir profinity && unzip Profinity-Portable.zip -d profinity

  3. Change into the folder and mark the startup script executable, because some archive tools do not keep the executable bit:

    cd profinity
chmod +x profinity.sh

  4. Start Profinity:

    ./profinity.sh

The extracted folder has this layout:

profinity/
├── profinity.sh      # startup script: runs preflight checks, then starts Profinity
├── update.sh         # updates the installation to the latest matching release
├── VERSION
├── edition.json
├── lib/
└── app/              # Profinity binaries

profinity.sh runs preflight checks before it starts Profinity. On the self-contained Linux archives, it checks the host architecture and the required system libraries. On the macOS and portable archive, it checks for a compatible .NET runtime and, if none is found, installs one from a checksum-verified Microsoft installer. Run ./profinity.sh --check-only to run these checks without starting Profinity.

The startup banner appears, followed by log lines that end with the address Profinity is listening on:

Prohelion Profinity - v2.3.x.x
Copyright © 2026 - Prohelion Pty Ltd.
------------------------------------------
Press Ctrl-C to shut the application down.

INFO: Starting Prohelion - Profinity
INFO: Profinity Profile : Default 11
INFO: Profinity Services Starting
INFO: Now listening on: http://127.0.0.1:18080

To open the web interface and sign in, refer to Open the web interface. On Linux, create the artefacts directory and set its ownership before the first start, or set PROFINITY_HOME to a writable path, as described in Where Profinity stores its data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• ./profinity.sh reports Permission denied: the archive tool did not keep the executable bit, so run chmod +x profinity.sh and start it again.
  • On the macOS and portable archive, a host without internet access cannot download the .NET runtime on first start: install the ASP.NET Core 10 runtime from Microsoft before you start Profinity, and run ./profinity.sh --check-only to confirm.
  • On Linux, Profinity cannot write to /var/lib/prohelion: refer to Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Install Profinity on Linux and macOS
docs.text:
Install Profinity on Linux or macOS with the bootstrap installer, or from a downloaded archive. For Windows, refer to Install Profinity on Windows, and for containers, refer to Docker installation.

Method Use when Result Bootstrap installer (install.sh) You install on a Linux server or embedded device, or any host where Profinity should start on boot Selects the right archive for the host, installs into /opt/profinity, creates the profinity service user, and on Linux with systemd creates the profinity.service unit Archive installation You are trying Profinity, running it interactively, or installing without root or systemd Files extracted into a folder of your choice, and started by hand with ./profinity.sh

docs.title: Install with the bootstrap installer
docs.text:
The installer downloads the release archive that matches the host operating system and CPU architecture, verifies it, and unpacks it into an install root, /opt/profinity by default. On Linux with systemd it also creates the profinity service user, the artefacts directory, and the profinity.service unit. Installing does not start Profinity.

On Linux, run the installer as root with sudo, unless you use --no-systemd with a writable --install-dir. The host needs internet access, or a local archive as described under Installer options.

  1. Download the installer and its checksum:

    curl -fsSL -o install.sh https://github.com/Prohelion/Profinity/releases/latest/download/install.sh
curl -fsSL -o install.sh.sha256 https://github.com/Prohelion/Profinity/releases/latest/download/install.sh.sha256

  2. Verify the checksum and run the installer:

    sha256sum -c install.sh.sha256 && sudo bash install.sh

    On macOS, use shasum -a 256 -c install.sh.sha256 in place of sha256sum -c.

  3. Start Profinity with /opt/profinity/profinity.sh to test the configuration, or start it as a service as described in Run Profinity as a service.

The installer can also be piped straight into the shell with curl -fsSL https://github.com/Prohelion/Profinity/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sudo bash. That trusts the network transport only and cannot verify the checksum, so avoid it on production hosts.

docs.title: Installer options
docs.text:
Option Effect --install-dir <path> Install into a different location than /opt/profinity --version <x.y.z> Install a specific GitHub release tag instead of the latest, ignored with --channel --channel <name> Download from a Prohelion file server channel instead of GitHub. Prohelion supplies the channel name and the installer address --package <archive> Install from a local .tar.gz or .zip with no download, for hosts without internet access. No checksum step is performed for a local package --no-systemd File-only install: skip the service user, artefacts directory, and systemd unit --dry-run Print the planned actions without changing the system

For a channel, download the installer from the address Prohelion supplies, then run it with the channel name:

sudo bash install.sh --channel <channel supplied by Prohelion>

docs.title: Update Profinity
docs.text: update.sh, installed alongside profinity.sh in the install root, fetches the matching release for the installed edition and swaps the application files in place. It takes the same --channel and --version options as the installer, and does nothing if the installed version is already current. Pass --force to reinstall anyway. If the profinity service is active, update.sh stops it before it applies the update and restarts it afterwards.

docs.title: Where Profinity stores its data
docs.text:
On Linux, Profinity 2.3 stores writable data under /var/lib/prohelion/profinity by default, not ~/.local/share, and there is no per-user fallback. On macOS the default is ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity.

The bootstrap installer creates this directory. For more information, refer to Artefacts directory.

docs.title: Open the web interface
docs.text:
Open the address that the Now listening on line of the log reports, or the httpAddress and httpPort values in config.yaml. By default Profinity listens on all network interfaces (0.0.0.0) on port 18080, so you reach it at http://localhost:18080 on the local machine, or at http://[host name or IP address]:18080 from another machine. Opening the web interface from another machine needs a Server licence, as described in Apply a licence.

The browser opens the Profinity sign-in page.

Profinity sign-in page

A fresh installation has only the administrator user active. Sign in with the username admin and the password password, and Profinity asks for a new password at the first sign-in. Choose one as described in the Security guide. After you sign in, the Profinity homepage appears.

Profinity homepage

To stop Profinity in a terminal, press Ctrl-C in that window. To stop it as a service on Linux, run sudo systemctl stop profinity, as described in Run Profinity as a Linux service.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: • On Linux, Profinity logs Unable to create directory '/var/lib/prohelion/...' and then fails to save its configuration: the account that runs Profinity does not own the directory, so run sudo chown -R profinity:profinity /var/lib/prohelion for the service user, or set PROFINITY_HOME to a path the account can write.

docs.title: Migrate from Profinity V1 to V2
docs.text:
Profinity V2 is a significant architectural upgrade from V1. It keeps the functionality of V1 and adds a web-based interface and an expanded API, but the two versions are not compatible. V2 profiles cannot be opened in V1, V1 and V2 system configurations cannot be used by the other version, and the API structure and endpoints have changed significantly. There is no downgrade path, so keep your V1 backups. To upgrade from Profinity 2.2 to Profinity 2.3, refer to Upgrade from Profinity 2.2.

Prohelion recommends a clean installation of V2, removing V1 before you install V2.

  1. Back up the V1 profiles, configuration files, DBC files, and any custom scripts or data. Write down the component settings and addresses, and any custom V1 settings you want to replicate in V2.
  2. Uninstall V1 with the standard uninstallation procedure, and remove the files in the V1 profile directory.
  3. Install V2 as a new installation, not as an upgrade of V1, for your platform: Windows, Linux and macOS, or Docker. Confirm that V2 is running.
  4. Recreate the configuration: create new profiles, add components in the V2 interface, import or recreate the DBC files, and set the system settings for your environment.
  5. Check that every component is detected and configured correctly, and test the critical functions before you put the system into production.
  6. Review the security settings and user accounts, starting with the default administrator password described in the Security guide.

docs.title: Run V1 and V2 on one machine
docs.text: Running both versions on one machine causes port conflicts, mixed-up profiles, and unsynchronised data, so Prohelion does not recommend it. If both versions must run for a while, give each version different ports and a different user account, keep their profiles and configurations separate, and complete the move to V2 as soon as practical.

docs.title: Get help
docs.text: If something goes wrong during migration, check the installation page for your platform and the System configuration documentation. You can also contact Prohelion Support, or report the issue with the Feedback feature in Profinity.

docs.title: Security guide
docs.text:
Profinity controls and monitors critical hardware, including industrial equipment, battery management systems, motor controllers, and charging systems. Treat security as a priority throughout deployment. A weak configuration can damage equipment, create a safety hazard, or stop the system.

This guide covers the security controls that matter when deploying and operating Profinity, and links to the pages for each feature.

docs.title: Security areas
docs.text: Profinity V2 provides control over critical industrial, automotive, and energy systems. Securing it involves six areas. HTTPS protects the network path, Docker settings isolate the container, and the security files and keys hold the secrets. Scripting controls what code runs with the engine's privileges, user accounts limit who can do what, and Kiosk Mode controls unattended displays. The checklist at the end summarises the steps for a production deployment.

docs.title: HTTPS configuration
docs.text:
When Profinity is accessed over a network rather than only through localhost, all communication uses HTTPS. Without it, usernames, passwords, API tokens, and system data can be intercepted.

Profinity supports HTTPS configuration through the System Configuration interface. Use a certificate from the Windows Certificate Store for a Windows deployment, or a .pfx or .p12 certificate file for a cross-platform deployment.

For production, turn on Redirect all Http traffic to Https so that every connection uses encryption. Use certificates from a trusted Certificate Authority (CA), and plan certificate renewal so that an expiry does not interrupt the service. Binding HTTP to localhost only and requiring HTTPS for remote access keeps credentials off the network, but Profinity Mobile connects over the local network, so keep the HTTPS port reachable from the networks that phones use. For the certificate steps, refer to System Configuration.

docs.title: Docker security
docs.text:
