The Profinity image runs as the non-root app user, so a container already runs without root privileges. Keep it that way, and make sure the host directory mounted at PROFINITY_HOME is writable by that user. Set CPU and memory limits on the container to prevent resource exhaustion, use Docker networks to isolate Profinity from other services, and use only official Profinity images from Prohelion repositories.

Give mounted volumes that hold profiles, configurations, or logs file system permissions that match their sensitivity. Mount configuration files read-only so that a container cannot modify them accidentally, and encrypt backups of sensitive data and keep them in a secured location. Publish only the ports you need to the host, restrict access to them with a host firewall, and place a reverse proxy such as nginx or Traefik in front of Profinity for production deployments. For deployment details, refer to Docker Installation.

docs.title: Protect the security files and keys
docs.text: security.yaml in the config/ folder of the artefacts directory holds users, roles, two-factor secrets, and the keys that sign sessions and encrypt secrets. Restrict read access to that folder to the account that runs Profinity, include security.yaml in encrypted backups, and never commit a file that contains real keys to source control. In a Docker container, security.yaml and its keys are written to the container's own storage when PROFINITY_HOME does not match a mounted volume. Replacing the image then regenerates the keys and resets Profinity to the default administrator account, so always set PROFINITY_HOME to the container path of a mounted volume.

docs.title: Scripting security
docs.text:
Profinity scripts execute with the same security permissions as the Profinity engine itself. A script can:

  • Access all system resources available to Profinity.
  • Send and receive CAN bus messages.
  • Modify system configuration.
  • Control connected hardware, including batteries, chargers, and motor controllers.

Scripting is switched off by default. An administrator turns it on with Enable Scripting under ADMIN > System Configuration. The setting is available only when the licence includes the Scripting feature (Desktop, Server, and Enterprise editions; an unlicensed instance does not include scripting). Enable it only when the use case needs it, and review script code before deployment, especially scripts from external sources. Keep production scripts under version control with a review process, and audit active scripts regularly. When Profinity runs as a service, give it the minimum operating system permissions it needs, and document each script and its purpose for security reviews. For the scripting pages, refer to Scripting.

docs.title: Default credentials
docs.text:
Change default credentials immediately

Fresh installations of Profinity Server on Linux, macOS, and Docker include a default administrator account:

  • Username: admin
  • Password: password

Profinity asks for a new password at the first sign-in with these credentials, and leaving the default credentials active exposes the system to unauthorised access.

The Windows desktop application does not create this account, and the desktop user signs in without a password. A Server licence does create the account. Refer to Windows Installation.

docs.title: User account practices
docs.text: Create an account for each person or system that needs access instead of sharing the administrator account. Enforce a password policy that suits the organisation (refer to Password Policy), rotate passwords on production systems, and disable or remove accounts that are no longer needed. Creating user accounts and roles needs the Profinity Server licensed feature.

docs.title: Sign-in, two-factor, and session controls
docs.text: Profinity offers a site sign-in method (Local or SSO), two-factor authentication for local users, a password policy, a session policy, SIEM export, and service accounts with long-lived tokens. Two-factor authentication needs the Server edition, and SSO and SCIM need the Enterprise edition. Refer to SSO and Sign-In, Two-Factor Authentication, SCIM and SIEM, and Service Accounts.

docs.title: Security roles
docs.text: Profinity uses 27 granular permissions grouped into roles, and users receive assigned roles. There are no security groups or per-user permission lists. Assign users only the permissions their work needs, give monitoring accounts read-only roles for dashboards and the Tag Explorer, and use individual administrator accounts. Review accounts and role assignments periodically. The Send CAN messages permission lets a user inject CAN frames onto the bus, so assign it only to trusted operators. Refer to Roles and Permissions for the full catalogue and the built-in Administrators role, and Managing Users for user management.

docs.title: Kiosk Mode security
docs.text: Kiosk Mode signs a selected user in automatically without a login, which needs careful configuration. Profinity does not restrict which enabled user is selected, including administrators, so anyone at the kiosk inherits that user's permissions. Use a dedicated user with only the view permissions the display needs, such as a read-only role, and review that user's permissions regularly. Monitor kiosk access through the logs. Secure the device physically, because Kiosk Mode bypasses the login page, isolate it on its own network segment in production, and disable Kiosk Mode when it is not needed. Refer to Kiosk Mode for the configuration.

docs.title: Production deployment checklist
docs.text:
Before deploying Profinity in a production environment:

  • Change the default administrator password.
  • Configure HTTPS with valid certificates and turn on the HTTPS redirect.
  • Create individual user accounts and assign minimum permissions.
  • Apply a Server licence if you need remote access, users, or roles.
  • Restrict read access to security.yaml and encrypt backups of it.
  • Review and audit all active scripts, and disable scripting if it is not required.
  • Configure firewall rules to restrict access to Profinity ports.
  • Review the logs on a schedule and forward them to your monitoring system.
  • Back up configurations and profiles on a schedule, and test a restore.
  • Write down the security configuration and who may change it.
  • If using Docker, mount a volume at PROFINITY_HOME and follow the Docker security guidance.
  • Review Kiosk Mode and disable it if it is not needed.

docs.title: Related documentation
docs.text:
• System Configuration: HTTPS and security settings.
  • Roles and Permissions: roles and permissions in 2.3.
  • SSO and Sign-In: Local and SSO sign-in.
  • Two-Factor Authentication: two-factor policy.
  • Managing Users: user accounts and role assignment.
  • Kiosk Mode: Kiosk Mode configuration and security.
  • Scripting: scripting security considerations.
  • Docker Installation: Docker deployment.

docs.title: Update the Profinity Docker image
docs.text:
Docker does not update a running container, so the latest tag only moves when you pull a newer image. To move to a newer Profinity image, use the compose file from Install Profinity with Docker. To upgrade a 2.2 container, read Upgrade from Profinity 2.2 first.

  1. In the directory that holds the compose file, pull the newer image:

    docker compose pull

  2. Start Profinity with the new image:

    docker compose up -d

Configuration and profiles are kept as long as PROFINITY_HOME names the container path of your mounted volume.

docs.title: Update automatically with Watchtower
docs.text:
To update automatically, add Watchtower, a community tool that replaces a container whenever a newer image appears, to the compose file:

services:
  profinity:
    image: prohelion/profinity:latest
    restart: always
    ports:
      - 18080:18080
      - 18443:18443
      - 4876:4876
    environment:
      - PROFINITY_HOME=/app/Prohelion
    volumes:
      - $HOME/Prohelion:/app/Prohelion:rw
    labels:
      - com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.enable=true

  watchtower:
    image: containrrr/watchtower
    restart: always
    command: --label-enable --cleanup --interval 86400
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock

The label limits updates to the Profinity container, --cleanup removes old images, and --interval 86400 checks once a day. Refer to the Watchtower documentation for the other options. An unattended update discards any data that is not in a host-mounted volume, so check that PROFINITY_HOME matches the mount before you enable it.

docs.title: Upgrade from Profinity 2.2
docs.text:
Upgrade a production system in the order below. Profinity 2.3 changes where data is stored, how security is configured, which features need a licence, and how the REST API reports errors, so read the breaking changes first.

Before you start, take the backup in step 1, and test the upgrade on a non-production instance if you can.

  1. Back up the config/ and profiles/ folders of the artefacts directory, together with license/ and certificates/. These folders are named Config and Profiles until 2.3 starts for the first time. On a 2.2 system the artefacts directory is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity on Windows, ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity on macOS, and ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity on Linux.
  2. Install Profinity 2.3 and start it once. The first start moves data from older locations into the 2.3 artefacts directory, renames Config, Profiles, and Logs to lowercase, and rewrites security.yaml and profile.yaml in the 2.3 camelCase format when it loads them. It rewrites config.yaml on that first load when the file still has legacy Pascal keys or an older version stamp. Profinity does not move data when PROFINITY_HOME is set, so copy anything you need into that location yourself.
  3. Open ADMIN > License and confirm the state and the edition. A 2.2 installation upgraded without a licence file is unlicensed once any trial ends, and remote web access, user and role administration, two-factor authentication, Profinity AI, and the Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT rule actions stop being available until you upload a licence. Refer to Apply a licence and Licensing.
  4. Sign in as an administrator, open ADMIN > Users & Groups, and check the Roles tab and each user's assigned roles. Change the default admin password if you have not already. A default admin account that Profinity creates must change its password at first sign-in.
  5. Open ADMIN > System Configuration and confirm the Sign-in method, the password policy, and the SSO, SCIM, and SIEM settings.
  6. Open ADMIN > Logs and read the messages from first start. On Linux, the migration messages name each file that moved.
  7. Open each custom dashboard in the dashboard editor and confirm it loads without schema errors.
  8. Unlock the firmware of each Gen2 battery management system once, and enter its passcode again, because 2.3 does not keep passcodes in the profile.
  9. Run every integration that calls /api/v2 against a test instance, because error responses changed. Refer to REST API errors.
  10. Open each BACnet component and set Device instance to the instance of its device, because Profinity now checks it. Refer to BACnet device instance.

To return to 2.2, reinstall 2.2 and restore the backup you took in step 1.

docs.title: Linux and Docker data locations
docs.text:
On Linux, 2.3 moves data from ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity, the 2.2 location, to /var/lib/prohelion/profinity the first time it starts. A Docker container follows the same rule unless PROFINITY_HOME is set, and the Docker compose file Prohelion publishes sets it to the container path that holds your mounted data.

For a Docker upgrade, set PROFINITY_HOME to the container path of your existing mount, keep that mount, and copy any legacy Config and Profiles folders into it before you start the 2.3 image. Refer to Docker installation.

docs.title: Install Profinity on Windows
docs.text:
The Profinity Setup Wizard installs Profinity as a desktop application on Windows. For Linux and macOS, refer to Linux and macOS installation, and for containers, refer to Docker installation.

The installer places Profinity in C:\Program Files (x86)\Prohelion\Profinity, and keeps configuration, profiles, and logs in the artefacts directory, which is %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity by default. To upgrade a 2.2 installation, read Upgrade from Profinity 2.2 first.

docs.title: Install Profinity
docs.text:
1. Obtain the installer, Profinity.Install.msi, from Prohelion.
  2. Open Profinity.Install.msi and follow the prompts in the Setup Wizard.
  3. Start Profinity from the Start menu.

Profinity opens its homepage in the desktop window. To stop Profinity, shut down the application.

Profinity homepage

docs.title: Open Profinity in a web browser
docs.text:
Web access needs a Server licence

The sign-in page opens on an unlicensed or Desktop installation, and signing in from the web needs a username and password. User accounts need a Server licence, so the page opens and sign-in fails until that licence is applied.

With Profinity running, open the URL set in the Profinity Web panel of System configuration, which you reach from ADMIN in the side menu. The default URL is http://localhost:18080, and the browser opens the Profinity sign-in page.

Profinity sign-in page

The desktop application signs in without a password. A fresh installation without a Server licence has no account for the sign-in page, so use the desktop application window. If the browser cannot reach the address, check that Profinity is running and that no other program is using port 18080.

docs.title: Remote access and user accounts
docs.text:
Without a Profinity Server licence, the desktop application binds its web interface to the local machine (127.0.0.1) on TCP port 18080 by default, whatever address is set in System configuration. Other machines cannot open the web interface, and the installer adds Windows Firewall exceptions for ports 4876 (TCP and UDP) and 42000 (UDP).

A Server licence changes this. Profinity then uses the address set in System configuration, so other machines can open the web interface and sign in with their own accounts. A Desktop licence does not provide this, because signing in from a browser on another machine always needs a Server licence.

User accounts and roles need the Server licensed feature, which the Server and Enterprise editions include. Without it, Users & Groups is unavailable and Profinity runs as a single built-in administrator. A Desktop host does not start the 14-day local trial, so apply a Server licence file under ADMIN > License, as described in Apply a licence, and restart Profinity so the new address takes effect. With a Server licence active, Profinity creates the default admin account, which must change its password at first sign-in. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text: With a Server licence applied, sign in as admin, change the password, and create your own accounts with Create a user. Then work through the Quick start guide, review the Security guide, and run Profinity in the background with Run Profinity as a Windows service.

docs.title: Run Profinity as a service
docs.text:
Run Profinity as a service to start it automatically on boot and restart it if it fails, which suits production environments where uptime matters. Install Profinity first, using the page for your platform: Windows, Linux and macOS, or Docker. In Docker, configure Docker to start the container on boot instead.

As of Profinity V2, Profinity runs in server mode on Docker, macOS, and Linux (x86-64 and 64-bit ARM, plus 32-bit ARM on Linux). On Windows the service runs the desktop application, and becomes a server when a Server licence is applied. In server mode the user interface is available only through a browser, and it is served by REST APIs that are also available to custom applications hosted on the Profinity Server.

A service serves the web interface to other machines. Opening the web interface from another machine, and creating user accounts and roles, need the Profinity Server licensed feature, which the Server and Enterprise editions include. A new installation that is not a Desktop host starts a one-time 14-day local trial with the Server features, so apply a licence file under ADMIN > License before the trial ends, as described in Apply a licence.

Each operating system has its own procedure:

  • Run Profinity as a Linux service: a systemd unit that runs profinity.sh.
  • Run Profinity as a macOS service: a launchd plist.
  • Run Profinity as a Windows service: the ProfinityService.cmd script.

docs.title: Run Profinity as a Linux service
docs.text:
Run Profinity as a systemd service on Linux to start it automatically on boot and restart it if it fails. Install Profinity first, as described in Install Profinity on Linux and macOS. A service serves the web interface to other machines, and opening it from another machine needs the Profinity Server licensed feature, as described in Run Profinity as a service.

On Linux, Profinity runs as a systemd service through the profinity.sh launcher in the install root, /opt/profinity by default. The bootstrap installer creates the profinity service user and the unit file. These steps cover systemd, which the installer supports, and on a distribution without systemd you follow that distribution's documentation for running a daemon.

profinity.sh supports two ways to start Profinity, selected by the -s (--service) flag. Running /opt/profinity/profinity.sh in a terminal starts Profinity in the foreground, which suits testing a configuration before you enable the service, and Ctrl+C stops it. Running systemctl start profinity starts the service, whose unit runs profinity.sh -s, and the -s flag does not select the account that Profinity runs under. Always start Profinity through profinity.sh and never by calling dotnet Profinity.dll, because the launcher resolves the installed edition and runs preflight checks.

docs.title: The systemd unit
docs.text:
The installer writes /etc/systemd/system/profinity.service with these contents:

[Unit]
Description=Profinity
After=syslog.target network.target

[Service]
Type=notify
User=profinity
Group=profinity
WorkingDirectory=/opt/profinity/app
ExecStart=/opt/profinity/profinity.sh -s
Restart=on-failure
TimeoutSec=900

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Adjust WorkingDirectory and ExecStart if you installed with a different --install-dir. If you installed with --no-systemd or from an archive, create the file yourself, and create the profinity user and the artefacts directory first:

sudo mkdir -p /var/lib/prohelion/profinity
sudo chown -R profinity:profinity /var/lib/prohelion

docs.title: Start the service
docs.text:
The installer already enables the unit, so the start command is normally all you need.

  1. If you edited the unit file, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload to reload the systemd configuration.
  2. If the service was disabled, run sudo systemctl enable profinity.service to enable it at boot.

  3. Start the service:

    sudo systemctl start profinity.service

docs.title: Service layout
docs.text:
A typical service layout is:

Path Purpose /var/lib/prohelion/profinity Artefacts: config, profiles, plugins, logs /etc/profinity/env JWT signing key and encryption key, when a deployment script keeps them outside security.yaml /opt/profinity Install root: profinity.sh, update.sh, VERSION, edition.json /opt/profinity/app Profinity binaries, self-contained or portable

To update an installed copy, refer to Update Profinity. Set environment variables for a service as Environment= lines in the [Service] section of the unit, because a service does not read ~/.bashrc, as described in Environment variables.

docs.title: Check that the service is running
docs.text: Run sudo systemctl status profinity.service.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
If the service does not start, read the log with journalctl -u profinity.service.

  • If Profinity logs Unable to create directory '/var/lib/prohelion/...' and then fails to save its configuration, the service user does not own the artefacts directory. Run sudo chown -R profinity:profinity /var/lib/prohelion.
  • A "file not found" error means the path to profinity.sh in the unit does not match where Profinity is installed. Correct the path in the service configuration and start the service again.

docs.title: Run Profinity as a Windows service
docs.text:
Run Profinity as a Windows service to start it automatically on boot and restart it if it fails. Install Profinity first, as described in Install Profinity on Windows. For what a service is and the licence it needs for remote access, refer to Run Profinity as a service.

The installation directory contains ProfinityService.cmd, which is at C:\Program Files (x86)\Prohelion\Profinity\ProfinityService.cmd with the default options. It registers Profinity.exe, the Windows desktop application, as the service. You need administrator privileges to run it.

A default installation installs the service under the LocalSystem user. Prohelion recommends a dedicated user account instead, because it holds fewer privileges than LocalSystem and keeps the artefacts directory out of the Windows directory. The service resolves its artefacts directory in the same way as the desktop application, as %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity of the account it runs under. For LocalSystem that folder is inside the system profile, which is difficult to work with and is beneath C:\Windows\SysWOW64\config\systemprofile\AppData\Local\Prohelion\Profinity on 64-bit Windows, because Profinity.exe is a 32-bit application.

  1. Search for cmd, right-click it, and select Run as administrator.

  2. Run the install command. To install under a user account, give the account name:

    ProfinityService.cmd install [Username to install under]

To install under LocalSystem, run it without a name:

```bat
ProfinityService.cmd install
```
  1. Open the Services app, find Profinity in the list, and start it like any other service.

To place the artefacts directory at a path of your choosing, set the PROFINITY_HOME system environment variable before the service starts, for example with setx PROFINITY_HOME "D:\ProfinityData" /M from an administrator command prompt, and restart the service so that it reads the new value.

Without a Server licence the service serves its web interface to the local machine only, on 127.0.0.1. With a Server licence applied under ADMIN > License, it uses the address set under Profinity Web and creates the default admin account, which must change its password at first sign-in, so other machines can sign in. A service has no application window, so apply the licence file before you rely on remote access, and expect the engine to restart when you apply it.

Starting a second instance with the same configuration on the same machine causes a port conflict on the API or web content ports. To serve content and develop on the same machine at the same time, install Profinity under a separate user account, and change the port in the config file for one of the instances.

To remove the service, run this command as an administrator:

ProfinityService.cmd uninstall

docs.title: Check that the service is running
docs.text: Open the Services app, find Profinity in the list, and confirm that its status is Running.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If the service does not start, read the log in the Event Viewer. A "file not found" error means the installation directory does not match where Profinity is installed, so correct the path in the service configuration and start the service again.

docs.title: Run Profinity as a macOS service
docs.text:
Run Profinity as a launchd service on macOS to start it automatically on boot and restart it if it fails. Install Profinity first, as described in Install Profinity on Linux and macOS. A service serves the web interface to other machines, and opening it from another machine needs the Profinity Server licensed feature, as described in Run Profinity as a service.

On macOS, Profinity is installed with the same bootstrap installer as Linux, into /opt/profinity by default, and launchd runs it as a service in the role systemd fills on Linux.

The plist and commands below are an example only. Prohelion does not ship a launchd plist for the Profinity engine, so check the labels, paths, and options against your own installation before you load the service.

  1. Create a plist file:

    sudo nano /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.profinity.service.plist

  2. Add these contents, adjusting /opt/profinity if you installed with --install-dir:

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.profinity.service</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/opt/profinity/profinity.sh</string>
        <string>-b</string>
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
    <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>

  3. Load the service:

    sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.profinity.service.plist

  4. Start the service:

    sudo launchctl start com.profinity.service

The plist uses -b (--background), which logs to a file and the console instead of depending on an interactive console session. It does not use -s (--service), which selects service-mode host integration only on Windows and Linux (systemd). Always start Profinity through profinity.sh, because it also bootstraps the .NET runtime for the portable macOS build when needed.

To check that the service is running, run sudo launchctl list | grep com.profinity.service, which lists the service when it is loaded. If the service does not start, read the profinity_<date>.log file in the logs folder of the artefacts directory (refer to Artefacts directory). Launchd discards console output unless you add StandardOutPath and StandardErrorPath keys to the plist. A "file not found" error means the path to profinity.sh in the plist does not match where Profinity is installed, so correct the path in the service configuration and start the service again.

docs.title: Integrating to Profinity
docs.text:
Connected equipment feeds into Profinity, which hosts web apps and scripts on top of its core platform (Tags, Collections, Rules, Alerts) behind Security. Profinity exposes that platform through REST APIs to business systems and applications, and through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to AI agents.

Profinity as the Hub of a Solution

docs.title: APIs
docs.text:
Profinity provides RESTful interfaces to integrate with and extend its functionality. The APIs are secured with Bearer tokens and use JSON, so custom applications can be built on them, or existing applications extended with them. They expose both real-time and historical data, so Profinity can be connected to other systems, to custom dashboards and to new applications built on Profinity's data.

Swagger documents the available APIs and how to call them, and the OpenAPI document that tools can import is at /swagger/v2/swagger.json. The Endpoint Reference lists the routes that complement the screens described elsewhere in the documentation. To make a first authenticated call, follow Make your first API call.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text: Profinity includes an MCP server, which lets AI assistants (such as AI Chat) and other MCP-aware tools query system data and metadata. The server exposes ten read-only tools for tag discovery, tag values and history, and alert state, over Streamable HTTP at /api/v2/Ai/Mcp. An MCP client can use it to answer questions about live tags and alerts, to pull history into an analysis tool, or to feed a monitoring or reporting system, all with the permissions of the account it authenticates as. Refer to MCP Server for how to connect and authenticate, and to the MCP tool reference for the full list of tools.

docs.title: Other ways to move data
docs.text: APIs and MCP are for systems that call Profinity. Data can also be pushed out of or into a Profinity instance without a custom client. MQTT Publisher and Webhook Publisher components send tag values to other systems, and MQTT Subscriber brings values in. Tag Relay shares live tags between Profinity instances, and the receiving instance needs the Receive external tags permission.

docs.title: Scripting vs APIs
docs.text:
Profinity offers two ways to extend its capabilities to meet the requirements of an application: Scripting and APIs. The table compares them.

Scripting APIs Scripts support C#, Python and Lua Any programming language that can call REST APIs and JSON can be used Scripts are built in to Profinity and need no external frameworks or hosting APIs are called from outside Profinity, in a custom environment, app, or cloud Scripts can be developed quickly to solve simple problems Applications can be as rich and complex as required and still use Profinity Scripts can run headless, on a schedule or triggered by CAN The application supplies its own logic for how it uses the API Scripts run inside Profinity Scripted API clients run outside Profinity and can be distributed

For compiled integrations and packaged components, refer to Developing with Profinity.

docs.title: Make your first API call
docs.text: This tutorial authenticates to the Profinity REST API and then uses the returned Bearer token to request the latest sample of a tag. At the end you have a token and have sent one authenticated request with curl.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A running Profinity instance. The APIs are running whenever Profinity is running. The examples use localhost:18080.

  • A way for the API calls to authenticate, which is one of:

    • A service account token, generated on the account's User Actions tab in Users & Groups.
    • The username and password of the Profinity user that the API calls run as.

    Either way, the account should be dedicated to the client, hold only the permissions the client needs, and for this tutorial it needs the View tags permission. Accounts are created in Users & Groups, which is shown only when the licence includes the Profinity Server feature, as described in Managing users. - The full path of a tag. The Tag Explorer shows tag paths, and GET /api/v2/Tags lists them (add ?flat=true for a flat list).

docs.title: Get a token
docs.text:
A service account token is used as it is, so with one you can skip to Call an endpoint with the token. A service account token never expires and has no refresh token, so the client sends the same token on every request until an administrator generates a new one, changes the account's roles, or disables the account.

Otherwise, exchange a username and password for a token:

  1. Send a POST request to http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Users/Authenticate, with the username and password of the Profinity user that the API calls run as in the JSON body. For example:

    {
  "username": "admin",
  "password": "password"
}

    An application that calls Profinity across a network should use HTTPS, because calling this API over HTTP can expose the password to network scanning. Custom applications running on the Profinity server can use the localhost address, which does not carry this risk.

    Keep passwords out of scripts

    Do not put a real password in a script, in shell history, or in a file under version control. For an application that runs unattended, use a service account instead.

  2. Read the token field in the response. If the username and password are valid, Profinity responds to a non-browser client with a JSON body like this (the permissions list is abbreviated):

    {
    "token": "eyJhbGciOi...",
    "refreshToken": "...",
    "username": "admin",
    "id": "admin",
    "permissions": ["TagView", "..."]
}

    A user who must complete two-factor authentication or change a password first receives a preAuthToken with requiresTwoFactor or requiresPasswordChange set instead of a token, which is completed through /api/v2/Users/Authenticate/TwoFactor or /api/v2/Users/Current/ChangePassword.

docs.title: Call an endpoint with the token
docs.text:
Pass the service account token, or the contents of the token field, in each request as a Bearer token. From a command line, this request returns the latest sample of a tag:

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Tags/Sample/{fullTagPath}

Replace <token> with the token and {fullTagPath} with the full path of the tag. The response includes the fullTagId, utcTimestamp, quality, and value of the sample. The call returns 404 unless the tag's quality is Good or Stale, and the tag must be visible to the user.

For the 401 and 403 responses and for renewing a token that is still valid, refer to Profinity REST APIs.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• The Swagger page, available by adding /swagger to the URL that Profinity is running on, lists every route and the parameters it accepts. To try routes there, apply a token with the Authorize button, as described in Profinity REST APIs. That page also covers historical data and the OpenAPI document.
  • The Endpoint Reference lists the routes that complement the screens described elsewhere in the documentation.
  • For a client that runs for a long time, use a service account, whose token never expires.

docs.title: Profinity REST APIs
docs.text:
Profinity V2 is built around its own Representational State Transfer (REST) APIs, which exchange JSON and are secured with Bearer tokens. Custom applications use the APIs to add capabilities to a solution, to provide custom user interfaces, or to extend the out-of-the-box functionality. A custom user interface can be hosted either externally or within Profinity itself (refer to Hosting).

As of Profinity 2.3, /api/v2 is the published shape of the REST API, errors are returned as application/problem+json documents, and the OpenAPI document that describes every route is checked against a committed snapshot, so an unreviewed change to a route or model is caught before release. Areas that are still being developed, such as firmware, can change between releases, and a client built on them should be tested against each new release.

The OpenAPI document is served at /swagger/v2/swagger.json, which API tools and AI skills can import to generate a client or to read the available routes and models.

API users can damage equipment

The Profinity APIs support security and can be encrypted, but an API user can change system and equipment state. Grant API access only to the users and applications that need it, and limit what each of them can do, so that nobody can accidentally damage the environment or equipment.

docs.title: Using Profinity APIs
docs.text:
Profinity V2 is built around its own APIs, so the APIs are running whenever Profinity is running. The Enable Profinity API and Enable Swagger on API settings apply to the Profinity Web server for extensions only (refer to Extensions Web), and the main Profinity host always publishes the API and Swagger.

The Swagger interface for Profinity is available by adding /swagger to the URL that Profinity is running on. For example, if Profinity is running on localhost:18080, the Swagger UI is at http://localhost:18080/swagger.

The Endpoint Reference lists the routes for alerts, collections, derived tags, Profinity AI chat, security, account resets, tag relay and themes.

Showing the Profinity APIs

docs.title: Profinity API security
docs.text: Profinity APIs require a Bearer token, which is either a service account token or a token returned by signing in with a username and password. Either way, the account should be dedicated to the client and hold only the permissions the client needs.

docs.title: Using a service account token
docs.text: A service account token is generated on the account's User Actions tab in Users & Groups, and it is already a Bearer token. A client that has one skips the /api/v2/Users/Authenticate call and passes the token directly in each request, and in Swagger the token is pasted straight into the Authorize dialog. The token never expires and has no refresh token, so it suits a client that runs for a long time or unattended. It stays valid until an administrator generates a new one, changes the account's roles, or disables the account.

docs.title: Signing in with a username and password
docs.text:
To test the APIs from the Swagger GUI without a service account token, execute a call against the /api/v2/Users/Authenticate API in the Swagger GUI and apply the returned token with the Authorize button in the top right of the Swagger page.

To get a token from any other client, send a POST request to http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Users/Authenticate, with the username and password of the Profinity user that the API calls run as in the JSON body. For example:

{
  "username": "admin",
  "password": "password"
}

Use HTTPS to protect passwords

Calling this API over an HTTP connection can expose the password to network scanning. Custom applications running on the Profinity server can use the localhost address, which does not carry this risk, while an application that calls Profinity across a network should use HTTPS for all API usage.

If the username and password are valid, Profinity responds to a non-browser client with a JSON body that carries the access token, a refreshToken (omitted for service accounts, whose tokens do not expire), the username, an id and the user's permissions, like this (the permissions list is abbreviated):

{
    "token": "eyJhbGciOi...",
    "refreshToken": "...",
    "username": "admin",
    "id": "admin",
    "permissions": ["TagView", "..."]
}

Generating an Authorization token via Swagger

A browser client receives the same session as cookies and a body without the token. A user who must complete two-factor authentication or change a password first receives a preAuthToken with requiresTwoFactor or requiresPasswordChange set instead of a token, which is completed through /api/v2/Users/Authenticate/TwoFactor or /api/v2/Users/Current/ChangePassword. A token that is still valid can be renewed with GET /api/v2/Users/Refresh.

docs.title: Passing the token
docs.text:
The service account token, or the contents of the token field, must be passed in each request as a Bearer token, and the documentation of the client-side tool calling Profinity describes how to do this for that tool. From a command line, curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:18080/api/v2/Tags/Sample/{fullTagPath} returns the latest sample of a tag. A call with a missing or expired token is answered with 401, and a call from a user that lacks the permission the route needs is answered with 403. A client that signed in with a username and password and starts receiving 401 should sign in again or renew the token with GET /api/v2/Users/Refresh. A client that uses a service account token and starts receiving 401 needs the current token from an administrator, because the old token stops working when a new one is generated or the account's roles change.

In Swagger the token is applied by clicking the Authorize button in the top right of the screen and pasting in the generated token:

Entering the token in Swagger

docs.title: Accessing historical data via APIs
docs.text:
APIs can provide both realtime and historical data when an InfluxDB database is configured in the profile. If no InfluxDB database is set up, only realtime data is available.

Historical data is retrieved in three steps, and the first two use POST /api/v2/TagQuerySet, which requires the TagView permission (View tags).

  1. Configure an InfluxDB database in the profile.
  2. Send POST /api/v2/TagQuerySet with a body that holds an optional srcSetId and a list of bindings. Each binding names a tag source and a store of Local or Logged. For the Logged store a binding also carries the timeRangeStart and timeRangeStop of the InfluxDB range, with optional seriesMode, aggregationWindow and aggregationFunction values. The response carries the matching values and a srcSetId.
  3. Send GET /api/v2/TagQuerySet/Delta/{sourceSet} to poll that set, which returns only the values that have changed since the previous poll.

Two further routes return the latest value of one item. GET /api/v2/DBC/{component}/{message}/{signal} returns the latest local value of a single DBC signal and needs the DBCView permission (View DBC definitions), and GET /api/v2/Tags/Sample/{fullTagPath} returns the latest sample of a tag.

For more information on configuring InfluxDB, refer to InfluxDB and Prometheus Logging.

docs.title: Endpoint Reference
docs.text: This page lists REST API routes that complement the screens described elsewhere in the documentation. The Swagger page on your Profinity instance lists every route and the parameters it accepts, and Profinity REST APIs explains how to authenticate. Each route needs the same permission as the matching screen.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Routes under /api/v2/Alerts return and manage the alerts shown in the Alerts Log.

Method Route Body GET /api/v2/Alerts/Active None. Optional query values componentId, tagPrefix, unacknowledgedOnly and level. GET /api/v2/Alerts/History None. Optional query values componentId, tagPrefix, pageIndex, pageSize, level, fromUtc, and toUtc. POST /api/v2/Alerts/Ack { "ruleId": "...", "tagId": "..." } POST /api/v2/Alerts/Unack { "ruleId": "...", "tagId": "..." } POST /api/v2/Alerts/Silence { "ruleId": "...", "tagId": "...", "durationMinutes": 60 }

Through the API a silence can last from 1 to 1440 minutes (24 hours), and a request outside that range is refused with "durationMinutes must be between 1 and 1440." The Unack route is the same revert that the Unacknowledge alert button uses.

docs.title: Collections and derived tags
docs.text: Method Route Purpose GET, PUT /api/v2/Tags/Collections Reads or saves the collections document, with JSON request and response bodies. Reading needs View tag collections and saving needs Modify tag collections. GET, PUT /api/v2/Tags/DerivedTags Reads or saves the derived tags document, with the same permissions as collections.

docs.title: Profinity AI
docs.text: Method Route Purpose POST /api/v2/Ai/Chat Streams a chat response for the calling user, using the instance's Profinity AI configuration.

docs.title: Component and collection security
docs.text:
The routes below work on the active profile only, and there is no route to edit security for a profile that is not currently loaded. A GET response includes an unresolvedRoles list alongside mode and allowedRoles, and a PUT accepts only mode and allowedRoles. Refer to Component and Collection Security for the policy itself.

Method Route Permission Purpose GET, PUT /api/v2/ActiveProfile/components/{componentName}/security Security administration Reads or writes the security policy for a component on the active profile. {componentName} is the component's display name. GET, PUT /api/v2/ActiveProfile/collections/{collectionId}/security Security administration Reads or writes the security policy for a collection on the active profile, including the reserved All collection.

docs.title: Account resets
docs.text:
These routes need the Security administration permission, and match Reset MFA and Reset Password in Managing Users.

Method Route Purpose POST /api/v2/Users/{username}/TwoFactor/Reset Clears the user's authenticator enrolment. POST /api/v2/Users/{username}/Password/Reset Requires a password change at the next sign-in and signs out active sessions.

docs.title: Tag Relay
docs.text: Method Route Purpose POST /api/v2/Relay/snapshot Receives a snapshot from a Tag Relay Sender that uses HTTPS. The caller needs a JSON Web Token (JWT) for a user with the Receive external tags permission (or Admin), the request body can be up to 5 MB, and an instance accepts relay posts for only one Tag Relay Receiver set to HTTPS.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text: The theme is read-only through the API. GET /api/v2/Themes is anonymous, so the sign-in page can use it before a user has authenticated, and returns appTitle, hasCustomTheme and a logos object with main, login and favicon URLs. The generated stylesheet is served from /Themes/theme.css, and each asset from /Themes/Assets/{file}. Changes are made by editing the theme file, as described in Themes and Branding.

docs.title: MCP Server
docs.text:
Profinity includes a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, which lets AI assistants and other MCP-aware tools query live data from a Profinity instance over a standard protocol. The server exposes read-only tools for tag discovery, tag values and history, and alert state, and it does not expose any tool that writes or changes Profinity data. An MCP client can use it to answer questions about live tags and alerts, to pull history into an analysis tool, or to feed a monitoring or reporting system, all with the permissions of the account it authenticates as.

Licence required

The MCP server requires the AI licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: About MCP
docs.text: MCP is a standard protocol that lets AI assistants and other external tools query a system's data without a bespoke integration for each tool. In Profinity, the MCP server answers queries about tags, tag values and alerts, scoped to the permissions of the authenticated caller. The built-in AI Chat uses the same server.

docs.title: Enabling the MCP server
docs.text:
The MCP server is configured from the Profinity AI settings page (select ADMIN in the side menu, open the System Configuration pill, then choose Profinity AI), under its own MCP Server field group, where the toggle is Enable MCP Server. Turning on Enable Profinity AI also enables the MCP server, since the assistant depends on it, and the MCP server can be enabled on its own, with Profinity AI left off, for external MCP clients such as Claude Desktop.

Restart required

Enabling or disabling the MCP server takes effect only after Profinity restarts. After saving the configuration, wait for the restart to complete before reloading the page, because the web client shows a restarting message while it waits for the engine to return.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text:
An MCP client connects to the endpoint at:

/api/v2/Ai/Mcp

resolved against the Profinity web server's host, port and protocol. An AI tool needs only this address and an Authorization header, and Connect Profinity to AI describes how to set one up.

docs.title: Available tools
docs.text: The MCP server provides ten read-only tools: get_all_components, search_tags, get_tag_catalog, get_tag_sample_by_canonical_id, get_tag_samples, get_tag_series, get_tag_series_batch, get_alert_rules, get_active_alerts and get_alert_history. Refer to MCP tool reference for the parameters and return values of each tool. A tool omits a tag or alert the calling user cannot view and never reports it as an error, so a response that looks smaller than expected usually reflects the caller's own permissions.

docs.title: Authentication and permissions
docs.text:
Every call to the MCP server requires a valid JSON Web Token (JWT) bearer token, checked against the MCP integration permission at the endpoint itself. Beyond that gate, each tool checks its own domain permission before returning data: the tag-related tools require View tags, and the alert-related tools require View alerts. In the permission list that the sign-in response returns, these appear as McpView, TagView and AlertsView.

The Profinity AI permission automatically grants MCP integration, so a user with access to Profinity AI does not need MCP integration granted separately (refer to Profinity AI Settings).

To authenticate directly against the MCP server:

  1. Create a user account with the required permissions, or use an existing one.
  2. Generate a JWT token for the user by signing in through POST /api/v2/Users/Authenticate, as described under Profinity API security. A personal token expires after the Security Token Expiration (minutes) setting in Application Config, whereas a service account token does not expire.

  3. Include the token in the Authorization header of every request:

    Authorization: Bearer YOUR_JWT_TOKEN_HERE

An external MCP client that runs for a long time should use a service account with the required permissions and a non-expiring token, rather than a personal user account.

docs.title: Troubleshooting connections
docs.text:
Response Cause Fix 401 The request has no token, or the token has expired Sign in again, or use a service account token 403 The user lacks MCP integration Add the permission to one of the user's roles (refer to Roles and Permissions) 404 The MCP server is not enabled, the AI feature is not licensed, Profinity has not restarted since the setting changed, or the request is not a Streamable HTTP MCP request, such as a browser request or one without the Accept header Turn on Enable MCP Server, check the licence and restart Profinity 429 with Too many MCP requests. Please try again later. The per-user rate limit on MCP requests was exceeded Reduce the request rate and retry later

A tool that returns fewer results than expected, rather than an error, reflects the caller's View tags or View alerts permission.

docs.title: Related documentation
docs.text:
• Profinity AI Settings: enabling the MCP server as part of, or independently of, Profinity AI
  • Service Accounts: long-lived credentials for external MCP clients
  • AI Chat: the built-in assistant that uses this MCP server
  • MCP tool reference: parameters and return values of the ten tools
  • AI Skills: an external toolkit that also uses this MCP server, for building dashboards and other configuration with an AI coding assistant
  • APIs: the REST API documentation
  • Scripting: Profinity scripting capabilities

docs.title: MCP tool reference
docs.text:
The MCP server provides ten read-only tools for tag discovery, tag values and history, and alert state. Refer to MCP Server for how to connect a client, authenticate, and troubleshoot a connection.

None of them acknowledge, unacknowledge, silence, or otherwise change alert or tag state, so those changes are made with the REST Alerts API or the Profinity UI.

A tag or alert the calling user does not have permission to view is omitted from a tool's response and is never reported as an error, so a response that looks smaller than expected on a shared instance usually reflects the caller's own permissions rather than a fault.

docs.title: get_all_components
docs.text:
The recommended first call, which returns a lightweight list of active component names visible to the caller, for use as the componentId argument to other tools.

Parameters: none

Returns: a collection of component name strings

docs.title: search_tags
docs.text:
Searches the live tag tree by name fragment, unit, meta-type, component, or tag-path prefix, without downloading the full catalogue. At least one of the filter parameters is required.

Parameter Type Description query optional Case-insensitive substring match against the tag path, its last segment, and its comment unit optional Exact unit match, case-insensitive (V is not the same as mV) componentId optional Restrict to a component name tagPrefix optional Restrict to a canonical tag path prefix; takes priority over componentId when both are set metaType optional Restrict to a meta-type, for example dbc.signal sampleLeavesOnly optional (default: true) If true, return only tags that carry a value includeMetadata optional (default: true) If true, include unit, comment, and scaling metadata on each result limit optional (default: 25) Maximum results, 1 to 50

Returns: {items, count, limit, truncated}, where items holds one object per matching tag with fullTagId, metaType, hasSample and isWritable, plus a metadata object when includeMetadata is true and the tag has metadata. count is the number of items returned, limit is the effective limit after clamping to the 1 to 50 range, and truncated is true when more tags matched than the limit allowed

docs.title: get_tag_catalog
docs.text:
Returns the tag catalogue for the active profile, nested by segment or as a paginated flat list. Use get_all_components first, then scope with componentId or tagPrefix, because an unscoped nested catalogue above roughly 200,000 characters is refused.

Parameter Type Description flat optional (default: false) If true, return a paginated flat list instead of a nested tree includeSamples optional (default: false) If true, include each tag's current value where available includeMetadata optional (default: false) If true, include unit, scaling, and comment metadata componentId optional Restrict to a component name tagPrefix optional Restrict to a canonical tag path prefix; takes priority over componentId when both are set pageIndex optional Zero-based page index pageSize optional Page size, 1 to 500 sampleLeavesOnly optional (default: false) Flat mode only: keep only tags that carry a value

Returns: with flat true, {items, totalCount, pageIndex, pageSize}, where each item is {fullTagId, metaType, hasSample, isWritable} plus sample when includeSamples is true and a value is available, and metadata when includeMetadata is true and the tag has metadata. Without flat, a tree keyed by path segment whose leaves are the same objects, or the same {items, totalCount, pageIndex, pageSize} wrapper when pageIndex or pageSize is supplied. A sample object holds utcTimestamp, quality, reason, and value and message when present

docs.title: get_tag_sample_by_canonical_id
docs.text:
Reads the current value of a single tag by its canonical full tag ID.

Parameter Type Description fullTagId required Canonical full tag ID, for example MyBMS/DBC/MessageName/SignalName

Returns: an object with fullTagId, utcTimestamp, quality, reason, and, only when present, value, message and a metadata object holding any of unit, comment, factor and offset. The reason is one of ok, notFound, notReadable, noValueYet, stale or error, so a path that does not exist returns notFound rather than nothing. The result is null only when the tag is not visible to the caller

docs.title: get_tag_samples
docs.text:
Batch-reads current values for up to 50 canonical tag IDs in one call.

Parameter Type Description fullTagIds required Canonical full tag IDs to read, maximum 50

Returns: an array of the same sample objects that get_tag_sample_by_canonical_id returns, one per visible requested ID, with blank and duplicate IDs skipped and IDs the caller cannot view omitted

docs.title: get_tag_series
docs.text:
Returns current or historical values for a single canonical tag ID, using the same range and aggregation rules as POST /api/v2/TagQuerySet (refer to Accessing historical data via APIs). Omit start/stop for the current value.

Parameter Type Description fullTagId required Canonical full tag ID start optional Start of the range, Flux-style, for example -1h stop optional End of the range, for example 0m, or omitted for now aggregationWindow optional Aggregation window, for example 10s, used only with a time range aggregationFunction optional (default: max) max, min, mean, sum, count, last, or first

Returns: an object holding a measurement (or, when more than one is returned, a measurements array). Each measurement has tagId, label, sample, dataPoints and, when known, unit and transmitter. sample carries utcTimestamp, quality, reason, and value and message when present, where reason is one of ok, stale, notFound, notReadable, notEnabled, noValueYet, noData, budgetExceeded, historianUnavailable, invalidTimeRange or error. dataPoints is a list of {time, value} pairs, which holds the single current value when no start or stop is given and is empty when the range returned no points. An ID that is a container rather than a readable tag is rejected with a validation error

docs.title: get_tag_series_batch
docs.text:
Batch-reads time series for up to 20 canonical tag IDs sharing one time range and aggregation.

Parameter Type Description fullTagIds required Canonical full tag IDs to read, maximum 20 start optional Start of the range, Flux-style stop optional End of the range aggregationWindow optional Aggregation window, used only with a time range aggregationFunction optional (default: max) max, min, mean, sum, count, last, or first

Returns: an array with one entry per visible requested ID, in request order, each shaped like the get_tag_series result. An ID that is a container or is not a valid tag returns an entry with an empty dataPoints list and a reason of notReadable or notFound instead of an error, and IDs the caller cannot view are omitted

docs.title: get_alert_rules
docs.text:
Returns the catalogue of defined alert rules, independent of whether any rule is currently active.

Parameter Type Description componentId optional Restrict to rules scoped under this component pageIndex optional (default: 0) Zero-based page index pageSize optional (default: 25) Page size, 1 to 500 includeDisabled optional (default: false) If true, include disabled rules

Returns: {items, totalCount, pageIndex, pageSize}, where each item has ruleId, ruleName, displayName, description, level, enabled, relatedTags, moreInformation, sourceKey, tagPathPrefix and collectionName. Text fields can be null when the rule does not define them, and pageSize is the effective size after clamping

docs.title: get_active_alerts
docs.text:
Returns currently active alerts.

Parameter Type Description componentId optional Restrict to alerts under this component or tag path prefix tagPrefix optional Restrict to alerts whose tag path starts with this prefix unacknowledgedOnly optional (default: false) If true, return only unacknowledged alerts level optional Restrict to a severity level, for example Warning or Error

Returns: {items, activeTagIds, componentNames}, where items lists the active alerts and the other two are sorted lists of the tag paths and component names those alerts belong to. Each alert has ruleId, ruleName, displayName, description, moreInformation, relatedTags, level, message, tagId, componentName, isActive, utcTimestamp, transition, isAcknowledged, acknowledgedBy, silencedUntilUtc and isSilenced

docs.title: get_alert_history
docs.text:
Returns a page of past alert state transitions (raised, cleared, acknowledged, silenced), newest first.

Parameter Type Description componentId optional Restrict to alerts under this component or tag path prefix tagPrefix optional Restrict to alerts whose tag path starts with this prefix pageIndex optional (default: 0) Zero-based page index pageSize optional (default: 25) Page size, 1 to 500 compact optional (default: false) If true, return rule definitions once with slim event rows, rather than repeating rule fields on every row level optional Restrict to a severity level fromUtc optional Inclusive UTC lower bound toUtc optional Inclusive UTC upper bound

Returns: {items, totalCount, pageIndex, pageSize}, where each item has the same alert fields as get_active_alerts and transition records the state change. With compact true the result is {ruleDefinitions, events, totalCount, pageIndex, pageSize} instead, where ruleDefinitions is keyed by ruleId and holds ruleId, ruleName and, when present, displayName, description, moreInformation and message, and each event holds only ruleId, tagId, isActive, isAcknowledged, isSilenced and, when present, componentName, utcTimestamp and transition

docs.title: Profinity Mobile
docs.text:
Profinity Mobile is a companion app for iOS and Android that connects to a Profinity engine over HTTPS and shows the web interface inside the app. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) heartbeat discovery lets phones on the same local area network (LAN) find servers without typing URLs.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Server["Profinity server"]
        Engine["Profinity engine"]
    end
    subgraph Phone["Phone"]
        List["Discovery list"] --> Interface["Web interface"]
    end
    Engine --> List
The Profinity engine broadcasts a UDP heartbeat that fills the discovery list in Profinity Mobile, and the app then connects to the chosen server over HTTPS and shows its web interface

To set up discovery and connect a phone, refer to Connect Profinity Mobile to a server. If no servers appear, refer to Troubleshoot Profinity Mobile.

docs.title: Install the app
docs.text: Prohelion does not publish the app in the public app stores. Contact Prohelion at the Prohelion Website to receive the installation files. Prohelion supplies the app as source code, and the organisation that distributes it builds and signs its own iOS and Android binaries, as described in OEM White-Label Mobile Builds.

docs.title: Login modes
docs.text: The Password mode is the standard Profinity web sign-in page, which the app opens inside the app and which follows the site's Local or SSO (single sign-on) sign-in method and shows the two-factor prompt when the site requires it. The app can save the username and password in the phone's secure storage. The Kiosk mode logs in automatically with a configured kiosk user (refer to Kiosk Mode). The app has no mode switch, because Kiosk Mode is a setting of the server, and the web sign-in page signs in automatically when the active profile has it enabled.

docs.title: Connect Profinity Mobile to a server
docs.text: To connect Profinity Mobile to a server, check the discovery settings on the Profinity engine, then select the server from the app's discovery list. You need the app installed on the phone (refer to Profinity Mobile). Phones reach the server only when remote web access is available, which needs the Profinity Server licensed feature (refer to Licensing).

docs.title: Enable server discovery on the engine
docs.text:
Phones find a server only while it broadcasts a heartbeat, so check these settings on the Profinity server first. Heartbeats are sent only while the web server is running and the machine has at least one network address other than loopback.

  1. On the Profinity server, select ADMIN in the side menu, then System Configuration, then the Discovery tab.
  2. Check the four settings described in Discovery.
Setting Description Profinity Server Name The friendly name shown in the mobile list, which defaults to the host name of the machine (for example Workshop-Profinity) Send Profinity Heartbeat Turns the broadcast on or off, and is on by default Heartbeat UDP port The UDP port of the broadcast, 49025 by default Heartbeat interval (seconds) The time between broadcasts, from 1 to 60 seconds, 3 by default

Server Discovery heartbeat settings

Saving System Configuration restarts Profinity. The mobile app listens for the broadcast on UDP port 49025 by default, so if you change the Heartbeat UDP port, the app build must use the same port (refer to OEM White-Label Mobile Builds). Each entry in the app's discovery list shows the server name, the active profile and the server's network addresses.

docs.title: Connect from the app
docs.text:
1. Connect the phone to the same Wi-Fi network as the Profinity server.
  2. Open Profinity Mobile. The discovery list shows the servers that are broadcasting a heartbeat.
  3. Select your server and connect. The app uses HTTPS when the server has it configured. The app opens the server's web sign-in page inside the app, where you sign in with your Profinity user name and password, or with your single sign-on and two-factor prompt. If the active profile has Kiosk Mode enabled, the page signs in automatically as the kiosk user.

To return to the server list, swipe from the left edge of the screen on iOS, or use the system back action on Android, which first steps back through the pages you opened in the app. A certificate warning that you accepted for a server stays accepted when you go back.

If the discovery list is empty or sign-in does not complete, refer to Troubleshoot Profinity Mobile.

docs.title: OEM white-label mobile builds
docs.text:
Original equipment manufacturer (OEM) partners can ship white-label builds of Profinity Mobile with their own branding and bundle identifiers.

The Profinity Mobile source package includes the build guide (BUILD.md) and the white-label guide (WHITE-LABEL.md), which list the prerequisites for building:

  • Node.js 22.11 or later and npm for every build.
  • macOS with Xcode 16 or later and CocoaPods for iOS.
  • Android Studio with SDK platform API 26 or later and JDK 17 for Android.

docs.title: Branding configuration
docs.text:
OEM partners rebrand the app by editing the build-time file app.config.yaml, which Prohelion supplies with the Profinity Mobile source code and the branding assets, and then building signed iOS and Android binaries. The file holds these fields:

Field Description appName Display name on the splash screen and in the app stores companyName Subtitle on the splash screen primaryColor Action colour for buttons and badges navBackground Navigation and toolbar background colour secondaryColor Muted text colour brandRed Accent colour of the Profinity logo splashLogo, landingLogo and appIcon Paths to the splash logo, the landing page logo and the app icon source artwork development.androidEmulatorHostConnect Set to true only for development builds that connect an Android emulator to a Profinity server on the host machine discovery.profinityHeartbeatPort Must match the Heartbeat UDP port on the Profinity server (default 49025) discovery.profinityHeartbeatVersion The Profinity product version that the heartbeat is expected to report, set to 2.3 for Profinity 2.3 discovery.staleTimeoutMs Time in milliseconds after which a server that has not been seen is removed from the discovery list

The iOS bundle identifier and the Android application identifier are set in the native projects, and each OEM sets them to its own namespace. The npm run configure command regenerates the application configuration from app.config.yaml, and npm run setup and npm run validate run it automatically. The app build regenerates the launcher icons from the appIcon artwork.

docs.title: What end users and operators get
docs.text:
End users install the OEM-branded app from the OEM's own store listing, or the OEM installs it on the phones of its service technicians. Server discovery and login behaviour are the same as in standard Profinity Mobile. The app only finds servers whose Heartbeat UDP port matches discovery.profinityHeartbeatPort. A server that uses HTTPS with a self-signed certificate shows the user a certificate prompt on first connection, so install a trusted certificate on the server where the app is deployed to staff. Sign-in through SSO (single sign-on) needs a Profinity site set to the Sso sign-in method.

Refer to the Release notes 2.3 for what changed in this release.

docs.title: Troubleshoot Profinity Mobile
docs.text:
This page lists the discovery, certificate, and sign-in problems that Profinity Mobile can show, with the remedy for each. To set up discovery first, refer to Connect Profinity Mobile to a server.

Issue Remedy No servers in the list Confirm that Send Profinity Heartbeat is on, that the phone and server are on the same subnet, that the firewall allows UDP port 49025, and that the network does not block broadcast traffic between Wi-Fi and wired segments or VLANs No servers in the list, and Profinity runs in Docker UDP broadcasts do not leave a Docker bridge network, so run the container with host networking on Linux (refer to Docker Installation) Android emulator list is empty Emulators cannot receive LAN broadcasts, so use a physical phone Certificate warnings Install a trusted HTTPS certificate on the server, or accept the prompt once per server SSO does not complete The site must use the Sso sign-in method, and the identity provider (IdP) sign-in is completed in the app's embedded browser

For single sign-on setup, refer to SSO and Sign-In. For the server-side discovery settings, refer to Discovery.

docs.title: Profinity AI
docs.text:
Profinity AI gives AI the context of a running Profinity system, so it can work across devices rather than one signal at a time. It comes in two parts: AI Chat, an assistant built into Profinity, and AI Skills, a toolkit for your own AI coding assistant.

AI Chat and the built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server require the AI licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

Context in, cross-system diagnosis out

docs.title: What Profinity AI can see
docs.text:
Profinity AI is connected to your running system and draws on four kinds of context:

  • Live data: every component in the Profile and its tags, with current values and data quality.
  • Rules and alerts: the alert rules you have defined, the alerts that are active, and the alert history.
  • History and trends: long-term values from the historian, not just the latest reading.
  • Documentation: manuals, procedures, and how-to material from docs.prohelion.com.

Live data, rules, alerts, and history reach the assistant through the MCP Server, which is read-only. Profinity AI cannot change tags, alerts, or configuration through it. Profinity AI sees only what the signed-in user could already see in Profinity, so tags and alerts you do not have permission to view are left out of its answers.

An administrator can also switch on web search for the Claude, OpenAI, and OpenRouter providers, which lets the assistant look beyond the documentation. Questions and tool results are sent to the configured AI provider, so refer to AI Chat before you discuss sensitive data.

docs.title: From context to diagnosis
docs.text: With that context in one place, Profinity AI gathers context from the whole Profile, correlates signals across devices, matches alerts to the relevant documentation, compares current readings against history and trends, and proposes a likely root cause and next steps with the evidence it used. A question such as "Why is Cell 12 overheating?" can therefore be answered from the alert, the neighbouring cells, the cooling system, and the service manual together.

docs.title: Choose how to use it
docs.text:
• AI Chat runs inside Profinity, from the side menu. Use it to ask questions about this instance: system health, alert investigation, and how-to questions.
  • AI Skills runs in your own AI tool (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT), outside Profinity. Use it to build dashboards, rules, collections, scripts, plugins, derived tags, and example apps from your live schema, and to develop with Profinity.

AI Chat answers questions and AI Skills helps you build things, and power users can pair AI Skills with the MCP Server to use their own AI tool instead of AI Chat. Users need the Profinity AI permission to open AI Chat, and the built-in Administrators role has it by default. Roles and Permissions lists the Profinity AI and MCP integration permissions. For administrator configuration, permissions, and data-handling notes, refer to Profinity AI settings.

docs.title: AI Chat
docs.text:
AI Chat is the chat assistant of Profinity AI, built into Profinity, available from the side menu once an administrator has configured it (refer to Profinity AI settings). It can answer questions about the live state of this Profinity instance, look up how-to and reference material from docs.prohelion.com, and, if the administrator has enabled it, search the web.

AI Chat requires the AI licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. Without it the feature is unavailable. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

Your messages may leave this instance

Profinity AI is answered by an external AI provider unless your administrator has configured a local, self-hosted model. Ask your administrator which provider is configured before discussing sensitive data with the assistant.

docs.title: Open Profinity AI
docs.text: Users with the Profinity AI permission see a Profinity AI entry in the side menu, above ADMIN, and selecting it opens the chat window. The built-in Administrators role has the permission by default. If the entry is missing, the signed-in user lacks the permission, the instance has no AI licence, or the administrator has not enabled and configured Profinity AI under ADMIN > System Configuration.

docs.title: Ask a question
docs.text:
The chat window opens with a short greeting and three example prompts to get started, covering a system-health question, a documentation search, and a how-to question. Type a question of your own and press Enter to send it, or Shift+Enter to add a new line without sending.

Profinity AI chat window with suggested prompts

While Profinity AI is answering, the status indicator at the top of the window reads Thinking…, and once a question has been answered it reads Connected to this environment. The response streams in as it is generated, rather than appearing all at once. Web search, when the administrator has enabled it, is available only with the Claude, OpenAI, and OpenRouter providers (refer to Profinity AI settings).

A conversation in progress

Profinity AI answers questions about this instance by querying live data through the same permissions you have, so it cannot see tags, alerts, or configuration that you could not otherwise see in Profinity.

You can send another question while Profinity AI is still answering the previous one, and it is queued and answered in turn. Use Stop to cancel a response in progress, and New chat to clear the conversation and start again.

docs.title: When AI Chat reports an error
docs.text: If the provider does not answer within the Response timeout (seconds) that the administrator set, the chat window shows a timeout message, and you can send the question again or ask the administrator to increase the timeout. Any other failure, for example an API key that the provider rejects or a provider that cannot be reached, shows Something went wrong. with a link to the logs, where the cause is recorded. The administrator corrects the provider settings under ADMIN > System Configuration.

docs.title: Limitations for 2.3
docs.text:
• Conversation history is kept only for the current browser tab and is cleared when the tab is closed. Profinity AI does not keep a record of past conversations across sessions or devices.
  • Profinity AI uses one configuration for the whole instance; there is no per-user choice of provider or model.
  • The example prompts shown in the empty state are suggestions only, and Profinity AI is not limited to those topics.

To build dashboards and other configuration with your own AI coding assistant instead, refer to AI Skills. For the live-data connection Profinity AI uses, refer to the MCP Server.

docs.title: AI Skills
docs.text: AI Skills is a pack of seven skills for AI coding assistants such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and ChatGPT that help you build Profinity dashboards, rules, collections, scripts, plugins, derived tags, and example apps. Every skill works from the live schema and API of your own Profinity instance and from curated examples drawn from Profinity's shipped content, so what it generates matches the conventions of your instance. AI Skills runs in your own AI tool, outside Profinity, while AI Chat is the assistant built into the product that answers questions about a running instance. To install the skills, refer to Install AI Skills. For the list of skills, their requirements, and the tools they support, refer to AI Skills reference.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Each skill is self-contained. Before it generates anything, it queries your instance's live schema (GET /api/v2/UI/schema for dashboards, and the matching live definitions for rules, collections, and derived tags), so it never relies on a schema remembered from a previous run. It also uses your instance's MCP Server for live data such as tags and alerts, and the REST API for the schema and for saving configuration, because the MCP Server does not serve dashboard, rule, collection, or derived tag documents. It grounds generation in Profinity's own example content rather than invented output. For skills that modify your instance (dashboards, rules, collections, and derived tags), the skill shows you the payload and asks for approval before any change goes live, while the read-only skills (script, plugin, and app) generate code and stop.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Outside["Outside Profinity"]
        Tool["Your AI tool"] --> Skills["AI Skills"]
    end
    subgraph Instance["Profinity instance"]
        API["REST API"]
        MCP["MCP Server"]
    end
    Skills --> API
    Skills --> MCP
A skill in your AI tool reads live data from the MCP Server and the live schema from the REST API of your Profinity instance, and for skills that modify the instance it sends the generated configuration back through the REST API after you approve

docs.title: Use AI Skills instead of AI Chat
docs.text:
AI Chat is for everyone with the Profinity AI permission and needs no setup on their machine. Power users can use their own AI tool for the same job, which suits people who want their own model or provider rather than the single provider configured for the whole instance, conversations that persist (AI Chat keeps history only for the current browser tab), or other work in the same session such as files, code, and other systems. To do this, connect your tool to the MCP Server using How to Connect Profinity to AI, which gives it the same read-only live data AI Chat uses: tags and their history, alert rules, active alerts, and alert history. Add AI Skills on top and the same tool can also build and change things, always showing you the payload before it saves.

Your own tool does not get AI Chat's built-in documentation lookup, so point it at docs.prohelion.com if you want it to cite the manuals. It sees only what your sign-in is permitted to see, and your messages go to whichever provider that tool uses, so check that provider against your organisation's data-handling rules.

docs.title: Developing with Profinity
docs.text:
AI Skills also helps people who build on Profinity, because each skill reads the schema and API of your instance and generates what your Profinity version accepts. Use the skill that matches what you are building:

  • A dashboard or component dashboard: Dashboard Builder.
  • Alert rules, tag collections, or derived tags: Tag Rules, Tag Collections, Derived Tags.
  • An in-profile script, with simulation before you deploy: Script.
  • A custom component plugin, packed for installation with the Component Pack CLI: Plugin.
  • An application or integration against the REST API: App.

The Script and Plugin skills work beside the Profinity developer kit (Profinity.Sdk, profinity-script, and profinity-component-pack), which Prohelion supplies on request. Refer to Developing with Profinity for the underlying SDK and plugin documentation.

For the next step, refer to Install AI Skills, to Profinity AI for how AI Chat and AI Skills fit together, and to the Profinity REST APIs, which the skills use to fetch your live schema and push generated configuration.

docs.title: AI Skills reference
docs.text: This page lists the seven skills in AI Skills, what they need to work, and the AI tools that can use them. To install them, refer to Install AI Skills.

docs.title: The seven skills
