docs.text: Skill Purpose Dashboard Builder Generate Profinity dashboard config (YAML) from your live UI schema Script Write in-profile scripts using profinity-script with SDK guidance Plugin Create a component plugin and package it with profinity-component-pack Tag Collections Build tag collection documents (group related tags for dashboards) Tag Rules Create alert and rule documents to trigger on tag conditions Derived Tags Define derived tags that compute from other tags App Write an example app that calls the Profinity REST API

docs.title: What AI Skills needs to work
docs.text: AI Skills needs no licence of its own. It uses the REST API, which every edition includes, with your sign-in, so the same credentials and permissions apply as for any other API call. A skill that saves a dashboard, rule, or collection needs the matching permission for the signed-in user, such as Modify dashboards, Modify tag rules, or Modify tag collections (refer to Roles and Permissions). Some skills can also use read access to the MCP server for extra schema discovery, which is read-only, never pushes changes, and needs the AI licensed feature. If MCP is unavailable, the skill falls back to the REST API alone. If the REST API is not available when a skill is asked to generate something, the skill says so and stops rather than guessing an endpoint or using a remembered schema.

docs.title: Supported AI tools
docs.text:
AI Skills ships in two forms.

Form Works with How you use it Agent skills (SKILL.md folders) Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and other agents that load SKILL.md skills Install with npx skills add; the agent discovers the skills and runs them ChatGPT Custom GPTs ChatGPT Someone builds a Custom GPT once from the files in the pack, then others use it

Agent skills give the full experience. When the tool can run commands, the script and plugin skills run profinity-script and profinity-component-pack themselves and read the output, and the skills reuse the MCP connection settings that Claude Code and Cursor already hold. Prohelion's setup guidance covers Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and ChatGPT, and other tools that load SKILL.md skills can use the agent skills without written guidance.

ChatGPT has more limits, because a Custom GPT has no shell and its connection is fixed when it is built. The dashboard, rules, collections, derived tag, and app GPTs can read and save through the REST API, but the script and plugin GPTs cannot, so they give you the commands to run yourself. Dashboards are written as YAML but the save endpoints accept only JSON, so the GPT converts the YAML and shows you the result first. To build a Custom GPT, refer to Install AI Skills.

docs.title: Install AI Skills
docs.text: Prohelion supplies AI Skills as profinity-ai-skills.zip with each Profinity release, and you install it into your AI tool with npx. Installing the skills with npx needs Node.js on your computer. Contact Prohelion for the zip that matches your release. For what the skills do and what they need once installed, refer to AI Skills and AI Skills reference.

docs.title: Install the agent skills
docs.text:
The zip has no wrapping folder, so create the destination folder when you extract.

Extract the zip into a folder, and point npx skills add at that folder:

unzip profinity-ai-skills.zip -d profinity-ai-skills
npx skills add ./profinity-ai-skills

On Windows, extract the zip with File Explorer or with Expand-Archive profinity-ai-skills.zip -DestinationPath profinity-ai-skills in PowerShell, then run the same npx skills add command. To see which skills the pack contains before installing, run npx skills add ./profinity-ai-skills --list.

After installation, the skills are available in your AI tool, and each skill's SKILL.md file gives step-by-step instructions, with API reference notes, examples, and schemas beside it in the skill's folder.

docs.title: Set up a ChatGPT Custom GPT
docs.text:
Profinity is deployed per customer, so there is no ready-made GPT to share. Whoever builds the GPT does a short one-time setup from the files in the pack, and others then use it:

  1. Paste the instructions.
  2. Upload the example files.
  3. Import the OpenAPI Actions file (the file that tells the GPT how to call the REST API) with your Profinity host in it.

For what a Custom GPT can and cannot do, refer to AI Skills reference.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
Release notes for Profinity V2 list the user-visible changes, what to do when upgrading, and the known issues that affect deployments.

  • Profinity 2.3.2 release notes: stale tags and quality in logs and history, component visibility, theme logos, and dashboard caption and chart colours.
  • Profinity 2.3 release notes: editions and licensing, Profinity AI, derived tags, publishers and subscribers, role-based access control (RBAC), single sign-on (SSO) and multi-factor authentication (MFA), mobile, Linux artefacts path, and known issues.
  • Profinity 2.3 breaking changes: what changes for existing installations, integrations, and plugins, including the security file format, licensing, REST API errors and data locations.
  • Profinity 2.2.5 release notes: data directory migration, installer alignment, stability, and validation improvements.

docs.title: Profinity 2.2.5 release notes
docs.text: The major change in this release is that the data folder moves from the Documents folder to the AppData folder on Windows, which improves reliability for users who have their home directory stored in OneDrive. The release also improves upgrade safety and reliability for desktop, Docker, and CAN adapter deployments, and surfaces dashboard and configuration errors earlier through stricter schema validation.

docs.title: Changes in this release
docs.text:
• Profinity's default artefacts directory moved to the operating system's application-data location, with automatic migration from the old locations.
  • Windows installer sample and profile content updated to match the new default location.
  • Improved reliability and diagnostics in the desktop application and for CAN adapter connections.
  • Stricter dashboard validation and updates to bundled dashboards and DBC (CAN database) handling.

docs.title: New default artefact location
docs.text: Profinity stores its artefacts in the operating system's local application data folder, under Prohelion/Profinity. This includes the Config/ and Profiles/ folders, logs, and other saved artefacts. Profinity 2.3 renames these folders to lowercase. Refer to the Profinity 2.3 release notes.

docs.title: Automatic migration from legacy locations
docs.text:
On startup, Profinity migrates an older Prohelion/Profinity folder into the new location when that folder contains Config/Config.yaml, moving or merging its files into the new location, depending on what the new location already holds.

Upgrade guidance:

  • If you have automation or backups that reference legacy paths (for example "Documents" or home-based paths), update them to the new location.
  • If you maintain custom profiles/config files, ensure you have a backup before upgrading.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: On Linux, Profinity 2.2.5 stores its data under $XDG_DATA_HOME when that variable is set and under $HOME/.local/share otherwise, so a root container with no overrides uses /root/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity/. Existing Docker Compose mounts that target /root/Prohelion/Profinity/... keep working in 2.2.5 when you set XDG_DATA_HOME=/root and keep your volume mappings. Profinity 2.3 on Linux ignores XDG_DATA_HOME and uses /var/lib/prohelion/profinity unless PROFINITY_HOME is set, so Docker users who move on to 2.3 should follow Upgrade from Profinity 2.2.

docs.title: Dashboards
docs.text:
• Dashboard examples and templates were refreshed to match the dashboard schema validation rules.
  • Validation of dashboards, schemas, and DBC files is stricter, so invalid content is reported when Profinity loads it rather than failing later at runtime.

If you maintain custom dashboards, validate them against the current schema and review any schema error messages during load.

docs.title: CAN and adapters
docs.text:
• Improved handling of connection edge cases including an adapter that is connected but sees no CAN traffic, which Profinity now reports as a warning rather than an error.
  • Virtual CAN adapters no longer try to connect when the required network capabilities are missing.
  • Ewert Energy CANdapter adapter reliability improvements:
  • Serial port selection is more reliable (handles COM port case differences such as com3 and COM3).
  • When no port is configured, Profinity scans the serial ports for a connected CANdapter for a limited time instead of failing with an unusable adapter.
  • When no device is detected, the settings page shows a warning and hides the empty fields until a CANdapter is available.
  • Improved error messages when the selected serial port is missing or invalid.

docs.title: Desktop GUI stability
docs.text: • Cleanup of the desktop application's embedded browser (WebView2) was hardened during reload and shutdown, which reduces the chance that shutdown is blocked.

docs.title: Battery Management Systems (BMS)
docs.text: • Updates across Prohelion D1000Gen1 BMS components and bundled DBC content to address issues found in the field, including engagement, heartbeat, and state machine improvements.

docs.title: Profinity 2.3 release notes
docs.text:
Profinity 2.3 introduces commercial editions with offline licensing, Profinity AI, derived tags, publishers and subscribers, role-based security with single sign-on and two-factor authentication, a visual dashboard editor, and the Profinity Mobile app. It also changes where Profinity stores data on Linux, how /api/v2 reports errors, and which features an instance without a licence can use. Anyone upgrading from 2.2 should read Upgrade from Profinity 2.2 and Profinity 2.3 breaking changes before they upgrade a production system. Changes after this release are in the Profinity 2.3.2 release notes.

This release is for operators, administrators, integrators, and OEMs who deploy Profinity on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Docker.

docs.title: Editions and licensing
docs.text: Profinity 2.3 limits commercial features by edition (Desktop, Server, and Enterprise) using a signed licence file that Profinity validates offline, with no activation service. An instance with no valid licence is unlicensed: it keeps the core product (the local web interface, the REST API, tags, dashboards, rules, device components, CAN utilities and file loggers) and loses the features that need an edition. A new installation that is not a Desktop host starts a one-time 14-day local trial with Server edition features (on builds that offer it), and drops to the unlicensed set when the trial ends. Remote web access, user and role administration, two-factor authentication, Profinity AI, the Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT rule actions and the data relay components need the Server edition, and single sign-on and SCIM provisioning need Enterprise. The ADMIN > License page shows the state, the edition, the machine fingerprint to send to Prohelion, and what each feature is blocked by. Refer to Licensing for the full feature table.

docs.title: Profinity AI
docs.text: Profinity AI adds a chat assistant inside the web interface that answers questions about a running instance by reading live tags, alert rules and alert history, and answers how-to questions from the Profinity documentation. An administrator configures one provider for the whole instance under ADMIN > System Configuration, and users with the Profinity AI permission open the chat from the Profinity AI entry in the side menu. The built-in MCP (Model Context Protocol) server lets other AI tools read the same data, and AI Skills packs help Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and ChatGPT build dashboards, rules, collections, derived tags and scripts against your instance. Profinity AI and the MCP server need the Server edition. Refer to Profinity AI, AI Skills, and MCP Server.

docs.title: Derived tags
docs.text: A derived tag is a tag whose value Profinity calculates from an expression over other tags. It appears in the tag tree and behaves like any other tag for dashboards, rules, history, and the API. Derived tags are created in the Derived Tags editor in the tag utilities menu, and are included in every edition. Refer to Derived Tags.

docs.title: Publishers and subscribers
docs.text: The MQTT Publisher and the new Webhook Publisher push the values of a tag collection to a broker or a URL, and the MQTT Subscriber receives Sparkplug B data into read-only tags. The MQTT Logger is now the MQTT Publisher, and the Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT rule actions send a message when a rule fires. These components need the Server edition. Refer to MQTT Publisher, Webhook Publisher, and MQTT Subscriber.

docs.title: Security and identity
docs.text: Profinity 2.3 replaces security groups with role-based access control (RBAC): each user is assigned roles, each role holds a list of the 27 available permissions, and changing a user's roles or a role's permissions revokes that user's active sessions. A site chooses one sign-in method, Local or SSO, and a Local site can require two-factor authentication for every local user, with recovery codes and an optional remember-this-device period. Administrators can reset another user's password or two-factor enrolment, and service accounts with long-lived tokens support automation and MCP. Component and collection visibility lets an administrator hide a component or tag collection from chosen roles, and the password policy and session policy are set under ADMIN > System Configuration. Firmware passcodes are no longer saved in the profile, and users enter them when they unlock a component's firmware. Refer to Roles and Permissions, SSO and Sign-In, and Component and Collection Security.

docs.title: Tags, rules, and alerts
docs.text: The tag layer adds the Tag Explorer for browsing the tag catalogue with quality indicators, visual editors for collections and rules, and an Alerts Log with Active and History tabs, live indicators on dashboards and in the Tag Explorer, and dwell and deadband evaluation. A rule can run a script on alert (C#, Python or Lua), and the script receives the tags that triggered the rule. Rule scripts and the Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT actions need the Server edition. Tag paths can now be absolute (starting with /) or relative to a component, and the Tag tree path setting mounts a component under a parent path. Refer to Tags, Alerts, and Tag Tree Path. Stale tags, quality in logs, and CAN Milliseconds Valid of -1 and 0 are in the Profinity 2.3.2 release notes.

docs.title: Components, plugins, and dashboards
docs.text:
The Plugin Manager under ADMIN > Components & Plugins uploads, enables, disables, and reloads external DLL plugins (.nupkg or zip). Custom Components support actions, firmware scripts and settings maps, and profinity-component-pack packs them for installation. The Dashboard component is a YAML-only profile component, and a menu layout editor places profiles and components in the side menu. The visual editor is now the main way to edit dashboards: add, arrange, and bind widgets in DESIGN mode, with the YAML tab as a fallback, and existing YAML dashboards keep working and open in the visual editor. Charts accept several data sources, and map bindings take latitude and longitude. Refer to Visual Editor, Components and Plugins, and Component Pack CLI.

Every component that holds a connection now starts even when the other end is down, shows Error with the reason in the log, and connects by itself when the broker, device, server, or database appears, including after a rejected login is corrected. Refer to Connections and Reconnecting.

docs.title: Installation and mobile
docs.text: Linux and macOS installs use a one-script installer (install.sh) and update.sh, with archives for each processor architecture, and Prohelion publishes a Docker image for linux/amd64, linux/arm64 and linux/arm/v7. On Linux the default data directory is now /var/lib/prohelion/profinity, and PROFINITY_HOME overrides it on every platform. Profinity Mobile for iOS and Android finds servers on the local network through a UDP heartbeat (port 49025 by default) and signs in with a password or a Kiosk Mode user. Refer to Linux and macOS Installation, Docker Installation, Artefacts Directory, and Profinity Mobile.

docs.title: Known issues
docs.text:
• Tag Relay shares live tags between Profinity instances and needs the Data Relay feature on both instances. It exports a sender's full tag tree with no field-level filtering, and a single path collision rejects the whole batch from that sender. Refer to Tag Relay.
  • Reciprocal tag linking, such as adding a rule from the collections editor context menu, is not available in 2.3, although the Tag Explorer context menu flows work.
  • Publishing plugins to a NuGet feed is not available in 2.3, so install a local .nupkg or zip through the Plugin Manager.
  • The central firmware updater is not part of 2.3. Each component flashes its own firmware.
  • Android emulators cannot receive local network UDP heartbeat broadcasts, so test mobile discovery on a physical device. Refer to Profinity Mobile.

docs.title: Profinity 2.3.2 release notes
docs.text:
Profinity 2.3.2 is the patch after Profinity 2.3.1. A tag that stops receiving data now shows as Stale and keeps its last value, logs and historians record that quality, and a component hidden from a role stays hidden on its page, its script log, its charge session, and its tag queries. Themes show the site logo in the side menu, a caption can take a status colour, and a chart can use a monochrome or categorical palette.

Read Upgrading from 2.3.1 before you upgrade a system that is already on 2.3.1. The Profinity 2.3 release notes and Profinity 2.3 breaking changes still describe the step from 2.2.

docs.title: Tags, rules, and history
docs.text:
A tag that stops receiving data shows as Stale with its last value, instead of reading as unavailable, and logs and rules can see the change. A derived tag takes the quality of its inputs by default, so a derived value built on a stale input is stale too. Set inputQuality: ignore on the derived tag when the output should stay Good regardless of the inputs. Refer to Derived Tags.

CAN Milliseconds Valid accepts -1 for traffic that never times out, and a value of 0 means nothing from that device is ever current. Batteries and chargers accept 1 to 60000 only. A frame for one multiplex group does not refresh a signal in another group, and each multiplexed signal expires from its own last frame. On a GStar GPS receiver, position, altitude, fix quality, speed, and heading go Stale about five seconds after the receiver goes quiet, and they keep the last value.

Because a timed-out CAN signal keeps its last value, tag.HasValue is still true for it. A rule or collection that means "has a current value" should use tag.HasValue && !tag.IsStale, and a "no data" rule should use !tag.HasValue || tag.IsStale. The sample endpoint returns the last value with quality Stale for such a signal, where it used to return not found.

Tag Change scripts run when a watched tag's value changes, not when only its quality changes. A tag removed from the tree is dropped from the rules engine. A rule that reads a tag's metadata is evaluated again when that definition changes and the value does not. Two rules cannot publish state to the same tag path: the rules file is rejected and the error names both rules. Each rule's state tag is written when the rules host starts, using the restored state, or false / -1 when there is none. Refer to Tags and Alerts.

Tags fed over Sparkplug or a tag relay become Stale when the connection is lost and recover when new data arrives. Tags for protocol points (S7, Modbus, EtherNet/IP, OPC UA and BACnet) become Stale when their connection closes, and a successful poll makes them Good again. An OPC UA client reading of Uncertain is stored as Stale with the last usable value. The OPC UA server reports a Stale tag with an uncertain status instead of good, and its RECEIVED and SENT counters count client requests and responses. The S7 Request timeout (ms) setting now bounds each read and each write. A register tag written by a script can set maxAgeMs in its metadata to go Stale when it is not written in time. Refer to S7 and OPC UA Server.

Loggers, historians, and the Webhook publisher record each sample with its quality. A Stale tag keeps its last value, and a tag that is Unavailable or Bad is recorded as a gap with no value. They no longer drop samples that were decoded more than a few seconds before the write. The MQTT publisher still sends good values only. InfluxDB v3 history queries skip points that have quality and no value, and the historian follows its health-check setting. Moving a component, including a change to its tag tree path, keeps that component's tags in the same logger and historian series. Refer to Tag file and SFTP loggers, InfluxDB historians, and Webhook Publisher.

File loggers, historians, publishers, and the other timed components share one interval setting, Update Interval (Seconds), from 1 to 86400. An Influx logger that was labelled Logging Interval (Sec) uses this name. The saved interval is unchanged.

docs.title: Component visibility and charging
docs.text:
A caller who cannot view a component gets the same result as for a component that is not there.

  • The component page returns 404.
  • The component's script log reads as empty, and clearing it does nothing.
  • MCP get_tag_series answers as a missing tag.
  • A wildcard DBC series query includes only components the caller can view.

A charge follows the charger and the battery on the session. A user who cannot view that equipment cannot set the charge up, start it, change the current or the target, or stop it, and the status reads as idle. Refer to Component and Collection Security.

docs.title: Dashboards and themes
docs.text:
The side menu shows the theme's main logo in place of the Profinity icon, and a themed sign-in logo is shown much larger than the default icon. Accordion tabs follow the theme colours. Refer to Themes and branding.

A caption's color is optional. It accepts red, green, amber or grey, the same colours as a lamp, and it can be bound to a tag. Any other value leaves the text in its normal colour. Refer to Caption.

A chart can set palette to mono or categorical. mono uses shades of the theme secondary colour, and categorical uses the chart categorical theme colours, so pie slices can be told apart without using the status colours. Leave palette out to keep that chart type's existing colours. A pie, doughnut, or polar area whose type is chosen in the visual editor starts on categorical. Refer to Charts.

docs.title: Sign-in, kiosk, and licensing
docs.text:
The desktop window signs in with a signed desktop-host claim and its own signing key, not by the username desktop. That name is no longer reserved, so a site can create a user called desktop.

The web client reads Kiosk Mode from kioskModeEnabled on the kiosk status response, so the sign-in page follows the profile setting. Refer to Kiosk Mode.

A local trial reports Expiring only in its last 7 days. For the rest of the 14 days it reports Trial. Refer to Licensing.

docs.title: CAN adapters
docs.text:
A PCAN or PCAN FD adapter that drops, goes bus-off, or loses its handle shows Error with the reason and connects again when the device returns. Discovery continues if listing attached channels fails. Refer to CAN bus adapters.

A Tritium adapter on protocol V2 accepts a bus number from 0 to 32767. Protocol V1 still accepts 0 to 13.

docs.title: Upgrading from 2.3.1
docs.text:
• Review rules and collections that treat tag.HasValue as "this signal is current". A stale CAN signal still has a value. Use tag.HasValue && !tag.IsStale for a current value.
  • CAN Milliseconds Valid of 0 means the device is never current. Use -1 when the signal should never time out. Batteries and chargers reject both 0 and -1.
  • A script saved with Milliseconds Valid 0 is loaded as 0. It is no longer treated as "never expires".
  • Tag Change scripts do not run when only the quality changes.
  • Log files, SQL history, Influx, and webhook payloads now include quality. Unavailable and Bad samples are gaps with no value. A consumer that assumed every row had a value needs to allow a gap.
  • Two rules that publish state to the same tag path cause the rules file to be rejected. Give each rule its own state tag path.
  • Users who were kept out of a component by role can no longer open its page, read its script log, query its tags, or operate a charge on that equipment. Confirm that charging operators can view the charger and the battery they are meant to run.
  • The desktop sign-in no longer depends on a user named desktop. A local account with that name is an ordinary user.

docs.title: Profinity 2.3 breaking changes
docs.text: These changes in Profinity 2.3 can affect an installation, integration, or plugin that works on 2.2. Read them with Upgrade from Profinity 2.2 before you upgrade a production system, and refer to the Profinity 2.3 release notes for the new features and known issues. If you already run 2.3.1, read the Profinity 2.3.2 release notes for the changes in that patch.

docs.title: Security file format
docs.text:
All installations that upgrade from 2.2 are affected. Security groups are removed: users receive assigned roles, and each role holds a list of permissions. Profinity migrates security.yaml automatically when it loads the file and writes version: "2.3" back. The default Administrators role holds every permission, including MCP integration.

Hand-edited security.yaml files, such as those kept in source control, need the new keys. On disk the keys are camelCase: securityGroups becomes roles, a user's securityGroups becomes assignedRoles, a group's securityRoles becomes the role's permissions, and Version becomes version: "2.3". Check that roles and assignedRoles are present before you start Profinity, and review role assignments afterwards. Refer to Roles and Permissions.

docs.title: Settings in config.yaml
docs.text: Administrators who configured OIDC single sign-on, SCIM provisioning or SIEM export in security.yaml now set them in config.yaml, under ADMIN > System Configuration in the Security section. security.yaml keeps users, roles, two-factor secrets and external identity links. Saving System Configuration restarts Profinity.

docs.title: Site sign-in method
docs.text: The per-user sign-in mode and the per-role two-factor setting are replaced by one site policy: an administrator chooses Local or SSO, and on a Local site can require two-factor authentication for every local user. SSO users sign in through the identity provider and link their account under External identities (SSO) in user settings. A site cannot mix Local and SSO sign-in. Refer to SSO and Sign-In.

docs.title: Licensing
docs.text: Features that were available without limit in 2.2 now depend on the edition (refer to Editions and licensing). A 2.2 installation without a licence file loses remote web access, users and roles, two-factor authentication, Profinity AI, scripting, the InfluxDB v2, InfluxDB v3 and TAG SQL historians, themes, and the Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT rule actions and rule scripts that run on alert. Upload a licence before you upgrade a production system that relies on any of them.

docs.title: REST API errors
docs.text: Every /api/v2 endpoint now reports failure with the HTTP status code and an RFC 7807 application/problem+json body, and no longer returns 200 OK with {"success": false}. Validation failures on settings return 422 or 400 with an errors object whose keys are dotted setting paths, creating a resource returns 201 Created with a Location header, and deleting one returns 204 No Content with no body. The users and roles endpoints return a fixed set of fields rather than the whole stored user or role. Integrations that read a success flag or a message field from the response body must read the status code and the problem body instead. SCIM keeps its own RFC 7644 error format, and the MCP tools are unchanged. The older data endpoints are no longer available under /api/v2, so integrations that call them must move to the tag, collection, rule, and alert endpoints. Refer to REST APIs.

docs.title: Data locations
docs.text: Linux moves from ~/.local/share/Prohelion/Profinity to /var/lib/prohelion/profinity. Windows stays at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Prohelion\Profinity and macOS stays at ~/Library/Application Support/Prohelion/Profinity, and on those platforms Profinity also moves data from ~/Documents/Prohelion/Profinity, ~/Prohelion/Profinity and the opposite-casing folder under the application-data location. Update backups, automation, and Docker volume mounts that refer to the old Linux path. Refer to Artefacts Directory.

docs.title: YAML documents
docs.text: Profinity writes every YAML document it owns with camelCase keys, lowercase file and folder names, and version: "2.3". Older PascalCase files still load. Profinity rewrites an older security.yaml, profile.yaml, config.yaml, theme.yaml or plugins.yaml in the new format when it loads it, and rewrites other documents when it saves them, so only tooling that reads these files directly needs to change. Re-save collections and rules in the visual editors after the upgrade if you edit their YAML by hand. The {COMPONENT_NAME} placeholder in dashboards still loads and is saved as a relative or absolute tag path the next time the dashboard is saved.

docs.title: Firmware passcodes
docs.text: Gen2 battery management systems no longer keep the firmware configuration key or setup passcodes in the profile. Users enter them in the component's settings dialog, and Profinity holds them only for that sign-in session, so anything that relied on a stored passcode must be unlocked again after each sign-in.

docs.title: BACnet device instance
docs.text: The BACnet component now reads the Device object of the device at its Remote host and compares the instance with Device instance, and it does not connect to, or read any point of, a device that reports a different number: the component shows Error with the reason and retries. A BACnet component that left Device instance at its default of 0 stops reading points until the setting is changed to the real instance of the device. The allowed range is now 0 to 4194302. Refer to BACnet.

docs.title: Auto Connect replaces Auto Start
docs.text: The setting that connects a component when the profile loads is now called Auto Connect on every component that holds a connection. Loggers, historians, publishers, the Tag Relay sender and the OPC UA server previously called it Auto Start, and the old setting is no longer read, so a profile that turned Auto Start off must have Auto Connect turned off. The MQTT Subscriber and Tag Relay receiver gain Auto Connect, on by default, and a Connect / Disconnect switch. Script components keep Auto Start Script.

docs.title: Connections start in Error instead of failing
docs.text: A component that connects to a broker, device, server, or database no longer refuses to start when the other end is unavailable. It starts, shows Error, and retries every 5 seconds, or at its own reconnect setting. A component that used to show Off after a failed start now shows Error, and anything that relied on a start failure to detect a missing device should watch the status instead. The MQTT and Tag Relay subscribers retry at a steady interval instead of backing off to 60 seconds. For plugin authors, ManagedConnection in Profinity.Sdk replaces the need for a plugin to keep its own reconnect scheduler, and PolledDeviceController<TPoint> in Profinity.Sdk.Components provides the whole connect, poll, sample, and write lifecycle for a device that is read by polling, so a protocol plugin supplies only how to open its transport and read and write one point. Refer to Connections and Reconnecting.

docs.title: Default series window is now ten minutes
docs.text: DataSource.DefaultLocalSeriesTimeRangeStart in the plugin SDK changed from -5m to -10m, so a data source that asks for a local series without its own range now starts ten minutes back. The value is a compile-time constant, so a plugin built against an earlier SDK keeps -5m until you rebuild it against the 2.3 SDK.

docs.title: Windows install with a Server licence accepts remote connections
docs.text: A Windows installation, including the Windows service that ProfinityService.cmd registers, used to serve its web interface to the local computer only, whatever licence it held. With a Server licence it now uses the address configured under Profinity Web, and it creates the default admin account (password change required at first sign-in) so people on other computers can sign in. Without a Server licence nothing changes. The built-in sign-in used by the application window is refused when it arrives from another computer. An engine restart, for example after you apply a licence, now keeps a desktop installation a desktop installation, where before it started behaving as a server host.

docs.title: OPC UA server listens on this computer only by default
docs.text: The OPC UA server now listens on 127.0.0.1 only unless you give it another address. An earlier build listened on every network interface by default while the documentation said localhost only, and the server uses no security policy and accepts anonymous clients. A Bind URL saved as 0.0.0.0 or localhost is treated as 127.0.0.1. If other computers connect to your OPC UA server, set the Bind URL to the IP address or host name of the Profinity computer, such as opc.tcp://192.168.1.20:4840/Profinity.

docs.title: Tag layer
docs.text:
The tag layer is Profinity's catalogue of live and configured tag values, and it is the foundation for Tag Explorer, collections, rules, and alerts, which are new in Profinity 2.3. Open TAG EXPLORER from the side menu, which requires the View tags permission, to browse the tag tree, switch to table views where available, and inspect the data quality indicator on each tag. Stale quality has its own icon, separate from the rule alert triangle. The TAG UTILITIES group in the side menu appears for users with the View tags permission. The collections and derived tags editors also need a loaded profile, and saving needs Modify tag collections for collections and derived tags, or Modify tag rules for rules.

A tag combines an address, value, quality flag and metadata

To start a collection, a rule, or a dashboard binding from tags selected in Tag Explorer, refer to Create collections, rules, and dashboard bindings from tags.

docs.title: Selecting tags
docs.text:
• Selecting tags: how a tag's path in the tree and the expression language work together to pick tags.
  • Tag tree paths and dashboard binds: how nesting a component in a folder of the tag tree affects scopes and binds.
  • Nest a component in the tag tree: mount a component inside a folder of the tag tree.
  • Tag expressions: the expression language shared by collections, rules, and derived tags.

docs.title: Tag collections
docs.text:
• Tag collections: group tags with a membership expression. Open COLLECTIONS under TAG UTILITIES, which opens an editor window and requires View tag collections.
  • Create a collection: build a restricted collection of cell voltages in the collections editor.

docs.title: Derived tags
docs.text:
• Derived tags: compute a tag from other tags. Open DERIVED TAGS under TAG UTILITIES, which opens an editor window and requires View tag collections.
  • Create a derived tag: convert speed from mph to km/h with an expression.
  • Create a derived tag with a script: publish a derived tag from a script.

docs.title: Tag rules
docs.text:
• Tag rules: evaluate tags and raise alerts. Open RULES & ACTIONS under TAG UTILITIES, which opens an editor window and requires View tag rules.
  • Create a rule: raise an alert when a battery pack temperature goes above a limit.
  • Complete rules.yaml example: read a full rules file with every setting explained.

docs.title: Rule actions
docs.text:
• Rule actions: choose what a rule does when it fires.
  • Email and Slack rule actions: settings for the Email and Slack notification actions.
  • Webhook and MQTT rule actions: settings for the Webhook and MQTT notification actions.

docs.title: Tag logs
docs.text:
• Tag logs: record tag values to a file and replay them onto live tags.
  • Log tags to a file: record tag values to a file with the TAG File Logger.
  • Replay a tag log: play a recording back onto your live tags from TAG LOG REPLAY under TAG UTILITIES, which requires Replay tag changes.

docs.title: Alerts and relay
docs.text:
• Alerts Log: review, acknowledge, and silence alerts. Open ALL ALERTS in the side menu, which requires View alerts.
  • Tag relay: share live tags between Profinity instances. One instance publishes periodic snapshots of selected collections, and another ingests them as remote, read-only tags under that site's own prefix.

Integrations can work with tags, tag collections, tag rules and alerts through the Representational State Transfer (REST) API under /api/v2. The Swagger page on your Profinity instance lists every endpoint and the parameters it accepts. The older data endpoint is not part of /api/v2, so use the tag endpoints for new integrations. All endpoints require the appropriate permissions, which are listed in Roles and permissions.

docs.title: Alerts Log
docs.text:
Profinity 2.3 surfaces rule-generated alerts in the Alerts Log, in live indicators across the UI, and through the API. Operators with the View alerts permission can view and acknowledge alerts and silence their actions, and an alert's text, level, and links come from the rule that raised it.

Alerts Log with Active and History tabs and the alert detail panel

docs.title: Open Alerts Log
docs.text:
Select ALL ALERTS in the side menu to open the Alerts Log, which shows the page heading ALERTS.

ALL ALERTS in the side menu

docs.title: Active and history tabs
docs.text:
The Active tab shows rule alerts currently firing, and the History tab shows a paginated history, newest first. Both tabs show the time (labelled Active Time on the Active tab, which is when the current episode began), the component, the rule, the level, the status and an actions column. Each row has a More info button that opens a detail dialog with the alert's message, tag, time, and status, followed by any relatedTags of the rule under RELATED TAGS, then the rule's description, which supports Markdown, and any moreInformation links under DOCUMENTATION. Both tabs can be filtered by level, the Active tab can also be filtered by acknowledgement status, and the History tab has a date range. Tables show 25, 50, 75 or 100 rows per page, and 25 by default.

Active alerts table

Alert history

docs.title: Alert levels
docs.text:
Set level on a rule, or on each threshold step, to classify alert severity, and the Alerts Log and the alert indicators combine the active rule state with that level.

The valid levels, from least to most severe, are Trace, Debug, Info, Warning, Error and Fatal. Level names are not case-sensitive, Information is accepted as Info and Warn as Warning, and a rule with no level is treated as Info. An unrecognised level on a rule, threshold step or triggerLevel stops the rules file loading and names the rule that holds it, so correct the spelling and save again. The same names are used as the triggerLevel of an action configured on a parent rule file or group.

A script receives the level as the string RuleLevel. The Webhook and MQTT JSON message has no level field, so add {RuleLevel} to the rule message if a receiver needs it. The level filter on the Active and History queries is not case-sensitive.

docs.title: Live indicators
docs.text:
The web client polls active alerts every four seconds and shows a yellow alert triangle at the bottom right of any dashboard widget bound to an alerting tag, an alert icon on tags in Tag Explorer that have an active alert, and a highlighted ALL ALERTS entry in the side menu while any alert is active. Hovering over an indicator shows a summary of the alert, and selecting it opens the Alerts Log when the user holds the View alerts permission. Stale data quality in Tag Explorer has its own icon, distinct from the alert triangle, so when both appear they indicate different conditions.

Dashboard alert indicator on a bound widget

Rule alert on a tag in Tag Explorer

docs.title: Acknowledge and silence
docs.text:
Acknowledging and silencing both need the View alerts permission, and both act on an alert that is currently active. Acknowledge marks the alert as seen and handled, and does not clear it. Silence suppresses the actions of the rule for that alert, so no Email, Slack, Webhook, MQTT, script, or log action runs, while the alert stays active and visible with a silence badge. Silence lasts one hour, and a silence expired entry then appears in the history. Actions that would have run during the hour are skipped, not queued or replayed, so actions run again only the next time the rule fires or clears. The silence lasts the full hour even if the alert clears first, so clear actions that fall inside the hour are skipped as well, and a new occurrence of the same alert inside the hour is still silenced.

The Acknowledge alert button and the Silence alert for 1 hour button sit in the actions column of the Active tab, and an acknowledged alert shows an Unacknowledge alert button in place of Acknowledge.

How a rule is evaluated, including dwell, deadband, and the evaluation tick, is described under Rule evaluation: dwell and deadband. The expression language is described in Tag expressions, and the actions a rule runs are described in Rules and Actions. For the rest of the tag layer, refer to Tag layer, Collections, and Roles and permissions.

docs.title: Create collections, rules, and dashboard bindings from tags
docs.text:
The Tag Explorer context menu creates collections, rules, and dashboard bindings from selected tags, so the selection does not need to be copied into the visual editors by hand. Tag Explorer itself requires the View tags permission. Each context menu action then checks its own permission, and an action whose permission is missing is shown disabled, while the whole menu is hidden from a user who holds none of these permissions. The permission for each action is listed under Menu actions.

To create one from selected tags:

  1. Open TAG EXPLORER from the side menu.
  2. Right-click a leaf tag or a branch to open the context menu. Several leaf tags and branches can be selected together, and the menu actions table shows which actions each kind of selection allows.
  3. Choose an action from the menu.
  4. Complete the configuration in the visual editor and save it.

Tag Explorer context menu

docs.title: Menu actions
docs.text:
Action Scope Permission Add tag(s) to dashboard… Leaf tags only Modify dashboards Create collection from tag(s)… Branch, leaf, or root Modify tag collections Create rule from tag(s)… Selected tags Modify tag rules Rules on this Tag Selected tags View tag rules Rules impacted by this tag Selected tags View tag rules

Selecting Add tag(s) to dashboard… opens a dashboard picker and creates a binding draft, and completing the bind still requires the dashboard editor. Selecting Create collection from tag(s)… opens a submenu for the primary filter (Branch, Meta type, Unit, Value or Quality), then an insert-location picker, and then the collections visual editor with a draft collection. Selecting Create rule from tag(s)… opens an insert-location picker and then the rules visual editor with a draft rule. Rules on this Tag lists the rules that reference the selection and opens the rules editor on the chosen rule source. Rules impacted by this tag lists the rules affected by the selection and opens the rules editor with that rule selected. Both list each matching rule as the rule source followed by a colon and the rule name, and show a disabled No matching rules entry when nothing matches, so they are the check in Tag Explorer that a rule is attached to a tag. These actions open the editor with a draft, and nothing is created until you save it in the editor.

Rules can also be started from two other places. Right-clicking a dashboard element that is bound to tags offers Create rule from this element…, and right-clicking a collection in the collections editor offers Create rule from collection….

docs.title: Expressions the menu generates
docs.text:
The create-collection and create-rule flows generate the expressions automatically. A selection of leaf tags becomes a set of tag.Is("…") matches. A single selected branch becomes a scope prefix with the expression tag.HasValue. Several selected branches become tag.MatchesPath("…") matches joined with || and combined with tag.HasValue. For collections, a primary filter other than Branch replaces this with an expression built from the selected tags' metadata type, unit, value, or quality. Refer to Tag expressions for the syntax.

For the next step, refer to Collections, Rules, and Actions, the Dashboard visual editor, or the Tag layer overview.

docs.title: Tag relay
docs.text:
Tag relay shares live tag data between two Profinity instances. One instance runs as a sender, publishing periodic snapshots of the tag collections it is set to export, and another runs as a receiver, ingesting those snapshots as remote, read-only tags under a prefix that identifies where they came from. It supports a fleet or head-office view spanning multiple sites, vehicles, or installations. Tag relay requires the Data Relay licensed feature on both the sending and receiving instance, and Licensing shows whether it is licensed and available on a given instance. Tag relay has no field-level filtering: a sender exports every tag that belongs to its selected collections, so create a collection that contains only the tags a receiver should see.

Each site runs its own tag pipeline, and relay adds a shared view at the central instance

Tag relay is Profinity-to-Profinity only, over its own snapshot format, and it does not speak Sparkplug. If the other end is a third-party Sparkplug B source, such as an edge gateway or a platform such as Ignition, rather than another Profinity instance, use the MQTT Subscriber instead. Refer to that page's own note for the reverse comparison.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Sender and receiver roles, with per-site tag prefixes on the receiving instance

A Profinity instance with a Tag Relay Sender component exports the member tags of the collections selected in the sender and sends them as a complete snapshot at a fixed interval, which defaults to 60 seconds. The receiver therefore always holds the values from the most recent snapshot rather than a stream of individual changes, and tags outside the selected collections are never sent. A Tag Relay Receiver component connects to one or more senders and mounts each sender's tags under a prefix that identifies that site, for example SiteA/…, so a single receiving instance can ingest many senders without their tag trees colliding. A sender is reached over HTTPS with a JSON Web Token (JWT) or over MQTT, and the choice is made per sender.

Relayed tags on the receiver are read-only, so the receiving instance cannot write back to a site through relay. Local tags, collections, rules, and alerts on the receiver can reference relayed tags the same way they reference any other tag.

docs.title: Collision rules
docs.text:
The receiver checks a whole snapshot against its live tag tree before it changes anything, and a single collision rejects the entire snapshot so that nothing is partially applied. A snapshot is rejected whole, with no tags created or updated, when any item in it meets one of these conditions:

  • The path is already occupied by a tag that did not come from relay, such as a local device tag, a script register or a derived tag.
  • A tag that came from relay already exists as a leaf where the snapshot needs a branch, or as a branch where the snapshot needs a leaf.
  • The snapshot itself asks for both a branch and a leaf at the same path.

A relayed leaf that already exists where the snapshot carries a leaf is not a collision, and its sample is updated. A path occupied by a tag that did not come from relay is never skipped on its own while the rest of the snapshot is applied.

docs.title: Troubleshooting a sender that stops updating
docs.text:
When the tags from one sender stop updating on the receiver, a path in that sender's latest snapshot clashes with a tag already on the receiver, and the receiver rejects the whole snapshot. Over HTTPS the sender receives a 409 Conflict response carrying the reason, and a malformed snapshot, for example an unsupported relay version, receives 400 Bad Request. Over MQTT the receiver writes a warning to the Profinity log and discards the snapshot. Remove the local tag that occupies the path or change the receiver prefix, and the next snapshot from that sender is accepted.

For the settings of each role, refer to Tag Relay Sender and Tag Relay Receiver. Refer to Roles and permissions for the permissions involved, and to the Tag layer overview for the rest of the tag pipeline.

docs.title: Tag collections
docs.text:
Collections group tags for filtering, dashboards, and rules. You build and manage them in the visual editor, and Create a collection walks through an example.

A collection matching tags in the tree by membership expression and scope

docs.title: Open the collections editor
docs.text:
Select COLLECTIONS under TAG UTILITIES in the side menu, which opens the collections editor as a window over the current page. The entry appears for users who hold the View tags and View tag collections permissions while a profile is loaded, and saving needs the Modify tag collections permission.

Collections visual editor

docs.title: Groups and collections
docs.text: The editor shows your collections as a tree on one side and the settings of the selected item on the other. A group organises collections into a hierarchy and passes its scope down to every collection inside it. A collection selects tags with a membership expression.

docs.title: Names and scope
docs.text:
Give each collection a display name, which you can change at any time. Rules refer to a collection by its identifier, which stays the same when you rename it, so rules keep working after a rename. Do not change an id in the YAML, because Profinity treats a changed id as a different collection and rules that use the old id stop resolving.

The Scope prefix, shown under Binding, limits a collection to the tags beneath a path in the tag tree. A scope on a collection is added to the scope of its group, so a group scoped to Vehicles/Car1 and a collection scoped to Battery together cover Vehicles/Car1/Battery. To ignore the group's scope, start the collection's scope with /.

docs.title: Saving and security
docs.text: A collection needs a display name and an expression before it can be saved. A user who holds the Security administration permission can also limit who sees a collection, by choosing Restricted and listing the roles that are allowed to use it. The built-in (All Tags) collection is read-only.

docs.title: Membership expression
docs.text:
Each collection filters candidate tags with a boolean expression over tag. The guided builder emits the published spellings, and free text uses the same language.

Examples:

tag.MatchesPath("Elmar Solar MPPT") && tag.MatchesName("OutputCurrent")
tag.Meta.Type == "dbc.signal" && tag.HasValue
tag.Value > 0

tag.HasValue is true for a stale tag as well as a good one. To keep only tags with a current value, use tag.HasValue && !tag.IsStale. A logger or publisher re-checks which tags match its collection once per interval, so a filter on staleness is approximate by up to one interval.

The full expression vocabulary, covering path matching, values, metadata and wildcards, is described in Tag expressions. For the rest of the tag layer, refer to Tag layer, Alerts Log and Derived tags. Integrators can use the Endpoint reference.

docs.title: Create a collection
docs.text:
This procedure gives the engineers on Car 1 a collection of its cell voltages that nobody else can see. Open the collections editor first, as described in Tag collections, which lists the permissions it needs. Choosing Restricted also needs the Security administration permission, as described under Saving and security.

  1. Create a group called Car 1 with the scope Vehicles/Car1.
  2. Inside it, create a collection with the Display name Cell voltages and the scope Battery.
  3. Set its expression to tag.Meta.Type == "dbc.signal" && tag.MatchesName("*Voltage") && tag.HasValue.
  4. Set its security to Restricted, and allow the Engineers role.

The collection now selects every cell voltage signal under Vehicles/Car1/Battery, and it appears in the collection picker of Tag Explorer under its display name. The editor generates the collection id itself (Collection1, Collection2, and so on), and the Collection id field is read-only, so the id is not taken from the name. Rules refer to the collection by its id, not its display name. A rule can use it, as in the cell_over_voltage rule in Complete rules.yaml example, which uses the id shown in the editor.

You can also start a collection from the Tag Explorer context menu with Create collection from tag(s)…, as described in Create collections, rules, and dashboard bindings from tags, and start a rule by right-clicking a collection in the editor and choosing Create rule from collection….

docs.title: Derived tags
docs.text:
A derived tag, also called a virtual tag, is a value that Profinity computes automatically and that then behaves exactly like a real tag to every consumer. Dashboards, the historian, rules, and the API all see the same quality and timestamp envelope and can subscribe to it the same way, so the computation is configured once and Profinity keeps it current. Profinity 2.3 computes a derived tag's value either from an expression, which recomputes whenever a source tag changes and needs no scripting, or from a script, which suits a computation that needs more than a single expression, and the table under Expression vs script shows which one fits a given case.

flowchart LR
    Source["Source tags"] --> Calc["Expression or script"] --> Derived["Derived tag"] --> Consumers["Dashboards, historian, rules, API"]
Profinity computes a derived tag from source tags with an expression or a script, and dashboards, the historian, rules and the API then use it like any other tag

docs.title: Open the derived tags editor
docs.text:
Select DERIVED TAGS under TAG UTILITIES in the side menu, which opens the editor as a window over the current page and needs the View tag collections permission and a loaded profile. The file the editor works on is named by the Derived tags YAML file (Optional) setting in the Tags category of the profile settings. Derived tags are organised into groups in a tree on the left of the editor, and selecting a group or derived tag opens its settings in an inspector on the right.

Derived Tags editor

docs.title: Expression-based derived tags
docs.text:
An expression-based derived tag names one or more dependencies, which are short aliases mapped to source tag paths, and a formula that combines them, and it recomputes the moment any dependency changes. To create one, refer to Create a derived tag. Groups exist only for organisation, and a group can set a mount path: a derived tag with a relative mount path mounts underneath its group's mount path, a derived tag that gives its own absolute path mounts there instead, and a nested group's mount path narrows further under its parent's.

Each alias exposes only the reading members (Value, Text, Bool, HasValue, Quality and IsStale), and path methods such as MatchesPath belong in collections and rules, as described in Tag expressions. An expression can be up to 4096 characters long.

docs.title: Quality of a derived tag
docs.text: A derived tag is only as trustworthy as its inputs, so by default its quality is the worst of its dependencies' qualities, from best to worst Good, Stale, Unavailable, and Bad. A derived tag built on a stale input is therefore stale (it still computes from the input's last value), and one built on an input with no value is unavailable. To handle missing inputs yourself, for example with a.HasValue, set inputQuality: ignore on the derived tag in the YAML; it then evaluates whatever the input quality, and is Good when the expression succeeds. The default is inputQuality: propagate.

docs.title: Deleting a derived tag that others depend on
docs.text: If another derived tag lists the tag being deleted under its dependencies, the editor names those derived tags and asks for confirmation before the delete goes through. Rule expressions are not checked.

docs.title: Expression vs script
docs.text:
When one expression is not enough, for example because the computation has several steps, carries state between runs or publishes several tags, write it as a script instead, as described in Create a derived tag with a script.

Use an expression when... Use a script when... The computation is simple real-time maths, a unit conversion, or combining a handful of tags The logic needs multiple steps, branching, or state carried between runs You want automatic history with no extra setup You need a timed or on-demand trigger rather than pure tag-change reactivity You want to populate several tags from one computation

A rule can publish its own current state to a tag, as described under Rule state publishing.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
The derived tags editor uses the same permission pair as collections: reading needs View tag collections and saving needs Modify tag collections. Refer to Roles and permissions for how permissions are granted. Integrators can also use the API.

For the rest of the tag layer, refer to Tag layer, Collections, and Script Types.

docs.title: Create a derived tag
docs.text:
This procedure creates a derived tag that converts a vehicle's speed from mph to km/h, grouped under that vehicle. Open the derived tags editor first, as described in Derived tags, which lists the permissions it needs.

  1. Create a group called Vehicle unit conversions with the mount path Vehicles/Car1.
  2. Inside it, create a derived tag with the mount path SpeedKmh. Because the path is relative, it mounts beneath the group's mount path.
  3. Add a dependency with the alias a that points at the tag Vehicles/Car1/SpeedMph.
  4. Set the expression to a.Value * 1.60934.

When you save, the editor shows "Derived tags saved", and a failed save shows "Save failed:" followed by the validation error. Vehicles/Car1/SpeedKmh is now a real tag that shows up in Tag Explorer at its mount path and in the rules engine, and history is available for it without further configuration.

Derived tag inspector with live preview

For the formula rules, refer to Expression-based derived tags. When the computation needs more than one expression, refer to Create a derived tag with a script.

docs.title: Create a derived tag with a script
docs.text:
A computation that does not fit one expression, such as multiple steps, state carried between runs, or publishing several tags from one computation, is written as a script instead of an expression-based derived tag.

Licence required

A derived tag computed by a script needs the Scripting licensed feature, included from the Desktop edition upward, and scripting enabled in Application Config. Expression-based derived tags work on every edition.

To set one up:

  1. Add a CSharp Script, Python Script or Lua Script component, or use an existing one.
  2. Set its mode to Run On Tag Change.
  3. Select the source tags in its Collections setting, as described in Script Types.
  4. In the script, publish the computed result with Profinity.Tags.SetValue(...).

Tag paths passed to Profinity.Tags are relative to the script's own host component, so a script is naturally suited to computing a derived value from, and publishing back to, tags on the same component. A path with a leading / starts at the root of the tag tree instead, which reaches tags on other components (refer to Tags in scripts).

C#PythonLua 
using Profinity.Sdk.Abstractions.Scripting;
using Profinity.Sdk.Models.Tags;

public class CSharpDerivedTagExample : ProfinityScript, IProfinityTagChangeScript
{
    private const string SourceTagPath = "SpeedMph";
    private const string PublishedTagPath = "SpeedKmh";

    public void OnTagChange(string tagId, DataTagSample sample)
    {
        if (!tagId.EndsWith(SourceTagPath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))
        {
            return;
        }

        double speedMph = Convert.ToDouble(sample.Value);
        double speedKmh = speedMph * 1.60934;

        Profinity.Tags.SetValue(PublishedTagPath, speedKmh);
    }
}

SOURCE_TAG_PATH = "SpeedMph"
PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH = "SpeedKmh"

def on_tag_change(tagId, sample):
    if not str(tagId).lower().endswith(SOURCE_TAG_PATH.lower()):
        return

    speed_mph = float(sample.Value)
    speed_kmh = speed_mph * 1.60934

    Profinity.Tags.SetValue(PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH, speed_kmh)

local SOURCE_TAG_PATH = 'SpeedMph'
local PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH = 'SpeedKmh'

function on_tag_change(tagId, sample)
    if not tostring(tagId):lower():find(SOURCE_TAG_PATH:lower() .. '$') then
        return
    end

    local speedMph = tonumber(sample.Value)
    local speedKmh = speedMph * 1.60934

    Profinity.Tags:SetValue(PUBLISHED_TAG_PATH, speedKmh)
end

Profinity offers a full starter template for each language when you create a script of that type.

Reading the published tag returns the last value the script published, and a read never re-runs the script. If nothing has triggered the script yet, the tag has no value rather than a freshly computed one.

Other trigger modes are available too, namely Run On Time Interval, Run On CRON Schedule and Run as Service, for a computation that is not purely reactive to a tag change. Refer to Script Types for each mode. For the expression-based alternative, refer to Create a derived tag and Tag expressions.

docs.title: Tag rules
docs.text:
A tag rule watches the tags in its scope and, when its condition changes, records an alert in the Alerts Log and runs the actions attached to it. This page covers writing rules, Create a rule walks through an example, and Complete rules.yaml example shows a full rules.yaml with every setting in one place. The Rule actions page covers the actions that a rule can run, such as Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT.

Licence required

Rules and the Alerts Log work on every edition. Without the Tag Rule Actions licensed feature a rule still evaluates and the alert is still recorded, and only the Email, Slack, Webhook, MQTT, and script actions are skipped. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

docs.title: Rules visual editor
docs.text:
Select RULES & ACTIONS under TAG UTILITIES in the side menu, which needs the View tag rules permission, or choose Edit Rules on a component that ships default rules, such as the Elmar MPPT and the C48 Gen2. The editor lists the profile's rules first and then each component's rules, and shows every rule with its level, scope, thresholds, and actions.

Rules visual editor with an expanded rule

The editor writes the same rules.yaml document that can be edited directly, and it exposes the settings that control how a rule is evaluated: Rule level and Rule type for each rule, Dwell seconds, Throttle minutes and the More information links, and the Evaluation tick (seconds) on the rules source. The valid alert levels, their aliases and the default are described under Alert levels. Each rule also has a description that the Alerts Log shows to the operator, and a condition written in the tag expression language, for example tag.Value > 4.2 to trip with tag.Value < 4.0 to clear, or tag.IsStale for a sensor that has stopped reporting.

Setting Publish state tag path on a rule, in its Rule State group, mirrors the rule's current state to a read-only tag, as described under Rule state publishing.

docs.title: Rule state publishing
docs.text:
A rule can publish its own current state to a tag. Set Publish state tag path in the Rule State group of a rule in the Rules editor, and Profinity mirrors the rule's state to that tag path whenever it changes: a boolean rule publishes true or false, and a threshold rule publishes the zero-based index of its active step, or -1 when no step is active. The tag is read-only, so only the rule can write to it. When the rules load, the tag takes the state the rule last had, which Profinity restores from the alert log, or false (-1 for a threshold rule) when the rule has no history, and it then changes whenever the rule changes state.

A rule has a single state tag even when its scope matches many tags, so every matching tag writes to the same state tag and the value shown is that of whichever matching tag changed state most recently, not a summary of all of them. Where the state of each tag matters, define one rule per tag, each with its own Publish state tag path, and do not give two rules the same path, because Profinity does not load the rules when two of them share a path, and the error names both rules. Refer to Rule actions for the actions a rule runs.

docs.title: Rule evaluation: dwell and deadband
docs.text:
Dwell, deadband and severity levels on a rule

Rules support dwell, where the condition must hold for a duration set with dwellSeconds or dwellMinutes, and deadband, where the alert clears at a different point from where it tripped, set on a threshold step with clearValue or clearExpression and on a boolean rule with clearExpression. Both are configured in the rules visual editor or in rules.yaml, and a complete example of each is shown in Complete rules.yaml example.

The Evaluation tick (seconds) setting, evaluationTickSeconds in YAML, takes a whole number from 1 to 3600. Rules evaluate whenever a tag in their scope changes, and the tick adds a periodic extra pass, which is the only way a tag.IsStale rule can fire for a tag that has stopped changing. When several rules files set a tick, the smallest value applies to the whole profile, so a low value in one file changes the evaluation cadence of every file. A rule that tests for stale or missing data needs the tick to be set in at least one loaded rules file.

Conditions use the same tag expression language as collections, so a numeric trip and clear pair is written as follows:

tag.Value > 4.2
tag.Value < 4.0

A no-data or stale sensor condition is written as follows, where a tag that has never had a value is caught by !tag.HasValue:

!tag.HasValue || tag.IsStale

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Task Permission View rules View tag rules Edit rules Modify tag rules View alerts View alerts

For the rest of the tag layer, refer to Tag expressions, Collections, Derived tags and Tag layer.

docs.title: Create a rule
docs.text:
This procedure creates a threshold rule that raises a Warning alert when a pack temperature goes above 45 °C and a Fatal alert above 55 °C. Opening the rules editor needs the View tag rules permission, and saving needs Modify tag rules, as listed under Permissions.

  1. In the side menu, select RULES & ACTIONS under TAG UTILITIES. The Editing Rules & Actions editor opens.
  2. In the Rule Set list, select the profile's rule set.
  3. Select + RULE. A new rule is added to the selected group, or to the rule set when no group is selected, and its settings open in the inspector.
  4. Set Rule id to pack_temperature and Display name to Pack temperature.
  5. In Item Scope, enter /Vehicles/Car1/Battery/PackTemperature. The leading / starts the path at the root of the tag tree, so the rule watches that tag whatever scope the rule set has.
  6. Set Rule type to Threshold rule, and leave Expression as tag.HasValue.
  7. Under Thresholds, select + Add step, and set the step as follows:
    1. Set Operator to > and Value to 45.
    2. Set Clear value (deadband) to 42.
    3. Leave Level as Warning, and set Enter message to Pack temperature above 45 C.
  8. Select + Add step again, and set Operator to >, Value to 55, Clear value (deadband) to 52, Level to Fatal, and Enter message to Pack temperature above 55 C.
  9. Optional: Set Dwell seconds to 10, so the temperature must stay above a limit for 10 seconds before the alert is raised.
  10. Select SAVE. The editor shows "Rules saved", and a failed save shows "Save failed:" followed by the validation error.

When the pack temperature next rises above 45 °C, a Warning alert for Pack temperature appears in the Alerts Log, and it clears once the temperature falls below 42 °C. The same rule is written out in YAML in Complete rules.yaml example.

A rule records its alert but runs only the actions it inherits from its rule set and groups until actions are attached to it, as described in Actions. A rule can also be started from a collection by right-clicking the collection in the collections editor and choosing Create rule from collection…, which fills in the collection as the rule's scope (refer to Create a collection).

docs.title: Complete rules.yaml example
docs.text:
The rules visual editor writes rules to a file, shown here in full so that every setting is in one place, and the file can also be edited directly. It has one rules source with a file-level scope, actions inherited by every rule beneath it, a group with its own action, a threshold rule and a boolean rule that uses a collection. It assumes a collection with the id Collection1, which is the id the editor generated for the collection created in Create a collection, and two actions named OpsSlack and OpsEmail that were added as described under Making an action available.

version: "2.3"
rules:
  displayName: Vehicle alerts
  enabled: true
  evaluationTickSeconds: 30
  scope:
    prefix: Vehicles/Car1
  actions:
    - action: ProfinityLog
      triggerLevel: Info
    - action: OpsSlack
      triggerLevel: Error
  clearActions:
    - action: ProfinityLog
      triggerLevel: Info
  groups:
    - group:
        id: battery
        displayName: Battery
        scope:
          prefix: Battery
        actions:
          - action: OpsEmail
            triggerLevel: Fatal
        rules:
          - rule:
              id: pack_temperature
              displayName: Pack temperature
              type: threshold
              description: >
                Pack temperature is above its normal range. Check the coolant
                pump and fan before the next drive.
              moreInformation:
                - description: Battery cooling guide
                  url: https://docs.example.com/battery-cooling
              relatedTags:
                - Vehicles/Car1/Battery/CoolantTemperature
              scope:
                prefix: PackTemperature
              expression: tag.HasValue
              dwellSeconds: 10
              throttleMinutes: 15
              thresholds:
                - condition: { operator: ">", value: 45 }
                  clearValue: 42
                  level: Warning
                  message: Pack temperature above 45 C
                  clearMessage: Pack temperature back below 42 C
                - condition: { operator: ">", value: 55 }
                  clearValue: 52
                  level: Fatal
                  message: Pack temperature above 55 C
  rules:
    - rule:
        id: cell_over_voltage
        displayName: Cell over voltage
        level: Error
        description: A cell voltage is above 4.2 V.
        scope:
          collection: Collection1
        expression: tag.Value > 4.2
        clearExpression: tag.Value < 4.1
        throttleMinutes: 5
        disableActions:
          - profile/ProfinityLog
        actions:
          - action: OpsEmail
            message: "Cell {TagId} is at {Value} V"
        clearActions:
          - action: OpsEmail
            message: "Cell {TagId} is back to {Value} V"

Its scope.prefix of Vehicles/Car1 is the default for every rule. A prefix written without a leading / in a group or rule joins beneath its parent, so pack_temperature watches Vehicles/Car1/Battery/PackTemperature, while a prefix with a leading / replaces the inherited one and / alone covers the whole tag tree. Every rule must end up with a prefix, a collection or both, and when both are present a tag has to satisfy both. A rules file that belongs to a component is written relative to that component, so its prefixes start from the component's own place in the tag tree.

The pack_temperature rule is a threshold rule, which holds an ordered list of steps in thresholds, each with a level and a message and either a structured condition (the operators are ==, !=, >, >=, <, <= and between) or an expression. The clearValue on a step is its deadband, so the Warning step stays active until the value falls below 42, and clearExpression does the same job for a step that uses an expression. A threshold rule still needs a rule-level expression, and tag.HasValue is the usual choice, but it takes its level from each step, so it must not set a rule-level level, actions or clearActions. The dwellSeconds value (or dwellMinutes, never both) makes the condition hold continuously before the first step activates, and the throttleMinutes value stops the actions of one rule on one tag from running again within that number of minutes, on both the trip and the clear. The cell_over_voltage rule is a boolean rule, which has a single level, a clearExpression that clears the alert even while the main expression is still true, and its own actions and clearActions.

The description is the text the operator reads in the detail dialog of the Alerts Log and supports Markdown. The moreInformation list adds links, each with a description label and an https:// url, which the dialog lists under DOCUMENTATION, and relatedTags stores tag paths that help diagnose the alert with the rule. Beyond the example, a rule, group or file takes enabled: false to switch everything beneath it off.

Actions written on the file or on a group are inherited by the rules beneath them, as described under Actions inherited down the rule tree, so in the example a Warning on pack_temperature runs only Profinity Log, an Error runs Profinity Log and OpsSlack, and the Fatal step also runs OpsEmail from the group.

For the editor, evaluation settings and permissions, refer to Tag rules.

docs.title: Rule actions
docs.text:
A tag rule watches the tags in its scope and, when its condition changes, records an alert and runs the actions attached to it. Profinity 2.3 has two built-in actions, Profinity Log and None. It also offers the Email, Slack, Webhook, and Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) actions as components, and any script set to Run On Alert mode. Every action receives the list of tags that caused the rule to fire, which is named TriggeredTags in a script and triggeringTags in the Webhook and MQTT JSON message.

Licence required

Rules, the Alerts Log and the built-in actions Profinity Log and None work on every edition. The Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT actions need the Tag Rule Actions licensed feature, included in the Server and Enterprise editions. A script set to Run On Alert needs both Tag Rule Actions and Scripting (included in the Desktop, Server and Enterprise editions). Without Tag Rule Actions the rule still evaluates and the alert is still recorded, and only the licensed actions are skipped. Refer to Licensing for what each edition includes.

flowchart LR
    Rule["Rule fires"] --> Context["Context: the tags that caused it"]
    Context --> Log["Profinity Log"]
    Context --> Msg["Email, Slack, Webhook, or MQTT"]
    Context --> Script["Run On Alert script"]
A rule firing passes the triggering tags to each action attached to it

docs.title: Action picker
docs.text:
When you edit a rule in the visual editor, you choose actions from the action picker, which lists the following:

  • Profinity Log, which writes a message to the Profinity log at the action's level and otherwise the rule's level.
  • None, which records the alert in the Alerts Log only and rejects message, level and tagId.
  • Every Email, Slack, Webhook, and MQTT action that has been added to the profile, listed by the name of its component.
  • Every CSharp Script, Python Script or Lua Script component whose mode is Run On Alert, as described in Rule scripts.

In YAML the two built-in actions are written ProfinityLog and None.

docs.title: Making an action available
docs.text:
An Email, Slack, Webhook, or MQTT action does not appear in the picker until it exists as a component. To add one:

  1. Add a new component from the Rule Actions group.
  2. Choose Email Rule Action, Slack Rule Action, Webhook Rule Action or MQTT Rule Action.
  3. Give the component a name.
  4. Fill in its settings.

A rule can then select the action from the picker. The component's name becomes the action id in the picker and in rules.yaml, so a component named OpsSlack is written action: OpsSlack, and renaming the component means updating the rules that use it. Several components of the same type, for example one Slack action per channel, can exist side by side. The settings of each action are described in Email and Slack rule actions and Webhook and MQTT rule actions.

docs.title: Actions inherited down the rule tree
docs.text:
Actions written on the file or on a group are parent actions, and each one needs a triggerLevel. A parent action runs for every rule beneath it whose alert level is at or above the triggerLevel, taking the level from the rule or, for a threshold rule, from the step that fired. In the complete rules.yaml example, a Warning on pack_temperature runs only Profinity Log, an Error runs Profinity Log and OpsSlack, and the Fatal step also runs OpsEmail from the group. Actions written on a rule or on a threshold step are local, take no triggerLevel and always run when that rule or step fires.

The clearActions lists work the same way when the alert clears. Each side can be switched off for one rule with disableActions and disableClearActions, which list an inherited action as the id of its parent, a slash and its name, as in profile/ProfinityLog. For a rules file that belongs to a component, the parent id is the component name instead of profile, and for a group it is the group id. Each parent can list a given action name only once, and a rule with thresholds cannot also have rule-level actions or clearActions, so its actions go on the steps.

An action entry may be a bare name or an object with action and optionally message and level, where message replaces the text sent for this rule and level sets the level that Profinity Log writes at. The tagId and value fields substitute a different tag path and value for those reported to the action. An action that is not found, or is not an action component, is reported as references unknown component when the rules file loads, and the rule file is not loaded until the name is corrected.

docs.title: TriggeredTags
docs.text: Every rule action receives the same firing context, which includes TriggeredTags, the list of tags in the rule's scope that are currently evaluating true.
